BBBB: US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier still counted as investment grade, from US and foreign companies, following a FTSE index. These pay more than higher-rated bonds but carry more risk of downgrades, and the fund is non-diversified.
BBBI: US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier of investment grade, with five to ten years left until maturity. It follows an index, so it holds a wide basket of bonds from industrial, utility and financial companies for income.
BBBL: A fund of US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest tier of investment grade, that mature in 10 years or more. Because the bonds are long, the price moves a lot when interest rates change, and the BBB rating means somewhat more default risk than higher grades.
BBBS: US dollar corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest investment-grade rating, maturing in one to five years. The short maturities mean its price moves less with interest rates than longer-term bond funds.
BBC: Small US biotech companies that are running clinical trials, held through an index. Most are early-stage and many have no approved product yet, so it is spread over lots of tiny positions, with the largest only about 2% of the fund.
BBCA: Canadian stocks traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange, weighted by company size. Banks lead: Royal Bank, TD and Bank of Montreal, plus Shopify, make up about 25% of the fund.
BBCB: A broad basket of investment grade US dollar corporate bonds, weighted by how much debt each company has outstanding. It is spread over a great many issuers, with banks like HSBC, Citibank and Morgan Stanley each only around 0.5% of the fund.
BBEM: Stocks from emerging market countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, following a market-cap weighted index. It is top-heavy, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix about 26% of it, and technology over 40%.
BBEU: A low cost fund that holds large and mid-sized companies across developed Europe, including the UK, France, Germany and Switzerland, tracked by an index. ASML is about 5% of it, and financials and industrials are the biggest areas.
BBH: About 25 US-listed biotech companies, which develop new medicines, tracked by the MVIS US Listed Biotech 25 Index. It is very top-heavy: Amgen, Gilead, Vertex and Regeneron together are more than 40% of the fund.
BBHL: An actively managed fund holding about 30 large US companies picked by the manager's research on quality and value. It is top-heavy in big tech, with Microsoft, Alphabet and Apple together about 20% of it.
BBHM: An actively managed fund holding a small group of mid-sized US companies that the managers think are high quality and reasonably priced. It is fairly concentrated, with the top five holdings making up about a quarter of the fund, led by industrial and technology firms.
BBHY: A broad basket of high-yield corporate bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, tracking an index of US dollar bonds from companies with below-investment-grade credit, weighted by how much debt each has. It holds many issuers, each around 0.4%, so no one company matters much.
BBIB: US Treasury bonds with between three and ten years left until they mature, following a JPMorgan index of those government bonds. Because it holds only Treasuries, there is little credit risk, but prices still move up and down as interest rates change.
BBIN: Large and mid-size companies from developed countries outside the US, such as Europe, Japan, Canada and Australia, weighted by market size. It is fairly spread out, with ASML at about 3% the biggest, and leans toward financials, industrials, technology and health care.
BBJP: Large and mid-sized Japanese companies, tracking a market-weighted index of stocks on the Tokyo exchange. It is a low-cost way to hold Japan, and Mitsubishi UFJ, Toyota, Sumitomo Mitsui and Hitachi are among the biggest holdings, each about 3% to 5%.
BBLB: US Treasury bonds with at least 20 years left until they mature, tracking an index of those long government bonds. Because the bonds are so long, its price moves a lot when interest rates change, and the government backing means very little credit risk.
BBLS: A fund focused on a small group of large energy companies it calls the Munificent Seven, with Chevron among its holdings. A large part of the fund is currently in short-term Treasury cash funds, so it is a narrow bet on the oil and gas business.
BBLU: An actively managed fund of large, established US companies, run by Bridgeway Capital Management, with income coming mainly from dividends. It is fairly spread out, but about 30% sits in technology, and AMD is the largest holding at roughly 8%.
BBMC: Middle-sized US companies, roughly the ones ranked just below the largest, tracking a JPMorgan US mid-cap index. It is very spread out: the top holdings are each under 1%, so no single stock makes much difference.
BBP: US biotechnology companies that already have at least one drug approved by the FDA, tracked by an index. It is a spread of many smaller biotech stocks, with none above about 3%, so it moves with the ups and downs of the biotech industry.
BBRE: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own buildings like apartments, warehouses and data centers, tracking an MSCI index weighted by company size. Welltower and Prologis are about 20% of the fund together, and it pays income from rents.
BBSB: US Treasury notes and bonds with between one and three years left until they mature, following a market index of such securities. Because the maturities are short, its price moves less when interest rates change than funds holding longer Treasuries.
BBSC: A broad group of smaller US companies, tracking an index of stocks in the lower middle of the market's size range. It is spread across hundreds of stocks, with no holding above about half a percent.
BBUS: A low cost fund that holds roughly the largest 85% of the US stock market by value, mostly large and mid-sized companies. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it, so it behaves much like a broad US market index.
BBYY: A fund that uses options on Alibaba stock to generate income. Selling options brings in extra cash but limits how much it can gain if Alibaba rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mostly backing for the option contracts.
BCCC: A fund that aims to pay income and track Bitcoin through ETFs, using a synthetic covered call strategy, which sells options on Bitcoin funds for income. That income comes in exchange for capping some gains if Bitcoin jumps.
BCD: Gains broad exposure to commodities like energy, metals and farm goods through futures contracts, following a Bloomberg index that looks at contracts further out in time. The Treasury bills in its list are collateral backing those futures, not the point of the fund.
BCDF: An actively managed fund investing in companies that stand to benefit from blockchain technology, mostly stock exchanges and financial firms rather than crypto itself. Singapore Exchange, Urbana, Cboe and TMX are the biggest holdings, together about 27% of the fund.
BCEM: An actively managed fund of growth companies in emerging markets, held in a fairly focused portfolio. Its biggest holding is another ETF, the Franklin FTSE India ETF at about 15%, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are also large.
BCFN: An actively managed fund of financial companies using innovative technology, including payments, banking, brokerage and asset managers. It is mostly financials, with Visa, Mastercard and Bank of America among the largest holdings at about 5% to 6% each.
BCGD: An actively managed fund of global stocks from companies Baron believes have lasting competitive strengths, in the size range of the MSCI ACWI index. Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA and Amazon are about 21% of the fund.
BCGS: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies from around the world, mostly common stocks. It holds a broad mix with no position above about 2.5%, including names such as SK Hynix, AppLovin, Spotify and Eli Lilly.
BCHP: An actively managed fund holding a small group of high-quality large US companies the managers believe are strong over the long run. It is concentrated: Amazon, NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft together are about 40% of the fund.
BCI: A broad bundle of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, tracked through futures contracts on the Bloomberg Commodity Index rather than physical goods. The fund holds Treasury bills as backing for those contracts.
BCIL: An actively managed fund of large companies outside the US, chosen by Bancreek for growth. It is spread across many countries and sectors, with no holding above about 4%, including Asics, SK Hynix and Codan.
BCKT: Holds US Treasury bonds and money market funds in a plan built to pay out income through about the year 2030. It is a near-term income fund, and its value moves with interest rates.
BCLO: An actively managed fund that buys collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of corporate loans packaged into bonds, focused on the lower investment grade and below investment grade slices rated BBB+ down to B-. These pay more interest than safer bonds but carry more credit risk.
BCOM: A fund tracking the Bloomberg Commodity Index, a broad basket of raw materials like energy, metals and farm products, mostly through futures contracts. It is a passive index fund, not actively managed, and gives wide commodity exposure instead of betting on one product.
BCOR: Holds companies that benefit from or are heavily tied to bitcoin, picked by an index from Indxx. It is very concentrated: Tesla is about 22% and Strategy about 13%, alongside crypto miners and exchanges, so it moves with bitcoin sentiment but owns no bitcoin directly.
BCPL: An actively managed bond fund mostly holding investment grade corporate bonds, plus government and other bonds, across all lengths of maturity. It is a broad core bond fund with a bit of added flexibility to look for extra income.
BCSM: An actively managed fund of small and mid sized US companies chosen by Baron's analysts for long term growth potential. It is well spread, with the largest holding, Axon, around 4%, and leans toward technology, industrials and health care.
BCTK: An actively managed fund of technology companies of all sizes, run by Baron Capital, that looks for businesses with durable growth. It is concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Lam Research and SpaceX each around 9% and Broadcom at about 6%.
BCUS: An actively managed fund of large US companies, chosen by the manager rather than an index. It leans toward industrials and technology, and its biggest holdings, such as Flex, Spotify and General Electric, are each only about 4 to 5%.
BD: An actively managed core-plus bond fund holding mostly investment-grade bonds, with room for some lower-rated and foreign debt for extra income. US Treasuries are a large share, with a spread of government and corporate holdings behind them.
BDBT: An actively managed fund that builds a bond portfolio by owning other bond ETFs, mostly from iShares, Schwab and State Street, covering US investment-grade bonds. Most of its money sits in just a handful of those funds.
BDEC: A defined-outcome fund using options on an S&P 500 ETF over a set one-year period starting in December. It aims to absorb a set amount of losses in return for a limit on gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
BDGS: An actively managed fund holding only 5 to 20 investments, mixing US stock index ETFs, large company stocks and a big slice of cash-like short-term Treasury funds. The manager shifts the mix over time, so it is flexible rather than tied to one index.
BDIV: An actively managed fund of US dividend-paying stocks, favoring companies whose dividends are growing faster than the market's. It is tilted toward technology and large names, with Microsoft, Apple and Lam Research making up about 17% of it.
BDRY: Futures contracts on the price of shipping dry bulk cargo like iron ore, coal and grain, spread across Capesize, Panamax and Supramax ships. It does not own any ships or companies, so it tracks freight rates, which can swing sharply with global trade demand.
BDVG: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends and have a track record of raising them. It is spread over many names, with Dell, Cisco, Nucor, JPMorgan and AbbVie the largest at about 4% to 7% each.
BDVL: An actively managed fund that mostly holds stocks from around the world, using a research process meant to limit big swings in the overall portfolio. It can also hold other ETFs, and it is broadly spread, with no single holding above about 2.5%.
BDYN: An actively managed fund that can hold stocks, bonds and cash worldwide, shifting the mix as managers see opportunities. It is mostly in stocks and leans on big US tech names, with Apple, NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft about 18% of it.
BEDY: An actively managed income fund that mainly holds dividend-paying US stocks, plus some bonds and preferred shares, and may use options to add income. It is diversified, with Texas Instruments, UnitedHealth and JPMorgan each around 4%.
BEEX: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US stocks, with a lean toward the tech giants. Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Texas Instruments and Microsoft are each about 4% to 7%, and together roughly a quarter of the fund.
BEEZ: A fund of US companies chosen by an adviser using a specific quality-focused approach, rather than tracking a standard index. It leans toward industrials and technology, with names like Lam Research, Watts Water and Badger Meter each around 4 to 6% of the fund.
BEMB: Bonds issued by governments and government-linked companies in emerging markets, all in US dollars, tracked by a JPMorgan index. It holds many bonds, with none above about 1%, so it spreads risk across countries like Argentina, Angola, Oman and Hungary.
BEMD: An actively managed fund of bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, which are developing economies. It is non-diversified and can use futures contracts to adjust its exposure.
BENJ: An actively managed fund that mostly holds US Treasury bills maturing in one to three months, or ETFs that hold such bills. Because the bills are so short, it works like a place to park cash and its price should move very little.
BESF: An actively managed fund of US-listed energy companies, with a tilt toward natural gas and pipelines. It is fairly concentrated, with NextDecade, Cheniere, Williams and Enterprise Products each about 5% to 9% of the fund, so it rides closely on one industry.
BESO: A fund holding three major cryptocurrencies, bitcoin, ether and solana, through other crypto ETFs. About half is bitcoin, with the rest split between solana and ether, and the ether and solana funds earn extra rewards by staking.
BETE: A fund that holds bitcoin and ether futures contracts in roughly equal amounts, giving exposure to both cryptocurrencies without owning the coins directly. Prices can swing sharply, and futures can behave a little differently from the coins themselves.
BETH: A fund that tracks bitcoin and ether together using futures contracts, weighted by the size of each coin's market value. It holds no actual coins, and since it is just two cryptocurrencies, its price can swing a lot.
BETZ: Companies in sports betting and online gambling, such as operators and the suppliers behind them, tracked by a Morningstar index. The biggest holdings, including Flutter, Allwyn, DraftKings and Evolution, are each around 7% of the fund.
BFAP: A fund that gets Bitcoin exposure through options contracts and aims to limit losses over a set one year period starting in April. It holds options rather than Bitcoin itself, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
BFEB: Uses options on the S&P 500 fund SPY to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in February. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold from the start of the period to the end.
BFEW: A fund of funds holding a ladder of four buffer funds on an equal-weighted version of US large companies. Each aims to limit some losses over its own one-year period in exchange for a cap on gains, and staggering them smooths out the timing.
BFIX: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment-grade US dollar bonds, with a lot of US Treasuries. Holdings are spread across a few Treasuries at about 5% each, and short maturities mean it should move less than longer bond funds.
BFJA: Aims to follow bitcoin's price using options, while setting a floor of 15% on losses over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, and it does not hold bitcoin directly.
BFJL: A Bitcoin fund that holds options on Bitcoin exposure and is built to limit losses to a floor over a set one-year period starting in July. In return the potential gain is capped, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the whole period.
BFLB: An actively managed fund that uses stock market options tied to the S&P 500 to soften a set amount of losses over a one year period. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
BFLX: An actively managed US stock fund that can use derivatives to adjust how much it moves with the market, aiming to cut the swings of an all-stock portfolio. NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 15% of it, so tech leads the mix.
BFOC: Gives exposure to bitcoin's price through options, and is built to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. The 15 in the name is the floor level, and the protection comes with a limit on how much it can gain.
BFOR: About 400 US stocks picked by a rules-based method that looks for companies with strong financial results, tracking the Barron's 400 Index. It is very evenly spread, with the largest holdings only about 0.5% to 1% each.
BFRZ: Gives exposure to large US stocks, with options that cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period and cap gains. Its holdings are top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
BFXU: Holds four First Trust Vest funds, each starting at a different time, to get stock market exposure to large US companies with accelerated gains when the market rises. It uses options, and the ladder spreads out when each fund resets.
BGCG: An actively managed fund of about thirty companies outside the US that the managers expect to grow strongly, in both developed and emerging markets. It is concentrated: Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 14%, and MercadoLibre, Spotify and ASML add roughly 22% more.
BGDV: A mix of dividend-paying US and foreign stocks picked by Bahl & Gaynor's managers, who look for companies that can keep growing their payouts. It is actively managed, and its largest holdings, like Taiwan Semiconductor, Western Digital and Broadcom, are each around 5%.
BGEG: An actively managed fund of companies in emerging markets, chosen by Baillie Gifford for long-term growth potential. It leans heavily on technology, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung Electronics together are about a quarter of it.
BGFI: An actively managed fund of bonds from governments and companies around the world, with the currency risk mostly hedged back to US dollars. A good part of its exposure comes through German government bond futures, which are contracts that track bond prices, rather than the bonds themselves.
BGGG: An actively managed fund of growth companies from around the world, held for the long term, with a small number of high-conviction picks. It leans toward technology and consumer stocks, with ASML, NVIDIA and Amazon making up about 22% of the fund.
BGIA: An actively managed fund of growth companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US. It is fairly concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung making up about 17% of the fund and tech and financials the biggest sectors.
BGIG: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large US companies, chosen by managers who look for growing payouts. It is fairly concentrated: Broadcom, UnitedHealth and Eli Lilly are each around 4% to 5% of it, with tech, health care and financials the biggest areas.
BGLD: Uses options tied to the SPDR Gold Trust to cushion part of the losses in gold over a set three-month period. In return, gains are capped each period, so it follows gold only partly and resets its terms every quarter.
BGRN: A fund of investment-grade US dollar bonds whose proceeds pay for environmental projects like clean energy and efficiency, tracking a green bond index. Issuers include development banks, governments and companies, and no single bond is more than about 2%.
BGRO: An actively managed fund of large US companies expected to grow faster than average, with the managers choosing the stocks. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA is about 13% of the fund, and technology is over half of it.
BGUS: An actively managed fund of US growth companies picked by Baillie Gifford, aiming for businesses it expects to grow fast. It leans on one name: NVIDIA is about 16% of the fund, and technology is around 40% overall.
BHDG: An actively managed fund that buys options on bitcoin funds to protect against a sharp drop in bitcoin, with most of its money in bonds and cash-like holdings. It is a hedge, so it does not simply track bitcoin up and down.
BHYB: A basket of US dollar junk bonds rated BB to B, excluding banks and other financial companies, tracking a subset of an ICE high yield index. It skips the lowest rated bonds, but still carries more credit risk than safer bonds, with thousands of small positions.
BHYP: Holds Hyperliquid's HYPE token directly, tracking its price through a published benchmark. It is a single-crypto fund, so its value moves with that one volatile digital asset, which is tied to the Hyperliquid trading platform.
BIBL: Holds about 100 large US companies selected by Inspire's impact score, a rating of how well each fits faith-based values. Caterpillar is the largest at about 9%, and KLA, Arista and Amphenol follow, so industrials and tech weigh heavily.
BIDD: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying companies outside the US, picked by iShares' systematic approach. Taiwan Semiconductor is the biggest holding at about 8%, and the fund leans toward financials, technology and industrials.
BIGY: Holds large US stocks from a list of 50 big companies and writes options on them to generate income. Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon and Alphabet are each roughly 5% to 7% of it, and the options give up some upside in exchange for regular payouts.
BIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in one to three months, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
BILD: Listed infrastructure companies around the world, such as utilities, pipelines, toll roads and airports, picked by an active manager. Utilities make up about half the fund, and the top holdings like Enbridge and United Utilities are each around 5%.
BILS: US Treasury bills that mature in 3 to 12 months, following a Bloomberg index. The bills are so short that the price barely moves, and the income it pays tracks short-term interest rates.
BILT: An actively managed fund of infrastructure companies worldwide, such as electric utilities, pipelines, railroads and airports. Utilities are about half the fund, and it differs from index infrastructure funds because managers choose holdings and weights themselves.
BINC: An actively managed bond fund that mixes high-yield corporate bonds, government debt and other loans, with managers choosing across the bond market rather than following an index. It is built for income and can shift between sectors as managers see fit.
BINT: An actively managed fund that gets global stock exposure by holding a handful of other index ETFs: US large companies, developed markets outside the US, and emerging markets. Just four funds make up all of it, so it works like a simple prebuilt global stock mix.
BINV: An actively managed fund buying large non-US companies, each worth more than $5 billion, that the manager believes are priced below their real worth. It is spread widely, with the largest holdings such as Sanofi and SAP each only about 2% to 3%.
BIOY: An actively managed fund that aims to pay weekly income by selling put options on a leveraged biotech ETF, which moves at three times the daily move of its index. Treasury bills back the options, and it gives up upside while carrying real downside risk.
BITA: Holds the iShares Bitcoin Trust and sells monthly call options on it to bring in extra income. The options help payouts but limit how much it gains when bitcoin jumps, while it can still lose when bitcoin falls.
BITB: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its US dollar price, so owning shares works like owning bitcoin without handling it yourself. It is passively managed, holds no stocks or bonds, and its value swings with the price of bitcoin.
BITC: An actively managed fund that shifts between bitcoin futures contracts and US Treasury securities depending on its trend signals. When it is in Treasuries it is mostly sitting in government debt, so its bitcoin exposure comes and goes rather than staying fixed.
BITI: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of bitcoin's daily move, using bitcoin futures contracts. It resets every day, so over longer periods its results can drift away from the opposite of bitcoin's total move, and it is built for short-term use, not as a long hold.
BITO: A fund that gets bitcoin exposure by holding bitcoin futures contracts, which are agreements tied to bitcoin's price, rather than owning bitcoin itself. Because futures roll over costs, its results can differ from bitcoin's price, and the rest of the money sits in cash-like holdings.
BITQ: Stocks of companies tied to the crypto industry, such as crypto exchanges, miners and firms that serve them, picked by a Bitwise index. It holds shares in these businesses, not crypto itself, and is concentrated: Coinbase, Iris Energy and Strategy are about 26% of it.
BITS: An actively managed fund that holds blockchain-related companies, along with bitcoin futures contracts. A big chunk is in a Global X Blockchain fund and short-term T-bill funds, so it is a mix of stock exposure and bitcoin price exposure.
BITW: A trust that holds a basket of cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin and Ether, tracking a crypto market index and rebalancing monthly. It holds the coins directly instead of stocks, so it is very volatile and moves with the crypto market.
BITY: A fund that aims for income by holding bitcoin exposure, mainly through the iShares Bitcoin Trust, and selling options on it. The options bring in extra income but cap some of the gains if bitcoin jumps, while falls still count in full.
BIV: A mix of US government bonds and investment grade company bonds that mature in five to ten years, weighted by size, following a Bloomberg index. It sits in the middle on risk among bond funds: more price movement than short bonds, less than long ones.
BIZD: Business development companies (BDCs), which are firms that lend money to mid-sized private businesses and pay out most of their income as dividends. It is concentrated in a few big names, as Ares Capital is about 14% and the top five holdings make up about a third of it.
BJAN: A defined-outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 to buffer a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each January. In return, gains are capped, and the buffer only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
BJUL: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 9% of losses over a one-year period that starts each July. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
BJUN: A buffer fund using options on the S&P 500 to absorb the first 9% of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are capped, and the cushion only works if you hold for the whole period.
BKAG: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, tracking the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is the standard core bond approach and is very spread out, with no single bond more than about 1%.
BKCG: An actively managed fund holding a small number of large US growth companies chosen by the manager. NVIDIA, Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft are each about 6% to 10% of it, so a few big tech names have a large influence.
BKCH: A fund tracking an index of companies tied to blockchain and digital assets, such as bitcoin miners, crypto exchanges and payment firms. It owns company stocks rather than crypto itself, and its biggest holdings, Iris Energy, Circle and Coinbase, are about a third of it.
BKCI: An actively managed fund holding a small group of large companies in developed markets outside the US, such as Taiwan Semiconductor, ASML and TotalEnergies. Because it holds relatively few stocks, each position matters, with the top ones around 5% to 7% each.
BKDV: An actively managed fund of US value stocks, meaning companies the manager thinks are priced below what they are worth. Amazon, Microsoft and JPMorgan are about 15% of it, and the mix covers tech, banks and health care.
BKEM: Large and mid-sized companies across emerging markets such as Taiwan, Korea, China and India, following the Solactive GBS Emerging Markets index. It leans on tech, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are together about 20% of the fund.
BKF: Large companies in Brazil, Russia, India and China, tracking the MSCI BIC index, though in practice the holdings today are mostly Chinese and Indian. Tencent and Alibaba together are around 13% of it, and banks and other financials are the biggest sector.
BKFI: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade bonds, with the manager adjusting how much interest rate and credit risk it takes. It aims to be a core bond holding, spreading across government, corporate and mortgage bonds rather than tracking a single index.
BKGI: Dividend-paying companies that own infrastructure around the world, such as utilities, pipelines, health care real estate and transport assets. It has about 40% in utilities and holds a modest number of companies, so each of the top holdings is roughly 7% of the fund.
BKHY: A broad basket of US high yield bonds, which are loans to companies with lower credit ratings that pay higher interest to compensate. It is spread across many small issuers rather than a few big ones, and it carries more default risk than investment grade bonds.
BKIE: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, tracking the Solactive developed markets ex-US index, with each stock weighted by its size. It is widely spread, with ASML the biggest holding at only about 2%, and financials and industrials the largest sectors.
BKLC: Roughly the 500 largest US companies, following a large-company US index weighted by company size. It works like a plain S&P 500 fund and is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of it, and technology is around 40%.
BKLG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers expect to grow faster than average. It aims to beat the market by picking stocks rather than copying an index, so its holdings can differ a lot from a plain large-growth index fund.
BKLN: Senior loans, which are loans made by banks to companies with weaker credit ratings, that rank first in line for repayment. Their interest rates float with short-term rates, and the fund spreads across many borrowers, each under about 2%.
BKMC: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, picked with a mix of computer models and research to hold a broad, balanced group. It is very spread out: the biggest holdings are each under 1% of the fund, across industrials, technology and health care.
BKMI: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, which are loans to US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It focuses on intermediate maturities, with an average of roughly three to ten years, so it sits between short-term and long-term muni funds.
BKMS: Short-term municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. Its average maturity is under three years, so the price is steadier than longer municipal bond funds.
BKSE: US small company stocks, tracked by an index, spread across tech, financials, industrials and consumer companies. It holds hundreds of names, and no single holding is much above 0.5% of the fund.
BLCK: An actively managed fund of companies that build crypto technology and platforms, such as exchanges and payment firms. Coinbase, BitMine, Circle and Robinhood are among the biggest holdings, and most of the fund is in financial companies.
BLCR: An actively managed fund from BlackRock that picks large US companies using a mix of computer models and analyst research, instead of following an index. NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet together are about 30% of it.
BLCV: An actively managed fund of large US value stocks, meaning companies that look cheap compared with their earnings or assets. Unusually, it is top-heavy in big tech: Microsoft, Amazon and Apple are about 23% of it.
BLDG: An actively managed fund of real estate companies around the world, including developed and emerging markets. It focuses on property owners like office and hotel landlords, and each top holding is only around 2% of the fund.
BLDX: Holds stocks of companies worldwide that build, run or supply infrastructure like power grids, water systems, railroads and data centers, with a focus on sustainability. It is actively managed and spread out, with the top holdings such as Iberdrola, Union Pacific and Keppel DC REIT each around 4% to 5%.
BLES: A global stock fund following an index of US and foreign companies, including emerging markets, picked to fit faith-based values screens. It is spread thinly across many companies, with no holding above about 0.5%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
BLGR: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs rather than individual stocks, to get exposure to large US growth companies. About half of it is one S&P 500 fund, with the rest in large-cap growth funds, so it is a mix of funds instead of a stock picker.
BLOK: An actively managed fund of companies involved in blockchain technology, like bitcoin miners, crypto exchanges and firms using digital assets. Holdings are spread fairly evenly at around 4% each at the top, but the whole fund is tied to the crypto industry and moves with it.
BLOX: An actively managed fund that mixes crypto-related company stocks with crypto ETFs, such as bitcoin and Ethereum funds, and uses options to try to generate income. It is a high-risk, income-focused way to get crypto exposure, with no single holding above about 8%.
BLST: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, held mostly through other ETFs such as Vanguard's short-term bond and corporate bond funds. Short maturities mean its price usually moves less than longer bond funds when interest rates change.
BLTD: An actively managed fund that gets its bond exposure mostly by holding other long-term bond funds, rather than picking individual bonds. About two thirds of it is a single Vanguard long-term bond fund, so its value moves a lot when interest rates change.
BLUC: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs: broad S&P 500, growth, total market and value funds. It is a mix of big US stocks, with the SPDR S&P 500 fund and Vanguard Growth ETF making up about three quarters of it.
BLUI: An actively managed fund of other ETFs that produce income, mainly bond funds, plus real estate and pipeline funds. Three bond ETFs are about 58% of it, and the rest adds real estate and energy income.
BLUX: An actively managed fund of other ETFs that aims for broad US stock exposure across company sizes. About half sits in an S&P 500 ETF and most of the rest in small-company ETFs, so it leans toward small stocks more than a plain total market fund.
BLV: US government and investment grade corporate bonds that mature in more than 10 years, tracked by a Bloomberg index. Long bonds pay more income but their prices move a lot when interest rates change, and the Treasuries are many small slices of about 1%.
BMAR: Uses options on the S&P 500 fund SPY to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in March. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
BMAY: A fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to buffer a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each May. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the whole period.
BMED: An actively managed fund picking health care companies working on medical innovation, such as drug makers and life science tool companies. Holdings are spread out: Moderna, Danaher, Gilead and AbbVie are each around 5%, and the entire fund is health care.
BMOP: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, which are loans to US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. The managers can buy a wider mix of credit quality and maturities than a plain muni index fund, so it aims for more tax-free income.
BMSI: An actively managed bond fund that spreads its money across several kinds of debt, such as corporate bonds, government bonds and higher-yielding bonds. The manager moves between these areas, aiming to earn income from whichever look better.
BMVP: Follows an index of 50 US mid-sized stocks chosen for strong momentum, steady prices, cheap valuations and high profitability. It spreads picks across sectors and sizes like the broader market, so no single stock is more than about 2% of the fund.
BNAV: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to bitcoin and shifts in and out of it depending on market signals. When it steps back from bitcoin it holds mostly cash-like investments, so it will not always follow bitcoin's price.
BND: One fund holding a broad mix of US investment-grade bonds: Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It spreads across thousands of bonds, so no single one is more than a sliver, and it earns its return mostly from interest.
BNDC: A core bond fund of US dollar investment grade bonds, held partly through other ETFs such as short-term and credit-focused bond funds. It is meant as a broad bond foundation, mixing government and corporate debt of different maturities.
BNDD: A mostly long-term US Treasury fund, held largely through a Vanguard long-term Treasury ETF, with a small side layer of options tied to the shape of the interest rate curve. The options are meant to limit losses and help when inflation and rates fall, so it behaves differently from a plain Treasury fund.
BNDI: An actively managed fund that holds two big US bond ETFs, iShares Core US Aggregate and Vanguard Total Bond Market, about half each. It adds a layer of options on bonds to boost income, which can limit some gains.
BNDP: A broad bond fund tracking an index of US investment-grade bonds, plus a small portion in higher-yielding and emerging market bonds. Most of it is Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate bonds, so it is more diversified than a basic US bond fund.
BNDS: An actively managed income fund split roughly evenly between bonds and preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of common shares. It mostly buys higher-yielding securities from corporate and real estate issuers, so it takes more credit risk than a plain bond fund.
BNDW: A fund of two Vanguard bond funds, one US and one international, that together track the global investment-grade bond market, with currency swings hedged back to US dollars. It splits about half and half between the two, so it is a one-fund mix of US and foreign bonds.
BNDX: Investment-grade bonds issued by governments and companies outside the US, with currency swings hedged back to US dollars. The hedge means returns follow the bonds rather than exchange rates, and holdings include UK gilts and French government bonds.
BNDY: An actively run fund of US investment-grade bonds, using a rules-based approach that weighs past returns and risk to decide how to tilt its holdings. Nearly all of it is held through another broad bond ETF, so it works like a core bond fund with some tilting.
BNGE: Companies behind streaming, video games and online gambling, picked by the S-Network Streaming and Gaming index from around the world. It includes names like Aristocrat, Take-Two, NetEase, Roku and Electronic Arts, each about 5% of the fund.
BNO: A fund that tracks the price of Brent crude oil by holding near-term Brent oil futures, which are contracts to buy oil later, instead of the oil itself. Its price follows oil closely, and it keeps cash and short-term holdings to back those contracts.
BNOV: Uses options on the S&P 500 fund SPY to protect against a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in November. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
BOAT: Shipping companies around the world, such as container lines, tanker operators and ship owners, picked by a rules-based global shipping index. It is a narrow bet on one industry, with the top eight holdings each around 4% to 5% of the fund, and it is sensitive to global trade and freight rates.
BOBP: A rules-based index of large US companies that can shift part of its money into cash to soften market drops. Around 90% is in stocks, spread across technology, industrials and other sectors, with a short-term bond ETF holding about a tenth of the fund.
BOCT: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion the first 9% of losses over a one-year period that starts each October, in exchange for a cap on how much it can gain. The protection only applies if you hold for the whole period.
BOND: An actively managed bond fund from PIMCO, mainly investment grade bonds such as US Treasuries and mortgage bonds, with managers choosing what to hold. It can also use derivatives, which are contracts that track other assets, so it is more flexible than a plain index fund.
BOTT: Companies that earn a big share of their revenue from designing and building humanoid and service robots, following a Themes index. The holdings come from around the world, including Chinese robotics makers, Teradyne and Tesla, and each of the top few is about 5% to 9% of the fund.
BOTZ: Companies around the world involved in robotics and artificial intelligence, such as makers of factory automation, sensors and chips. It is concentrated: Keyence, ABB, Fanuc and NVIDIA are about 36% of the fund, with a heavy Japan weighting.
BOUT: Follows an index of stocks showing breakout patterns from the Investor's Business Daily research, mainly smaller growth companies. Holdings are concentrated in a few dozen names, with the top ones like Hinge Health and Guardant Health each making up about 7%.
BOXA: An actively managed fund that aims to beat a broad US bond index, the Solactive U.S. Aggregate, using options on a bond ETF and the S&P 500. The holdings listed are mostly option contracts, so it behaves differently from a plain bond fund.
BOXX: A fund built around box spreads, which are paired options contracts on the S&P 500 that behave like a short-term loan. It aims to act like a very short-term Treasury bill, with a steady price and returns that follow short-term interest rates.
BPAY: An actively managed fund of companies in financial technology, such as payments, online brokerage and digital banking firms. Holdings like Global Payments, Robinhood, Chime and Capital One are each around 4% to 5%, and it keeps a notable share in cash.
BPH: A single stock fund holding American depositary receipts of BP, the British oil company, with currency swaps meant to hedge the pound against the dollar. It is a bet on one company, so it moves with BP's shares.
BPI: An actively managed fund that gets bitcoin exposure by holding bitcoin ETPs (funds that own bitcoin) and then using options to generate extra income. The options can limit gains when bitcoin rises, and the fund's price still swings with bitcoin.
BPRO: An actively managed fund that aims to gain when currencies lose buying power, by holding gold, silver, gold mining stocks and bitcoin. Most of it is in physical gold and bitcoin products rather than ordinary stocks, so it behaves differently from the stock market.
BRAZ: An actively managed fund of Brazilian companies, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It leans toward banks, energy and mining, with Petrobras, Itau Unibanco and Nu Holdings together about a third of it.
BRCE: Large US companies chosen by MFS using a mix of computer models and human research. It looks a lot like the broad market and is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 27% of the fund.
BREE: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, using a blend of research and quantitative screening. It is heavy in technology: Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and Samsung together make up about a third of it.
BREM: An actively managed bond fund that buys debt from governments and companies in emerging market countries, mostly priced in US dollars and other major currencies. Managers pick the bonds, so it can differ from a plain index, and emerging market debt carries more credit risk than US bonds.
BRES: An actively managed fund holding a small group of US stocks of any size, with the managers picking names they find undervalued. It is concentrated: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Expedia are each around 6 to 8% of the fund.
BREW: An actively managed fund of companies in coffee, energy drinks and other beverages, plus restaurants. Starbucks and Coca-Cola make up about a third of the fund together, so it is concentrated in a few well known names.
BRF: Small Brazilian companies, chosen by a VanEck index, covering industries like homebuilding, utilities, materials and real estate. It is concentrated in one country and spread over many names, with no holding above about 4%, so it swings with Brazil's economy and currency.
BRHY: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, which are rated below investment grade, with maturities of ten years or less. Higher interest comes with a higher risk of default, and the holdings are spread over many companies.
BRIB: An intermediate-term ladder of high-quality corporate bonds from companies that score well on the manager's Bright Score, a measure of benefit to the common good. It aims for steady income and keeping capital safe, and it is spread across many issuers at about 1% each.
BRIE: A fund of large and mid-sized stocks from developed markets outside the US, picked by MFS using a mix of computer models and research. It is spread across technology, financials and industrials, with Taiwan Semiconductor the largest holding at about 5%.
BRIF: An actively managed fund holding a focused group of large US companies that its model says are in strong profit cycles. It is tech heavy, with NVIDIA, Broadcom and Palo Alto Networks among the largest, and the top holding is about 8%.
BRKC: An options income fund tied to Berkshire Hathaway's B shares, aiming to pay regular distributions by selling call options rather than owning much of the stock. The Treasury bills shown are mostly collateral, and the options approach limits gains if Berkshire shares rise sharply.
BRKW: An actively managed fund aiming for about 1.2 times the weekly return of Berkshire Hathaway's Class B shares, using swaps and some stock. It resets every calendar week, pays out income often, and the Treasury bills it shows mostly back the swaps.
BRLN: An actively managed fund of floating rate loans, which are loans to companies whose interest payments rise and fall with short term rates. These loans go to companies with weaker credit, and the fund also holds some cash and other iShares bond funds.
BRNY: An actively managed fund of US stocks that shifts between investing styles, such as value, growth and quality, depending on what its model favors. It holds many mid and large companies, and NVIDIA, Expedia, Alphabet and Apple are the largest at around 5 to 8% each.
BROL: An actively managed fund of large US companies that aims to manage downside risk while still owning growth stocks. It is fairly top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 15% of it, and technology is over a third of the fund.
BRRR: A fund that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its price, so owning it is a way to get bitcoin exposure through a regular brokerage account. Its value rises and falls with bitcoin, which can swing sharply, and it pays no income.
BRSM: A fund of small and mid-sized US companies chosen by the manager using a blend of research and quantitative screens. It is widely spread across industrials, technology, financials and health care, with no holding above about 1%.
BRSV: An actively managed fund of small US value stocks, meaning smaller companies that look cheap compared with their finances, chosen using a statistical approach. It holds many names, with banks common, and each is only around 1% of the fund.
BRTR: An actively managed bond fund from BlackRock holding a wide mix of investment-grade bonds, like corporate, mortgage-backed and government debt, and sometimes other kinds of debt. Managers can shift between sectors to seek income, so it differs from a plain index bond fund.
BSCA: Investment grade US corporate bonds that mature in 2036, tracked by an index. The fund is designed to close around then and pay back its money, a bit like a single bond that matures, so its yield and risk are tied to that date.
BSCQ: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2026, from many well-known companies. The fund has a set end date, returning cash as the bonds mature, and no single bond is above about 2%.
BSCR: A basket of US investment grade company bonds that all mature in 2027. As bonds mature, the fund steadily winds down and then closes at the end of 2027, so it behaves a bit like a single bond, with spread out holdings from big banks and tech companies.
BSCS: A basket of investment-grade US company bonds that all mature in 2028. The fund shuts down around the end of 2028 and hands back what is left, and no single company is more than about 1%.
BSCT: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2029, from many well-known companies. The fund has a set end date, returning cash as the bonds mature, and no single bond is above about 1.5%.
BSCU: A basket of US investment-grade company bonds that all mature in 2030, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It holds hundreds of issuers such as Boeing, Meta and Oracle, each around 1% or less, and pays income along the way.
BSCV: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2031, tracked by an Invesco BulletShares index. As the bonds near that year they get paid back, so the fund is designed to wind down around then rather than run forever.
BSCW: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2032. As bonds drop out, the fund winds down around that year and returns the money, so it behaves more like a single bond with a set end date than an open-ended bond fund.
BSCX: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, tracking an index of such bonds. The fund is designed to wind down around that year and return the money, so its average maturity shortens over time like a set of bonds held to maturity.
BSCY: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2034, tracking an Invesco BulletShares index. The fund has a set end date: as the bonds mature it winds down and pays out the cash, so it acts more like a single bond than an open-ended fund.
BSCZ: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2035, tracking an Invesco BulletShares index. As bonds mature the fund winds down in 2035 and returns the money, which works somewhat like a single bond with a set end date.
BSEP: Uses options linked to the S&P 500 to absorb the first 9% of losses over a one-year period starting in September, in return for a cap on gains. The protection only applies to someone who holds for the full period.
BSGR: A fund of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2027, tracking the Invesco BulletShares index. The bonds are held until they mature and then the fund winds down, so it behaves like one bond with a known end date.
BSGT: A bundle of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2029, tracked by an Invesco index. As the bonds reach maturity the fund winds down and returns the cash, so it works more like a single bond with an end date than an ongoing fund.
BSJQ: A basket of US high-yield corporate bonds, riskier company bonds that pay more interest, all maturing in 2026. Unlike a regular bond fund, it has an end date: as the bonds mature, the fund winds down and returns cash, and it is concentrated in a few issuers.
BSJR: A basket of US dollar junk bonds (from lower-rated companies) that all mature in 2027. As the bonds come due, the fund winds down and pays out the money, so it behaves more like a single bond than an ongoing fund, with about 90% in bonds.
BSJS: A basket of US high-yield corporate bonds, riskier company bonds that pay more interest, all maturing in 2028. Unlike a regular bond fund, it has an end date: as the bonds mature, the fund winds down, and it is spread across many issuers.
BSJT: High yield (junk) US dollar corporate bonds that all mature in 2029, tracking an Invesco BulletShares index. It has a set end date, paying back cash as the bonds mature, and its higher income comes with a greater chance that issuers fail to pay.
BSJU: A basket of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, all maturing in 2030. The fund is built to wind up around then, returning its holdings as the bonds mature, instead of staying invested forever like most bond funds.
BSJV: Holds US dollar high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds because the companies are riskier, that mature in 2031. The bonds are held until they mature and the fund then closes, so it acts like a bond with one end date.
BSJW: A basket of US high yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. High yield bonds come from companies with weaker credit, so they pay more income but carry more risk of loss.
BSJX: A set of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature in 2033, tracked by an Invesco index. The fund ends around that year, returning the money as the bonds mature, so its payout is more predictable than a typical bond fund's.
BSJY: US high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature in 2034. The fund is designed to wind down at the end of 2034, so it behaves more like holding a set of bonds to maturity than an open-ended fund.
BSMA: A basket of US municipal bonds that all mature in 2036, with income generally free from federal income tax. As bonds mature the fund winds down toward that year and returns the cash, so it behaves more like a single bond than an open-ended fund.
BSMC: An actively managed fund of small and mid sized US companies that Brandes believes are priced below their real worth, a style called value investing. It is spread across many stocks, none above about 3%, and leans toward health care, technology and consumer staples.
BSMQ: Investment-grade municipal bonds that mostly mature in 2026, held in a basket that winds down as the bonds come due. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and it holds a lot of cash now because many bonds are nearing maturity.
BSMR: A basket of investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2027, so the fund winds down that year and returns the money. Muni interest is generally free from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 1% of it.
BSMS: A basket of investment grade municipal bonds, issued by US states, cities and agencies, that all mature in 2028. The fund is built to wind up around then, returning its holdings as the bonds mature, and no single bond is more than about 0.5%.
BSMT: A fund of US municipal bonds that all mature in 2029, so it winds down around that year. The bonds' interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the holdings are spread over many issuers, each under 1%, including states, counties and transit agencies.
BSMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds that mostly mature in 2030, held in a basket that winds down as the bonds come due, like a bond ladder in one fund. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 1%.
BSMV: Holds US investment-grade municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, that mature in 2031. The fund is designed to wind down by then, so it behaves more like a bond held to maturity than an endless bond fund.
BSMW: A portfolio of US municipal bonds all maturing in 2032, tracked with an Invesco BulletShares index. Because the bonds mature in the same year, the fund winds down then and returns principal, and the interest is generally exempt from federal income tax.
BSMY: A basket of investment-grade US municipal bonds that all mature in 2034, tracking an Invesco index. Because the bonds end in the same year, the fund is designed to wind down then and return its money, and interest is generally exempt from federal income tax.
BSMZ: A basket of US municipal bonds, issued by cities and states, that all mature in 2035, tracking an Invesco index. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, and as the bonds mature the fund winds down at the end date.
BSOL: A trust that holds the cryptocurrency Solana directly and prices itself off a Solana reference rate. It also stakes some of its Solana, meaning it helps run the network to earn extra tokens, and it moves with Solana's price, which can swing sharply.
BSR: An actively managed fund of funds that holds mostly other ETFs, with a large chunk in S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds. It may trade actively and mixes in some bonds, so it behaves like a stock heavy blend.
BSSX: A basket of investment-grade US municipal bonds that all mature in 2033, tracking an Invesco index. Because the bonds end in the same year, the fund is designed to wind down then and return its money, and interest is generally exempt from federal income tax.
BSTP: An actively managed fund that uses exchange-traded options on a large US stock ETF to buffer part of the losses over a set outcome period. Several layers of buffer are staggered so that protection steps up over time, and gains are capped.
BSTS: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2028, following an Invesco BulletShares index. The fund is set to close around that year, so it behaves more like a single bond that returns your money at the end.
BSTU: Holds US Treasury bonds that mature in 2030 and tracks an index of them. Bonds are held until they mature, so the fund winds down in that year and returns the money, working like a set maturity date.
BSTV: A bundle of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2031, tracked by an Invesco index. As the bonds reach maturity the fund winds down and returns the cash, so it works more like a single bond with an end date than an ongoing fund.
BSV: US government and investment-grade corporate bonds maturing in 1 to 5 years, weighted by size. The short maturities mean it moves less when interest rates change than longer-term bond funds, and US Treasuries are its largest holdings.
BSVO: An actively managed fund of small US companies the managers consider cheap compared with their fundamentals, known as value stocks. It owns a very wide range of names, with no holding above about 1%, and financials are the biggest sector at about a third.
BTA: An actively managed fund of other ETFs in non-traditional areas: managed futures, commodities, the US dollar and short-term bonds. A large share is a bullish US dollar fund at about 36%, so it behaves differently from stocks and bonds.
BTAL: A market-neutral fund that buys US stocks that tend to move less than the market and shorts ones that tend to swing more, in equal dollar amounts within each sector. It aims to do well when the broad market falls, and no single position is more than about 1% of it.
BTC: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its price, so shares let you get bitcoin exposure through a regular brokerage account without owning it directly. It holds nothing but bitcoin, so it moves with the price of one volatile digital asset.
BTCC: An income fund that uses options on a Bitcoin ETP, a bitcoin-tracking exchange-traded product, to generate regular payouts. Selling those options limits how much of bitcoin's gains it can capture, and the Treasury holdings listed are cash backing the options rather than the point of the fund.
BTCI: An income fund tied to Bitcoin that holds Bitcoin ETFs along with Treasuries and uses options to generate extra income. That options approach gives up some of Bitcoin's upside in exchange for regular payouts.
BTCK: Follows an index that is 80% Bitcoin and 20% carbon credit futures, using futures contracts to get that exposure. It mixes crypto with a carbon price bet, so it is volatile and does not pay income.
BTCO: Holds bitcoin directly, so its value follows the bitcoin price, which can swing sharply. The fund values its coins using a daily price from the data company Lukka, and it owns the actual coins rather than bitcoin company stocks.
BTCW: Holds bitcoin directly, so its value follows the price of bitcoin, based on the CME CF Bitcoin Reference Rate. It holds no stocks or bonds and pays no income, and bitcoin prices can swing a lot.
BTGD: Gives exposure to both bitcoin and gold, partly through other ETFs like iShares Bitcoin Trust and SPDR Gold MiniShares, plus derivatives. The name points to about 100% in each, so total exposure is roughly double the money in the fund, which makes it more volatile.
BTOT: Holds the whole US dollar bond market in one fund, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and corporate bonds. It is made of many bonds and no single one is more than about 2% of the fund.
BUCK: Aims to pay steady income from US Treasuries and bond ETFs, then adds an options strategy that earns extra premium income. It holds mostly short-term, low-risk bonds, so the options layer is what makes it different from a plain Treasury fund.
BUFB: A fund of buffered ETFs from Innovator, with start dates spread across the year. Each uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion some losses over its period, while capping gains, and each holding is about 8% of the fund.
BUFC: A defined outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion some losses over a set one-year period, in exchange for capping gains. The protection only applies if you hold for the full period, and the options contracts are the main holdings.
BUFD: A fund of twelve other buffer funds on US large-company stocks, each cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the layers start on staggered dates to smooth the timing.
BUFE: A set of emerging-markets buffer funds from First Trust, each with a different start date, so the fund always holds options with staggered one-year periods. Each layer is meant to absorb part of the losses, while capping gains.
BUFF: A fund that holds twelve Innovator Power Buffer ETFs, each starting in a different month, to spread out timing. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion some losses on the S&P 500 over a one-year period, in exchange for capped gains.
BUFG: A fund of funds that holds seven First Trust buffer ETFs, each tied to the S&P 500's price over a one year period. Each buffer absorbs a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and the seven are spread across different start dates.
BUFH: A fund of funds holding twelve FT Vest buffer ETFs, each starting at a different month, so the protection periods are staggered across the year. Each one cushions a set amount of S&P 500 losses while capping gains, with each about 8% of the fund.
BUFI: A fund that uses options on an ETF tracking developed markets outside the US and Canada (the MSCI EAFE index) to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, so it will not fully follow the index when markets rise.
BUFM: A buffer fund that uses options on a US stock ETF to cushion the first chunk of losses over a set one-year period. The trade-off is that gains are capped, and the bank holdings listed are option and collateral positions.
BUFP: A fund of twelve S&P 500 buffer ETFs, each starting at a different time of year, which softens the first part of losses on the S&P 500 over each one-year period. The buffers come with capped gains, and staggering the start dates smooths out the timing.
BUFQ: A fund that holds four FT Vest Nasdaq-100 buffer ETFs, each starting at a different time of year. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion some losses over a set one-year period, in exchange for a cap on gains, and spreading the start dates smooths out those limits.
BUFR: A fund that holds 12 other First Trust buffer funds, each using options to limit S&P 500 losses up to a set level over a year in exchange for a cap on gains. Their start dates are staggered, and it holds nothing else.
BUFS: Holds four FT Vest small-cap buffer ETFs, each starting at a different time of year, to spread out when protection resets. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion a set amount of losses on small US stocks in exchange for capping the gains, and the four are held in equal parts.
BUFT: A fund of buffer ETFs tied to the S&P 500, held in different mixes so each one protects against part of the losses over its own period. It aims for a smoother ride than stocks alone, but gains are capped on every one.
BUFX: A bundle of twelve one-year options-based funds, each starting in a different month, that aim to boost gains up to a cap while cushioning a set amount of S&P 500 losses. Because the start dates are staggered, it avoids depending on the timing of a single entry date.
BUFY: A set of four international buffer funds, each tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF of developed market stocks outside North America, with start dates staggered through the year. This ladder aims to soften part of the losses while capping gains on each one.
BUFZ: A fund that holds twelve FT Vest buffer ETFs, each starting at a different month, to spread out timing. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion some losses on the S&P 500 up to a point, in exchange for capped gains.
BUG: Cybersecurity companies, such as firms making network protection and identity software, selected by the Solactive Cybersecurity index. The holdings are spread fairly evenly, with Okta, CrowdStrike, Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks each around 7% of it.
BUIL: An actively managed fund of companies helping rebuild US infrastructure, including electrical equipment, construction materials, machinery and energy makers. It has no single huge holding, with Flex, First Solar, Bloom Energy and Caterpillar each about 5% to 7%.
BUL: Holds US mid and large companies that produce a lot of cash relative to their price, and tilts toward ones that are also growing, following a Pacer index. Booking Holdings, HCA Healthcare and Uber are each about 5% of it, with consumer, health care and tech names leading.
BULD: Follows an index of global companies that earn at least half their revenue from robotics and 3D printing. It is concentrated in design software and chip equipment makers like Autodesk, Proto Labs, Applied Materials and ASML, each around 8%.
BUSA: An actively managed fund of US stocks that Brandes thinks are priced below what the companies are worth, a style called value investing. It is spread out, with the biggest positions such as Merck and Bank of America each around 2% to 3%.
BUXX: An actively managed fund that aims to beat cash by holding short-term, investment-grade bonds, many of them packages of car loans and similar debts. It is spread across hundreds of small positions, none above about 1%, and the short maturities keep price swings small.
BUYB: Tracks an index of S&P 500 companies that have cut their share count every year for at least ten years, usually by buying back their own stock. It holds roughly equal-sized positions, so it leans toward industrials, financials and consumer companies rather than mega-cap tech.
BUYO: Small US companies chosen to resemble the kinds of businesses that private equity firms tend to buy out, using a rules-based index. It holds a wide mix with no single stock above about 2%, tilted toward technology, industrials and health care.
BUYW: A fund of other US and international stock ETFs that also sells call options on them to bring in extra income. Selling those options caps its gains in a strong market, and about 41% sits in one broad US ETF.
BUYZ: An actively managed fund of global companies that the managers think are changing how people shop and pay, such as online marketplaces. It is fairly concentrated: Amazon and Shopify together are about 19% of it, and over 40% is consumer discretionary.
BUZZ: Tracks an index of about 75 US stocks picked by scanning social media, news and blogs for the most positive talk about them. Technology is almost half of it, and holdings include Nebius, AMD, Micron and Tesla at around 3% each.
BVAL: An actively managed fund that gets its large-company value exposure by holding other ETFs instead of individual stocks. Four underlying funds make up nearly all of it, so it is really a blend of large-cap value index funds, with about a third in one State Street fund.
BWET: Gives exposure to the cost of shipping crude oil on tankers by holding freight futures, contracts that track Baltic Exchange shipping rates. It does not own ships or oil, and its price can swing sharply with tanker rates and with how those futures roll over time.
BWQG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that its managers believe have above average growth potential. It is concentrated in a few names, with NVIDIA, Meta and Micron about 26% of the fund, and leans toward technology.
BWTG: Large and mid sized stocks picked from about 1,400 companies in the Brendan Wood Shareholder Conviction Universe, using a model portfolio from the sub-adviser. It is fairly spread, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Broadcom and Micron each around 5%, and mixes tech, energy, real estate and industrials.
BWX: Government bonds from investment-grade countries outside the US, paying in local currencies, tracking a Bloomberg international Treasury bond index. Japan, Austria, Belgium and the Netherlands appear among the top holdings, though each is small, and currency moves affect results as well as interest rates.
BWZ: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US, with one to three years left until they mature. They are paid in local currencies, such as the yen, euro and Australian dollar, so the fund's value also moves with exchange rates.
BYLD: A fund of bond funds, mostly other iShares ETFs holding high-yield, emerging market, floating-rate and corporate bonds, aiming for higher income than a plain bond index. Its biggest piece, about 20%, is a US high-yield bond fund, so credit risk is higher than in government bonds.
BYRE: An actively managed fund of real estate companies, mainly US real estate investment trusts (REITs) that own properties like data centers, cell towers and senior housing. Equinix, Welltower and American Tower are together about 22% of it, so it leans on a few big names.
BZZ: An actively managed fund investing in companies tied to drones and flying taxis, including defense firms, sensor makers and drone suppliers. It is a narrow theme, with Northrop Grumman, Teledyne and Unusual Machines making up about 22% of the fund.
CAAA: Commercial mortgage backed securities rated AAA, meaning bonds backed by loans on office buildings, apartments and other commercial property. The AAA rating is the top credit rating, and the fund spreads its money across many separate bond issues.
CABZ: An actively managed fund investing in companies working on robotaxis, self-driving vehicles and the technology behind them. It is fairly concentrated: Tesla, Alphabet, Uber, Baidu and WeRide together are about 30% of the fund.
CAFG: US small companies with strong free cash flow, the cash left over after running the business, and growth potential, picked by a rules-based index. It holds many small names, such as Iridium and Liquidia, none above about 4%.
CAFX: An actively managed fund of US-dollar, investment-grade bonds, meaning bonds from borrowers rated as fairly safe, with an average maturity of up to about ten years. US Treasury bonds are its largest holdings, and each is a small slice of the fund.
CAGE: An actively managed fund that uses Treasuries and options on a growth stock index to chase equity growth with a built-in structure, an autocallable approach. It can pay out under set conditions but gives up some upside, so it behaves differently from a plain index fund.
CAIE: An options-style income fund that gets its stock market exposure through swaps (contracts that pay the return of an index) tied to a MerQube large-cap volatility index with autocallable features. Most of the portfolio is a collateral ETF, so results depend on that derivative strategy rather than on owning stocks directly.
CAIQ: An actively managed fund that tries to pay income by using options tied to the Nasdaq-100, with returns linked to autocallable notes that can end early when set price levels are met. Most of the fund sits in another Calamos collateral ETF holding safe assets.
CALF: US small companies that generate lots of free cash flow, meaning cash left after running the business, relative to their stock price. It is evenly spread, with no holding above about 3%.
CALI: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment-grade California municipal bonds maturing in five years or less, with income generally exempt from federal tax. Short maturities mean smaller price swings, but it is tied to issuers in one state.
CAM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds issued in California, whose interest is generally free of federal and California state income tax. It is actively managed with a target duration, and the biggest holding is City of Los Angeles bonds at about 4%.
CAML: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies chosen by the Congress adviser. NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 25% of it, and technology is around half the fund.
CAMX: An actively managed fund that holds just 20 to 30 stocks, mostly in the US but with some elsewhere, which Cambiar considers undervalued. Each of the top few is about 4% to 5%, so it is fairly concentrated, with health care and industrials the biggest areas.
CANC: Companies focused on cancer treatments and diagnostics, picked by an active manager. It is concentrated in drug and biotech names: Revolution Medicines, Eli Lilly, Roche and Cogent Biosciences are each between about 4% and 8%.
CANE: Gives exposure to sugar prices through futures contracts, which are agreements to buy sugar at a future date, rather than holding physical sugar. Futures funds can drift from the spot price, and sugar prices can swing with weather and crop conditions.
CANQ: A mix of options, equity ETFs and bond ETFs meant to act like a convertible security tied to the Nasdaq-100, which blends bond and stock features. Most of what it holds is bond funds, such as mortgage, emerging markets and high yield bond ETFs.
CAOS: An actively managed fund that mostly holds options tied to the US stock market, aiming to gain when markets fall sharply. Because it is built from put options that expire and get replaced, it is a hedging tool and not a normal stock fund.
CAPA: Companies that make capacitors and other small electronic parts used in AI data centers and equipment, tracked by a rules-based index. It is a narrow technology theme, and some of the fund sits in cash-like money market holdings.
CAPE: An actively managed fund of US large companies picked using the Shiller CAPE ratio, which compares prices with ten years of average earnings. It favors sectors that look cheaper on that measure, so it differs from the S&P 500 and is spread widely, with Eli Lilly the top holding at about 4%.
CARK: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, picked by the CastleArk team. It is concentrated in a few names: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple, Eli Lilly and Broadcom together are about 40% of it.
CARY: An actively managed bond fund focused on income, holding mortgage-backed securities, loans bundled into securities and other debt, plus some Treasuries. It mixes many types of debt, with no holding above about 1.5%, and can take on more risk than a plain bond fund.
CARZ: Stocks tied to electric and autonomous vehicles and the technology behind them, tracking the S-Network Future Vehicles and Technology index. In practice it is mostly chipmakers, with Micron, AMD and Intel making up about 25% of it.
CAS: A fund that holds Chinese stocks listed on mainland exchanges (China A shares), and adds income from options. Much of the fund is currently in a Simplify government money fund, so it is a mix of mainland China exposure and an income strategy.
CATF: Intermediate-term municipal bonds issued in California, whose interest is exempt from federal and California income tax. The bonds come from many issuers such as airports, school districts, transportation agencies and hospitals, so it is a spread of California public projects rather than one borrower.
CATH: The S&P 500 with companies removed if their activities conflict with Catholic values, based on guidelines from the US Conference of Catholic Bishops. It still looks a lot like the regular index, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 20% of it.
CAUG: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
CBIL: US Treasury bills with maturities of roughly three to twelve months, tracking an index of them. Because the bills are so short, the price moves very little and the income follows short-term interest rates.
CBLS: An actively managed fund that buys stocks with strong financial returns and sells short others it expects to lag, aiming to soften market swings. Shorting means betting on price drops, and the stock picks are spread out, with none above about 3%.
CBOA: An actively managed fund that follows the price of bitcoin for about a year, up to a set maximum gain, while aiming to protect against drops in bitcoin over that same period. This is the April version, so its yearly cycle starts and ends in April.
CBOJ: An actively managed fund tied to the price of spot bitcoin over roughly a one-year period, using options. It aims to share in bitcoin's gains up to a cap while protecting against a set amount of losses, so upside is limited in exchange.
CBOL: A fund of four Calamos Bitcoin structured protection ETFs, laddered across quarters, that tracks bitcoin's price while using options to limit part of the downside. Each holds about a quarter of the fund, and the protection comes with a cap on gains.
