CBON: Holds Chinese government and corporate bonds priced in renminbi, China's currency, following a FTSE Russell index of fixed-rate bonds. Besides interest rate moves, its value also rises and falls with the renminbi against the US dollar.
CBOO: An actively managed fund giving exposure to bitcoin's price gains up to a cap over about a year, while aiming to protect against part of the losses. It uses options to do this and resets each October, so the result depends on when you buy.
CBOT: An actively managed fund of companies involved in robotics, automation and humanoid robots. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 25% of it, and the rest spreads across technology, industrials and autonomous vehicle firms.
CBOX: An actively managed fund that uses box spreads, a pair of option trades that combine to act like a loan with a fixed interest rate, to produce a tax-aware cash-like return. It does not pick stocks, and the options positions are the whole point, so its holdings look unusual.
CBOY: An actively managed fund that follows the price of bitcoin for about a year, up to a set maximum gain, while aiming to protect against drops in bitcoin over that same period. This is the July version, so its yearly cycle starts and ends in July.
CBSE: An actively managed fund of global small and mid-sized companies that the manager thinks are undervalued or have room to grow. It is spread across many stocks, with none above about 3% to 4%, and its mix spans technology, energy and health care.
CBTA: An actively managed fund giving exposure to bitcoin's price gains up to a cap over about a year, while aiming to protect against a set amount of the losses. It uses options to do this and resets each April, so buying mid-period changes the outcome.
CBTJ: A defined-outcome fund tied to bitcoin that uses options to protect part of the losses over a one-year period starting in January. Most of the money is in short-term Treasuries and cash, with options providing the bitcoin exposure.
CBTL: Holds four Calamos bitcoin funds that start in different quarters, giving exposure to bitcoin's price with protection against a set amount of losses over each fund's one-year period. The 80 in the name refers to that level, and gains are capped.
CBTO: An options-based fund that aims to follow bitcoin's price gains up to a cap over about one year, while protecting against a set amount of losses. It does not hold bitcoin directly, and the cap and protection only apply if you hold through the full October-to-October period.
CBTY: An actively managed fund that tracks the price of bitcoin up to a set cap over about a year, while aiming to protect against part of the losses. It uses options to do this, so gains are limited and the protection only applies over its full period.
CBXA: An actively managed fund that follows the price of bitcoin for about a year, up to a set maximum gain, while aiming to protect against losses beyond the first 10% over that period. This is the April version, so its cycle starts and ends in April.
CBXJ: Holds short-term US Treasuries plus options to follow bitcoin's price gains up to a cap over about one year, while shielding against a set amount of losses. The protection and cap only work across the full January-to-January period, so the starting date matters.
CBXL: Holds four Calamos bitcoin funds that start in different quarters, giving exposure to bitcoin's price with protection against a set amount of losses over each fund's one-year period. The 90 in the name refers to that level, and gains are capped.
CBXO: An actively managed fund giving exposure to bitcoin's price gains up to a set cap over about a year, while aiming to protect against part of the losses. It uses options to do this, and the outcome resets each October, so buying mid-period gives a different result.
CBXY: An actively managed fund giving exposure to bitcoin's price gains up to a cap over about a year, while aiming to protect against part of the losses. It uses options to do this and resets each July, so buying mid-period changes the outcome.
CCEF: An actively managed fund that buys shares of other closed-end funds, which often trade for less than the value of their holdings, aiming for high income and growth. It spreads across many funds, with none above about 5%.
CCFE: An actively managed fund holding a small number of US small and mid-size companies the managers think are priced below their worth. It is concentrated: Cooper-Standard, WESCO, Advance Auto Parts and Premium Brands are about a third of the fund, and it holds some cash.
CCML: Companies that make multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) and other electronic components, the tiny parts found inside phones, cars and computers. It is concentrated: Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics together are about 40% of the fund.
CCNR: Stocks of companies that produce or own natural resources, mainly miners, energy producers and agriculture firms, from around the world including emerging markets. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward materials and energy companies.
CCOM: Aims to give exposure to commodities tied to China, such as metals and farm goods, using futures contracts instead of owning the physical goods. The details of its holdings are limited, so it is best understood as a commodity bet that does not issue a K-1 tax form.
CCOR: Holds high quality US large company stocks that pay and grow dividends, then uses options to try to lower the swings. Its largest positions are Alphabet, Morgan Stanley and Johnson & Johnson, each about 4% to 5% of it.
CCRP: An actively managed fund of US corporate bonds, which are loans to companies that pay interest. Its largest holdings are big banks like Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan and Bank of America, each at around 3% to 4%, along with companies like Amgen.
CCSB: Holds short-term green and sustainability bonds, whose proceeds are meant to pay for climate-friendly projects, with an average life of about five years or less. Issuers are mostly utilities, banks and property companies, and no single bond is more than about 5%.
CCSO: An actively managed fund of US companies the manager sees as helping the world cut carbon emissions, such as waste handlers, building efficiency and materials firms. Industrials make up about half of it, and Nucor, Republic Services, Johnson Controls and Waste Management are each around 5% or 6%.
CDC: US large company stocks with high dividend yields, picked from a Nasdaq Victory index and weighted so that steadier, less volatile stocks count for more. It leans toward utilities and financials, and each top holding is only about 2% of the fund.
CDEI: US large company stocks selected using an index that favors firms with stronger diversity, equity and inclusion practices. It looks a lot like the broader market: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are about 24% of it, with technology near half.
CDIG: An actively managed global stock fund with a concentrated portfolio spread across consumer, energy, utility and financial companies. Its top eight holdings are about 57% of the fund, led by Talen Energy and Tidewater at roughly 10% each.
CDL: About 100 large US companies with high dividend yields, picked by a Victory index and weighted so that steadier, less volatile stocks count for more. It leans toward utilities, financials and consumer staples, and no single stock is much above 2%.
CDPI: Mostly large US dividend-paying stocks, combined with options that generate extra income. The options give up some of the gains in strong markets in exchange for that income, and the biggest holdings, like ExxonMobil, JPMorgan and Johnson & Johnson, are each only about 2 to 3% of the fund.
CDX: A high yield bond fund that buys other bond ETFs and adds a derivative based hedge meant to cut credit losses. Much of the fund sits in Treasury bills and cash as backing for those derivatives, so it is not a plain junk bond fund.
CEF: A trust that holds physical gold and silver bullion in storage, so its price follows the two metals. It owns the metal itself rather than mining companies or futures, and it pays no income.
CEFA: Large companies from developed markets outside the US, tracking an S&P index that screens out companies that conflict with Catholic values. It is widely spread across many holdings, with ASML the largest at only about 3%.
CEFS: An actively managed fund that buys closed-end funds, often when they trade below their underlying value, and uses hedges to reduce stock market risk. Closed-end funds are pooled funds with a fixed number of shares, and the hedging means it will not simply rise and fall with the market.
CEFZ: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and cash, mostly built by buying closed-end funds, which are pooled funds that trade like stocks. Its top holdings are other funds such as Pershing Square USA at about 10%, so it holds a fund of funds.
CEMB: Bonds issued by companies in emerging markets, such as Latin America, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia (excluding Japan), following a JPMorgan index. It holds hundreds of bonds with no issuer above about half a percent.
CEPI: Holds stocks of companies tied to crypto and digital assets, such as PayPal, Mastercard and NVIDIA, and sells options on them to generate income. The options can pay out regular income but cap how much it gains when those stocks rise.
CERY: A broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm products, held through futures contracts (agreements to buy at a set price later) rather than physical goods. It aims to pick contracts that lose less when rolled forward, and the cash on hand is collateral for those contracts.
CEW: A currency fund that follows a basket of emerging market currencies against the US dollar, using currency contracts alongside short term money market holdings. It tends to gain when those currencies rise against the dollar and lose when they fall.
CFA: About 500 large US stocks, but weighted so that calmer, less volatile companies get bigger shares instead of the largest companies by size. It tilts toward steadier names like utilities and insurers, and no holding is much above 0.5%.
CFIT: An actively managed fund of ETFs that uses a computer model to move between bond areas such as emerging markets, preferred stocks and Treasuries. Its mix shifts with market trends, and a big part can sit in short-term Treasuries when the model turns cautious.
CFO: About 500 large US companies, weighted by how little their share prices swing, so steadier stocks get more weight, unlike a regular index weighted by size. No stock is more than a small slice, and it leans toward financials, industrials and utilities.
CGBL: A manager-run mix of roughly 60% stocks and 36% bonds in one fund, with the bond part held through two Capital Group bond ETFs. It spreads across sectors, with technology the biggest at about 32%, and the manager shifts the stock and bond mix within set ranges.
CGCB: A manager-run fund of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, aiming for steady income and protecting capital. It is spread across many issues, with no single bond above about 1.3%.
CGCP: An actively managed bond fund from Capital Group holding US Treasuries, mortgage bonds, corporate bonds and some higher risk debt. The managers choose the bonds instead of following an index, aiming for income with a broad mix.
CGCV: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen for steady, sustainable dividends and lower risk than the broad market. Microsoft and Broadcom are about 11% of it, and the rest is spread over health care, consumer staples and financials.
CGDG: An actively managed global fund of large companies that the manager expects to pay and grow dividends over time. It holds a limited number of stocks spread across financials, tech, industrials and health care, with Broadcom and TSMC the largest at about 4% each.
CGDV: An actively managed fund from Capital Group of large US companies that pay dividends, picked by the firm's research analysts rather than an index. It leans toward big tech, with Microsoft, NVIDIA and Broadcom about 17% of it.
CGFS: An actively managed fund that mostly buys other ETFs to get large-company US stock exposure, mixing broad funds with specialty ones like aerospace and defense. It is a fund of funds, so about 10% sits in a single large-company index fund.
CGGE: An actively managed fund of stocks from around the world that its managers think can grow, many also paying dividends. It holds a fairly small number of companies, with Alphabet, Broadcom, Taiwan Semiconductor and Microsoft making up about 18% of it.
CGGG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, picked by Capital Group's team of portfolio managers. It is concentrated at the top, as NVIDIA, Broadcom, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta make up roughly 45% of the fund.
CGGO: An actively managed global stock fund from Capital Group, holding companies around the world its managers think can grow. Chip makers loom large: Taiwan Semiconductor, Micron and SK Hynix are about 18% of it.
CGGR: US stocks that Capital Group's managers think offer strong growth potential, with a small slice allowed outside the US. It is actively managed rather than tracking an index, and Meta, Tesla, Broadcom and NVIDIA are its biggest holdings at about 24% together.
CGHM: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It focuses on lower-rated, higher-yielding bonds, so it takes more credit risk, and has some exposure to Puerto Rico issuers.
CGHY: An actively managed fund of high-yield (junk) bonds, which are issued by companies with lower credit ratings and pay more interest to make up for the risk. It holds many different bonds, with none above about 1%, plus a small cash position.
CGIB: An actively managed fund of government and corporate bonds from around the world, with currency moves hedged back to the US dollar. The hedging reduces swings from exchange rates, and top holdings include Chinese, UK, German and Italian government bonds.
CGIC: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US, including emerging markets, that the managers think can grow or pay dividends. Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest holding at about 6%, and financials and technology each make up over a fifth.
CGIE: An actively managed fund of growth-oriented stocks from companies outside the United States, picked by Capital Group's managers. It holds a limited number of stocks, and companies like ASML, TotalEnergies and Taiwan Semiconductor are among its biggest positions, with industrials and financials leading by sector.
CGMM: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, picked by Capital Group's managers. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings, such as Bloom Energy and Exelon, only about 2% each.
CGMS: An actively managed US bond fund mixing different kinds of income-paying debt, such as company bonds, mortgage-related bonds and higher-yield bonds, to aim for a high level of income. It is widely spread, with no single holding above about 3%.
CGMU: Municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, chosen by Capital Group managers, with interest mostly exempt from regular federal income tax. Most are medium maturity, and the holdings are very spread out, with the biggest only around 1%.
CGNG: An actively managed fund of companies with significant business in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and India, even if the companies are based elsewhere. It holds a small number of stocks, with Taiwan Semiconductor and SK Hynix about 18% of it.
CGOV: Very short-term US Treasury bills with 0 to 3 months left until they mature, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. The bills are so short that the price barely moves, and income follows short-term interest rates.
CGPT: Stocks of companies tied to AI inference, the step where trained AI models answer real requests, such as chip, networking and cloud names. It is a narrow technology bet, with Astera Labs, Cerebras and NVIDIA among the largest holdings, each roughly 7% to 9% of the fund.
CGRO: An actively managed fund of growth companies in Greater China, covering mainland China, Taiwan and Hong Kong. It is led by Tencent and Alibaba at around 16% combined, with a heavy tilt toward consumer discretionary stocks.
CGSD: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mainly investment-grade corporate and government-backed mortgage bonds, plus some cash. Because the bonds mature soon, its price should move less than a longer-term bond fund, and it pays income from the interest.
CGSM: An actively managed fund of short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. Short maturities mean its price should move less than a longer-term muni fund, and it is spread across many issuers around the country.
CGUS: An actively managed US stock fund from Capital Group, holding companies its managers expect to grow in value or pay dividends. NVIDIA, Broadcom, Microsoft and Amazon are about 24% of it.
CGV: An actively managed global fund buying stocks of smaller and mid-sized companies that look cheap and financially sound. It is spread worldwide across materials, industrials, energy and consumer staples, with no holding above about 4%.
CGVV: An actively managed fund of large US value stocks, chosen by Capital Group managers who look for companies that seem priced below their worth. Holdings are spread out, with Amazon, Alphabet, Intel and Starbucks each about 3 to 5%.
CGW: Water-related companies around the world, such as utilities that supply water and makers of pumps and treatment equipment, tracked by the S&P Global Water Index. American Water Works, Xylem and Brazil's Sabesp are the biggest, at roughly 8% each.
CGXU: A manager-picked fund of growth-oriented companies based outside the US, including emerging markets. It holds a limited number of stocks, and Taiwan Semiconductor, SoftBank and First Quantum Minerals are among its largest, with tech the biggest sector at about 26%.
CHAT: An actively managed fund of global companies tied to generative AI, from chip makers to software and internet firms, including some in emerging markets. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Broadcom about 17% of it and semiconductors making up a big share.
CHDG: An actively managed fund that holds other equity funds tracking large US stocks and uses hedging, such as options, to reduce the effect of market declines. The aim is a smoother ride than a plain stock fund, which usually means giving up some gains.
CHGX: About 100 US large and mid-sized companies, equally weighted, and screened for sustainability by Stance. Because every stock gets a similar weight, the largest holdings are only around 1% each, unlike cap-weighted funds dominated by a few giants.
CHIP: Companies in the chipmaking supply chain, including makers of the equipment used to build semiconductors, following an index chosen for AI related chip exposure. Holdings are spread fairly evenly, with Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA and Tokyo Electron each around 5%.
CHIQ: Tracks Chinese consumer companies in the MSCI China Index, such as online retailers, carmakers, travel and restaurant firms. It is top-heavy in a few names: Meituan, PDD and Alibaba are about 26% together, and it moves with China's economy and its regulations.
CHNL: A fund that gets exposure to Chainlink, a crypto token, through futures contracts rather than holding the coins directly. Futures can track the price a little differently than the coin, and the cash it holds is collateral for those contracts.
CHPS: Semiconductor companies that also meet certain sustainability screens, tracked by an index. It is a narrow bet on chips: Micron, SK Hynix and AMD are each around 7%, and the top eight holdings are close to half of the fund.
CHPX: Companies in the artificial intelligence chip and quantum computing worlds, such as memory makers, chip equipment makers and chip designers. It is nearly all technology, and Micron, SK Hynix and ASML are about 27% of the fund.
CHPY: Holds US semiconductor stocks and sells options on them and on chip ETFs to generate monthly income. The options give up some of the upside in strong rallies, and the portfolio is concentrated in one industry, with NVIDIA, Broadcom and AMD each around 5% to 6%.
CHRI: The S&P 500 with companies screened out if they conflict with Christian values, such as those tied to things like abortion, adult entertainment or gambling. What is left looks a lot like the regular index: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
CHYG: Short-term high yield corporate bonds with 0 to 5 years left to maturity, following an index of them. These are bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, so they pay more income but carry more risk of default than safer bonds.
CIBR: Companies that make cybersecurity software and hardware, such as firewalls, threat detection and network protection, tracked by the Nasdaq CTA Cybersecurity index. Concentrated: Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, CrowdStrike and Cisco make up about 35% of it.
CIEI: US Treasury bonds with about three to seven years left until they mature, tracked by an index. That puts it in the middle of the range, with more interest rate sensitivity than short-term Treasuries but less than long-term ones.
CIVG: US investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies with solid credit, with one to five years left until they mature. The shorter lifespan generally means the price moves less when interest rates change than with longer bond funds.
CJUL: A defined-outcome fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in July. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
CJUN: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a broad US large-company stock fund to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in June. The name points to a 15% buffer, and it works only if held for the full period.
CLCG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, meaning ones expected to grow faster than average, drawn from the Russell 1000 Growth index. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are about 37% of it, and technology is over half.
CLCV: Large US companies that look inexpensive, chosen from the Russell 1000 value universe by an active manager. Even so, it holds big names: Amazon, Apple and Microsoft are about 11% of it, with technology and financials the largest sectors.
CLIM: Real estate investment trusts (companies that own property and pay out rental income) picked by an index built around climate resilience. Holdings are spread widely, with Welltower, American Tower, Prologis and Digital Realty each about 3% to 4% of the fund.
CLIP: Very short-term US Treasury bills with one to three months left until they mature, tracked by an index. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, and because the bills are so short, the price barely moves while income follows short-term rates.
CLNK: Holds Chainlink, a cryptocurrency that supplies real world data to blockchain applications, directly rather than through futures. Its price follows the price of Chainlink, which can swing a lot, and it owns no stocks or bonds.
CLOA: An actively managed fund of AAA-rated collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of corporate loans sliced into layers, with the AAA layer first in line to be paid. These floating-rate securities are the safest layer, so income moves with short-term interest rates.
CLOB: An actively managed fund holding collateralized loan obligations, bundles of corporate loans cut into slices, mainly those rated AA down to BB. It aims for higher income than regular bonds, though these slices can lose value quickly if loan defaults rise.
CLOC: An actively managed fund of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans to companies sliced into bonds that pay interest. It spreads its money across many CLOs, each around 2.5% of the fund.
CLOD: Holds companies in cloud computing, such as cybersecurity and software firms, from developed markets. Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are about 15% of it combined, and technology makes up over 80%.
CLOI: An actively managed fund that buys the investment-grade slices of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are pools of loans to companies that are sold off in layers by risk. It focuses on the safer layers, which pay floating interest rates, and spreads across many separate CLOs.
CLOO: Investment-grade tranches of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of corporate loans sliced into layers by risk. It holds the safer upper layers, spread across many CLOs, with each holding around 1% or 2% of the fund.
CLOU: Companies that sell cloud computing services, such as data storage, software delivered online and web infrastructure, tracking the Global X Cloud Computing Index. It is almost entirely technology, with Snowflake, Datadog and DigitalOcean each at roughly 5% to 6%.
CLOX: An actively managed fund holding the safest, AAA rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of corporate loans packaged into bonds. It holds many different CLOs, none above about 2%, and its income tends to follow short term interest rates.
CLOZ: An actively managed fund buying the lower-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans made to US companies. These BBB to B slices pay higher income but carry more credit risk, and it spreads across many CLOs.
CLSE: An actively managed fund that buys stocks it likes and bets against stocks it doesn't (short positions), while staying net long overall. It is tilted to tech and chips, with NVIDIA, Micron and Lam Research among the largest long positions.
CLSM: An actively managed fund that moves its money among US sector ETFs, with the manager choosing the sectors it thinks are leading. Right now it is concentrated: about 33% in a tech sector fund, 30% in a Nasdaq-100 fund, 29% in consumer staples, and some gold.
CLUB: An actively managed global stock fund that buys companies where famous billionaire investors have large stakes. Holdings are spread widely, with Dell, SoftBank, Oracle and ArcelorMittal each around 4% to 6%, and technology is the biggest sector at roughly 30%.
CMAG: An actively managed fund holding the largest US-listed tech and tech-related giants, weighted by company size. NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 38% of it, and a large chunk sits in government cash funds, so it is very concentrated.
CMAY: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 15% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on when you hold it.
CMBO: An actively managed fund that takes positions on US interest rates mainly through options on Treasury-related investments, alongside a base of short-term government securities. It aims to profit from rate moves, so it is quite different from a plain short-term bond fund.
CMBS: Investment-grade commercial mortgage-backed securities, which are bonds backed by pools of loans on office buildings, apartments and other commercial property. Much of it is issued or guaranteed by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, and it follows a broad index of this market.
CMCI: A broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, tracking the UBS Bloomberg CMCI index through futures contracts rather than physical goods. The cash and bonds it holds are collateral behind those contracts, not the main point of the fund.
CMDT: An actively managed fund that gets commodity exposure through derivatives, which are contracts tracking prices of things like energy, metals and crops. Those are backed by a portfolio of bonds PIMCO manages, so returns come from both the commodity moves and the bonds.
CMDY: A broad commodity fund that holds futures contracts, agreements to buy a commodity later, on 24 commodities including oil, gold, copper and crops. It owns no stocks, and the futures roll forward to new months over time.
CMF: Bonds issued by California cities, schools and agencies, tracked by an index of investment grade California municipal bonds. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and holdings are very spread out, with no single bond above about 1% of the fund.
CNAV: An actively managed fund that shifts across the sub-industries of the S&P 500 using a quantitative model, so it can lean heavily on whatever it favors. It is very tech-heavy right now, with Western Digital, Sandisk and Astera Labs among the top holdings.
CNBS: US-listed companies tied to cannabis and hemp, such as growers, suppliers and cannabis-focused real estate firms. It is a narrow, volatile corner of the market, and Curaleaf is one of its biggest named stock holdings at about 16%.
CNEQ: An actively managed fund holding a small number of large US growth companies, with bigger bets on its best ideas. It is concentrated: NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nebius are about 36% of the fund.
CNQQ: Chinese technology and innovation companies listed in China and abroad, picked by an index with an eye toward newer industries. It is a concentrated bet on one country: Alibaba and Tencent are about 9% each, and tech makes up nearly half of it.
CNRG: Companies in clean power, such as fuel cells, solar, wind and grid equipment, tracked by the S&P Kensho Clean Power Index. It is spread fairly evenly, with the top holdings like FuelCell Energy and GE Vernova each only around 3% to 6%.
CNXT: Tracks an index of the 100 largest and most liquid companies on China's ChiNext board, a market for young, fast-growing firms. It is concentrated: Zhongji Innolight and Contemporary Amperex Technology are about 29% together, and over half is technology.
CNYA: Holds large and mid-sized Chinese companies whose shares trade on mainland China's stock exchanges (A-shares), tracking an MSCI index. Technology, financials, industrials and materials lead, and battery maker CATL and liquor maker Kweichow Moutai are the biggest holdings at under 4% each.
COAL: Follows an index of coal companies worldwide, from mining to transport, covering both steelmaking (met) coal and power plant (thermal) coal. It is concentrated in a few miners: Warrior Met Coal, Yancoal and Alpha Metallurgical are about 27% of it.
COIW: An actively managed fund that aims for about 1.2 times the weekly return of Coinbase stock, using swaps and some direct shares, and it pays out income weekly. The Treasury bills it holds are collateral, so this is a leveraged bet on a single stock.
COLO: Companies in Colombia, tracked with the MSCI Colombia index. It is a narrow, concentrated fund: Grupo Cibest (a bank) is about a quarter of it, and financials, utilities, energy and materials fill most of the rest.
COM: Futures contracts across many commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, tracking an index that tries to ride upward trends and cut risk in downtrends. It holds futures rather than physical goods, with cash and Treasuries backing them.
COMB: An actively managed fund that gives exposure to a broad basket of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, using futures contracts. It does not track an index exactly, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly collateral, with no K-1 tax form needed.
COMD: An actively managed fund giving exposure to commodities such as metals, oil, natural gas and farm products, mostly through futures contracts. Much of the fund sits in short-term Treasury bills as backing for those contracts.
COMT: Futures contracts on a broad mix of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, tracking an S&P GSCI index. It picks which contract months to hold to reduce losses from rolling contracts forward, and the cash and bonds shown are mostly backing for the futures.
CONY: Earns income by selling options tied to Coinbase stock, which is closely linked to the crypto market. The options strategy limits gains if Coinbase rises but still leaves most of the losses, and the Treasury bills listed are mainly collateral backing the options.
COOL: Invests in companies behind the power and cooling needs of AI data centers, such as Vertiv, Vicor and Navitas, and may use options or swaps for exposure. A fifth of it sits in a government money fund, and the rest is split between technology and industrials.
COPA: A fund holding copper mining and refining companies from around the world, following an index of firms that earn much of their revenue from copper. Freeport-McMoRan is the largest holding at about 9%, and nearly everything is in materials companies.
COPJ: Small and mid sized copper mining companies that earn at least half their revenue or assets from copper, tracking a Nasdaq index. It is spread over many miners, each around 5% or less, so it moves with copper prices and mining stocks.
COPP: A fund of companies that earn most of their revenue from copper mining, tracking an index of global copper miners. It is concentrated, with Freeport-McMoRan about 24% and Teck and Antofagasta adding about 19% more, so it moves with copper prices.
COPX: Global companies that mine copper, tracked by a Global X index. It is a bet on one industry, nearly all materials, with BHP, Teck, Hudbay, Southern Copper and First Quantum each at about 5%.
COPY: An actively managed fund of US and foreign small and mid-sized companies the manager thinks are cheap, with a special interest in firms whose own executives and directors are buying shares. It is diversified, with no single holding above about 2% of the fund.
CORB: An actively managed core bond fund, holding a mix of US Treasuries, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, with an average quality of A or better. Treasuries are the largest holdings, and it is meant as an all-round bond holding.
CORN: Tracks the price of corn by holding futures contracts, which are agreements to buy corn at a set price later, spread across three contracts traded in Chicago. It never holds actual corn, and the rest sits in cash-like holdings, so its price follows corn futures and can swing with weather and crop news.
CORO: An actively managed fund that holds other iShares country funds, shifting money toward countries outside the US that its managers favor. Japan is about 20% and Canada about 13%, so a few countries drive the result at any time.
CORP: US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds, loans to financially solid companies, tracking the ICE BofA US Corporate Index. The Treasury holdings listed near the top are likely cash management and collateral, not the main point of the fund, which is corporate debt with at least a year left.
COSW: A single-stock fund that gets its exposure to Costco through swaps, contracts that pay the stock's returns, plus some direct shares. It aims to pay distributions weekly, and much of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing for those swaps.
COWG: US large companies that produce a lot of free cash flow, meaning cash left over after running the business, picked by a rules-based index that favors growth. It is about 70% technology, and its top holdings are mostly mid-sized names rather than the usual giants.
COWS: US dividend-paying stocks that produce strong cash flow, picked by a rules-based index from Amplify. It holds mid-sized companies from many sectors, such as tech hardware, with no stock above about 4%.
COWZ: About 100 large and mid-sized US companies that generate the most free cash flow (cash left over after expenses and investments) relative to their value. It is rules-based and spread fairly evenly, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward energy, health care and industrials.
COYY: An income fund tied to Coinbase stock through options on another Coinbase ETF, aiming to pay out regularly. The options cap how much of any rise it can capture, while the Treasury bills that fill most of the portfolio mainly support the strategy.
CPAG: A fund giving exposure to the broad US investment-grade bond market, built by holding two other bond ETFs, iShares Core US Aggregate and a Dimensional core bond fund, about half each. It follows an index designed to track total return without reinvesting the interest it earns.
CPAI: An actively managed fund that uses computer models to pick at least 50 US-listed stocks, mostly mid-sized companies. It leans toward technology at about a third of the fund, with energy and health care next, and no stock above roughly 2%.
CPER: A fund that gains exposure to copper prices by holding copper futures contracts traded on COMEX, instead of owning actual metal. Its price follows copper but can drift from it as the contracts roll forward over time.
CPHY: A fund that gets high yield corporate bond exposure by holding other bond ETFs, mainly from Invesco, State Street and iShares. High yield bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, pay more interest because the companies are riskier, and this fund is built around three funds rather than individual bonds.
CPII: An actively managed fund built to protect against rising US inflation, using inflation-linked Treasury bonds along with inflation swaps and options. Most of it sits in a handful of inflation-protected Treasuries, so it is aimed at inflation rather than stock-like growth.
CPLB: An actively managed fund of US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, with the freedom to add some lower-quality bonds for extra income. A good part of it is in US Treasuries, with the largest few holdings making up about 20%.
CPLS: An actively managed bond fund holding a broad mix of US government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, plus some riskier types for extra income. The managers choose bonds themselves rather than following an index, and US Treasuries are the largest holdings.
CPNJ: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq-100) to protect against part of the losses over a set period starting in June. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full period.
CPNM: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to follow the index up to a cap while protecting against a set amount of losses. The period starts in March, and the outcome only applies if held for the full period.
CPNQ: Uses FLEX options, customizable exchange traded options, tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, a Nasdaq-100 fund, to seek protection from a set amount of losses over a set period that starts each December. In return, the upside over that period is limited.
CPNS: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, over a set period starting in September. It aims to protect against part of the losses, and in return gains are capped.
CPRA: An actively managed fund using options on the iShares Russell 2000 fund, which tracks small US companies, over a set one-year period starting in April. It aims to cushion part of the losses in exchange for limited gains, and it is not a plain small-cap fund.
CPRJ: An options-based fund tied to the Russell 2000 small-company index through a one-year outcome period starting in July, designed to protect against some losses in exchange for limited gains. The protection only applies to those who hold for the full period.
CPRO: Uses options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which holds US small company stocks, to follow that index over a set period starting in October. It aims to protect against part of the losses, and in return gains are capped.
CPRY: Options on an iShares Russell 2000 fund, which tracks US small companies, designed to absorb part of the losses over a set one year period starting in January. In exchange, gains are limited by a cap, so results depend on timing.
CPSA: A defined-outcome fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in August. The price of that protection is a cap on how much of the market's gain it can pass on.
CPSD: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to protect against part of the losses over a set period starting in December. In exchange, the gains are capped, and the protection is meant for those who hold the full period.
CPSF: Options on an S&P 500 index fund designed to cushion part of the losses over a set one year period starting in February. In exchange, the upside is capped, so the outcome depends on when you buy and sell relative to the period.
CPSJ: A defined-outcome fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to shield part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in July. In return, gains are limited to a cap, so it will not capture all of a big market rally.
CPSL: A fund that holds twelve staggered defined outcome funds on the S&P 500, each resetting at a different month. It aims to follow large US stocks while limiting a set amount of downside, with gains held back by a cap.
CPSM: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow large US stocks while protecting against a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each May. Gains are capped, and the protection applies fully only if you hold through the whole period.
CPSN: A defined outcome fund that uses customized options tied to the S&P 500 (via the SPDR S&P 500 ETF) to protect against part of the losses over a set one year period starting in November. The trade-off is that gains are capped.
CPSO: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to protect part of the losses over a one-year period starting in October, in return for capping how much of the gains it can keep. Results depend on when you buy relative to that period.
CPSP: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 (through the SPDR S&P 500 ETF) to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period that starts in April. In return, gains are limited, so it will not fully keep up if the market rallies.
CPSR: A defined outcome fund that uses customized options tied to the S&P 500 (via the SPDR S&P 500 ETF) to protect against part of the losses over a set one year period. In exchange, gains are limited, and the fund is non-diversified.
CPST: Uses customized options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in September. It aims to protect against a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and is built to be held to the end.
CPSU: A structured protection fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a set one-year period starting in June. It aims to cushion part of the losses in exchange for limited gains, and it only works as intended if you hold the full period.
CPSY: A structured protection fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a set one-year period starting in January. It aims to cushion part of the losses in exchange for limited gains, and it only works as intended if you hold the full period.
CPTL: Large US companies picked by Morningstar for how well they use their cash, such as reinvesting it wisely and returning it to shareholders. It leans toward tech, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet making up about 18% of the fund.
CPU: Stocks of semiconductor companies, the makers of computer chips, held directly or through swaps and options that track them. It is focused on one industry, and the fund is non-diversified, so a few chip names can drive its results.
CQQQ: Chinese technology and internet companies, such as Meituan, PDD, Tencent and Baidu, following an index. It is concentrated and tied to one country: the top four holdings are about 40% of the fund.
CQTM: An actively managed fund focused on companies working on quantum computing, a new kind of computer technology. It is very concentrated: IonQ is about 18% of it, and D-Wave, Rigetti and Quantinuum add roughly another 25%.
CRAK: Companies that refine crude oil into fuels like gasoline and diesel, from around the world, following a VanEck index. It is a narrow energy bet, with Reliance Industries, Marathon Petroleum, Valero and Phillips 66 together making up about 30%.
CRAM: A fund tracking companies in mainland China and Hong Kong that make memory and storage chips. It focuses on one narrow corner of the chip industry in one region, so it can be quite volatile.
CRBN: Large and mid-sized companies from developed and emerging markets worldwide, tracking an MSCI index tilted to have a lower carbon footprint and less exposure to fossil fuel reserves. It resembles the global market, with NVIDIA and Apple each around 4.5%.
CRCO: A fund tied to the stock of Circle (ticker CRCL) that uses options to try to pay out high income. It does not own the shares directly, mostly holds Treasury bills as backing, and its gains are capped while it can still lose heavily if the stock falls.
CRDD: A fund that gets its exposure to Cardano's ADA token mainly through futures contracts traded on a US regulated exchange, with cash and similar holdings set aside as collateral. It does not hold the coin directly, and it is a narrow, concentrated bet on a single cryptocurrency.
CRDT: An actively managed income fund that mixes corporate bonds, mortgage and consumer-loan securities, preferred stock and other income assets. A big share sits in mortgage real estate companies like Rithm, Dynex, MFA and Annaly, and it also uses leverage, meaning borrowed money.
CRIB: Holds real estate companies from around the world, such as property owners and landlords. Welltower, Equinix and Prologis are about 21% of the fund, and nearly all of it is real estate.
CROB: Holds Chinese robotics companies, directly or through derivatives that give similar exposure, such as makers of industrial robots and automation parts. The cash-like holding in its list is just collateral, and the fund is a narrow bet on one theme in one country.
CRPT: Companies in the crypto industry and digital economy, such as bitcoin holders, exchanges and brokers, plus some bitcoin ETFs. Metaplanet is the biggest holding at about 11%, and the fund is concentrated, so it tends to move with crypto prices.
CRSH: An actively managed fund that aims to make money when Tesla stock falls, and pays income from options. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, so it gives up gains if Tesla rises, and it is a bet against one company.
CRTC: Large and mid-size companies in areas defined as critical technologies, such as AI, semiconductors and biotechnology, in developed countries. It follows an index, and its top holdings, like Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and NVIDIA, are each around 5%.
CRUX: An actively managed core bond fund holding investment-grade US dollar bonds, with a large share in mortgage-backed bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac plus some corporate bonds. It can also hold foreign bonds and loans, so it is not tied to a single index.
CRXP: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds US investment-grade bonds like mortgage-backed securities, with some room for riskier ones. It aims for income plus a bit of extra return than a plain core bond index, and holds many small positions.
CRY: An options income fund tied to Circle (CRCL) that sells call options on a leveraged ETF of the stock to generate weekly style payouts. It holds derivatives rather than shares, so the income can be large, but the upside is capped and losses can be steep.
CSB: About 100 US small companies with high dividend yields, picked by the Nasdaq Victory US Small Cap High Dividend 100 Volatility Weighted Index, which gives calmer stocks bigger weights. It leans toward utilities and financials, and no single holding is more than about 2%.
CSD: US companies that were recently spun off from a larger parent, tracked with the S&P Spin-Off Index. It is concentrated, with GE HealthCare, Veralto and GE Vernova each at roughly 7% to 8%, and about 40% in industrials.
CSEN: An actively managed fund of energy companies, including oil and gas as well as renewable and clean energy and utilities. Today it is mostly traditional energy, with ExxonMobil, Phillips 66, Suncor and ConocoPhillips among the biggest holdings.
CSEP: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
CSHI: An actively managed fund that holds very short-term US Treasury bills and also sells put options on the S&P 500 to earn extra income. The option income comes with stock market risk that plain T-bills don't have, so it is not just cash.
CSHP: An actively managed fund aimed at short-term bond-like returns that also uses stocks and currencies opportunistically. About half is bonds, with a smaller part in stocks such as NVIDIA and Apple, so it takes more risk than a plain ultrashort bond fund.
CSIO: An actively managed fund of infrastructure companies around the world, such as utilities, railroads, pipelines and communications. Utilities are over half of it, and CSX, Williams and Entergy are among its larger holdings at around 6% to 7% each.
CSM: Follows an index built on a 130/30 idea: it goes long on the leading large US companies it likes and shorts those it doesn't, with the net exposure close to the market. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 13% of it.
CSMD: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that the managers expect to grow faster than average. It is spread over health care, technology and industrials, and no single stock is much above 4% of the fund.
CSNR: An actively managed fund holding companies that own or earn money from natural resources, such as oil and gas, mining, fertilizer and farm goods. It is about 41% energy and 40% materials, and ExxonMobil is the largest holding at around 6%.
CSPF: An actively managed fund mostly holding preferred securities and other income paying bonds, which are hybrids of stock and debt. Large global banks such as Citigroup, BNP Paribas and Royal Bank of Canada show up often, so it leans heavily on financial companies.
CSRA: An actively managed fund spread across real assets: real estate, energy, utilities, materials, commodities and gold, often through other funds. It aims to hold up better when inflation rises, and it mixes stocks with commodity and bond exposure.
CSRE: An actively managed fund of real estate companies, mostly REITs (companies that own properties and pay out the rent income). It is concentrated: Welltower and Digital Realty alone are about 24%, and holdings include data centers, cell towers and health care properties.
CSSD: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income bonds, mostly from banks and financial companies, with shorter maturities. The shorter terms are meant to make its price less sensitive to interest rate changes, and it focuses on investment grade issuers.
CSTK: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers see as undervalued and out of favor. It is broadly spread, with Alphabet, Microsoft and Cisco each only around 3% to 4% of it.
CTA: An actively managed trend-following fund that takes bets through futures on stocks, Treasuries, commodities and currencies, going long or short as trends develop. It is meant to behave differently from stocks and bonds, and much of its portfolio is Treasuries held as collateral.
CTAG: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized growth companies, mostly in the US, picked by the manager through hands-on research. It leans toward technology, industrials and health care, with the top holding, Dave Inc, at about 5%.
CTAP: An actively managed fund that combines two strategies: US stock market exposure with an options overlay, and a managed futures strategy that trades across markets such as commodities, currencies and bonds. It uses leverage, so it holds more than 100% in total exposure.
CTAU: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 30% of losses over a set one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
CTEC: Tracks an index of companies that benefit from technologies aimed at fighting climate change, such as solar power, batteries and clean energy equipment. It is fairly concentrated, with Bloom Energy, Samsung SDI and First Solar together about 23% of the fund.
CTEF: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, chosen by the manager rather than an index. It is concentrated and tilted toward technology: Micron is about 10% of it and Western Digital, Lam Research and Jabil each add another 6 to 7%.
CTIF: An actively managed fund of US companies with a record of growing dividends, which also uses options to boost income. The holdings are spread fairly evenly, with Broadcom, Analog Devices, Caterpillar and Eaton each around 6%, and the options can limit gains.
CTJL: A fund that holds options on US stocks to give a set amount of protection against losses over a one-year period that starts in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and buying in mid-period changes how much protection and upside remain.
CTJN: A fund that holds options on US stocks to give a set amount of protection against losses over a one-year period that starts in June. In exchange, gains are capped, and buying in mid-period changes how much protection and upside remain.
CTMA: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 30% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains are limited, and the protection only applies over the full period.
CTSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion the first 30% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
CTWO: A trust that holds European Union carbon allowances, permits that companies must buy to emit carbon dioxide. Its price follows the carbon market, so it is a commodity style bet and pays no income.
CUST: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, so it is a low-risk way to hold government debt. Because the bonds are short, the price moves less when interest rates change than it would for long-term Treasuries.
CUT: Follows an index of companies around the world that own timberland or make wood, paper and packaging products. International Paper, Smurfit Westrock, Amcor and Packaging Corp are each around 6% of it, so it leans heavily on packaging and paper makers.
CVAR: An actively managed fund holding roughly 50 to 100 stocks across company sizes and sectors, with a small slice in Treasuries. It leans toward health care and technology, and the manager picks holdings rather than following an index.
CVGD: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying companies in the US and abroad, picked for being financially strong. It leans toward health care, financials and consumer staples, with CVS, Verizon and Elevance each making up around 4%.
CVIE: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed and emerging markets outside the US, selected by an index that screens for environmental, social and governance practices. Chip makers lead the holdings, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix together around 12%.
CVLC: Large US companies from an index that screens for the Calvert Principles for Responsible Investment, which cover environmental, social and governance issues. It looks much like the broad market, with NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft about 22% of the fund.
CVMC: Mid-sized US companies that meet the Calvert Principles for Responsible Investment, tracked by an index. It is extremely spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and spans technology, industrials, financials and health care.
CVNY: Aims to pay income while tracking the Carvana (CVNA) share price indirectly, using a synthetic covered call strategy built from options instead of owning the shares. Gains are limited if the stock soars, and it does not protect against falls.
CVRD: A fund of dividend-paying US stocks that also sells covered call options on much of the portfolio, earning extra income in exchange for giving up some gains in strong rallies. It is spread over many companies, with technology, financials and health care the largest areas, and none above 5%.
CVRT: An actively managed fund of convertible securities, which are bonds and preferred shares that can turn into company stock. It targets those that move more like stocks, and it leans toward health care and utilities, with Boeing and Alphabet preferreds among the top holdings.
CVSM: An actively managed fund of small and mid sized US companies, those in between the giants and the tiniest firms. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3%, and leans toward financials, consumer companies and industrials.
CVY: A mix of income-paying holdings, mainly dividend stocks from the US and abroad, plus some preferred shares and bonds, selected by Zacks research. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward financials, energy and real estate.
CWB: Convertible bonds, which are company bonds that can be swapped for shares of the issuer's stock, tracking a Bloomberg convertibles index. They combine some bond-like income with stock-like swings, and they are spread across many companies, mostly in technology.
CWI: Stocks from developed and emerging countries around the world, except the United States, following the MSCI ACWI ex USA index. It is broadly spread across thousands of companies, with Taiwan Semiconductor the biggest at about 5% and financials and technology each making up over a fifth.
CWS: An actively managed fund of a small group of US stocks picked with a model that favors steady, high quality businesses with consistent earnings. It is concentrated, with Comfort Systems USA and IES Holdings about 16% together, and includes a mix of industrials, health care and technology.
CWY: Earns income by selling options linked to CoreWeave through a leveraged fund, so it does not simply hold the stock. The options income comes with caps on gains and the underlying leverage adds big swings, so the price can move sharply.
CXSE: Chinese companies that are not controlled by the state, tracked by a WisdomTree index of private-sector firms. Tencent and Alibaba are about 13% of the fund, and consumer and technology companies each make up around a quarter.
CZA: 100 US mid-sized companies chosen by Zacks using a ranking model, then weighted by a set formula. It holds a wide mix such as financials, industrials and health care, with no stock above about 2%.
DABS: An actively managed fund of asset-backed securities, which are bonds backed by pools of consumer loans, auto loans and similar debt. Holdings are spread across many issues, with Upstart and SoFi loan pools among the larger ones.
DACL: A fund that uses derivatives to follow an autocallable index, a strategy that pays income and can end early if certain price levels are met. Its holdings are mostly options and similar contracts rather than stocks, so the results depend on how the index's rules play out.
DADS: An actively managed fund of debt, such as bonds, convertibles and preferred shares, from companies involved in digital assets like bitcoin mining. Core Scientific, Riot and Galaxy Digital are among its holdings, so it is tied to the crypto industry.
DAK: An actively managed fund that builds a portfolio of large US stocks, partly through other ETFs such as S&P 500 funds. About half of it sits in a few dozen names and funds, with Apple the largest at about 6%.
DALI: An actively managed fund that holds First Trust AlphaDEX ETFs and rotates among asset classes, such as US sectors, company sizes and foreign stocks, based on which are showing the strongest recent price momentum. It is a fund of ETFs, so its holdings change as the rankings change.
DANA: An actively managed fund of high-quality, short-term bonds, aiming to protect capital while paying income. Mortgage-backed bonds from Fannie Mae are the biggest holdings, and the focus on short maturities is meant to keep price swings small.
DAPP: Stocks of companies involved in digital assets and blockchain, including crypto exchanges, payment firms and bitcoin miners. It does not hold any cryptocurrency directly, and it is fairly concentrated: Block, Coinbase and Iris Energy are about 23% of the fund.
DAPR: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each April. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
DARP: An actively managed fund that holds 30 to 60 growth-focused stocks, looking for companies tied to innovation and disruption. It is fairly concentrated and tech-heavy: Alphabet, Amazon, NVIDIA and Micron together are about 38% of the fund.
DAUG: Uses exchange-traded options on the S&P 500 to deliver a set outcome over a one-year period starting in August. A deep buffer is meant to absorb a large slice of any market losses, but in return gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
DAX: Large German companies, tracked with the DAX index of the biggest firms listed in Germany. It is top-heavy: Siemens, Allianz and SAP together are about 30% of the fund, with industrials and financials the largest sectors.
DBA: A fund that tracks agricultural commodity futures, contracts on crops and livestock such as corn, wheat, sugar and soybeans, rather than owning any farm companies. Its prices follow farm commodity markets, and the Treasury and cash holdings listed are just collateral backing those contracts.
DBAR: An actively managed fund that combines a managed futures strategy, which trades contracts across markets, with a US stock strategy, aiming for steadier results through different market conditions. It is non-diversified and its futures part can behave very unlike stocks.
DBAW: Stocks from developed and emerging markets outside the US, from the MSCI All World ex USA index, with the currency swings hedged back to the US dollar. Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are the biggest holdings, together about 10% of the fund.
DBB: Tracks base metals prices by holding futures contracts, which are agreements to buy aluminum, zinc and copper at set prices later. It does not own metal or mining stocks, and much of the fund sits in Treasury bills and cash as collateral.
DBC: A fund that tracks a basket of commodity futures, contracts on oil, natural gas, metals and farm products. It does not hold the goods themselves, and its Treasury and cash holdings are only margin to back the futures contracts.
DBE: A fund that tracks an index of energy futures, contracts to buy oil, heating oil, gasoline and natural gas at a set future price, instead of owning any physical fuel. Much of the money sits in short-term government funds as backing, so it is a bet on energy prices.
DBEF: Stocks of large companies in developed markets outside North America (Europe, Japan, Australia), tracked by an MSCI EAFE index, but with currency hedging. The hedge offsets moves between those currencies and the US dollar, so mostly the stock prices matter to you.
DBEM: Large and mid-sized stocks from emerging markets like Taiwan, Korea, China and India, with the currency risk reduced by hedging against the US dollar. It follows an MSCI index, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung alone are about 22% of the fund.
DBEU: Large and mid-sized European stocks that also hedges against currency swings, so changes in the euro and pound against the dollar mostly do not affect results. It follows an MSCI Europe index, with ASML, HSBC and Roche among the top holdings at roughly 2% to 4%.
DBEZ: Large companies from countries using the euro, following an MSCI Eurozone index, with currency swings against the US dollar hedged away. ASML is the largest holding at about 7%, and financials and industrials lead the sectors.
DBJP: Large Japanese stocks, tracking an MSCI Japan index, with a currency hedge to cancel out changes between the yen and the US dollar. Its return follows Japanese stocks without the effect of the yen, led by banks, Toyota and tech names.
DBMF: A managed futures fund that tries to copy how trend-following hedge funds trade, using futures contracts on currencies, bonds, stock indexes and commodities. It goes long or short as trends change, so it can behave differently from stocks and bonds, and much of it sits in cash and short-term bonds.
DBND: An actively managed bond fund that mixes US Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds, corporate bonds and other debt, including some emerging market and global bond funds. The manager has wide freedom to shift between bond types, so it differs from a plain index of investment-grade bonds.
DBO: A fund that tracks the price of crude oil (light sweet WTI) by holding oil futures, which are contracts to buy oil at a set future price. The Treasury and cash-like holdings you see are just collateral, so its results follow oil futures rather than oil company stocks.
DBP: Futures contracts on gold and silver, tracking an index of precious metals prices rather than owning the metals themselves. Its cash and Treasury holdings back the futures, and returns can differ from the spot price of the metals.
DCAP: An actively managed fund aiming for income by holding preferred stocks (shares that pay set dividends) issued by companies that keep bitcoin on their balance sheets. It is very concentrated: about 45% sits in a single Strategy preferred, with options used on top.
DCMT: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to a broad basket of commodities, including industrial and precious metals, energy and farm products. It mostly does this through futures and swaps, and the cash and bonds on its books are there to support those contracts.
DCOR: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, run by Dimensional, which tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market index would. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are still about 16% of it.
DCRE: An actively managed fund of bonds backed by commercial real estate loans, such as office, apartment and retail mortgages, including some government-backed ones from FNMA. The income depends on those loans being repaid, and about 5% is cash.
DDDD: Holds about 100 large US stocks like Abbott, Amgen, Merck and Coca-Cola while using options to pay out roughly double the usual income. The options mean it gives up some gains when stocks rise strongly.
DDEC: Uses exchange-traded options on the S&P 500 to deliver a set outcome over a one-year period starting in December. A deep buffer is meant to absorb a large slice of any market losses, but in return gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
DDFA: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting each April. It aims to gain when the market rises or falls up to a limit, while buffering a set amount of losses, and it only works as designed if held for the full period.
DDFD: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a gain whether the market rises or falls modestly over a set period, with a cushion against part of the losses. The period ends in December, and results only apply if held to then.
DDFF: Uses customized options tied to the S&P 500 so it can gain whether the market rises or falls modestly over a one-year period starting each February. It also cushions part of the losses, but gains are capped, and the terms only apply if you hold the full period.
DDFG: Options on an S&P 500 fund built to give a positive result whether the index rises or falls up to a point, with a 15% buffer against losses, over a one year period starting in August. Gains are capped, and results depend on timing.
DDFJ: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a 15% buffer against losses over a one-year period beginning in January. It also gains when the market dips slightly, but upside is capped and it fits the full period.
DDFL: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in July. It aims to gain when the market rises or falls up to a limit, with a buffer against part of the losses.
DDFM: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock fund to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in March. Its dual-directional design can also benefit if the market falls a little, though gains are capped.
DDFN: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in November. It also tries to gain when the market falls a little, but gains are capped if it rises.
DDFO: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a gain whether the market rises or falls modestly over a set one year period, with a cushion against part of the losses. Results only apply if shares are held for the whole period.
DDFS: A defined outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 so that it can gain when the market rises or falls up to a point, while covering a set amount of losses over a one year period starting each September. Both the upside and the protection are limited by caps.
DDFY: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a 15% buffer against losses over a one-year period beginning in May. It also gains when the market falls slightly, but it caps the upside, so it only fits the full period.
DDFZ: Gives exposure to the S&P 500 through options, with a defined outcome over a set one-year period starting in June. It aims to gain when the market rises or falls modestly, while a set amount of losses is buffered, though a cap limits the upside.
DDIV: About 50 US dividend-paying stocks picked for both high yield and strong recent price momentum, following a Dorsey Wright index. Financials and real estate make up about half, and the stocks are spread fairly evenly.
DDLS: Small companies from developed countries outside the US and Canada, weighted by dividends paid. It also hedges currency, which means it aims to cancel out swings in foreign currencies against the dollar, and it holds many tiny positions, none above about 1%.
DDNQ: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, over a set period that resets each quarter. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses and pay out gains whether the market rises or falls, within limits.
DDSQ: Uses options on US large-company stocks to profit when the market moves up or down by a modest amount over a set period, while cushioning part of the losses. The upside is capped, and the period resets quarterly.
DDTA: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim for gains whether the market rises or falls, up to a cap, over a set period starting in April. It buffers only part of the losses, and it works as intended only if held for the full period.
DDTD: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 (through the SPDR S&P 500 ETF) over a one-year period starting in December. It aims to gain when the market rises or falls, up to a limit, while absorbing a set amount of losses.
DDTF: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim to gain if the market rises or falls modestly, while cushioning losses of up to 10%. It works over a one-year period starting each February, so results depend on when you buy.
DDTG: A fund that holds options on an S&P 500 fund and aims to gain if the index rises up to a cap, or if it falls modestly, while shielding a set amount of larger losses. The outcome runs one year from August, and it applies only to those who hold for that full period.
DDTJ: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim to gain if the market rises or falls modestly, while cushioning losses of up to 10%. It works over a one-year period starting each January, so results depend on when you buy.
DDTL: Holds options tied to the S&P 500 that give a set amount of protection against losses over a one year period, while also gaining if the market rises or falls up to a limit. It is a defined outcome fund, so the protection and limits only apply if shares are held for the full period.
DDTM: An actively managed fund using options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting in March. It aims to give a gain if the market rises or falls modestly, and to cushion a set amount of losses, but with limits on upside.
DDTN: A fund that holds options on an S&P 500 fund and aims to gain if the index rises up to a cap, or if it falls modestly, while shielding a set amount of larger losses. The outcome runs one year from November, and it applies only to those who hold for that full period.
DDTO: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a set period that resets each October. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses and pay out gains whether the market rises or falls, within limits.
DDTS: A fund that holds options on an S&P 500 fund and aims to gain if the index rises up to a cap, or if it falls modestly, while shielding a set amount of larger losses. The outcome runs one year from September, and it applies only to those who hold for that full period.
DDTY: Options on an S&P 500 fund built to give a positive result whether the index rises or falls up to a point, with a 10% buffer against losses, over a one year period starting in May. Gains are capped, and results depend on timing.
DDTZ: A fund that holds options on an S&P 500 fund and aims to gain if the index rises up to a cap, or if it falls modestly, while shielding a set amount of larger losses. The outcome runs one year from June, and it applies only to those who hold for that full period.
DDV: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs, mainly US Treasuries with a small amount of stock funds, aiming to be less risky than a typical balanced fund. Its name suggests a fixed target for how sensitive it is to interest rates, and it is mostly bonds.
DDWM: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked from a WisdomTree index that weights by dividends and then hedges currency moves. Because of the hedge, changes in the dollar versus foreign currencies should matter less, and no holding is above about 2%.
DDX: A fund of funds that mixes US Treasuries with stock ETFs, such as Vanguard Value and emerging markets funds, over a set ten-year period. The Treasuries are about 45% of it, so it blends safer bonds with a smaller dose of stocks.
DDXX: An actively managed fund of funds that holds broad stock ETFs, such as value, minimum volatility, total market, emerging markets and small cap funds, trying to beat a plain market weighted index fund. About 24% sits in one SPDR portfolio fund, and the rest is spread across Vanguard and iShares ETFs.
DECM: Options on a US stock market index fund that aim to protect against a large part of losses over a one year period starting in December, as its Max Buffer name says. In exchange, gains are capped, and results depend on when you buy.
DECO: Stocks of companies tied to crypto and blockchain, plus funds and futures that track bitcoin and ether. Bitcoin miners and data center firms lead the holdings: Riot Platforms, Keel Infrastructure and CleanSpark together are about 31% of the fund.
DECP: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in December, the buffer being 12 in the fund's name. In return, upside is capped, and the options are nearly the whole fund.
DECT: Uses options tied to the S&P 500, through the SPY fund, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in December. It is built to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, so timing within the period matters.
DECU: A fund using options to follow US stock market returns over a one year period starting in December, with a set amount of losses cushioned. Gains are not capped by a fixed limit, but the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
DECW: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each December, with the 20 in its name referring to the buffer level. In return, gains are capped, so it works best held for the full period.
DECZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set one-year period starting in December. The options track part of the market's gains while limiting some losses, with most of the money held in Treasuries.
DEED: An actively managed bond fund focused on securitized debt, meaning pools of loans bundled into bonds, mainly mortgage-backed securities from agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It also holds some asset-backed and commercial mortgage bonds for extra income.
DEEF: Stocks of companies in developed countries outside the US, chosen using five factors: quality, value, momentum, low volatility and small size. It is spread very thinly, with the biggest holdings each under 1% of the fund, and leans toward industrials and financials.
DEEP: Holds small and micro-cap US stocks that an index flags as cheap compared with their business value, a style called deep value. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward consumer and industrial companies.
DEFR: An actively managed fund that uses options, total return swaps and Treasury bills to deliver a tax-efficient stream of returns tied to large US stocks, mostly technology. The Treasury bills are collateral for those contracts, so it is not a typical bond fund.
DEHP: Large emerging market companies that Dimensional's rules rate as highly profitable. It leans heavily toward technology at about 47%, and SK Hynix, Taiwan Semiconductor, Tencent and Samsung are together about 28% of the fund.
DEM: Large emerging market companies that pay high dividends, weighted by how much cash they pay out rather than by size. Holdings are spread over Taiwan, China, Brazil, South Africa and others, and tilt toward chipmakers and big banks like MediaTek and China Construction Bank.
DEMZ: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen with a focus on firms that support Democratic Party causes and policies. It leans toward technology at close to half the fund, with chip names such as Lam Research, KLA and AMD among the top holdings.
DEPW: Invests in companies tied to Google DeepMind's AI ecosystem, such as chip makers, suppliers and Alphabet itself. It is concentrated, with Alphabet at about 19% of the fund and technology and utilities making up much of the rest.
DES: Small US companies that pay dividends, with the index weighting each by how much it pays out. Holdings are tiny slices of about 1% each, spread over financials, consumer companies, industrials and energy, so it has little single-stock risk.
DESK: A fund of US office and commercial real estate companies, which own and rent out office buildings and similar properties. It is concentrated: Vornado, Cousins Properties and BXP are each about 10%, and every holding is in real estate.
