DEUS: A fund tracking an index of US stocks from the Russell 1000, weighted toward companies that score well on factors like value, quality, momentum and low volatility. It holds a broad mix of mid-sized and large companies, with no stock above about 1%, so it is widely diversified.
DEW: A global fund of large companies that pay high dividends, picked from the WisdomTree Global High Dividend index. It leans toward financials, energy, health care and real estate, with ExxonMobil, Johnson & Johnson and Chevron among the larger holdings.
DEXC: Stocks from emerging markets other than China, picked and weighted by Dimensional's research-driven, rules-based approach. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13%, and with SK Hynix and Samsung, the chip and electronics giants, it makes up about 27% of the fund.
DFAC: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes, run by Dimensional, which tilts toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms than a plain market index would. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are still about 15% of it.
DFAE: A broad mix of emerging market stocks (such as Taiwan, China, India and Korea), chosen by Dimensional using its own size and value rules rather than a single index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13% of it, and technology is around 40%.
DFAI: Thousands of stocks from developed countries outside the US, of all sizes, with extra weight on smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than a plain market index would hold. It is spread very thin: the biggest holding, ASML, is only about 1.6% of the fund, and financials lead.
DFAL: Large US companies chosen by Dimensional using a broad rules-based approach that covers most of the large-company market, with a slight tilt toward cheaper and more profitable stocks. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 20% of it, similar to a regular large-company index fund.
DFAR: US real estate companies, mostly REITs that own property such as apartments, warehouses, data centers and shopping centers, weighted by size. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are about 20% of it, and REITs usually pay out a lot of income.
DFAS: Small US companies of all styles, bought in proportion to their market value using Dimensional's rules. It holds well over a thousand stocks, so no single holding is more than about 0.3% of the fund.
DFAT: A broad group of US small and mid-sized companies that look cheap compared with their size and are also more profitable, picked by Dimensional's rules rather than an index. It is spread across hundreds of stocks, with financials the largest sector at about 29%.
DFAU: A broad mix of US stocks of all sizes, tilted by Dimensional toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable companies than the overall market. The biggest names are still NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, which together are about 18% of it.
DFAW: A fund of funds that owns other Dimensional stock funds to cover the whole world, with roughly half in US stocks and the rest split between developed markets abroad and emerging markets. It holds thousands of companies through those funds, tilted toward smaller and cheaper stocks.
DFAX: Stocks of companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US, run by Dimensional with a tilt toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable firms. It is very spread out, and Taiwan Semiconductor, the largest holding, is only about 3% across its two listings.
DFCA: Investment-grade California municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, whose interest is exempt from federal and California income tax. Holdings include the State of California, Bay Area Rapid Transit and Los Angeles schools, each a small slice around 1%.
DFCF: A broad US investment grade bond fund from Dimensional, mixing government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that mostly mature within about 20 years. It is actively managed rather than tracking a standard index, and several of its largest positions are mortgage bonds.
DFE: Small European companies that pay dividends, picked and weighted by dividend payments from a WisdomTree index. It holds many small stocks, none above about 2%, and leans toward industrial companies, with European banks and consumer firms also in the mix.
DFEB: Uses exchange-traded options on the S&P 500 to deliver a set outcome over a one-year period starting in February. A deep buffer is meant to absorb a large slice of any market losses, but in return gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
DFEM: A broad mix of emerging market stocks (such as Taiwan, China, India and Korea), chosen by Dimensional using its own size and value rules rather than a single index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 10% of it, and technology is around 40%.
DFEV: Emerging market stocks that the managers see as cheap relative to their size or fundamentals, known as value stocks, across companies of all sizes. It can include frontier markets, and SK Hynix, Chinese banks and Reliance Industries are among its larger holdings.
DFGP: Government and company bonds from the US and abroad, mostly investment grade, including US mortgage bonds and Japanese government bonds. Dimensional runs it with a rules-based but flexible approach, and it aims to hedge foreign currency back to US dollars.
DFGR: Real estate companies from around the world, including emerging markets, weighted by company size. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix, which own health care properties, warehouses and data centers, are about 20% of the fund.
DFGV: US government and agency bonds that mature in about five to fifteen years, chosen by Dimensional's rules for low risk. It sticks to high quality government debt, so it is a middle-length bond fund with little credit risk and no stock exposure.
DFGX: An actively managed fund of high-quality bonds from outside the US, maturing within twenty years, and currency swings hedged back to US dollars. Japanese government bonds make up most of the top holdings, and it holds many issuers across several countries.
DFIC: A broad mix of stocks from developed countries outside the US, covering companies of all sizes and leaning toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones. Thousands of holdings keep it spread out: the top few, such as ASML and Shell, are only about 1% each.
DFII: Gets exposure to bitcoin through derivatives rather than holding the coin directly, and also aims to pay out income. Because it relies on options style contracts, its results can differ a lot from simply owning bitcoin, and it is non-diversified.
DFIP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), government bonds whose value rises with inflation, focused on maturities of about five to twenty years. It is held almost entirely in a handful of Treasury issues, so it is a simple, very high-credit-quality holding.
DFIS: Thousands of small companies in developed countries outside the US, bought in roughly market-size proportions, with a lean toward cheaper and more profitable ones. It is extremely spread out, with every holding under 1%, and industrials, materials and consumer firms are the largest groups.
DFIV: Large companies from developed countries outside the US that look cheap relative to their book value, picked by Dimensional's rules-based approach. It also tries to limit taxable gains by timing its trades, and Shell, TotalEnergies and Santander are among its larger holdings.
DFJ: Small Japanese companies, weighted by a WisdomTree index that focuses on dividend payers. It is very spread out, with the top holdings each under 1%, and it leans toward industrials, financials and consumer companies.
DFLV: Large US companies that Dimensional considers cheap relative to their size, with extra weight on the cheapest and most profitable. JPMorgan, Amazon and Exxon Mobil are among the biggest holdings, and it leans toward financials, health care, energy and industrials.
DFMC: A broad basket of very small US companies (micro caps), bought in proportion to their size by Dimensional Fund Advisors. It holds a great many tiny stocks, none above about 0.5%, so no single company moves it much.
DFNL: An actively managed fund of roughly 15 to 35 financial companies, such as banks, insurers and card lenders, picked by Davis Advisors. It is concentrated, with Capital One alone about 10% and the top eight holdings roughly half of the fund.
DFNM: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term municipal bonds, loans to US states and cities, whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It holds a very wide range of issuers, none above about 1%, and keeps its sensitivity to interest rates close to a standard muni index.
DFSB: A broad mix of investment-grade bonds from governments and companies around the world, including mortgage-backed bonds, that screens out issuers with weaker sustainability records. Foreign currency risk is hedged back to the US dollar, and no holding is more than about 2%.
DFSD: A mix of investment-grade bonds, mostly government and corporate, that mature within about five years, chosen by Dimensional's managers. Because the bonds are short term, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than a regular bond fund, and the holdings are very spread out.
DFSE: A broad fund of emerging market stocks (companies in developing countries like Taiwan, Korea and China) of all sizes, tilted toward smaller and cheaper companies, with some companies screened out on sustainability grounds. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 8% of it, and technology is roughly 40%.
DFSI: A broad, spread-out mix of companies of all sizes in developed markets outside the US, tilted toward cheaper, more profitable firms and ones with better sustainability scores. No holding is above about 2.5%, with ASML the largest.
DFSU: A broad fund of US companies of all sizes that leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones than the overall market, while adjusting holdings for sustainability factors. NVIDIA and Apple are about 13% of it, and technology is about a third of the fund.
DFSV: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their book value, picked by Dimensional's rules-based but actively run approach. It holds hundreds of stocks, with no single one above about 1%, and leans toward financials, industrials and energy.
DFTT: Tracks an index that holds 30 of the 100 largest US stocks, picked by recent price momentum, and can shift toward safer assets when markets look risky. It is concentrated, with the top holdings each about 4% to 5% and technology over half.
DFUS: The whole US stock market, buying companies of all sizes in proportion to their market value. It works like a broad index fund, so it is top-heavy toward big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of the fund.
DFUV: US companies of all sizes that Dimensional considers value stocks, meaning priced low relative to measures like their book value. It holds a wide range, led by JPMorgan, Amazon, Exxon and Johnson & Johnson, each between roughly 3% and 5%.
DFVE: The largest US companies from the Fortune 500 list, held in roughly equal amounts rather than weighted by size. Because every company gets a similar slice, the biggest firms count for far less than in a usual index fund, and no single holding is much above half a percent.
DFVX: Holds large US companies, tilted by Dimensional's research toward cheaper, more profitable stocks rather than just the biggest ones. It is actively managed with rules rather than an index, and Microsoft and Amazon are each about 5% to 6% of it.
DGAP: Uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in April: a buffer against part of the losses, plus a fixed digital return if the market is up. Gains are limited, and the terms only apply if held for the full period.
DGCB: A global bond fund focused on investment-grade corporate bonds (from mostly solid companies) maturing within twenty years, with currency risk hedged back to the US dollar. It is actively run with a rules-based approach and widely spread, with no holding above about 1%.
DGIN: Indian companies that help power the country's digital economy, such as telecom, online services, payments and fintech, tracked through a benchmark index. It holds a small number of stocks, with Reliance, Bharti Airtel and Eternal each making up around 7% to 8%.
DGJA: A fund of options on an S&P 500 fund that cushions a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each January. It also pays a fixed extra return if the market is up, but gains beyond that are not captured.
DGJL: A fund of options on an S&P 500 fund that cushions a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each July. It also pays a fixed extra return if the market is up, but gains beyond that are not captured.
DGLO: A US stock fund built around companies expected to gain from supply chains moving closer to home, tracking an index from RBA. It is mostly industrial companies such as railroads and defense, plus energy and materials, with no holding above about 3%.
DGOC: A fund of options on an S&P 500 fund that cushions a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each October. It also pays a fixed extra return if the market is up, but gains beyond that are not captured.
DGRE: Emerging market companies that pay dividends and show growth traits, picked by WisdomTree's index. It is heavy in technology, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung together are about 25% of the fund.
DGRO: US companies with a record of growing their dividends that are expected to keep paying them, following a Morningstar index. Holdings are weighted by dividends paid, so it is spread out: the top names, such as Microsoft and JPMorgan, are each about 3%.
DGRS: Smaller US companies that pay dividends and show strong profitability and earnings growth, chosen and weighted by a WisdomTree index. No single holding is above about 3%, and financials, industrials and consumer companies make up most of it.
DGRW: US companies that pay dividends and have strong profitability and growing earnings, weighted by the dividends they pay rather than by size. It still leans on big tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple together are about 17% of the fund.
DGS: Small companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Africa, Brazil and India, picked and weighted by a WisdomTree index of small-cap stocks. It is very spread out, with the largest holding around 3% of the fund, and leans toward technology, financials and industrials.
DGT: 150 large companies from around the world, selected as leaders in their industries under the Global Dow index and weighted roughly equally. This keeps it less top-heavy than most global funds, with no holding above about 3%, and it is spread across technology, financials and industrials.
DHDG: A defined outcome fund that uses exchange-traded FLEX options on the S&P 500 and resets every quarter, aiming to absorb losses between about 2.5% and 15%. Gains are limited, and nearly all the fund is in those options.
DHLX: An actively managed fund holding only a small group of large US companies that the managers believe are undervalued. It is concentrated: Microsoft, ConocoPhillips, Berkshire Hathaway and Amazon each make up around 6% to 8% of it.
DHS: The higher-dividend payers among US companies, picked and weighted by dividends paid in a WisdomTree index. It is built for income, so it leans toward financials, health care, consumer staples and energy, and AbbVie, Merck and Altria are each around 4% of the fund.
DHSB: An actively managed fund that holds mostly a broad US stock ETF, about 98%, and adds a hedging approach meant to soften some losses. The protection comes from other positions in S&P 500 funds, so it behaves differently from a plain index fund.
DIA: The 30 big US companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, weighted by share price rather than company size. That odd weighting means the higher-priced stocks count more: Goldman Sachs, Caterpillar and Microsoft are about 26% of the fund.
DIAL: A broad mix of US bonds, including mortgage-backed securities, Treasuries and corporate debt, aiming to track a diversified bond index. Mortgage-backed bonds are loans pooled together, and the fund is actively spread across many issuers rather than relying on any one.
DICE: Holds companies that profit from trading and betting on markets, such as online brokers, exchanges and crypto platforms. IG Group, Coinbase, Intercontinental Exchange, Interactive Brokers and Robinhood each make up about 5%, and financials are most of it.
DIEM: Emerging market stocks that pay dividends, picked from a Morningstar index and tilted toward higher-yielding companies. It is top-heavy in chips: Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics are about 30% of the fund.
DIHP: Large companies outside the US that Dimensional rates as highly profitable, bought in a size-aware way. Roche, ASML and Nestle are the biggest names, and holdings are spread over industrials, technology, health care and financials.
DIM: Mid sized dividend paying companies from developed markets outside the US, picked and weighted by dividends in a WisdomTree index. It holds many stocks, each about 1%, with financials and industrials the largest groups.
DINE: An actively managed income fund mixing dividend stocks, bonds and options strategies, with the manager aiming to keep taxes on the payouts low. It holds mostly bonds and cash-like investments today, rather than being a pure stock or pure bond fund.
DINT: An actively managed, fairly concentrated fund of companies outside the US, picked by the Davis team's long-term approach. The top four holdings, JBS, Full Truck Alliance, Sea and Trip.com, are each about 6% of the fund, with a lot in Asian and emerging market firms.
DIPR: An actively managed fund holding companies involved in space and satellite communications, including rockets, satellites and defense contractors. SpaceX is about 13% of the fund, and Rocket Lab and Lockheed Martin follow, so a few names carry a lot of weight.
DIPS: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income while moving opposite to NVIDIA's share price, using options rather than owning the stock. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and its gains from falling NVIDIA shares are partly capped.
DISK: An actively managed fund of memory and data storage chip companies from around the world. It is very concentrated: SanDisk, Kioxia and SK hynix together are about 50% of the fund, so it rides on one corner of the tech industry.
DISV: Small, cheaper-looking companies in developed countries outside the US, picked by Dimensional using value measures such as low prices relative to book value. It holds thousands of names, with no holding above about 1%, spread across industrials, materials, financials and consumer firms.
DIV: An equal-weighted group of 50 US stocks with some of the highest dividend yields, including real estate trusts and pipeline partnerships. It focuses on income rather than growth, leans toward energy, real estate and utilities, and no single holding is more than about 3%.
DIVB: US companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks, tracking the Morningstar US Dividend and Buyback Index. It is spread out, with ADP and Accenture the biggest at about 5% each, and many tech and finance names.
DIVD: A global fund holding dividend-paying large companies, with at least 30% of its assets outside the US. It is spread fairly evenly, with no holding above about 3%, and leans toward health care, financials and consumer staples.
DIVE: An actively managed fund holding roughly 25 to 35 US dividend-paying companies picked for dividends and solid finances. It is concentrated, with Philip Morris the largest at about 9%, and spreads across health care, consumer staples, technology and financials.
DIVG: US companies from the S&P 500 that have raised their dividends and pay relatively high yields, picked and weighted by an S&P index. It leans toward financials, technology, utilities and consumer staples, with no holding above about 3.5%.
DIVH: An actively managed fund of US dividend-paying stocks, chosen with income in mind. It is broadly spread, with the largest holdings such as Broadcom, Chevron and AbbVie each around 4%, across technology, financials, energy and consumer staples.
DIVI: Stocks of large companies in developed markets outside North America, tilted toward those paying higher dividends, using an index based on a Morningstar benchmark. It is spread across many countries and names, with ASML the biggest at about 3% and financials the largest sector.
DIVL: US companies with market caps over $1 billion that have paid dividends and look able to raise them. It leans toward energy, financials and health care, and Johnson & Johnson, Exxon and Texas Instruments are about 14% of the fund.
DIVN: An actively managed fund of dividend paying US large companies that also uses options to add income. Its holdings are fairly spread out, with Qualcomm the largest at about 6%, and it leans toward staples, energy and health care.
DIVO: A fund of dividend-paying US companies picked by a manager, which also sells covered call options on some of them to bring in extra income. The options give up some of the gains in strong markets; Caterpillar, Apple and Microsoft are each about 5 to 7% of it.
DIVP: Dividend-paying US stocks, chosen on value, with covered call options sold on part of them to bring in extra income. Selling those calls can limit gains in strong markets, and the top holdings are spread across many sectors at about 4% or less.
DIVS: An actively managed global fund of companies that pay dividends and that the managers think can keep raising them. It is led by Cisco, Texas Instruments, Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom at about 4% each.
DIVY: Holds about 30 US dividend-paying companies picked by an active manager, spread across financials, health care, energy and more. It leans toward mid-sized, steady companies like Cisco, Omnicom and UPS, aiming for income rather than fast growth.
DIVZ: An actively managed fund holding just 25 to 35 US stocks that pay dividends, expect to grow them, and look reasonably priced. It is concentrated and spread across health care, energy, technology and utilities, with UnitedHealth, Philip Morris and MPLX each around 6%.
DJAN: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each January. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
DJD: Dividend-paying companies from the Dow Jones Industrial Average, weighted by how much yield they pay instead of by size. It holds about 30 US blue chips, and the top picks UnitedHealth, Chevron, Cisco and Merck are about a quarter of the fund.
DJIA: Holds the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average and sells one-month call options on them to earn extra income, which is paid out regularly. The options cap how much it gains in strong markets, and Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar alone are about 21%.
DJUL: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each July. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
DJUN: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each June. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
DLAG: A defined-outcome fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for gains whether the index rises or falls, up to a cap, over a set period starting in August. It buffers a set amount of losses, and the stated outcome only applies if held for the full period.
DLCU: The 500 large US companies of the S&P 500, held in about the same proportions as the index, managed by Dimensional. It is top-heavy with tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of the fund.
DLFE: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to give a limited share of gains whether the market rises or falls slightly, while cushioning part of larger losses, over a one-year period starting in February. It holds options, not stocks, so timing of purchase matters.
DLMY: A fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to let investors gain when the market rises or falls modestly, over a set one-year period starting in May. It does not hold stocks directly, and its outcome only applies if you hold for the full period.
DLN: About 300 of the largest US dividend-paying companies, with each one weighted by the total dividends it pays rather than by its size. That tilts it toward steady payers like banks, health care and consumer staples, and it is far less top-heavy than most large-company funds.
DLNV: Uses FLEX options, customizable exchange traded options, on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to seek a set amount of protection from losses over a set period that starts each November. Protection and gains only apply when held for the full period, and results are limited either way.
DLS: Small companies from developed markets outside the US, chosen from a WisdomTree index with a value focus. It is spread across hundreds of tiny positions, none above about 1%, with a lean toward industrials, financials and consumer companies.
DMAR: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each March. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
DMAX: A fund that holds the S&P 500 through an iShares ETF plus options, to buffer a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each December. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
DMAY: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion losses between 5% and 20% over a one-year period that starts each May. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if you hold for the full period.
DMBS: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans whose payments pass through to investors. Much of it is government-backed agency mortgages, and the managers pick the mix themselves.
DMX: An actively managed bond fund from DoubleLine that spreads across several bond types, including mortgage-backed securities, corporate loans and other debt. It is aimed at steady income, and the portfolio is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%.
DMXF: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US and Canada, such as Europe and Japan, screened for environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. ASML is the biggest holding at about 6%, and the rest is spread widely.
DMXU: Large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US and Canada, such as Europe, Japan and Australia, tracking a Bloomberg index. It is spread widely: the largest holding, chip equipment maker ASML, is only about 5% of it, and financials are the biggest sector.
DNL: Quality, faster-growing companies from developed and emerging markets outside the US, selected by a WisdomTree index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 11% and ASML about 8%, so a few big names have a large influence.
DNOV: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb a deeper chunk of early losses over a one-year period starting in November. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
DOCK: An actively managed fund of companies that move goods around, such as railroads, trucking, shipping and port operators. Union Pacific is the biggest holding at roughly 9%, and nearly everything in the fund is an industrial company.
DOCT: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb a deeper chunk of early losses over a one-year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
DOGG: A strategy built on the Dow Jones 10 highest yielding Dow stocks (the Dogs of the Dow), combined with options that aim to pay extra income on top. The options limit upside gains, and it holds just a concentrated set of about ten large companies.
DOJE: A fund giving exposure to Dogecoin, the meme-inspired cryptocurrency, held partly directly and partly through other crypto products. About 59% is Dogecoin itself, so it moves with the price of one crypto asset and pays no regular income.
DOL: Large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted by dividends paid instead of by size, following a WisdomTree index. It leans toward established dividend payers, and Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are the biggest names at about 5% and 3.5%.
DON: US mid-sized companies that pay dividends, with each stock weighted by the dividends it pays rather than by its size. It is spread thin, with the largest holding only about 1% of the fund.
DPRE: An actively managed fund of real estate companies, mostly REITs (companies that own and rent out property), with a focus on income. It holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and Welltower is the largest at about 9% of the fund.
DQJN: A defined outcome fund holding options on the Nasdaq-100 over a one-year period starting each June. It aims to give some gains when the market rises and shield part of the losses when it falls, within limits, so it works best held for the full period.
DQSE: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to offer a set amount of protection from losses and a set amount of gains over a one-year period starting in September. Its gains are capped, and it pays off whether the index rises or falls, within limits.
DRAI: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs covering stocks, bonds and more, based on the manager's view of risk and reward. Despite a conservative label, it holds several leveraged ETFs that multiply daily moves, alongside bond funds.
DRAM: Companies that make memory chips and related storage products, such as Samsung, SK hynix and Seagate, sometimes held through swaps (contracts that mimic owning the stock). It is a narrow theme fund, with Samsung and SK hynix making up roughly a third of it.
DRAY: Aims to pay high income based on DraftKings stock, using options rather than owning the shares. The options bring in payouts but cap how much it can gain when the stock rises, while it can still fall if the stock drops, and its Treasury bills are mostly collateral.
DRES: An actively managed fund of US companies the manager thinks will gain as supply chains move back home and away from globalization. It is mostly industrials and materials, with Union Pacific, WillScot, Carlisle and Martin Marietta each about 4% to 5%.
DRGN: Chinese companies listed in the US or Hong Kong, or reachable through the Stock Connect trading link, that earn meaningful revenue from generative AI. It leans hard on chip and computing hardware makers like Hygon, Montage and Cambricon, with technology about three quarters of the fund.
DRIV: Companies involved in electric and self-driving vehicles, including carmakers, chip makers and battery material suppliers, tracking a Solactive index. It is spread across technology, auto and materials firms, and Intel is the largest at about 5%.
DRKY: An actively managed fund that holds stocks chosen by the BITA VistaShares DRUKMacro Select Index and also uses options to generate income. It is very concentrated: Natera alone is about 27% of the fund, and health care and technology make up most of the rest.
DRLL: US energy companies, mainly oil and gas producers and refiners, following the Bloomberg U.S. Energy Select Index. It is very top-heavy: ExxonMobil and Chevron are each over 20%, so these two make up about 44% of the fund.
DRMP: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies tied to computer memory and storage, the chips and hardware that hold data. It is non-diversified, so it bets on a narrow group of companies, and its listed holdings are mostly cash-like backing.
DRMY: A fund of memory-chip and data-storage companies, such as SK Hynix, Samsung, Western Digital and Seagate, that also uses options to generate income. It is concentrated in one corner of tech, and the options can limit gains.
DRNZ: Companies that make drones and the technology that supports them, tracking an index of global drone and unmanned aircraft businesses. It is concentrated, with AeroVironment and Ondas each around 13% and the top three about 37%, and it includes many small companies.
DRSK: An actively managed fund that puts most of its money in a basket of bond funds with set end dates, and uses a small options position on stocks for extra return or protection. It is mainly a bond fund with a stock-market twist.
DRUP: About 100 large US-listed companies picked by Nasdaq for strong disruptive potential, mostly in technology, health care and communication. Microsoft is around 10% of the fund, and Meta and Alphabet are each about 7%, so the top names carry real weight.
DRVR: S&P 500 companies chosen for their dividends and the ability to keep paying them, following an Amplify index. Holdings are fairly even, with Accenture the largest at about 6%, and mixed across financials, consumer and technology.
DSCO: An actively managed fund of securitized credit, which means bonds backed by pools of loans such as mortgages, car loans and credit cards. It is spread across many such bonds, with a small slice in cash-like funds, and pays income from the underlying loans.
DSEP: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb a deeper chunk of early losses over a one-year period starting in September. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
DSI: About 400 large US companies chosen for strong environmental, social and governance records, tracking the MSCI KLD 400 Social Index. It is tech-heavy and top-heavy: NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 23% of it, and technology is around 45% of the fund.
DSMC: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, favoring those that generate lots of cash relative to their price. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 1%, and it is spread across consumer, tech, industrial and energy businesses.
DSPY: An actively managed fund of S&P 500 stocks, weighted using the index's older, more even weights rather than today's top-heavy ones. That means the biggest companies, like NVIDIA at about 4% and Apple at about 3.5%, count less than in the regular index.
DSTL: An actively managed fund of US stocks, chosen for steady cash flow and a solid balance sheet at a fair price, rather than by size. Holdings are spread out: AbbVie, Merck and Qualcomm are the biggest at only about 3% each.
DSTX: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized companies outside the US, chosen for steady finances and reasonable prices. It is spread across many countries and industries, with no single holding above about 3% of the fund.
DTAN: Stocks of large non-US companies that its manager thinks are cheap once you count intangible assets like brands and research, which regular accounting often misses. Holdings are well spread, with Roche, Novartis and L'Oreal each only around 3% of the fund.
DTCR: Companies that own the buildings and networks behind the internet: data centers, cell towers and fiber, tracking the Solactive Data Center REITs & Digital Infrastructure Index. Equinix, Digital Realty and American Tower are about a third of it, and about 40% is classed as technology.
DTD: Dividend-paying US companies of all sizes, with each stock weighted by the total dollars of dividends it pays rather than by its size. It is broad, with the biggest holdings, NVIDIA, Microsoft and JPMorgan, each around 3%, and spreads across technology, financials and health care.
DTEC: Companies using disruptive technologies across ten areas such as healthcare, robotics, cybersecurity and clean energy, following an ALPS index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 2%, and technology is over half.
DTH: Dividend-paying companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen and weighted by the dividends they pay under a WisdomTree index. It leans toward banks, industrials and utilities, with HSBC, Nestle and Intesa Sanpaolo among the largest holdings, each at roughly 2 to 3%.
DTRE: Real estate companies that own the physical backbone of technology, such as data centers, cell towers and warehouses, tracked using an Alerian index. The top five, including Equinix, Prologis, Digital Realty and American Tower, are about 30% of the fund.
DUBS: An actively managed fund that holds mostly low-cost US large-company stock ETFs and adds total return swaps, contracts that pay the stock returns, to try to boost its total return. Over 70% of it sits in one S&P 500 fund, so it looks a lot like the index.
DUHP: Large US companies chosen by Dimensional because they are unusually profitable compared with their peers. NVIDIA, Apple, Eli Lilly and Microsoft are about 24% of it, so it still leans toward big names.
DUKH: An actively managed fund that moves between other ETFs, mainly high-yield bond and senior loan funds, long-term Treasury funds and cash. It is concentrated, with a single senior loan ETF making up about 70% of it.
DUKQ: An actively managed fund of funds that shifts money among other US stock ETFs and cash-like holdings as the manager sees fit. Large positions in Vanguard S&P 500 and Schwab large-cap growth funds make up almost half of it.
DUKX: An actively managed fund of funds that shifts money between international stock ETFs and cash depending on market conditions. Nearly 45% sits in Vanguard's Total International Stock ETF, and about 25% in an emerging markets ETF.
DUKZ: An actively managed income fund that shifts its money between other bond ETFs and cash depending on market conditions. Because it holds other funds rather than individual bonds, it is a mix of whatever bond funds the manager favors at the time, including senior loans.
DUNK: An actively managed, concentrated fund of US-listed companies that the managers think benefit from disruptive technology. Software and AI names dominate: Datadog, Snowflake and ServiceNow are about 31% of it.
DURA: Large US companies with high dividend yields and strong finances, picked by a VanEck index that also screens on valuation. It leans toward health care, energy and consumer staples, with Merck, Philip Morris, Bank of America and Coca-Cola about 5% each.
DUSA: An actively managed fund holding only about 15 to 35 US companies chosen by the Davis team for long-term value. Because it is so concentrated, single names matter: Capital One, US Bancorp, Amazon and Devon Energy are each roughly 6% of it.
DUSG: A broad basket of US small companies with growth characteristics, picked by Dimensional using company size, profitability and price measures. It holds a huge number of stocks, with no holding above about 1%, so it is very spread out across industries.
DUTY: US defense companies that earn at least half of their revenue from areas such as weapons systems, defense technology and cybersecurity, tracked by an index. The biggest holdings are General Dynamics and Lockheed Martin at about 7% each, with tech names like Palantir also in the mix.
DVAL: An actively managed fund of large, lower priced US companies, chosen by Brandywine as being good value. Financials make up about 30% of it, with companies like General Electric, Cisco, JPMorgan and Bank of America each around 4% to 5%.
DVDN: An actively managed fund that buys dividend-paying companies, with a heavy focus on mortgage real estate investment trusts. Annaly, AGNC, Dynex and Invesco Mortgage Capital are each about 7%, so it is concentrated in companies that earn money from mortgage lending and pay it out.
DVGR: An actively managed fund of US-listed dividend-paying companies, picked for dividends that look likely to keep growing. Large names like Microsoft, Broadcom, Oracle and JPMorgan are among its biggest holdings, each around 4% to 6%.
DVLU: Holds 50 US mid-sized and large companies picked by NASDAQ for being cheap compared to their size while also showing strong recent price strength. It is spread thinly, with Dell the largest at about 6%, and leans toward financials and industrials.
DVND: An actively managed fund holding large US companies that have a history of paying dividends. It tilts toward technology, financials and health care, with Microsoft, Broadcom and KLA each around 3% to 4% of the fund.
DVOL: About 50 US stocks picked for strong recent price momentum and low volatility, following a Dorsey Wright index. It leans toward financials, industrials and real estate, with no single holding above about 3%.
DVQQ: A fund that follows the Invesco QQQ Trust (the Nasdaq 100) but adjusts its exposure using options and cash to aim for a smoother ride. About half is held in QQQ itself, so it tracks the Nasdaq 100 only partly.
DVSP: A fund that follows the SPDR S&P 500 ETF but adjusts its exposure using options and cash to aim for a smoother ride. About 43% is held in the S&P 500 fund itself, so it tracks the market only partly.
DVVY: Holds large US companies that pay dividends, picked by the manager to be diversified across industries rather than concentrated in a few. It aims for income from those dividends along with some growth in the stocks' prices.
DVY: About 100 US stocks with some of the highest dividend yields (annual dividend relative to share price), subject to rules on dividend history and payout. It leans toward financials, utilities and consumer companies, and holds more mid-sized firms than the big tech names.
DVYA: Around 30 high dividend-paying companies from Australia, Japan, Hong Kong, New Zealand and Singapore, picked by dividend yield. Financial companies make up about a third of it, and miners like BHP and Fortescue are among the larger holdings.
DVYE: One hundred emerging market companies that pay high dividends, picked and weighted by dividend yield. It spans many countries, with energy and financial firms like Petrobras, Vale and China Construction Bank among the larger holdings, each around 3%.
DWAS: About 200 US small companies chosen by Dorsey Wright for strong price momentum, meaning stocks that have been rising relative to others. The list changes often and leans toward health care, technology and industrials, with no single holding above about 3%.
DWAW: An actively managed fund of other ETFs that shifts between global stocks and safer holdings based on trend signals. Right now it holds mostly iShares stock funds covering US value and quality, so it may sit in cash or bonds at times.
DWLD: An actively managed, concentrated fund of stocks from the US and abroad, including emerging markets, picked with the Davis Investment Discipline. Full Truck Alliance, Trip.com and JBS lead at about 4% to 6% each, with a sizable share in Asian companies.
DWM: Dividend-paying companies in developed countries outside the US, with holdings weighted by their earnings through a WisdomTree index. It owns many hundreds of stocks, with financials and industrials the largest sectors, and top holdings such as HSBC, Novartis and Nestle are about 1 to 2% each.
DWMF: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US and Canada, picked by a model that scores companies on several traits such as value, quality and momentum. It is spread across many holdings, led by financials, industrials and technology.
DWSH: An actively managed fund that bets against US stocks by short selling, borrowing shares and selling them so it gains when they fall. It holds many small short positions picked by a trend-following model, and it tends to lose when the stock market rises.
DWUS: An actively managed fund of funds that mostly holds other ETFs full of large US companies, and can shift into short-term bonds and cash for defense. Two ETFs, one broad US stock fund and one Nasdaq 100 fund, are each about half of it.
DWWN: An actively managed fund of long-term US government bonds, mostly Treasuries. Because the bonds mature far in the future, its price tends to swing more when interest rates move than a short-term bond fund's does.
DWX: Tracks an index of 100 high-yielding stocks from outside the US, chosen for dividends. The mix includes TotalEnergies, Evonik, DCC, Pembina and Orange, each only about 2%, so no single company dominates.
DXIV: Thousands of international stocks across developed markets outside the US, with extra weight on smaller and lower-priced (value) companies, chosen by Dimensional's research-driven approach. It is very spread out, with the biggest holding, ASML, only about 1% of the fund.
DXJ: Large Japanese companies, mainly exporters, with a currency hedge added that protects against a falling yen versus the US dollar. Banks like Mitsubishi UFJ and Sumitomo Mitsui, plus Toyota, are among its biggest holdings, and it leans toward industrials and financials.
DXUV: A broad mix of US companies of all sizes that leans toward smaller, cheaper and more profitable ones than the overall market, following Dimensional's research-based rules. Despite that tilt, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Apple are still around 14% of it.
DYFI: An actively managed fund of bond ETFs, spreading money across multisector bonds, fallen angel high yield, mortgage bonds, CLOs and inflation-protected Treasuries. It is a fund of funds, so it holds other ETFs instead of individual bonds, and the mix is adjusted by the manager.
DYLD: An actively managed bond fund that mixes corporate bonds, government and agency securities, private debt and foreign debt, aiming for steady income. A large share is currently held in cash, so it is more of a flexible income strategy than a plain bond index.
DYLG: The 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average with one-month covered calls sold on them, an options strategy that earns income but caps some of the gains. Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar are the biggest holdings at about 10% each.
DYNB: An actively managed bond fund that mixes investment grade and lower rated bonds, including US Treasuries, across the bond market. The manager changes the mix as conditions shift, so it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
DYNF: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US stocks that shifts its mix of investing styles, such as value, quality or momentum, based on a model's view of the market. It currently looks like the big tech heavy market, with NVIDIA and Apple about 15%.
DYTA: An actively managed fund that moves between other ETFs and mutual funds covering US, foreign and emerging markets stocks, depending on how the managers see the market. It can hold a lot of cash, about a third here, so it may act more cautiously than a stock index fund.
EAFG: Holds growing companies from developed markets outside the US, picked for strong free cash flow, which is cash left after running the business. It has a tilt toward chip equipment makers like Advantest, Tokyo Electron and ASML.
EAFH: Stocks of large and mid-size companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, tracking the MSCI EAFE index, with about half the foreign currency exposure hedged. Hedging reduces the effect of dollar swings on returns.
EAGG: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage bonds, like a standard aggregate bond index but screened for environmental, social and governance factors. It is spread across thousands of bonds, none above about 0.5%.
EAGL: An actively managed fund where Eagle Capital picks a small group of companies, US and foreign, that it thinks are good businesses at fair prices. It is concentrated: Amazon, MercadoLibre, UnitedHealth and Taiwan Semiconductor are each about 7%.
EALT: Uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses on large US stocks, with the protection range named in the fund's 5 to 15 buffer label. In exchange, gains are capped, and it resets every quarter.
EAPR: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF to cushion part of the losses over about a year starting each April. In return, gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
EART: Miners and producers of rare earths and other critical materials, such as copper and lithium, tracked by an index. About 90% of it is in materials companies, and Anglo American, Grupo Mexico, Freeport-McMoRan and Southern Copper are each about 5%.
EASY: An actively managed fund of US companies with a record of raising their dividends, chosen for steadier, more defensive businesses. It leans toward health care, consumer staples, industrials and utilities, with Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and Cardinal Health each around 6% of it.
EBI: An actively managed fund that buys US stocks of many sizes and industries, with the managers picking the holdings. Apple and NVIDIA are each around 5 to 6% of it, and technology and financials make up almost half of the fund.
EBIT: Small US companies that are profitable, picked by an index that screens for earnings. Holdings are spread thin, with no stock above roughly 1%, and it tilts toward financial companies, consumer businesses, industrials and energy.
EBIZ: Tracks an index of companies that benefit from online shopping and e-commerce, including online retailers, travel booking sites and food delivery. It holds companies from around the world in roughly similar sized positions, with none above about 5%.
EBND: Government bonds issued by emerging market countries in their own currencies, such as Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, tracked by a Bloomberg index. Because the bonds are in local currencies, exchange rate swings against the US dollar matter as much as interest rates.
EBUF: A fund using options on an emerging markets stock ETF to cushion part of the losses over a set period. It resets every three months, and in exchange for that protection, its upside over each period is capped.
ECH: Large and mid-sized Chilean companies, weighted by size, giving a one country bet on Chile. It is concentrated in a few names: lithium maker SQM is about 16%, and Banco de Chile and Latam Airlines are about 11% each.
ECML: An actively managed fund of small US companies that the manager believes are undervalued, using a rules-based, data-driven approach. It is spread widely, with the largest holdings such as Mueller Industries, Matson and Owens Corning each only about 2% of it.
ECNS: Small Chinese companies, tracking the MSCI China Small Cap index, with shares listed in places like Hong Kong. It is widely spread across many tiny holdings, none more than about 4%, and health care and technology are among the biggest sectors.
ECON: Large and mid sized stocks from emerging markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and China, selected by an index that tilts toward stocks expected to do better. It is tech heavy, with SK Hynix, Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor about 20% of the fund.
ECOW: Holds 100 large and mid-sized emerging market companies that generate lots of free cash flow compared with their price, using a rules-based Pacer index. It spreads across many sectors, with communication, energy, consumer and materials companies leading, and no single stock above about 2%.
EDEN: Large and mid-sized Danish companies, tracking the MSCI Denmark Index. It is top-heavy in a few names: Novo Nordisk alone is about 21% of the fund, and health care and industrials make up roughly two thirds.
EDGE: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to get stock market exposure, rather than owning the stocks directly. Nearly all of it is one long-dated option position on the SPY fund, so its returns can behave differently from owning the index.
EDGF: An actively managed bond fund that shifts between types of fixed income, and currently holds mostly short-term Treasury bill ETFs and inflation-protected bonds. Its mix moves with the managers' view, so it can look more like cash than a typical intermediate bond fund.
EDGH: An actively managed mix of funds covering commodities, gold and inflation-protected Treasuries, aiming to hold up when prices rise. Roughly half sits in two broad commodity funds and about a fifth in physical gold.
EDGI: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs holding stocks outside the US, including developed markets and emerging markets. Japan makes up about 29% through two Japan ETFs, and the mix of regions is adjusted by the manager.
EDGQ: A fund that holds a Nasdaq-100 ETF and sells weekly call options on it to generate income. Selling those options limits gains when the Nasdaq-100 rises sharply, in exchange for regular payouts, and nearly all of the fund is the Nasdaq-100.
EDGU: An actively managed fund that invests in US stocks mainly by holding other ETFs, shifting between sectors and company sizes as the manager sees fit. About half of it sits in a technology sector fund and a Nasdaq-100 fund, so it leans heavily toward tech.
EDGX: An actively managed fund that holds large US stocks, mostly through other S&P 500 funds, and sells call options each week to generate income. Selling those options limits how much it gains in a strong rally, in exchange for regular payouts.
EDIV: One hundred high-dividend emerging market companies, picked and weighted by dividend yield from a State Street S&P index. It is spread across countries and sectors, with financials the biggest at about 30%, and the top holding is only about 3.5%.
EDOG: Holds the highest dividend paying stocks in a basket of large emerging market companies, a so-called dividend dogs approach that picks the top payers in each sector. It is spread across industrials, energy, health care and technology, with Indian and European-listed names among its largest holdings.
EDOW: The 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average, but each held in roughly equal amounts instead of weighted by share price. That means every company counts for about 3% to 4%, so the biggest names have less pull than in the regular Dow.
EDV: US Treasury STRIPS that mature in 20 to 30 years. These are zero-coupon bonds that pay nothing until the end, which makes their price swing a lot when interest rates change, much more than a normal Treasury fund.
EEE: About three quarters of this fund is in the S&P 500, the 500 largest US companies, and about a quarter is in Ethereum, a cryptocurrency. It mixes a broad stock index with a risky crypto bet.
EELV: Emerging market stocks that have historically bounced around less than the market, picked from the S&P Emerging Markets index by the S&P Low Volatility approach. It is spread over many countries and companies, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward financials.
EEM: Large and mid-sized stocks from emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India, South Korea and Brazil, following an MSCI index. It is concentrated in a few giants: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 22% of it.
EEMA: Large and mid-sized companies in emerging Asian countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India, following the MSCI Emerging Markets Asia Index. It is top-heavy, with Taiwan Semiconductor alone about 16%, and technology is nearly half of the fund.
EEMO: Tracks an S&P index of emerging market stocks that have recently been rising fastest, so the picks change as trends change. It is heavy in technology, and SK Hynix and Samsung together make up about a quarter of it.
EEMS: Small companies from emerging markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, tracking the MSCI Emerging Markets Small Cap Index. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward technology and industrial firms.
EEMV: Emerging market stocks chosen and weighted to swing less in price than the broader emerging market index, following an MSCI index. It is spread out, with the largest holding, SK Hynix, only about 3%.
EEMX: Emerging markets stocks, tracking an MSCI index that leaves out companies that own fossil fuel reserves. It is top-heavy in Asian chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 32% of the fund.
EES: Small US companies chosen and weighted by their earnings through a WisdomTree index, so profitable firms count for more. It holds many hundreds of stocks, with financials and technology the largest sectors, and no single holding is above about 1%.
EETH: A fund that gives exposure to the price of ether, the cryptocurrency on the Ethereum network, by holding ether futures contracts rather than the coin itself. Futures can differ from ether's price, and crypto can swing sharply.
EFA: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, such as Japan, the UK and France, tracking the MSCI EAFE index. It excludes the US and Canada, and financials and industrials are the biggest sectors.
EFAA: Stocks in developed countries outside the US and Canada, following the MSCI EAFE index, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to add income. A large chunk of the fund sits in cash and money market holdings to support those options.
EFAD: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada that have raised their dividends every year for at least 10 years, tracking an MSCI index. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3.5%.
EFAS: The 50 highest dividend-paying stocks in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, held in equal amounts. It leans toward banks, insurers, utilities and real estate, and no single company is more than about 3%.
EFAV: Stocks from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and Asia (excluding the US and Canada) picked to have lower price swings than the broader market, using the MSCI EAFE Minimum Volatility Index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
EFAX: Stocks from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and the Far East, with companies that own fossil fuel reserves left out. It otherwise follows the broad MSCI EAFE market, with ASML the largest holding at about 4%.
EFFE: An actively managed fund of emerging market companies chosen for how efficiently they use resources such as energy and water, by Osmosis. It is spread across many countries, with top holdings like Wistron, Wiwynn, Kia and Taiwan Semiconductor each about 4%.
EFFI: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked for using resources like energy and water efficiently. It is widely spread, with names like Recruit, Keyence and L'Oreal each around 3% to 4%.
EFG: Growth-oriented large and mid-sized companies from developed markets in Europe, Australasia and the Far East (not the US or Canada), tracking the MSCI EAFE Growth index. ASML is the biggest holding at about 6%, and industrials and technology lead.
EFIV: The S&P 500 with companies screened out or reduced for weak environmental, social and governance (ESG) scores. Tech is heavy, as NVIDIA, Microsoft and Alphabet make up about 28% of it, so it behaves much like the regular S&P 500.
EFNL: Finnish companies, tracking the MSCI Finland index. It is quite concentrated: Nokia and Nordea Bank are close to 40% of it, so a handful of firms drive results in this small market.
EFRA: A fund of companies tied to environmental infrastructure and industrial work, such as water, waste and clean transport, following a FTSE index. Industrials are about 60% of it, utilities about a quarter, and Xylem and American Water Works are among the top holdings.
EFV: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US and Canada that look cheap on measures like price relative to earnings or book value. It leans heavily toward financials, about 40% of the fund, with banks like HSBC among the top holdings.
EFZ: A fund that aims to go up about as much as the MSCI EAFE index of developed markets outside North America goes down, resetting each day. The money market holdings are collateral, and it is meant for short-term use as returns can drift over longer periods.
EGGQ: An actively managed fund that owns growth stocks, some directly and some through options, and also sells options to bring in extra income. It is heavily tilted to tech and industrial names like Seagate, Bloom Energy and Lumentum, and the options income can limit gains.
EGGS: An actively managed fund that holds growth stocks, either directly or through options, and sells options to generate income. This gives it some protection against falling prices, but it also limits how much it gains, and it is concentrated in tech hardware names.
EGGY: An actively managed fund that holds US stocks, some through options, and sells options to generate high income while hedging against very large drops. It is heavily tilted to technology and concentrated, with Seagate, Bloom Energy and Micron about 27%.
EGLE: Holds the S&P 500 companies with the largest revenues, rather than weighting by company value. It still leans toward tech: Microsoft and NVIDIA together are about 20% of the fund.
EGUS: US growth stocks chosen from an index that also screens for environmental, social and governance, or ESG, characteristics. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 38% of it, and technology is over half the fund.
EHCC: An actively managed fund that aims for income by selling call options on Ethereum exchange-traded products, which caps how much it can gain if Ether rises. It gets its Ether exposure indirectly through options and holds Treasury bills alongside them.
EHLS: An actively managed fund that buys stocks it expects to do well and sells short ones it expects to lag, using a proprietary model. Shorting is borrowing shares to bet on a price drop, so it is meant to be less tied to the overall market.
EHY: An actively managed fund that gives exposure to the price of ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, mostly through ether funds. It also sells options on them to earn income, which limits gains if ether rallies and still leaves large losses if it falls.
EIDO: Large and mid-sized Indonesian companies, following the MSCI Indonesia index. It is concentrated in banks: Bank Central Asia, Bank Rakyat and Bank Mandiri alone are about a third of it, and financials are around half the fund.
EINC: Energy companies that move and process oil and gas, mainly pipelines, following a VanEck index of them. They tend to pay income, and the top names are Williams, Enbridge, TC Energy and Kinder Morgan, about 30% of the fund.
EIPI: Mostly North American energy companies, especially pipeline and midstream firms, plus an options strategy that sells call options to bring in extra income. Enterprise Products, Energy Transfer and MPLX are about 19% of it, and the options income can limit gains in a rally.
EIPX: An actively managed fund that holds energy company stocks, with many pipeline and midstream partnerships among its top holdings. Enterprise Products and Energy Transfer are the largest, each about 7%, and the focus is on energy businesses that pay income.
EIRL: Companies in Ireland, following the MSCI Ireland index. It has only a few big names: Ryanair, AIB Group and Bank of Ireland together are about 44% of the fund, so it leans toward banks and airlines.
EIS: Large and mid-sized Israeli companies, following the MSCI Israel Capped Index. It is concentrated in a few names, with Teva, Bank Leumi, Bank Hapoalim and Tower Semiconductor about 31%, and financials the largest slice.
EJAN: Gives exposure to emerging market stocks through options on the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF, over a set one-year period starting in January. A set amount of losses is buffered, but gains are capped, and the full benefit applies only if held the whole period.
EJUL: A defined-outcome fund using options on an emerging markets ETF over a set one-year period starting in July. It aims to absorb part of the losses in exchange for a limit on gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
EKG: Companies where healthcare meets technology, such as medical devices, digital health and health data firms, picked by a Nasdaq Lux index. It is fairly concentrated: IQVIA, Veeva, DexCom, Guardant and Intuitive Surgical are each about 6% to 8%.
ELCV: An actively managed fund holding dividend-paying US stocks, with the goal of steady income plus some growth. It spreads across energy, technology, health care and utilities, and no single stock is large: the top names, Prologis, Entergy and Williams, are each around 4% or 5%.
ELD: Government and agency bonds from emerging market countries, all paid in those countries' own currencies such as Brazilian, Hungarian or South African money. That means the fund is exposed to currency moves as well as interest rates, and its bonds typically have maturities of two to ten years.
ELFY: Companies helping build the electric grid and the equipment around it, such as power gear, electrical components and utilities, tracking a rules-based index of large and mid-sized firms. It is spread thinly, with no stock above about 2%.
ELM: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other ETFs: roughly 60% global stocks, with the rest in short-term Treasury bills and inflation-protected bonds. The managers shift the mix over time, so it works as a one-fund balanced portfolio with a large cash-like cushion.
EMAG: An actively managed fund giving exposure to three major artificial intelligence-linked companies in emerging markets, such as China, Taiwan and India. With so few holdings, it is a concentrated bet, and it also carries the extra risks of emerging markets.
EMAU: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on an emerging markets stock ETF (iShares MSCI Emerging Markets) to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
EMB: US dollar bonds issued by governments and government-linked companies in emerging markets, tracking a J.P. Morgan index. It pays more interest than US Treasuries because these borrowers are riskier, and Argentina and Ecuador appear among its larger holdings.
EMBD: An actively managed fund of bonds from emerging market governments and companies, such as Brazil, Argentina and Eskom in South Africa. It is spread across many issuers, each around 2% or less, and pays more income than US bonds in exchange for higher risk.
EMBX: A fund investing mainly in bonds issued by governments and companies in emerging markets, in both US dollars and local currencies. Holdings are mostly government debt from places like Mexico, Poland, Peru and Indonesia, so it carries currency and country risk beyond a typical bond fund.
EMC: An actively managed fund of emerging-market companies tied to consumer spending, such as retail, food and leisure, but it holds big tech names too. Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor lead, with Samsung about 11% and Taiwan Semiconductor about 12% across two lines.
EMCB: Holds corporate bonds issued by companies in emerging markets such as Latin America, Asia and Africa. It is actively managed and spread out, with no single bond above about 2%, and it keeps average sensitivity to rate changes between two and ten years.
EMCR: Large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets that meet certain environmental standards or have promised to cut greenhouse gas emissions. It is tech heavy, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix making up about 23% of the fund.
EMCS: Emerging market stocks (companies in developing economies) chosen from an index that screens a large global list for climate-related factors. It is concentrated in Asian chips: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 19%, Samsung about 11% and SK Hynix about 9%.
EMDM: Stocks from emerging market countries that are rated as democracies, picked by a Bloomberg index. It leans on tech and Asia, with Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor each around 12% and SK Hynix near 9%.
EMDV: Companies in emerging markets with a record of growing their dividends, following the MSCI Emerging Markets Dividend Growers index. It holds many names, with the largest, such as Lotes and NAURA Technology, each only around 3%.
EMEM: An actively managed fund holding stocks of companies in emerging markets, which are developing economies such as Taiwan, South Korea and China. Chipmakers are a big theme: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung together are about a quarter of the stock holdings.
EMEQ: An actively managed fund of a small number of emerging market stocks, picked by the manager from companies in countries like Taiwan, Korea and China. It is very concentrated: SK Square, Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics together are around half of it, and technology is over half.
EMES: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and China. It is heavy in tech, with Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and SK Hynix together over a quarter of the fund and Tencent around 4%.
EMET: Global companies that mine and process metals used for electrification, mainly copper but also others used in batteries and power grids. It is concentrated in mining firms, with Freeport-McMoRan, Anglo American and Grupo Mexico about 23% of the fund.
EMFI: An actively managed fund buying bonds from emerging market governments and companies. It is spread across many countries, with Egypt, Nigeria, Guatemala and Kenya among the larger holdings, and these bonds pay more yield but carry more risk.
EMGF: Emerging market stocks picked and weighted to favor five traits: momentum, quality, value, low volatility and small size. It looks like a standard emerging market fund, with Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung about 19% of it.
EMHC: US-dollar bonds issued by governments and government-related borrowers in emerging markets, following a Bloomberg index. It holds a very wide mix of countries, such as Argentina and Brazil, with each single bond under about 2% of the fund.
EMHY: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies that are rated below investment grade, all in US dollars, tracking a J.P. Morgan index. Higher yields come with higher default risk, and Ecuador, Argentina and Ghana show up among the larger holdings.
EMIF: Infrastructure companies in emerging markets such as airports, water utilities and power companies, tracked using an index. It is concentrated: two Mexican airport operators and Airports of Thailand are among the top holdings, and industrials and utilities are around 40% each.
EMJL: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on an emerging markets stock ETF (iShares MSCI Emerging Markets) to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
EMJN: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on an emerging markets stock ETF (iShares MSCI Emerging Markets) to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
EMKT: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks that Lazard's managers think are priced below what their earnings and assets are worth. It is tilted to tech: Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and SK Hynix together make up about a third of it.
EMLC: Bonds issued by emerging-market governments, such as Brazil, South Africa and Mexico, paid in each country's own currency rather than US dollars. Returns depend on both the bonds and how those currencies move against the dollar; it tracks a J.P. Morgan index.
EMLP: Mostly pipeline and other energy infrastructure companies in the US and Canada, picked by a manager rather than an index. Many are partnerships that pay out lots of income, and Enterprise Products and Energy Transfer are about 16% of it.
EMM: An actively managed fund of stocks in emerging markets that leaves out China. It is tilted to tech and heavy in a few places: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and a Global X India fund make up around 40%.
EMMF: Emerging markets stocks picked and weighted using several factors like value, quality and momentum, instead of just company size. It still leans on the big names, with Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and Samsung about 21% of the fund.
EMMY: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to an emerging markets stock ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 15% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited.
EMNT: An actively managed fund of very short-term bonds, mostly corporate debt with a mix of government and mortgage bonds, that aims to earn a bit more than cash. It screens holdings for environmental, social and governance factors, and its price moves very little.
EMOP: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks, picked by managers who look for profitable companies at reasonable prices. It is top-heavy in Asian chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK hynix together are about 35% of it.
EMOT: Holds S&P 500 companies that an index judges to have a lasting competitive edge, called an economic moat, and are priced reasonably. It is spread widely, with chipmakers like Applied Materials, KLA and Lam Research each around 3%, and leans toward technology.
EMPB: An actively managed fund that uses a computer model to pick which parts of the US market are likely to beat it, then mostly holds other ETFs. Its largest holdings are solar, semiconductor, Nasdaq-100 and ARK funds, each around 10% to 12%.
EMQQ: Internet and e-commerce companies in emerging markets such as China, India and Latin America, tracking the EMQQ Emerging Markets Internet and Ecommerce Index. It is concentrated, with MercadoLibre, Reliance, Alibaba and PDD together making up about 30% of the fund.
EMSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on an emerging markets stock ETF (iShares MSCI Emerging Markets) to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
EMSF: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks chosen for sustainability and good governance standards as well as quality. It is tech-heavy: SK Square, Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 25% of it, with banks and consumer companies making up much of the rest.
EMTY: A fund that aims for the opposite of the daily move of an index of US retailers that are likely to suffer as shopping moves online. It uses derivatives and resets daily, so over longer periods the results can differ a lot from simply the reverse.
EMXC: Stocks from emerging markets such as Taiwan, India and South Korea, but leaving out China, tracking the MSCI Emerging Markets ex China index. It is chip-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix together are about 36% of the fund.
EMXF: Large and mid-sized emerging market stocks that score well on environmental, social and governance ratings, with fossil fuel companies removed. It leans on tech and financials: SK Hynix alone is over 11% of the fund.
ENDW: An actively managed fund that owns other Cambria funds to spread across stocks, bonds, real assets and alternatives in the US and abroad. It is modeled on the way big university endowments invest, so it is a mix in a single ticker.
ENFR: Tracks an index of North American midstream energy companies, the pipelines, storage and processing businesses that move oil and gas. Enbridge, Energy Transfer and Enterprise Products are the largest, together about 23%, and many holdings pay sizeable income.
ENHE: An actively managed fund of emerging market stocks, with the managers choosing holdings to try to beat the market. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 27% of it, and technology is around 42%.
ENHI: An actively managed fund of large company stocks from developed markets outside North America, aiming to stay close to the MSCI EAFE Index while trying to do a bit better. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest holding at only about 3%.
ENHU: An actively managed fund of large US companies that stays close to the Russell 1000 index but uses computer models to try to do a little better. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 20% of the fund, much like the broad market.
ENOR: Large and mid-sized Norwegian companies, tracked with the MSCI Norway index and weighted by market value. Energy and banks dominate: Equinor and DNB are each roughly 12% of the fund, so it leans heavily on oil, gas and finance.
ENRG: An actively managed fund investing worldwide in companies that explore for, produce or distribute oil, gas, coal or uranium, including some in emerging markets. It is a bet on the energy industry, so its value tends to follow commodity prices.
ENZL: New Zealand stocks, tracking the MSCI New Zealand index, which covers the country's large and mid-sized companies. It is a small, concentrated market: Fisher & Paykel Healthcare is about 21% of the fund, and Infratil and Auckland Airport add roughly another 28%.
EOCT: Uses options on an emerging markets stock fund (the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each October. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only works if held the full period.
EPAI: An actively managed fund of companies that the managers think will benefit from artificial intelligence, such as chip equipment makers. It is concentrated in technology, about 60% of the fund, with Applied Materials, Teradyne and Lam Research among the largest holdings.
EPEM: An actively managed fund of stocks in developing countries such as Taiwan, South Korea, India and others. It is top-heavy: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 14% and Samsung about 8%, so chip companies make up a big part of the fund.
EPHE: Philippine companies of all sizes, tracking the MSCI Philippines index. It is concentrated in one country and one name: International Container Terminal Services is about 24%, and banks, ports, property and utilities make up most of the rest.
EPI: Indian companies, chosen and weighted by how much profit they earn rather than by their market value. This tilts it toward earnings-heavy areas such as financials, energy and materials, and Reliance Industries, ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank together are about 17% of it.
EPIN: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Taiwan, the Netherlands, South Korea and the UK. It is spread broadly, with the largest holding, Taiwan Semiconductor, at only about 5% of the fund.
EPMB: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies, picked by the manager rather than an index, with a blend of growth and value stocks. It is widely spread, with the top holdings such as Keysight, Woodward and Cummins each around 3%.
EPMV: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized companies that the manager considers undervalued, using the Russell Midcap Index as its yardstick for company size. It is fairly spread out, with its largest positions, such as Flex and Cummins, each around 3% of the fund, and leans toward industrials, financials and technology.
EPOL: Large and mid-sized Polish companies, tracking the MSCI Poland index. It is concentrated in a single country and a few sectors: two big banks and the oil company Orlen make up roughly 15% each or less, with banks and energy dominating.
EPP: Large and mid-size companies in the developed Asia-Pacific region outside Japan: Australia, Hong Kong, New Zealand and Singapore, tracked by an MSCI index. Australia dominates, with BHP and Commonwealth Bank about 19% of the fund, and financials are nearly half.
