The Treasury bills shown mostly back those futures, so it is a trend-following strategy, not a bond fund.
FMHI: Municipal bonds from states, cities and public projects, paying interest that is generally free from regular federal income tax, with a focus on higher yielding, lower rated issues. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, none above about 1%.
FMKT: An actively managed US stock fund that looks for companies expected to gain from lighter regulation, including in heavily regulated areas like health care and finance. Holdings are spread out, with no single stock above about 4% of the fund.
FMNY: Municipal bonds from New York issuers, such as state authorities and local projects, whose interest is generally exempt from federal, New York State and New York City income taxes. It targets higher yields and can hold bonds of any maturity, including lower rated ones.
FMQQ: Internet and online-finance companies in emerging markets such as India, Latin America and Africa, following an index built for that theme. Holdings are spread across several countries, and the top names, such as Bajaj Finance and MercadoLibre, are each only about 8% of the fund.
FMTL: Follows an index of companies that mine and process critical metals, such as copper, lithium and other minerals used in batteries and electronics. It is mostly materials companies from around the world, and BHP, Freeport-McMoRan, Glencore and Anglo American are about a third of it.
FMTM: An actively run basket of US stocks that have been rising over recent periods, based on the idea that winners tend to keep winning for a while. Holdings change often and sit mostly in technology and health companies, with the top names each around 3 to 4% of the fund.
FMUB: An actively managed fund buying US municipal bonds whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It can put up to 30% in lower-quality bonds, so it takes more credit risk than a plain muni fund, and holds many small positions.
FMUN: US municipal bonds issued by states, cities and public agencies, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It follows a Fidelity index of intermediate-term bonds and holds a broad mix, with the biggest position about 2%.
FNCL: The financial sector of the US stock market, including banks, payments companies, insurers and brokers, tracked by an MSCI index. JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway, Visa and Mastercard are about 30% of it, and it holds only this one sector.
FNDA: Small US companies, picked and weighted by business size such as sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. It holds about a thousand names with none above 1%, so it is very evenly spread.
FNDB: A broad US stock fund that weights companies by business size, such as sales, cash flow and dividends, instead of by stock market value. This makes it different from a plain index fund, and Apple, Intel, Alphabet and Microsoft are only about 11% of it.
FNDC: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted by fundamentals like sales, cash flow and dividends rather than by market size. It holds a very large number of tiny positions across Japan, Europe and elsewhere, with none above 1%.
FNDE: Large emerging market companies (such as Taiwan, China, Brazil and India) chosen and weighted by business size measures like sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 6% of it, and financials, technology and energy are the biggest areas.
FNDF: Large companies from developed countries outside the US, chosen and weighted by sales, cash flow and dividends rather than market value. Samsung, Shell and TotalEnergies are among its top holdings, and it tilts toward value-style stocks like banks and energy firms.
FNDX: Large US companies picked and weighted by business size measures like sales, cash flow and dividends, rather than by stock market value. That makes it less tilted toward the biggest stocks than a regular index fund, though Apple, Intel, Alphabet and Microsoft are still its largest holdings.
FNGS: An exchange-traded note (a bond-like IOU from a bank, not a fund of shares) that follows an index of 10 highly traded tech and internet growth stocks, in equal amounts. Micron, Meta, Palantir, NVIDIA and Broadcom are each about 10%, and it also carries the bank's credit risk.
FNK: Mid-sized US value stocks, selected and weighted from a NASDAQ index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks companies on value and growth traits instead of size. It holds many stocks in similar amounts, none above about 1%.
FNOV: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to buffer the first 10% of losses over a one-year period that starts each November. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
FNX: A broad basket of US mid-sized stocks, picked from a Nasdaq mid-cap index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value-style measures instead of company size. No holding is above about 0.5%, so it is very evenly spread across financials, consumer and industrial companies.
FNY: Growth-leaning mid-size US stocks from the Nasdaq US 600 Mid Cap Index, re-ranked by First Trust's AlphaDEX method to try to beat the usual weighting. Holdings are spread thin, none above about 1%, with health care, technology and industrials leading.
FOCT: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to buffer the first 10% of losses over a one-year period that starts each October. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
FOPC: A fund of other bond ETFs, usually six to twelve of them, that together give broad exposure to US bonds of varied types and quality. Four holdings, including TCW Flexible Income and JPMorgan Core Plus Bond, make up about three quarters of it, so it is a fund of funds.
FORH: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized company stocks from around the world, with some derivatives and Treasury bills mixed in. It is concentrated, with Acacia Research about 10% of the fund, and it also has some volatility-linked holdings for defense.
FOTO: Holds companies whose main business is photonics, which means using light and lasers in things like fiber optic networks and manufacturing. Lumentum, IPG Photonics and Coherent make up about a third of it, and some exposure comes through swaps rather than shares.
FOWF: Companies that build defense and military technology for the US and its allies, tracked using a rules-based index. It is concentrated in a few big contractors: RTX, Lockheed Martin and General Dynamics are each about 8%, with industrials and technology making up most of the fund.
FOXY: An actively managed fund that trades currency forward contracts, which are agreements to exchange currencies at a set future rate, backed by short-term Treasuries. It is a currency-trading strategy, so returns depend on exchange rate moves rather than on stocks or bonds.
FPA: Stocks from Asia Pacific countries outside Japan, picked from a NASDAQ index using the AlphaDEX method, which scores and ranks stocks on growth and value factors rather than just size. Samsung and SK group companies are prominent, and industrials and technology lead the sectors.
FPAA: An actively managed mix of stocks and bonds that holds other FPA funds. About 60% is in a global stock fund and about a third is in short-term government bonds, so it works as a ready-made balanced portfolio.
FPAG: An actively managed fund of stocks from around the world, chosen by the manager as good businesses priced below their worth. It tends to hold a smaller number of companies, with Analog Devices and Alphabet each around 4 to 5%, and it also keeps some money in short-term Treasury bills.
FPAS: A fund holding short-term US government debt, mostly Treasuries with a small share in agency debt, kept short so prices move little when interest rates change. It is actively managed and aims for income with low volatility rather than higher returns.
FPE: Preferred stocks and other income-paying bonds, mostly from big banks, insurers and utilities, which pay a fixed dividend and rank ahead of regular shares. It is actively managed and built for income rather than growth, and it is roughly half preferred stocks and half bonds.
FPEI: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income-paying debt issued by institutions, mostly big banks and financial firms around the world. Preferreds are hybrids that pay set income and rank ahead of common stock, and this fund is about 70% bonds and 27% preferreds.
FPFD: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and other income-paying investments, which are stock-like shares that pay fixed dividends. Issuers include banks, pipelines and utilities, and the focus is on steady income.
FPRO: An actively managed fund of real estate companies, mostly REITs that own property such as warehouses, data centers and cell towers. Prologis, Equinix and American Tower are the largest holdings at around 9% each, and it does not publish its full holdings every day.
FPWR: An actively managed fund of North American energy and power companies picked for steady income, such as pipeline firms and electric and gas utilities. Utilities make up about 63% and energy about 33%, with Energy Transfer and Enterprise Products among its largest holdings.
FPX: Newly public US companies, tracking an index of the largest recent IPOs and spin-offs. It is concentrated and shifts often: GE Vernova and Sandisk are about 21% of it together, and it tends to hold mid-sized companies.
FPXE: Roughly the 100 largest recent IPOs, spin-offs and carve-outs of European companies, picked by the IPOX Europe index. Because it focuses on newly listed firms, it is concentrated: ARM Holdings alone is about 9% of the fund.
FPXI: A fund of non-US stocks tracking a market-cap weighted index of growth-oriented companies. It is concentrated in tech and industrial names, with Advantest, Kioxia and Contemporary Amperex Technology each around 8% to 9%.
FQAL: Large and mid-sized US companies that score well on quality measures like profitability and stable earnings, tracking a Fidelity index. NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet are about 26% of it, so it looks like a top-heavy market fund.
FRDM: Emerging market stocks, with countries weighted by how free they score on personal and economic freedom measures. Chip makers lead: Samsung, SK hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor are about a third of the fund.
FREI: An actively managed mix of real estate related investments: mostly bonds and loans, with some real estate company stocks and preferred shares. It is built for income, and well known property owners like American Tower, Welltower and Prologis show up as small holdings.
FREL: US real estate companies, mostly REITs that own properties like apartments, warehouses, data centers and cell towers, tracking the MSCI USA IMI Real Estate 25/25 Index. Welltower and Prologis are the largest holdings at about 9% and 8%, and most REITs pay out income.
FRGN: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US, across both developed and emerging markets. Its biggest holdings are Taiwan Semiconductor, ASML and Samsung, and technology and financial companies make up around 40% of it.
FRI: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like apartments, warehouses and data centers, tracking an S&P index. Welltower and Prologis are about 21% of the fund, and REITs are required to pass most of their income to shareholders.
FRIZ: An actively managed fund of US companies with long records of paying and raising dividends, or that the manager expects to raise them. It is led by big names, with Microsoft, Apple, Broadcom and JPMorgan together about 20% of the fund.
FRNW: Tracks an index of global companies in clean energy, such as wind, solar, fuel cells and power equipment. It is fairly concentrated, with GE Vernova, Vestas and Bloom Energy about 15% together, and mostly utilities and industrials.
FRTY: An actively managed fund of about 40 mid-sized US growth companies. It is concentrated and tilted toward health care and technology, with names like Twist Bioscience, Western Digital and Nebius each around 4% to 5%.
FRUT: Follows an index of big, fast-growing US tech and related companies, nicknamed MANGOS. It is very concentrated: Space Exploration Technologies and NVIDIA are about 16% each, and tech makes up around three quarters of it.
FRWD: An actively managed fund of technology companies expected to benefit from major shifts, such as AI and chips. It is concentrated: NVIDIA, AMD, Seagate, Lam Research and Taiwan Semiconductor make up about 37%, so it is a narrow bet on semiconductors and hardware.
FSCC: An actively managed fund of small US companies, using a computer-driven model to pick stocks it expects to do well. It is spread out, with no holding above about 2% of the fund, and leans toward health care, financials and industrials.
FSCS: Holds about 200 smaller and mid-sized US dividend-paying companies picked for strong financial health, following a First Trust Capital Strength index. It is spread widely, with no company above about 1.5%, and leans toward financials and industrials.
FSEC: Mortgage-backed and other securitized bonds, which bundle many loans together and pass on the payments, mostly backed by US government agencies. It is actively managed, and it is built for steady income with investment grade quality.
FSEG: A fund of US small growth stocks, based on the Russell 2000 Growth Index, with the manager tilting the picks to try to beat the index. Health care and technology make up over half, and no single company is more than about 1% of the fund.
FSEP: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion the first roughly 10% of losses over a one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, so it only fully works if held for the whole period.
FSEV: An actively managed fund of small US companies that look cheap, built around the Russell 2000 Value Index, with the manager adjusting weights to try to beat it. It holds many names, none above about 1% of the fund, and leans toward financials.
FSGS: Holds small and mid-sized US companies that the index picks for strong market positions and healthy finances. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward technology, health care and financials alongside industrial firms.
FSIG: An actively managed basket of investment-grade corporate bonds, chosen so the fund's overall sensitivity to interest rates stays fairly low. It spreads across a lot of companies, with no single bond above about 1.5%, and pays interest income.
FSMB: An actively managed fund of short-term US municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments, with interest that is generally exempt from federal income tax. The shorter maturities mean its price moves less when interest rates change, and it is spread across many small positions of around 1% or less.
FSMD: US small and mid-sized companies chosen using several factors: attractive prices, strong quality, rising share prices and low volatility. It is very spread out, with only Sandisk above about 1% of the fund.
FSML: An actively managed fund of small US companies that tries to beat the small company market, using derivatives alongside the stocks. It spreads across many names, with health care, financials and technology the biggest groups and no holding above about 3%.
FSOL: A fund that holds the Solana cryptocurrency (SOL) directly and tracks its US dollar price using a blended price from several trading markets. It holds no stocks or bonds, so its value moves with the price of a single, volatile digital asset.
FSPC: Follows a Bloomberg index of companies tied to the space economy, such as aerospace and defense makers, satellite operators and related technology firms from several countries. It is mostly industrials, and each of its top holdings, like Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Thales, is only about 5%.
FSTA: US consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks, household products and tobacco, tracking the MSCI USA IMI Consumer Staples 25/50 Index. Walmart, Costco, Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble together make up about 42% of the fund.
FSTB: An actively managed fund of investment-grade bonds with short maturities, run to have interest rate risk similar to a 1 to 3 year government and corporate bond index. US Treasuries make up a large share, so price swings are small compared with longer bond funds.
FSYD: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, often called junk bonds because they are rated below investment grade, that Fidelity picks partly on sustainability factors. It is spread over many issuers, each under 2%, and pays higher income for higher risk.
FSZ: Swiss stocks picked from the NASDAQ Switzerland Index using a scoring system called AlphaDEX, which favors stocks with stronger growth and value traits. It holds Swiss industrials, financials and health care, with no single stock above about 5%.
FTA: A broad basket of large US value stocks, picked from the Nasdaq US 500 Large Cap Index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on value and growth-style measures instead of company size. No holding is above about 1%, spread over financials, energy, utilities and technology.
FTAG: Companies tied to agriculture, from farm equipment and seeds to fertilizer and crop chemicals, in a global index weighted by company size. It is fairly concentrated: Deere, Corteva, Bayer and BASF are each roughly 9% to 10%, so about 40% sits in those four.
FTBD: An actively managed bond fund that can invest across the whole bond market, from US Treasuries to high yield and emerging markets debt. The manager shifts between sectors and maturities as conditions change, with Treasuries as the biggest piece at roughly a third.
FTBI: A fund of other First Trust ETFs, set in fixed proportions across income-focused stocks, bonds and commodity strategies. Roughly 55% is in stocks and about a third in bonds, so it blends several approaches that are built to pay income.
FTC: A broad basket of large US growth stocks, picked from the Nasdaq US 500 Large Cap Index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value-style measures instead of company size. Holdings are fairly evenly spread, none above about 1%, with technology and industrials the biggest groups.
FTCA: Holds investment-grade California municipal bonds with maturities of three years or longer, so the interest is generally free of federal and California income tax. It is actively managed, and some of its income may still be subject to the alternative minimum tax.
FTCB: An actively managed bond fund holding investment-grade bonds, such as government-backed mortgage bonds, Treasuries and corporate debt. Its managers choose the bonds rather than tracking an index, and it aims for a broad, fairly safe core bond portfolio that pays income.
FTCE: Large US companies chosen by a First Trust index that favors firms with strong, high quality earnings, based on a cleaned up measure of profit. It is spread fairly evenly, with Seagate, IBM, Qualcomm and CrowdStrike each around 4% to 5%, and tilted to tech.
FTCS: Large US companies chosen for strong finances, such as lots of cash and high returns on their capital, from a Nasdaq index of big US stocks. It holds about 50 names in similar-sized stakes of around 2%, spread over financials, industrials, consumer staples and health care.
FTDS: US mid-sized companies and REITs with long records of raising their dividends, picked by a First Trust index that screens for financial strength. It is spread widely, with no holding above roughly 2%, and leans toward financials, energy and industrials.
FTEC: US technology companies, from software to chips to hardware, tracking the MSCI USA IMI Information Technology 25/50 index. It is very top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 44% of the fund.
FTG: An actively managed fund buying US growth companies, mostly mid-sized, using a behavioral approach that tries to take advantage of common investor biases. About half of it is in technology, and no single stock is more than about 4% of the fund.
FTGC: An actively managed fund that gains exposure to a broad mix of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, mainly through futures contracts. The Treasury bills shown in its holdings are mostly collateral backing those contracts, so its ups and downs follow commodity prices.
FTGS: US large and mid-sized stocks chosen for traits like strong return on equity, low debt and growing revenue and cash flow. It is evenly spread, with the top holding, Palo Alto Networks, at only about 4%, and technology and health care are the biggest sectors.
FTHB: An actively managed bond fund that invests in companies chosen to match biblical values, with about 40% in US Treasuries. It also holds corporate bonds and some preferred stock, so it works as an income fund with a faith-based screen.
FTHF: Emerging market companies chosen by First Trust's index for criteria around human flourishing, such as freedom and social factors, instead of just size. It is concentrated, with SK Hynix, Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor making up about 38% of the fund.
FTHI: US large-company stocks combined with a covered call strategy: it sells options on the S&P 500, collecting extra income in return for giving up some gains when the market rises sharply. Apple and NVIDIA are about 12% of the stock portfolio.
FTIF: A fund of US mid-sized stocks picked to hold up when inflation rises, following a Bloomberg index. It leans heavily toward energy at about 44% of the fund, along with industrials, materials and real estate companies.
FTKI: Holds a mix of US small company stocks and earns extra income by selling call options on small-cap indexes, which means giving up some gains when prices jump. It is fairly spread out, with its largest holding, Argan, at about 4% of the fund.
FTLS: An actively managed fund that buys US stocks it likes and bets against others, so it can profit when some shares fall. Because of that and a sizable cash holding, it moves less with the market than a regular stock fund, and Apple is about 7%.
FTMA: A fund of Massachusetts municipal bonds, which pay interest that is generally exempt from federal and Massachusetts income taxes. It mainly holds bonds from state and local issuers in that state, so it is concentrated in one state's finances and mostly appeals for tax-free income.
FTMH: Mostly municipal bonds whose interest is exempt from federal income tax, split between lower-rated and investment-grade, with intermediate to long maturities. The high yield mix means more income but more credit risk, and the interest may be subject to the alternative minimum tax.
FTMN: Investment-grade municipal bonds whose interest is generally free from federal and Minnesota income tax, with intermediate to long maturities. It is actively managed and focused on one state, so it mainly suits residents who want to avoid state tax and it carries Minnesota-specific risk.
FTMS: Mostly investment-grade municipal bonds with short maturities, paying interest generally exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds are short, the price should move less than longer municipal bond funds when rates change.
FTMU: Investment-grade municipal bonds with intermediate to long maturities, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed, mostly bonds with a small cash holding, and income may still be subject to the federal alternative minimum tax in some cases.
FTN: Investment-grade US dollar corporate bonds with five to ten years left until they mature, from US and foreign companies, following a FTSE index. These mid-length bonds sit between short and long ones in how much their prices move when rates change.
FTNJ: Investment-grade New Jersey municipal bonds with intermediate to long maturities, paying interest generally exempt from federal and New Jersey income tax. It is actively managed and concentrated in one state's issuers.
FTNY: Mostly New York municipal bonds, aiming for income that is exempt from federal and New York State and City income taxes. Because the bonds all come from one state, the fund depends on the finances of New York issuers.
FTOH: A fund of investment-grade Ohio municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal and Ohio income tax, though some may be subject to the alternative minimum tax. It is actively managed and focused on tax-free income for Ohio residents.
FTPA: Bonds issued by Pennsylvania state and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax and from Pennsylvania state tax for residents. It focuses on one state, so its results depend on the finances of Pennsylvania issuers rather than the whole US municipal market.
FTQI: Large Nasdaq stocks combined with a strategy of selling call options on the Nasdaq-100 for extra income, which pays out regularly but caps gains in strong rallies. Apple, AMD and NVIDIA are the biggest, together about 18% of it.
FTRB: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds investment-grade US dollar bonds, with a smaller share in riskier or foreign bonds. A good part of it is held through other Federated funds, including a mortgage bond fund of about 16%, and the managers adjust the mix.
FTRI: The 50 highest-dividend-paying global companies in the upstream part of natural resources, including miners, energy producers and some utilities. Barrick Mining and TotalEnergies together are nearly 19% of it, and about half the fund is in materials like gold mining.
FTSD: A short term bond fund holding mostly US government debt, including Treasuries and government backed mortgage bonds. Because the bonds mature quickly, its price moves less than longer bond funds, and it may use Treasury futures to adjust its interest rate risk.
FTSL: Senior loans, which are floating-rate loans made to lower-rated companies and sit first in line to be repaid if the company struggles. Because the interest rate resets with short-term rates, income moves with them, and no single borrower is more than about 2% of the fund.
FTSM: Short-term US dollar bonds, mostly government and investment-grade corporate, run actively to keep average maturity under three years. Because of that the price barely moves, and income tracks short-term interest rates, with holdings spread very widely.
FTWO: Companies tied to natural resources and national security, such as farm equipment, energy, mining and defense firms, following a Bloomberg-based index. Deere, Constellation Energy, ExxonMobil and General Electric make up about a third of it.
FTXG: US food and beverage companies chosen by a Nasdaq index for their size and trading activity. It is fairly concentrated: Archer Daniels Midland, Coca-Cola, Kraft Heinz and Mondelez are each around 8% to 9%, and almost all of it is consumer staples.
FTXH: US pharmaceutical companies picked and weighted by a Nasdaq index. It is concentrated in big drugmakers: Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Merck and Johnson & Johnson are each around 7%, and the top five are about 36% of the fund.
FTXL: US semiconductor companies chosen from a Nasdaq index based on trading volume and ranking. It is concentrated in one industry, with Intel and Micron each around 12% to 13% and the top eight holdings making up about 60% of the fund.
FTXN: US oil and gas companies, from producers to refiners, selected and weighted by a Nasdaq index. It is concentrated in a few big names: ConocoPhillips, ExxonMobil and Chevron are each around 7%, so energy prices drive it heavily.
FTXO: US banks, following the Nasdaq US Smart Banks index. It is all financial companies, with Citigroup, Bank of America and JPMorgan each around 8% to 9% and Wells Fargo and Truist about 7%, so it moves with bank profits and interest rates.
FTXR: About 30 to 50 US transportation companies, such as automakers, railroads, airlines and delivery firms, picked by a ranking of factors like value and growth. It is concentrated, with Tesla, Union Pacific, Ford and General Motors each around 7%.
FUTY: US utility companies, such as electric, gas and water providers, tracking the MSCI USA IMI Utilities 25/50 Index. NextEra, Southern and Duke are about 25% of it, and many of the holdings pay steady dividends.
FV: A fund that holds five First Trust sector funds, picked by a rules-based ranking of which sectors have recently done best. Each gets about 20%, so the mix changes as the rankings do.
FVAL: Large and mid-sized US stocks that look attractively priced compared with measures like earnings and book value, following Fidelity's value factor index. Despite the value label, it holds big tech, with NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet making up about 26% of it.
FVC: Holds just five other First Trust ETFs at a time, chosen by Dorsey Wright's strength-ranking method that favors recent winners. Each gets about 20%, so the mix of sectors can change a lot as the picks are updated.
FVD: About 200 US dividend payers that Value Line rates as safe and financially sound, weighted roughly equally. Because each stock is only a sliver (around 0.4%), no company dominates, and it leans toward financials, utilities and industrials.
FWD: An actively managed global stock fund that looks for companies likely to benefit from big technology and industry shifts. It is spread out, with Broadcom, AMD, Samsung and NVIDIA each only about 2% to 3%.
FXA: Tracks the Australian dollar by holding actual Australian dollars in a bank deposit. Its price moves with the exchange rate against the US dollar rather than with any stocks or bonds, and it earns little or no interest.
FXB: Tracks the British pound by holding actual pounds in a bank deposit. Its price moves with the exchange rate against the US dollar rather than any stocks or bonds, and it earns little or no interest.
FXC: Holds actual Canadian dollars in a bank deposit, so its price follows the exchange rate between the Canadian and US dollar. It owns no stocks or bonds, and gives a simple way to hold the currency without opening a foreign bank account.
FXD: US consumer discretionary stocks, the companies selling things people want rather than need, chosen by the AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value measures. It holds each stock at close to equal weight, so no single company is above about 2%.
FXE: A trust that holds actual euros in a bank deposit, so its price follows the euro against the US dollar. It holds no stocks or bonds, which makes it a way to bet on the currency itself, and it pays a small amount of interest.
FXED: An actively managed income fund that mixes corporate bonds, preferred stock and other bond ETFs, plus shares of lenders such as Ares Capital and Hercules Capital. It aims for higher income than a plain bond fund, with more risk than one.
FXF: Holds Swiss francs in a deposit account, so its value follows the franc against the US dollar. It holds no stocks or bonds, and pays little interest, since the money sits in a bank deposit.
FXG: Holds consumer staples stocks (food, drinks and household goods makers) from the Russell 1000, picked and weighted by the AlphaDEX method that scores stocks on value and growth. Weights are close to equal, so JBS, Smithfield, Ingredion and General Mills each make up about 4% to 5%.
FXH: US health care stocks from the Russell 1000, picked and weighted by a rules-based score of growth and value rather than by company size. That makes it roughly equal-weighted, so no holding is much above 3% and smaller names count as much as giants.
FXI: About 50 of the biggest Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong, tracked by an index of large caps. It is fairly concentrated: Alibaba, Tencent and two huge state banks make up about a third of the fund.
FXL: US technology stocks from the Russell 1000, chosen by a formula that scores growth and value and weights them more evenly than a typical index. Because of that, no stock is much above 2%, so it is less dominated by the giant tech names than most tech funds.
FXN: US energy stocks from the Russell 1000, picked by a scoring system for growth and value and held in roughly equal dollar amounts. That gives smaller oil and gas producers and refiners more weight than a normal index, with each top holding near 5%.
FXO: US financial companies from the Russell 1000, such as insurers, banks and exchanges, picked and weighted by AlphaDEX, a rules-based ranking on growth and value. Holdings are close to equal weighted, so no stock is above about 2.5% and smaller names count more than usual.
FXR: US industrial companies picked and weighted by a First Trust AlphaDEX method that ranks stocks on growth and value traits, so it differs from a regular market-weighted fund. It holds around 100 stocks in similar amounts, each only about 1 to 2% of the fund.
FXU: US utility companies, such as gas, electric and water providers, picked from the Russell 1000 by a rules-based method that favors stocks with strong growth and value traits. Holdings are roughly equal in size, each at about 4%, instead of favoring the largest.
FXY: Holds Japanese yen in a bank account and tracks the yen's price against the US dollar. It owns no stocks or bonds, so its value moves only with the exchange rate.
FXZ: US materials stocks, such as chemicals, metals and mining, picked from the Russell 1000 by a scoring system and held in roughly equal dollar amounts. That gives smaller companies more weight than usual, with top holdings near 5% each.
FYC: A broad basket of US small growth companies, picked from a Nasdaq small-cap index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value-style measures instead of company size. No holding is above roughly 1% of the fund, and health care and technology make up nearly half.
FYEE: A fund of large US companies similar in size to the S&P 500, picked with computer models that weigh value, growth and quality. It also aims for extra income on top of the stocks, and tech is big: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
FYLD: An actively managed fund of developed market stocks outside the US, especially smaller and mid-sized companies, picked for paying cash back to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. It leans toward energy and financials, with no holding above about 1%.
FYT: About 200 small US value stocks, picked and weighted by First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which scores stocks on value and growth measures instead of by size. No holding is much more than 1%, and it differs from a plain small-cap value index.
FYX: A broad basket of US small-company stocks, picked from a Nasdaq small-cap index using First Trust's AlphaDEX method, which ranks stocks on growth and value-style measures instead of company size. No holding is above about 0.5%, so it is very spread out across financials, health care and industrials.
GAA: A fund of funds that spreads money across many other ETFs covering stocks, bonds, real estate and commodities around the world. It is actively managed to hold a wide mix rather than follow a single index.
GABF: An actively managed fund of financial services companies such as banks, insurers and asset managers, with no limit on company size. It is about 88% financials, and Berkshire Hathaway, Neostellar Capital and Cohen & Steers are each around 5% to 6%.
GAEM: An actively managed fund of bonds from governments and companies in emerging markets, in US dollars or local currencies. A manager chooses the bonds rather than following an index, and local-currency bonds mean exchange rate swings can affect results.
GAIQ: An actively managed global stock fund that looks for companies it thinks will grow through technology, communications or innovative management. It is tilted to tech, with Advanced Micro Devices, Thermo Fisher, Microsoft and Apple each making up about 4% of the fund.
GAL: A fund of funds that spreads money across other State Street ETFs covering US and foreign stocks, bonds, commodities and inflation protected Treasuries. It aims for around 60% in stocks, though the manager can shift that mix.
GALX: Companies tied to the space industry, from rocket makers to satellite and electronics suppliers, chosen by VistaShares. It is a narrow, non-diversified theme, mostly industrials and technology, with Rocket Lab and MACOM each around 4% of the fund.
GAMR: Companies in the video game business, from chipmakers and platforms to game publishers, tracked by an index that weights them by size within limits. It is concentrated, with AMD, Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA each about 10% of the fund.
GANZ: An actively managed fund that holds US-listed stocks and uses options on individual stocks and indexes, following a thematic approach. It is non-diversified, so a few positions can matter a lot, and the options can change how much of the market it captures.
GAPR: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set part of losses over a one-year period that starts in April. In return, gains are capped, and it works as intended only if held for the whole period.
GARA: An income focused fund of real assets companies around the world, such as utilities, infrastructure, data centers and health care real estate. Holdings are spread widely, with names like Infratil, Elia, Welltower, Equinix and Ventas each around 3%.
GARP: A fund of US stocks that screens for quality companies growing at reasonable prices, an approach called growth at a reasonable price. It leans on tech, with KLA and Micron near 6% each and Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft each around 4%.
GARY: An actively managed fund of US-listed stocks the manager believes have strong, consistent growth in sales and earnings. It leans toward chip and tech names: Applied Materials, ASML, Mastercard, NVIDIA and AMD are each roughly 5% of it.
GASZ: An actively managed fund of companies tied to natural gas power, such as engine makers, turbine builders and pipeline companies. It is concentrated: Caterpillar and GE Vernova are about 25% of it, and nearly two thirds of the fund is industrials.
GAUG: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a moderate amount of losses over a one-year period starting in August. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
GAVA: A fund that gives exposure to AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain, without having to buy and store the crypto yourself. It holds AVAX directly and may earn staking rewards, so its value moves with the price of one volatile crypto asset.
GBHI: An actively managed fund holding high-yield bonds, which are loans to companies with weaker credit ratings that pay higher interest to make up for the added risk. It spreads money across many issuers, and no single one, such as SoftBank, is more than about 3% of the fund.
GBIL: US Treasury bills and notes maturing in one year or less, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bonds are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
GBND: An actively managed fund of investment-grade US bonds, mainly Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It is a core bond fund, meant as a broad, fairly steady slice of the US bond market rather than a high-risk one.
GBTC: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and aims to follow its price, so its shares rise and fall with bitcoin. It holds no stocks or bonds, and bitcoin prices can swing widely.
GBUG: An actively managed fund of gold and silver mining companies, including explorers, producers and royalty firms. Miners can swing more than the metals themselves, and the top holdings are each only about 5% of the fund.
GCAD: An actively managed fund of companies in commercial aerospace and defense, including parts makers and aircraft builders like Boeing. It is concentrated in smaller suppliers, with Albany International and Moog each at about 6% or 7%.
GCAL: Holds bonds issued by California and its local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax and often California tax. It is actively managed, with managers choosing bonds of varying maturities, and its holdings are spread across many small positions.
GCB: A mix of US government bonds and investment-grade corporate bonds with intermediate maturities, following a FTSE index. It is a core bond fund, a basic building block spread across Treasuries and companies' debt.
GCC: An actively managed fund giving broad exposure to energy, farm goods, industrial metals and precious metals through futures contracts, rather than by holding physical commodities. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills as collateral, and a small slice is in a Bitcoin fund.
GCLO: An actively managed fund that invests in investment grade collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are bundles of loans to companies sliced into bonds. Investment grade CLOs are the safest slices, so they pay less than lower-rated ones.
GCOR: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, following a core bond index. It spreads money across thousands of bonds, with US Treasury notes as the biggest pieces.
GCOW: Large companies from around the world that pay high dividends and also produce lots of free cash flow, meaning cash left after running the business. It is spread out, with the largest holdings only about 2% each.
GCPB: An actively managed fund of US bonds, mostly investment grade, with room for some lower-rated and other debt for extra yield. Goldman Sachs analysts pick the bonds instead of following an index, aiming for income plus modest price growth.
GCPU: Companies that supply computing power for artificial intelligence and bitcoin mining, including data center and cloud providers, following an index built around that theme. It is concentrated in a handful of volatile names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, DigitalOcean, Hut 8 and IREN.
GDE: Gives exposure to both US large company stocks and gold futures in one fund, using futures for the gold part. About 85% is in stocks like NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet, with the rest in gold-linked contracts.
GDEC: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 15% of losses over a one-year period that starts each December. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
GDIV: An actively managed fund of US large companies that pay dividends and are expected to grow them over time. It is spread across financials, industrials and health care, with Apple and Eli Lilly the biggest holdings at about 4% to 5% each.
GDLC: A fund that holds a basket of the five largest cryptocurrencies directly, following a CoinDesk index, rather than owning crypto company stocks. Bitcoin and Ether are the biggest pieces, and its value moves with crypto prices, which can swing sharply.
GDMA: An actively managed mix of other ETFs spread across stocks, bonds, inflation-linked Treasuries, gold and cash-like holdings, shifted over time as the managers see fit. Roughly 60% sits in two low-risk holdings, short-term inflation-protected bonds and a box-spread ETF, so it is a cautious blend.
GDMN: Gold futures combined with shares of gold mining companies, so it gets both the metal's price and miners' stock moves. Newmont, Barrick and Agnico Eagle are the largest miners, together roughly a quarter of the fund.
GDOC: An actively managed fund of US and international health care companies tied to themes like new technology and better patient care. Eli Lilly is about 13% and Johnson & Johnson about 8%, so a few large drug makers drive a good share of how it behaves.
GDOG: A fund that holds actual Dogecoin, a cryptocurrency that began as an internet joke, so buyers get its price movements without handling a crypto wallet. It holds only that one coin, so its value swings with Dogecoin alone.
GDT: An actively managed mix of inflation-protected US Treasury bonds and gold, which the fund holds directly or through a subsidiary. It combines two traditional inflation hedges, so part of its movement follows the price of gold.
GDX: Companies that mine gold and a few that mine silver, held in proportion to their size, tracking the NYSE Arca Gold Miners index. It is concentrated, with Agnico Eagle, Newmont and Barrick making up about 29%, and it swings with gold prices.
GDXJ: Smaller gold and silver mining companies from around the world, tracked by a VanEck index. Miners tend to swing more than gold itself, and it is spread across many names, with Evolution, Equinox and Alamos each about 6%.
GDXW: A fund that aims for about 1.2 times the weekly return of a gold miners stock group, using swaps and shares. It resets every week, so results over longer periods can drift from that, and it pays out income often.
GDXY: An actively managed fund that uses options on a gold miners fund to produce regular income. It gets only part of the gains if gold miners rise, and still takes much of the losses, so it trades upside for income.
GEEQ: An actively managed fund that holds stocks plus derivatives to give stock-like returns, and aims to pay out extra income from options. Selling options for income tends to cap gains in strong markets compared with owning the stocks alone.
GEM: Emerging markets stocks selected from an index that tilts toward factors like value, momentum, quality and low volatility rather than just company size. Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 28% of it, so chip makers matter a great deal.
GEMD: A bond fund that tracks a rules-based index of investment grade and high yield bonds issued by emerging market governments and related entities, all in US dollars. It is spread across many countries, with no single issuer more than about 2% of the fund.
GEME: An actively managed fund holding a concentrated set of large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and India. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 17% of it, and technology is around 40% of the total.
GEMQ: A fund of emerging market stocks that uses Goldman Sachs' data-driven models to choose and weight them rather than just tracking an index. It covers companies in developing economies, so it tends to be more volatile than funds of developed markets.
GEND: About 25 to 50 US dividend-paying companies chosen by the manager, spread across health care, financials, energy and industrials. No holding is much bigger than about 5%, including Northern Trust, CVS, Enbridge and JPMorgan.
GENM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds, loans to US states and local governments whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It focuses on higher-quality bonds, is spread across many issuers, and the largest holdings are only about 3% each.
GENT: An actively managed fund of investment-grade US bonds with medium-term maturities, meaning borrowers rated as fairly safe. About half of it is in US Treasuries, with the rest mainly in corporate bonds, so it is a core, middle-of-the-road bond holding.
GENW: About 25 to 50 dividend-paying companies outside the US, chosen by the manager, with a tilt toward banks and financials. Barclays, BBVA, ABB, BNP Paribas and Mitsubishi UFJ are each about 4% to 5% of the fund.
GENZ: Companies built around the digital economy, such as gaming, online platforms and digital finance, from a VanEck index. Its biggest holdings are Shopify, Uber, NetEase and Electronic Arts, each about 8%, so it is fairly evenly spread.
GEQ: A global stock fund that spreads money roughly equally across holdings, including other ETFs, instead of favoring the biggest companies by size. That makes it less top-heavy than a normal index fund, with no single holding above about 3%.
GEW: An actively managed fund of stocks worldwide, partly directly and partly through other ETFs, aiming to weight holdings equally rather than by company size. That makes it more spread out than a typical global index, with the largest position around 6%.
GFEB: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 15% of losses over a one-year period that starts each February. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection applies only if shares are held for the full period.
GFGF: An actively managed fund of high quality US and global stocks favored by well known long term investors, at prices the manager sees as reasonable. Microsoft is about 8% and Alphabet about 5%, and technology and financials are the biggest areas.
GFLW: Large US growth companies that generate positive free cash flow (cash left after running the business and investing), chosen and weighted by a rules-based index. It leans heavily on technology at about 47%, with companies like Sandisk, Caterpillar and NVIDIA each at roughly 3% to 4%.
GGM: An actively managed fund of funds that holds sector ETFs and may trade them often. Nearly all of it sits in five funds, including consumer staples, utilities and energy, so it is a bet on a few sectors rather than the whole market.
GGME: Tracks an index of companies in next-generation media and gaming, such as streaming, social platforms, chips and software. It leans heavily into big tech: Apple, NVIDIA, Meta, AMD and Netflix each make up roughly 7% to 8% of the fund.
GGOV: An actively managed fund of government bonds from countries around the world, with the currency exposure hedged back to US dollars. The hedging removes most of the swings from foreign currencies, so results depend mainly on interest rates in those countries.
GGRW: An actively managed fund of stocks in companies it believes are driving innovation, mostly in technology and industrials. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon and Applied Materials are each about 5% to 9% of it, so a handful of big names drive much of the fund.
GGTL: An actively managed fund buying technology companies from around the world. It leans on Taiwan Semiconductor, which is about 9% of the fund, and holds a smaller slice of Treasury bills alongside the stocks.
GGUS: Tracks the Russell 1000 Growth Index, holding large US companies expected to grow faster than average. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA and Apple each about 11% and Microsoft, Broadcom and Tesla adding another 13% or so.
GHTA: An actively managed fund of other ETFs, mixing stocks and bonds and shifting between them as conditions change. Right now it holds mostly bond and floating-rate funds, with stocks only a bit over a quarter, so it works as a tactical balanced portfolio.
GHYB: A broad basket of US high-yield (junk) corporate bonds, tracking an index built on the FTSE US High-Yield Market Index. The borrowers are riskier companies that pay more interest, and the fund holds so many bonds that none is above about 0.4%.
GHYG: Tracks an index of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, from companies in the US and abroad, paying higher interest because the issuers are riskier. It holds well over a thousand bonds, so no single issuer is more than a small slice of the fund.
GIAX: A fund that holds a basket of stock ETFs covering global markets and sells call spreads, a type of options trade, to earn income. The options trade some upside for income, and it holds mostly large US and international stocks.
GIEQ: Stocks of companies outside the US, picked by a Goldman Sachs model that uses data to tilt toward stocks it rates as more attractive while staying broadly diversified. It looks like a normal international fund, with ASML, Nestle and Roche among its biggest holdings, each at a few percent or less.
GIGB: Corporate bonds from investment grade companies, meaning firms with relatively strong credit, tracked by a rules-based index. It holds a large number of bonds from banks and big industrials, and no single issuer is above about 0.3%.
GIGL: Investment-grade bonds from US companies, meaning businesses with solid credit ratings, held in an actively managed portfolio. It is very spread out across many issuers, mainly banks and other large corporations, with each holding around 1% of the fund.
GII: About 75 of the largest infrastructure companies around the world, such as airports, toll roads, power utilities and pipelines, tracked by the S&P Global Infrastructure Index. It is spread across countries and companies, with the biggest holdings, like Aena and Transurban, around 5% each.
GINC: An actively managed bond fund aiming for income from many types of debt, including corporate bonds and a small share of preferred stock. Rather than tracking an index, the managers choose across sectors, which makes it broader than a plain bond index fund.
GIND: A fund of stocks from companies in India, run by Goldman Sachs with a focus on the country's fast-growing economy. Banks are the largest group, and ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank and Reliance Industries are among the top holdings.
GINN: Global stocks of companies using new technology to change their industries, tracking a Goldman Sachs innovation index. It is spread thin, with the biggest names, Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Amazon and Alphabet, only about 2% each, and has a big weighting in tech and health care.
GINX: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying global companies that trade on US exchanges, plus a short-dated options strategy meant to generate extra income. Banks and financials are the largest part, and the options income comes at the cost of some upside.
GISC: An actively managed bond fund built mostly from securitized debt, meaning pools of loans like mortgages, car loans and credit cards bundled into bonds. It aims for income, and it is spread across many pools instead of a few holdings.
GJAN: Uses exchange-traded options on the S&P 500 to deliver a set outcome over a one-year period starting in January. A moderate buffer is meant to absorb the first slice of any market losses, but gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
GJUL: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a moderate amount of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
GJUN: A buffer fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first chunk of losses (about 15%) over a one-year period that starts in June. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
GK: An actively managed fund that holds US stocks of companies of any size, with a focus on growth and technology. It is concentrated in a few names: Micron, Alphabet, Eli Lilly and NVIDIA together are about a third of the fund.
GKAT: An actively managed global stock fund from Scharf, which looks for companies it believes have more upside than downside over the long run. It is fairly diversified, with no holding above about 5%, and tilts toward health care, financials and technology.
GLAM: An actively managed fund holding companies in beauty, skincare and aesthetics, from cosmetics sellers to health care firms. It is concentrated, with AbbVie, the maker of Botox, about 15% of the fund, followed by Colgate-Palmolive and Estee Lauder.
GLBL: Large companies from developed countries, chosen from the MSCI World Index by picking those with the biggest weight in each of 25 industry groups compared with the index. Tech is heavy here, and Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, Alphabet and NVIDIA are each around 5% of the fund.
GLCR: Companies based in Iceland, plus foreign companies closely tied to its economy, following a Nasdaq Iceland index. It is a small, narrow market, with two Icelandic banks, Islandsbanki and Arion Banki, together making up over a quarter of the fund.
GLD: A fund that holds physical gold bars in vaults, so its price follows the price of gold. It owns no companies and pays no income, so what it is worth depends only on gold.
GLDB: Blends bitcoin and gold, mainly through other ETFs that hold them, and shifts the mix up or down over time using a set strategy. It is a two-asset fund with no company stocks, so its results depend on bitcoin and gold prices.
GLDI: An exchange-traded note (a bank-issued debt security, not a fund) that follows a covered call strategy on the SPDR Gold Trust: gold exposure plus income from selling monthly call options. The options income comes at the cost of capping some gold gains, and it carries the issuer's credit risk.
GLDM: Physical gold bars held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of gold. It holds no companies and pays no income, so any gain or loss comes only from the price of gold.
GLDN: A fund that holds gold mining and royalty company stocks along with a gold ETF, then sells options on them to generate extra income. The options give up some of the upside when gold stocks surge, and the fund is concentrated in a single industry.
GLDW: A leveraged fund that aims for about 1.2 times the weekly return of a gold ETF, using swaps and other contracts, and pays out distributions weekly. Because the leverage resets each week, its results over longer periods can differ from 1.2 times gold's move.
GLIN: Indian companies chosen as growth leaders, held through a subsidiary based in Mauritius, a common route for investing in India. It leans toward financials, with BSE, Trent and Bharti Airtel among the largest holdings at about 5% each.
GLIX: Stocks of infrastructure companies around the world, such as railroads, power and gas utilities, toll roads and airports, picked by an active manager. It is fairly concentrated: Canadian National Railway, National Grid and Vinci together are about a quarter of the fund.
GLNK: Holds Chainlink's LINK token directly, so its value follows the LINK price. It is a crypto fund that can swing a lot, and it does not hold stocks or bonds.
GLOF: Holds large and mid-sized companies from around the world, chosen by an optimized method that aims to tilt toward five traits: momentum, value, quality, size and low volatility. Because it is global but heavy in tech, NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 16% of it.
GLOW: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs to spread money across US and international stocks, with at least 40% of it in ETFs focused outside the US. Much of it sits in sector funds, with technology, financials and health care the biggest pieces.
GLRY: An actively managed fund of mid sized US companies chosen under faith-based screening rules from Inspire, with a focus on growth. It is spread across about equal holdings, with the biggest around 6%, and tilts toward technology and industrials.
GLTR: Physical gold, silver, platinum and palladium bars held in vaults, with each share backed by a basket of those metals. Its value follows precious metals prices, with gold making up the largest part, and it pays no income.
GMAC: An actively managed global macro fund that can invest in stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities anywhere in the world. It can bet on prices rising or falling, following big economic trends, so it has no fixed mix like a normal index fund.
GMAR: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a moderate amount of losses over a one-year period starting in March. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
GMAY: Uses exchange-traded options on the S&P 500 to deliver a set outcome over a one-year period starting in May. A moderate buffer is meant to absorb the first slice of any market losses, but gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
GMEY: Aims to pay high income based on GameStop stock, using options rather than owning the shares. The options bring in payouts but cap the gains when GameStop rises, but it can still fall if the stock drops, and its Treasury bills are mostly collateral.
GMF: Large and mid-size companies from emerging Asia Pacific markets, such as Taiwan, China, India and South Korea, excluding Japan. It is top-heavy on chip makers: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 18% across its two listings in the fund.
GMIE: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, run by GMO and focused on companies that look cheap compared with their value. It is spread across many names, with ASML, BBVA, Toronto-Dominion and Banco Santander each around 3% to 4%.
GMMA: A tactical allocation fund that mostly holds an S&P 500 index fund plus a short-term Treasury bond fund, and shifts between them as its strategy sees fit. About two thirds is in US large stocks and a third in short-term government bonds.
GMMF: A money market fund that keeps nearly everything in cash, Treasury bills and other short-term US government obligations. It aims to hold a stable price while paying interest that follows short-term rates, and it is a place to park cash rather than to grow money.
GMNY: An actively managed fund of New York municipal bonds, mostly with intermediate maturities, whose interest is generally free of federal and New York income tax. Holdings are spread thin, with no single bond more than about 1% or 2% of the fund.
GMOD: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and alternative strategies, mostly built from other GMO and third-party funds. The top holdings are GMO's US Quality, International Value and US Value ETFs, each about 10% of it.
GMOI: An actively managed fund that buys stocks outside the US that GMO thinks are cheap compared with their true worth. Financials are over a third of it, and big holdings include Toronto-Dominion Bank, TotalEnergies and BHP at about 3 to 4% each.
GMOM: A fund of funds from Cambria that owns other ETFs across stocks and assets around the world, favoring those that have been moving up recently, a style called momentum. It is actively managed and spreads money over several Cambria funds, mostly at 11% to 13% each.
GMOV: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that GMO considers cheap relative to their value. It is spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and has bigger positions in Meta, Alphabet, Qualcomm, Merck and Exxon than a typical value fund.
GMUB: An actively managed mix of intermediate-term municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It holds hundreds of bonds from many states and territories, and none is much above 1% of the fund.
GNMA: US government-backed mortgage bonds issued through Ginnie Mae, where homeowners' monthly payments flow through to the fund as income. Because the government guarantees these bonds, credit risk is low, but prices still move with interest rates and how fast people repay their mortgages.
GNMX: An actively managed fund buying health care companies working on genomics and precision medicine, such as gene-based drugs and DNA tools. It is concentrated: Thermo Fisher and Moderna are about 8% each, with Vertex and Illumina next.
GNOM: Tracks an index of companies working in genomics, the study and use of DNA, and biotechnology. It spreads fairly evenly across smaller, research-driven health companies, with the largest holdings at about 4% to 6% each, which makes it volatile.
GNOV: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set part of losses over a one-year period that starts in November. In return, gains are capped, and it works as intended only if held for the whole period.
GNR: Large global companies tied to natural resources: energy, mining, agriculture and timber, tracking an S&P index of 90 of them. Materials are about half and energy about a third, with BHP, Nutrien, ExxonMobil and Shell among the largest holdings.
GOAU: Stocks of gold and precious metals companies, with a strong tilt toward royalty and streaming firms that fund miners in return for a share of output, instead of running mines themselves. Franco-Nevada, Osisko and Wheaton Precious Metals are about 29% of the fund.
GOCT: A buffer fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in October. In exchange, gains are capped at a limit, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
GOEX: Holds gold mining companies around the world that are mainly searching for new gold deposits rather than running big established mines. Hecla, DPM Metals, Coeur and Eldorado Gold are each about 4% to 5%, so its price can swing with gold.
GOIB: Aims to pay high income from Alphabet, Google's parent company, by combining swaps and options on the stock, rather than just owning shares. Because it sells upside through options, it will not fully share in big gains.
GOLI: An actively managed fund that aims to pay income while following the price of gold through the SPDR Gold Shares ETF. It sells options on gold to earn that income, which caps how much it can gain if gold rises.
GOLS: An actively managed fund of companies in live entertainment and sports, such as team owners and venue operators. It is concentrated: Madison Square Garden Sports, Atlanta Braves Holdings and Liberty Media are together about a quarter of it.
GOLY: A fund that aims to earn income on top of gold exposure, using gold-linked investments alongside a large holding of investment-grade corporate bond funds. Much of what it owns is other bond ETFs, so it is a mix of gold and bonds, not a pure gold fund.
GOOP: Aims to pay income while following Alphabet (Google) stock by using options on it, which limits how much of a rise in the share price it can capture. Most of the fund is held in Treasury bills, so it is not simply a pile of Google shares.
GOOW: A fund that seeks about 1.2 times the weekly move in Alphabet (Google) stock, using swaps and some shares, and pays out distributions every week. It is a bet on a single company, and the Treasury bills listed are backing for the swaps.
GOOY: A fund that earns income by selling options tied to Alphabet (Google) stock. It collects option payments to pay out a high yield, but this limits gains if Alphabet rises, and the fund still takes most of the losses if it falls.
GOP: An actively managed fund of US stocks that tracks what sitting Republican members of Congress are buying, based on their public disclosures. It is fairly concentrated: Comfort Systems, Intel and JPMorgan Chase are about 20% of the fund.
GOVI: US Treasury notes and bonds from zero to thirty years in maturity, with each of up to 30 securities weighted about equally. Because it spreads evenly across short and long maturities, it has less tilt toward long bonds than a typical market-weighted Treasury fund.
GOVM: US Treasury bonds that mature in one to ten years, tracking an index of those government bonds. Backed by the US government and spread across hundreds of issues, with a middle-of-the-road sensitivity to interest rate changes compared with very short or very long Treasuries.
GOVT: A broad mix of US Treasury bonds of all lengths, from short to very long, weighted by size. Backed by the government, it gives a middle level of interest rate sensitivity, since the short and long bonds balance out.
GOVZ: Treasury STRIPS that mature in about 25 years or more, which are zero-coupon bonds that pay no interest along the way and instead are bought at a discount. Their prices swing a lot when interest rates change, much more than ordinary bonds.
GPIQ: Holds the Nasdaq-100's large, tech-heavy stocks and sells call options on them to earn extra income, which pays a premium but caps gains in strong rallies. Technology is about 60% of it, with NVIDIA and Apple among the biggest holdings.
GPIX: Holds the S&P 500's large US companies and sells call options on them to collect extra income, which brings in a premium but caps gains when stocks surge. NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are the largest holdings, and technology is about 40% of it.
GPRF: Preferred stocks and hybrid securities from US issuers, following an index, which pay fixed dividends and sit between bonds and common stock. It is built for income and spread out, with no single holding above about 1%.
GPT: A global large-company stock fund that uses artificial intelligence to pick stocks and hold them in roughly equal amounts. The AI looks at major trends to choose names, so it leans toward technology, industrials and health care, and is spread out with no holding above about 5%.
GPTY: An actively managed fund holding AI and technology stocks and using options on them to generate income. NVIDIA, Snowflake and Alphabet are each about 6% of it, and the options strategy aims to pay out regular income but limits how much it gains when stocks rise.
GPZ: Stocks of companies that run alternative asset businesses such as private equity, tracked with a VanEck index. It is concentrated: Blackstone, Brookfield, KKR and Apollo together make up about 40% of the fund.
GQGU: An actively managed, concentrated fund of US stocks chosen by GQG Partners. Despite its growth label, it currently leans toward defensive areas, with ExxonMobil, Philip Morris, Altria, AT&T and Verizon each between 5% and 6.5% of the fund.
GQI: An actively managed fund of high-quality large US stocks that also sells call options on an index to produce extra income. The options limit some upside, and the stocks are top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are about 20% of it.
GQQQ: An actively managed fund of US growth companies that the managers rate as high quality, with a Nasdaq-100-like look. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it, and roughly half the fund is in technology.
GQRE: Global real estate companies, mostly property owners and landlords, picked by an index that favors those scoring well on quality, value and momentum. It is spread across countries and property types, with Equinix, Prologis and Welltower the largest holdings at about 16% combined.
GREK: Large and mid-sized Greek companies, tracked through an MSCI index. It is a single-country fund heavy in banks: National Bank of Greece, Eurobank, Piraeus and Alpha Bank are together about 45% of it.
GRID: Companies that build and equip the electric grid, such as makers of grid equipment, smart meters and power infrastructure, tracking a Nasdaq Clean Edge index. Eaton, Schneider Electric, ABB and Quanta are each about 8%, around a third together.
GRIN: Growth companies from developed countries outside the US, picked by an index that looks for businesses producing strong free cash flow, meaning cash left after expenses. It leans heavily to chips and tech, with Kioxia, ASML and Advantest each making up several percent.
GRNB: Tracks an index of dollar-denominated green bonds, whose proceeds fund environmental projects like clean energy and efficient buildings. Issuers include development banks, governments and companies from many countries, so it is a diversified bond fund with a climate-focused use of money.
GRNI: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked by Fundstrat's growth-focused themes, paired with an options strategy that aims to pay regular cash distributions. The options can limit gains in strong markets, and holdings are spread out, none above about 3%.
GRNJ: An actively managed fund of US small and mid-sized companies, using the Granny Shots approach of picking stocks that fit several investing themes at once. No single holding is above about 3% of the fund.
GRNY: An actively managed fund of about 35 large US stocks picked by Fundstrat using a mix of research and what it sees as major market themes. Each holding is a small slice, around 2% to 3%, so it is more evenly spread than most big stock funds.
GROZ: An actively managed fund of US growth companies chosen by Zacks using its own research ratings. It is top heavy, with Apple, NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft together making up about 34% of it, and technology is over half the fund.
GRPM: The top 60 stocks in the S&P MidCap 400 that combine growth with good quality and reasonable price, a style called growth at a reasonable price. With only 60 stocks, each is a few percent of the fund at most.
GRPZ: About 90 US small companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that score well on both growth and reasonable price, a style called growth at a reasonable price. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings each only around 2%, and tilts to financials and health care.
GRW: An actively managed fund of US and global companies the manager thinks will benefit from change driven by technology and shifting customer habits. It holds a small group of stocks, with TransDigm, Broadcom and General Electric around 20% of it.
GSC: An actively managed fund of small US companies, using a mix of research and quantitative screening to pick them. It holds many stocks with none above about 2%, so it behaves like a broad small-company fund rather than a bet on any single name.
GSEE: A broad basket of large and mid-sized stocks across emerging markets, covering roughly the largest 85% of each country's market. It is top-heavy in Asia's chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix together are about 27% of the fund.
GSEP: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each September. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold from the start to the end of that period.
GSEU: Developed European stocks selected and weighted by Goldman Sachs using factors like value, quality, momentum and low volatility, rather than size alone. ASML is the largest holding at about 4%, and financials are the biggest sector.
GSEW: Large US companies held in nearly equal amounts, instead of weighting by size, so small and big firms count about the same. The top holdings are each about 0.4% of the fund, so it is much less top-heavy than the S&P 500.
GSG: A commodities fund that holds futures contracts tracking the S&P GSCI index, which covers energy, metals and farm goods. It holds no physical goods, and energy like oil is the largest slice, so oil price swings drive much of how it moves.
GSGO: An actively managed fund of US growth stocks that Goldman Sachs expects to expand faster than average. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 31% of it, and technology makes up around half.
GSIB: An actively managed fund of stocks in the world's largest and most important banks, the ones regulators watch closely because their failure would shake the whole system. It is all financials, and the top holdings are each about 4%.
GSID: A low-cost fund holding large and mid-sized companies from developed markets outside the US, tracking a broad index in roughly market proportions. It is widely spread, with ASML the biggest at under 3%, and it leans toward financials and industrials.
GSIE: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked to tilt toward four traits: low risk, value, quality and momentum. It is very spread out, with the biggest holding, chip equipment maker ASML, only about 2% of the fund, and financials are around 29%.
GSJY: Tracks an index of Japanese stocks that is built to follow Japan's market while tilting toward certain traits, such as value, quality and momentum. It spreads across many companies, with Mitsubishi UFJ, Toyota and Advantest each about 3% to 4%.
GSKH: A way to own GSK, the UK drugmaker, through its US traded shares while hedging out changes in the British pound versus the dollar. It holds one company, so its value follows GSK alone, apart from the currency swings.
GSLC: Large US companies in roughly the same mix as the broad market, but with a rules-based tilt toward stocks showing good value, momentum, quality and low volatility. Tech giants still dominate: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of the fund.
GSOL: A trust that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, and aims to track its price less expenses. It also stakes some coins to earn rewards, so it is crypto exposure and can swing sharply in price.
GSPY: An actively managed take on the S&P 500, mostly holding its companies but with the manager adjusting which stocks and how much of each. It looks a lot like the index, with Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft making up about 19% of it.
GSSC: Small US companies chosen and weighted by a rules-based index that tilts toward stocks with traits like value, quality and low volatility. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, so it is a broad small-company fund with a factor twist.
GSUI: Holds the SUI cryptocurrency directly, so its value follows the price of one digital coin. It also stakes the coins, meaning they help run the network and earn rewards, which carries the usual risks of a single volatile crypto asset.
GSUS: A low-cost fund that holds large and mid-sized US companies, tracking a broad index of the US stock market. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together make up roughly 20% of the fund.
GSWO: A fund of stocks from around the world, including the US, that uses Goldman Sachs' ActiveBeta approach. It tilts toward traits like value and quality using set rules instead of a manager's picks, so it differs a bit from a plain global index.
GTEK: An actively managed fund of technology companies around the world, aimed at those the manager thinks will lead future innovation. It holds many mid-sized names like MediaTek, Delta Electronics and Marvell, each about 3% to 5%, so it is less dominated by the biggest US tech giants.
GTIP: A fund holding US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, government bonds whose value adjusts up with inflation. It follows an index of these bonds, so it is made up almost entirely of US Treasuries and is often used as a hedge against rising prices.
GTND: An actively managed fund that holds mostly big US stock ETFs, like the Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500, and shifts toward defensive positions based on trend-following signals. The goal is to cut exposure when markets fall, though signals can lag.
GTO: An actively managed bond fund that can hold bonds of any credit quality and maturity, with a big share in US Treasuries and government-backed mortgage bonds. The managers have wide freedom to shift between bond types, so it is not tied to a single bond index.
GTOC: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade bonds, such as government, corporate and mortgage-backed securities, aiming for steady income and capital preservation. It holds a broad, diversified mix of bonds rather than following a single index.
GTOH: High-yield bonds, issued by companies with lower credit ratings, with short times left until they mature. Shorter maturities mean it reacts less to interest rate changes, and its biggest holdings are each about 2% of the fund, so it is spread thinly.
GTOP: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in technology companies, chosen by the manager rather than an index. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Alphabet alone are over 20% of it, with Microsoft, Micron and Amazon next.
GTOQ: An actively managed fund of high-yield (below investment grade) corporate bonds, picked by a rules-based, data-driven process. It spreads across many issuers, with none above about 1% of the fund.
GTOS: An actively managed bond fund holding a mix of short-term bonds, including US Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-related securities. Because the bonds are short-term, prices tend to swing less than in longer bond funds, and the fund aims for steady income.
GTPE: A fund that tries to approximate the returns of private equity, which is investing in privately owned companies, by holding public stocks and similar instruments tracked by a Goldman Sachs MSCI World index. Because it uses stand-ins rather than real private firms, it is mostly technology, industrial and financial stocks.
