GTR: An actively managed fund that uses options on global stocks to aim for returns within a target range, limiting both gains and losses. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills that support the options, so it is a hedged strategy.
GUNR: Global companies that produce natural resources, such as miners, oil and gas producers, fertilizer and farming firms, and timber. About half is in materials and a third in energy, with Exxon Mobil, Corteva and BHP among the biggest holdings.
GURU: US stocks picked from the biggest positions reported by well-known hedge funds in their public filings. It tilts to health care and tech, and holds many smaller companies, with no single name above about 3%.
GUSA: Roughly the 1,000 largest US companies, tracking an index that covers large and mid-size stocks and aims to match the broad US market. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of the fund.
GUSE: An actively managed fund of US large, mid and small companies that starts from the market and tilts toward stocks its models like. It is top-heavy in big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
GVAL: An actively managed fund of cheap-looking stocks from developed and emerging markets, selected by Cambria's rules-based formula. It leans toward financials, materials and energy and toward smaller markets such as Austria, Czechia and Poland, rather than the biggest US companies.
GVI: A mix of US Treasuries, other government-backed bonds and bonds from solid companies, with medium-term maturities, following a Bloomberg index. It holds thousands of bonds, so no single one is more than about 1%.
GVIP: US large company stocks that hedge funds hold most heavily in their long positions, picked by a Goldman Sachs index. It leans toward technology at about a third, and holdings are fairly evenly spread, none above about 3% of the fund.
GVLE: An actively managed fund of large US companies the manager thinks are priced below their worth, spread across financials, health care, technology and more. Alphabet, Micron, Amazon and Chevron are the top holdings at about 5% to 7% each.
GVLU: An actively managed fund holding roughly 400 to 600 mid-sized and large US companies that its model rates as cheap compared with their finances. Positions are small and spread out, with no single stock more than about 1% of the fund.
GVUS: A low-cost fund tracking US large and mid-size stocks that look cheap relative to their size, using the Russell 1000 Value index. It holds hundreds of companies, with Micron, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase the largest at about 2% to 3% each.
GWX: Small companies from developed countries outside the US, following an S&P index of developed-market small caps outside the US. It holds a very large number of stocks, none more than about half a percent, spread over industrials, technology, materials and consumer companies.
GXC: Large Chinese companies tracked by the S&P China index, including those listed in China and ADRs. Tencent and Alibaba are about 17% of the fund, with consumer, financial and communications companies making up much of the rest.
GXDW: A fund that holds other Global X thematic ETFs in roughly equal slices, chosen by an index based on which themes have had strong momentum. Its five biggest holdings, covering blockchain, AI, hydrogen, data centers and lithium batteries, are each about 17 to 22%.
GXIG: An actively managed fund of investment grade corporate bonds, loans to financially solid companies, held directly and through other bond funds. It is spread over many issuers, with some US Treasuries too, and pays regular interest income.
GXLC: The 500 largest US companies, tracking an index similar to the S&P 500 in how it weights them. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of the fund, and technology is around 40%.
GXPC: Holds US communication services companies like Alphabet, Meta and Netflix, but caps how big each one can be so the largest stocks do not dominate as much. Even so, Alphabet's two share classes together are about 58% of it, and Meta is around 20%.
GXPD: US consumer discretionary stocks, the companies selling things people want rather than need, from an MSCI index with a cap-style twist on weights. It is top-heavy: Amazon is over 40% of the fund and Tesla is about 19%.
GXPE: US energy companies from the MSCI USA index, such as oil producers and pipeline firms, weighted so that no single company dominates as much as in a plain market-cap fund. Even so, ExxonMobil and Chevron together are close to half of it.
GXPS: Large US consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of everyday goods, from an MSCI index that caps each stock's weight. It is concentrated, with Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola about half of it.
GXPT: The technology sector of the US market, following an MSCI index, but with limits on how large a few stocks can become. Even so, it is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 50% of the fund.
GXRP: Holds XRP, a cryptocurrency, directly through a Grayscale trust, so its price follows XRP rather than any company's earnings. Crypto prices can move sharply in either direction, and the fund holds the coins instead of stocks or bonds.
GXUS: A low-cost fund covering large and mid-sized companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US, roughly the largest 85% of that market by size. It is broad, with financials, technology and industrials the biggest areas, and Taiwan Semiconductor the largest holding at about 5%.
GYLD: Follows an index of about 150 high-yielding stocks, bonds and other income assets from around the world. It is a mix, with real estate and energy stocks leading, aimed at producing a high payout rather than growth.
HACK: Companies that provide cybersecurity products and services, such as network protection and threat detection software, tracking the ISE Cyber Security index. Broadcom, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Cisco and Cloudflare are about 30% of the fund.
HAIL: Tracks an index of companies tied to smarter, cleaner transportation, such as electric vehicles, self-driving technology, chips and mobility services, from developed and emerging markets. It is spread across many small and mid-sized names, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward technology and consumer discretionary.
HAKY: Holds the cybersecurity stocks of the Amplify Cybersecurity ETF, such as CrowdStrike, Okta, Fortinet and Cloudflare, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. The options give up some of the upside when those stocks surge, and the fund is almost all technology.
HALX: Holds US stocks of companies with lots of physical equipment and property, which an index judges to be hard to make obsolete. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 3%, and leans toward utilities, energy and industrials.
HAP: Global companies in natural resources, covering farming, oil and gas, renewable energy, metals and forestry. It holds big names such as Deere, ExxonMobil and Chevron, and about two thirds of it is in materials and energy.
HAPI: About 150 large US companies chosen by an index that favors firms that invest heavily in their workforce, weighted mostly by company size. Because of that weighting, Amazon, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are each roughly 5% to 6% of the fund.
HAPS: About 200 small US companies picked by an index that favors firms investing heavily in their workers, using measures like pay and staff spending. Holdings are weighted by size, and no stock is large, with the biggest around 3%, tilted toward health care and financials.
HARD: Invests in futures contracts on a broad mix of commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, with a Treasury bill portfolio backing them. It is set up to avoid the K-1 tax form, and its moves follow commodity prices rather than stocks or bonds.
HAUG: Uses options on the S&P 500 to protect against all losses over a one-year period starting each August, in exchange for giving up part of the gains. It only works if you hold the full period, and the 100% in the name is the buffer level.
HAUS: An actively managed fund of real estate investment trusts (REITs) whose income comes from housing-related property, including senior housing and medical properties. Its biggest holdings are Welltower, Ventas and Public Storage, and REITs pay out much of their income.
HAUZ: Real estate companies outside the US, like property developers and landlords, weighted by company size. Japan, Australia and Hong Kong firms such as Goodman Group, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan lead, and no single holding is above about 5%.
HAWG: Holds big US stocks tracking indexes of large companies and tech, with a hedging strategy meant to soften market drops. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up around 29% of the fund, and about half of it is technology.
HAWX: Holds a fund of large and mid-sized stocks from developed and emerging markets outside the US, then uses currency contracts to cancel out swings in foreign currencies against the US dollar. So results mostly reflect the stocks, not exchange rates.
HBDC: A basket of corporate bonds issued by business development companies (BDCs), lenders that make loans to mid sized private firms. It follows a rules based index, and the largest holdings are bonds from firms like Ares, Apollo and Blue Owl at about 1% each.
HBIL: A fund holding very short-term US Treasury bills, which are loans to the US government that mature within a year. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
HBIT: An actively managed fund that gets Bitcoin exposure mainly through other Bitcoin ETFs and uses options to reduce swings and manage downside. Because of the options, it will not track Bitcoin exactly, and it can lag if Bitcoin rises sharply.
HBMX: A concentrated fund of companies in the memory chip supply chain, from memory makers like Micron and SK Hynix to equipment and testing firms. All of it is technology, and the top holdings are about 5% to 10% each.
HBR: A trust that holds HBAR, the token of the Hedera network, and tracks its dollar price using a benchmark rate. It owns only that one digital asset, so it moves with the crypto market and can swing sharply.
HBRD: A bond fund tracking an ICE index that mixes ordinary corporate bonds with hybrid securities, which blend features of bonds and stocks and often pay higher income. About 95% is bonds and about 5% convertibles, so it carries more risk than a plain corporate bond fund.
HBTA: An actively managed fund holding large US growth stocks, with a big share in tech, plus an options strategy meant to cushion losses. NVIDIA, Alphabet and Apple are each roughly 7% to 8%, and a Magnificent Seven fund is another 9%, so it is top-heavy.
HBTC: A fund that aims to give Bitcoin exposure while hedging part of the risk, based on its name and category. Holdings details are limited, so it is best seen as a Bitcoin strategy that uses derivatives rather than a plain fund that just holds Bitcoin.
HCMT: An actively managed fund that gets its exposure to large US stocks mainly through derivatives like futures and options, rather than owning all the shares, aiming for enhanced returns that follow the US market. Much of it is in non-stock holdings, with NVIDIA and Apple the largest stocks at roughly 6% each.
HCOW: Holds a fund that picks cash-rich US companies and adds covered calls, which means selling options for extra income. Those options limit how much it gains when stocks rise, and the portfolio is spread out, with each top holding near 4% to 5%.
HCRB: A broad portfolio of mostly investment-grade US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt, with some foreign issuers. It is actively managed, aiming to work as a core bond holding, and the mortgage bonds shown as TBA are forward purchases of such bonds.
HDEF: Large companies from developed markets in Europe, Australia and Asia outside North America that pay higher-than-average dividends, tracking an MSCI index. It leans toward financials, consumer staples and health care, and Roche, Nestle and Novartis are about 15% of it.
HDG: A fund that tries to mimic the returns of the hedge fund industry, using a mix of stock futures and other financial contracts instead of owning hedge funds. Most of it sits in cash as collateral, and it follows the HFRI Composite Index.
HDMV: Holds stocks of developed-market companies outside the US that are picked to be less volatile, meaning steadier in price. It leans toward utilities, telecom and real estate, with no holding above about 2%, so it is broadly spread.
HDUS: Large US companies picked by a Hartford index that uses a disciplined, rules-based method to select stocks. It looks a lot like the big-company market, with NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet together making up about 24% of the fund.
HDV: About 75 US companies with high dividend yields and strong financial health, from the Morningstar Dividend Yield Focus index. It is concentrated in a few sectors: consumer staples and energy are over half, and Exxon, AbbVie and Chevron are each around 6% to 8%.
HEAL: About 50 companies that use technology to improve health care, such as medical devices, health data and digital health firms, tracked through a theme index. It is spread fairly evenly, with DexCom, IQVIA, Oscar Health and GE HealthCare each around 4% to 5%.
HECA: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and other assets that shifts its allocation as the manager sees conditions change. It mostly invests through other funds, so its top holdings are other ETFs and mutual funds, and it holds a sizable amount of cash.
HECO: Companies tied to the digital asset economy, such as bitcoin miners and crypto-related businesses, with currency hedging aimed at reducing the effect of foreign exchange moves. It is concentrated: Riot Platforms, Keel Infrastructure and CleanSpark are about 31% of it, and it holds stocks, not crypto itself.
HEDG: Holds S&P 500 funds and sells call options on them, which hedges against market drops by giving up some of the gains. Almost all of it is two big S&P 500 ETFs, so it is mostly a lower-volatility version of large US stocks.
HEDJ: Large European companies that earn much of their revenue from exports, with the euro's swings against the US dollar hedged away. Because of the hedge, it follows European stocks without the effect of currency moves, and ASML is about 8% of it.
HEEM: A fund that holds an emerging markets stock ETF and adds currency hedges so that swings in emerging market currencies against the US dollar matter less. It follows the MSCI Emerging Markets index, so it holds stocks from countries like China, Taiwan and India.
HEFA: Developed-market stocks outside the US and Canada (Europe, Japan, Australia and more) held through the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, with currency hedges added. The hedges reduce the effect of the US dollar moving against the euro, yen and pound on what you earn.
HEFT: An actively managed fund that holds a mix of other funds and takes both bets that rise and bets that fall, with long exposure up to about 150% and short exposure up to about 50%. It is built around the manager's view of a cycle called the Fourth Turning.
HEGD: An actively managed fund that holds a large US stock fund tracking the S&P 500, then uses options to protect against big drops. The hedging costs some upside in strong markets, and about 90% of it sits in a single S&P 500 ETF.
HELO: A large US stock fund that also uses options to cushion the fund against big market drops. The options are rolled forward in stages, which limits some of the upside too, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 20% of the stocks.
HELX: Invests in health care companies tied to genomics, the study and use of genes in medicine and diagnostics. It is fairly concentrated, with Guardant Health and Natera together about 17% of the fund, and nearly all of it is in health care.
HEMI: Large US stocks with an options strategy layered on top to generate extra income. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple and Microsoft are about 28% of it, and selling options pays more income but gives up some gains when the market surges.
HEQQ: A fund that holds big Nasdaq stocks and adds an options overlay, set up in a ladder across different dates, to soften the effect of falling markets. Tech dominates: NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 30% of it, though hedging limits some upside.
HEQT: A fund holding an S&P 500 ETF almost entirely, with an options overlay called a collar that limits big losses. In return, gains in strong markets are capped, so it tends to lag a plain S&P 500 fund when stocks rise a lot.
HERD: A fund of funds that holds five Pacer Cash Cows ETFs in roughly equal parts, covering US large, small, growth and international stocks. All of them pick companies with strong free cash flow, which is cash left after running the business.
HERO: Companies around the world that make or benefit from video games and esports, such as game publishers, developers and hardware makers. Holdings are spread across the US, Japan, China and Korea, with no single name above about 7% of the fund.
HEWJ: Japanese stocks held through the iShares MSCI Japan fund, with a currency hedge that aims to offset changes in the yen against the US dollar. So its returns mostly follow Japanese stocks, without the effect of yen moves.
HEZU: Eurozone stocks, held through another iShares fund, with a currency hedge that aims to cancel out the effect of euro-to-dollar moves. Returns therefore follow European shares in local terms, mostly financials, industrials and tech, not the changing exchange rate.
HF: An actively managed fund of other ETFs, mixing US value and growth stocks, international stocks and dividend funds. It also holds an inverse S&P 500 fund, about 19% of it, which rises when the market falls, as a hedge meant to soften downturns.
HFEQ: A fund of funds that mostly holds other ETFs, including Vanguard value, mid-cap and momentum funds, and takes both long and short positions in stocks. It is actively managed, so the mix of what it owns changes over time.
HFGM: A fund aiming to behave like the hedge fund industry's global macro strategies, but with about twice the ups and downs. It does this with long and short positions in 10 to 30 other ETFs and futures, such as emerging markets and China funds.
HFGO: An actively managed fund of large US companies expected to grow faster than average. It is concentrated in a few giants: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Broadcom are about 33% of the fund, and technology is around 60%.
HFIX: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, also called junk bonds, which are issued by companies with lower credit ratings. They pay more interest than safer bonds, but the borrowers are more likely to struggle to repay.
HFMF: An actively managed fund that tries to copy the results of managed futures hedge funds, which trade futures contracts to follow price trends in markets like commodities, currencies and bonds. It mostly holds cash and futures, not company stocks.
HFND: A fund of other ETFs and futures that takes both long and short positions across stocks, bonds and commodities. It tries to copy the broad behavior of hedge fund style strategies, holding about 30 to 50 funds, with no single one above roughly 6%.
HFSI: An actively managed bond fund that mixes several types of debt, including US Treasuries and mortgage-backed bonds, and can reach into riskier corporate bonds. The manager shifts the mix over time to chase income.
HFSP: An actively managed fund that mixes large US company stocks with cash and uses an AI driven process to decide the balance. Holdings details are limited, so the exact mix of stocks and cash can shift as the manager's models change.
HFXI: Large company stocks from developed markets outside the US, with about half of the currency risk hedged back to the US dollar each month. That cuts the swings from exchange rates, though it does not remove them; Samsung, SK Hynix and ASML are among the biggest holdings.
HGER: Gets exposure to a broad mix of commodity futures (things like energy, metals and farm goods) through a quantitative index, using swaps held in an overseas subsidiary. Most of the money actually sits in Treasuries and similar safe assets as backing, so the commodity swaps drive the results.
HGRO: An actively managed fund of US stocks chosen for quality and growth, with a heavy tilt toward technology at around 47%. Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA are about 21% of it, so it behaves a lot like a big tech fund.
HH: US dollar corporate bonds rated below investment grade, often called junk bonds, from US and foreign companies, following a FTSE index. They pay more interest than safer bonds but the companies are more likely to struggle to repay.
HIAI: An actively managed fund of mostly US large company stocks, where artificial intelligence helps pick which ones to hold. It is fairly concentrated: Apple is about 9% of it, and technology makes up around 40% of the whole fund.
HIDE: A mix of three other ETFs: intermediate-term US Treasury bonds, real estate and commodities, shifted around by a rules-based trend system. The idea is to hold up when inflation or deflation hits, and about half of it is usually in Treasuries.
HIDV: An actively managed fund of US stocks with higher-than-average dividend yields, picked by the managers instead of following an index. Despite the income focus, it is tilted to big tech: NVIDIA and Apple are about 16% of the fund together.
HIGH: Holds mostly short-term US Treasuries and another Simplify fund, and adds an options strategy to try to pay more income than Treasuries alone. The options layer adds risk beyond ordinary Treasuries, and income can change from month to month.
HIMU: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, loans to US states and cities, with a focus on higher-yielding and lower-rated ones. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, but the lower credit quality of many holdings means more risk than a standard muni fund.
HINC: An actively managed fund of high-yield corporate bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, issued by companies with lower credit ratings. They pay more interest than safer bonds but carry a higher chance the issuer fails to repay, and the managers choose the bonds themselves.
HIPS: Tracks an index of up to 40 US-listed investments that pass most of their earnings to shareholders as cash, such as energy partnerships, real estate companies and income funds. It is built for high payouts, and energy, financials and real estate make up most of it.
HIS: An actively managed fund of US companies, mostly large ones, chosen by its managers in a focused way. It is tilted toward the biggest tech names: Apple, Alphabet, NVIDIA and Microsoft are each about 6%, or roughly 24% of the fund together.
HISF: An actively managed fund that invests in a set of other First Trust bond ETFs following the firm's High Income Model. It aims for a steady income stream by blending different kinds of bonds, with one underlying fund making up about 28% of it.
HIYY: An actively managed fund that aims for income using options tied to Hims & Hers Health stock, which limits gains if the stock rises. It holds mostly Treasury bills to back those options, so it is a single-company bet rather than a normal stock fund.
HJLY: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a very large buffer against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in July. The name points to a 100% buffer, which only applies if held for the full period.
HJUN: A fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim to protect against losses over a one-year period starting each June, in exchange for capping the gains. The name says it targets a 100% buffer, and it resets every year.
HLAL: Large and mid-sized US companies that pass Shariah (Islamic law) screens, which exclude things like banks, alcohol and gambling. It ends up very tech heavy, with Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Broadcom making up about 35% of the fund.
HLTH: An actively managed fund of health care companies that use artificial intelligence or data in areas like genetics, diagnostics and medical devices. It is concentrated, with 10x Genomics, Twist Bioscience and Illumina together making up about 20% of the fund.
HMAY: A defined outcome fund that uses options on large US company stock funds to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 100% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on when you hold it.
HMOP: Municipal bonds, issued by US states, cities and agencies, that are generally free from federal income tax, picked by Wellington Management's managers. It holds both investment-grade and lower-rated bonds in search of more income, and is spread across many issuers, each around 1% to 2%.
HMYY: A fund that uses options on a leveraged ETF tied to HIMS, a health and wellness company, to generate income. Leverage and options make its results very different from the stock itself, and the Treasury bills it shows are backing for those contracts.
HNDL: A fund of other ETFs that follows the Nasdaq 7HANDL index, which splits money between stocks and bonds and is built to pay out a high, steady income. It holds mostly other funds, including bond funds and an energy pipeline fund, and the payout can include a return of your own capital.
HODL: A trust that holds actual bitcoin and tracks its price, valued daily from a bitcoin benchmark rate. It holds no stocks or bonds, so its value swings with bitcoin alone, and it pays no income.
HOID: Companies that earn at least half their revenue from humanoid robots, the human-shaped machines, or commit that much of their assets to making them or their parts. It is a narrow theme fund, so a small group of robotics firms drives its results.
HOLA: A fund holding international stocks, but with a built-in options strategy meant to reduce how much it moves with the market, and the options are layered over time. This hedging may limit its gains in strong markets, and ASML, Siemens and AstraZeneca are among the larger holdings.
HOLD: Holds a fund that tracks the S&P 500 and layers a trend-following futures strategy on top, so each dollar gets both stock market exposure and a bet on price trends in other markets. About 40% is in an S&P 500 fund, with the rest in cash and futures.
HOMZ: About 100 US companies tied to housing, such as homebuilders, home improvement stores, real estate trusts and mortgage lenders, tracked through a rules-based index. No holding is large, with Home Depot and Lowe's each around 3%, so the bet is spread across the whole housing industry.
HOOW: Aims to deliver about 1.2 times the weekly return of Robinhood stock, using swaps and the stock itself. It is a leveraged bet on one company that resets each week, and it pays distributions weekly, with Treasury bills held as collateral.
HOOY: An income fund that gets exposure to Robinhood (HOOD) stock using options rather than owning it directly. It sells call options to produce high monthly payouts, which caps the upside, and the Treasury bills listed are mainly backing for those options.
HOYY: An income fund tied to Robinhood stock that uses options and swaps instead of owning the shares directly, aiming to pay large distributions. Most of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing, and the strategy limits how much it can gain if the stock rises.
HQDG: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends and have raised them over time. It is a concentrated group of about 30 or so stocks, with Microsoft, KLA, Texas Instruments and Casey's around 5% each.
HQGO: US large companies chosen for high quality and growth, picked by an index and weighted toward technology. It is fairly top-heavy: NVIDIA, Amazon, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft each make up about 5% of the fund.
HRSK: US large company stocks, held through S&P 500 futures, index funds and individual stocks, with a hedging layer meant to reduce losses in downturns. A sizeable share is held in cash, so it is more cautious than a plain S&P 500 fund.
HRTS: Health care stocks of companies earning much of their revenue from GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs or from heart and metabolic disease treatments. Eli Lilly is about 12% of it, and the top eight holdings are about 42%.
HSBH: A fund tied to a single stock, HSBC Holdings, the large London-based global bank, with currency moves hedged so the US dollar value follows the share price more closely. Almost all of it, about 96%, is that one company, so it moves with one bank.
HSCZ: Small and mid-sized stocks in developed countries outside North America, held through another iShares ETF, with currency hedging that reduces the effect of the euro, yen and pound moving against the dollar. It follows the MSCI EAFE Small Cap index.
HSEP: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim to cover all losses (a 100% buffer) over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
HSMV: A fund of US small and mid-sized stocks chosen because they have tended to move less than the overall market. It leans toward real estate, financials, industrials and utilities, and no holding is more than about 2% of the fund.
HTAB: An actively managed bond fund aiming for income that is lightly taxed, mostly holding municipal bonds plus some mortgage-linked and Treasury bonds. The manager considers taxes when choosing bonds, so it differs from a plain muni or bond index fund.
HTAX: Municipal bonds, which are loans to US state and local governments, with interest generally free from federal income tax. It focuses on higher-yielding, riskier issuers, including a notable share tied to Puerto Rico.
HTEC: Stocks of companies that use technology in healthcare, such as genetic testing, diagnostics and lab tools, following the ROBO Global healthcare technology index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 3% of the fund.
HTRB: An actively managed bond fund that mixes US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds, aiming for both income and price gains. It can hold some lower-rated junk bonds and foreign debt, and a manager picks the bonds rather than following an index.
HTUS: An actively managed fund that mostly holds an S&P 500 index fund, then adjusts how much stock market exposure it has using its own models. Because it can shift toward or away from the market, it will not move in lockstep with the index.
HULL: An actively managed fund of companies in shipping, delivery and global logistics. Amazon is the largest holding at about 13%, with FedEx, UPS and Expeditors close behind, and nearly a third of the fund is in energy.
HUMM: Companies that help supply the high-voltage power systems used in AI data centers, such as power chips and electrical equipment makers. It is a narrow, non-diversified theme, with Vicor, Navitas and Infineon each making up about 6 to 8% of the fund.
HUMN: An actively managed fund of companies working on humanoid robots, including makers of the parts and software that power them. It is concentrated in a young theme, with UBTech and Tesla about 5% each, and has holdings in several countries.
HUSV: US stocks selected to be steadier than the overall market, aiming for smaller ups and downs by favoring less volatile companies. Its largest holdings, such as Cisco, Gen Digital and VeriSign, are each only around 3% of the fund.
HVAC: An actively managed fund holding US industrial companies tied to heating, cooling, building systems and the electrical equipment behind them. Sterling Infrastructure and Comfort Systems are the two largest at about 7% to 9% each, and industrials plus some technology make up the whole fund.
HWGV: An actively managed fund buying global stocks that managers think are cheap compared with what the companies are worth, known as value investing. It holds many companies without big bets, with its top holdings Workday, SAP and AIG each around 3% to 4%.
HWIV: An actively managed value fund of companies outside the US, bought when they seem cheap compared with what the managers think they are worth. It is spread over many countries and sectors, and its largest holdings include Akzo Nobel, SAP and Shell.
HWMV: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies that the manager believes are priced below their worth, often out-of-favor or recovering businesses. It holds a modest number of stocks, with the top five, including Workday, AIG and Kosmos Energy, making up about 19%.
HWO: An actively managed fund from Hotchkis & Wiley that buys stocks it thinks are undervalued, plus some bonds including junk bonds. It is concentrated and flexible, with Workday alone about 12% and sizable stakes in technology, energy, materials and industrial firms.
HWSM: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that the manager thinks are priced cheaply compared to their worth. It is widely spread, with no holding above roughly 3%, and leans toward financials, consumer companies and technology.
HXA: An actively managed fund that tries to copy hedge-fund style corporate arbitrage strategies, using stocks, other funds, closed-end funds and derivatives. Its biggest positions are other ETFs, such as a minimum-volatility fund at about 11%, so it is a mix of funds rather than a simple stock basket.
HXC: An actively managed fund that gains exposure to a broad mix of commodities through futures and related contracts, partly held through a Cayman Islands subsidiary. A large share of the fund sits in cash and short-term bonds that back those contracts.
HXE: An actively managed fund that mostly holds other ETFs, such as S&P 500 quality, Russell 1000 and Russell 2000 funds, and adjusts them using a hedging approach. Technology is about half of the stocks underneath, so it is a US stock mix that can change.
HXF: An actively managed managed futures fund that takes long and short positions across stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, trying to follow big market trends in either direction. It does not hold a fixed basket of stocks, and its results can differ a lot from stock markets.
HYBB: US corporate bonds rated BB, the top tier of high-yield bonds, so they are riskier than investment-grade bonds but usually safer than lower-rated junk. It holds hundreds of bonds, each well under 1% of the fund.
HYBI: An actively managed fund that holds other high-yield (lower-rated, higher-interest) bond ETFs and also sells S&P 500 put options to bring in extra income. Roughly equal thirds sit in three high-yield bond funds, and the options add stock market risk on top of the bond risk.
HYBL: An actively managed fund of US dollar high yield debt: junk corporate bonds, senior loans and pieces of CLOs (pools of company loans). Higher income comes with higher default risk, and holdings are spread thin, with the largest around 1% of the fund.
HYBX: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds, often called junk bonds, which are loans to companies with weaker credit that pay higher interest. Most of the money sits in bonds, with a small slice held in cash.
HYD: Tax-exempt bonds from US states, cities and agencies with weaker credit ratings, so they pay higher interest but carry more risk of default. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%, including some Puerto Rico and tobacco settlement bonds.
HYDB: US high-yield bonds, also called junk bonds, which are loans to companies with weaker credit ratings that pay higher interest in return for more risk. Rather than following an index by size, it uses a rules-based approach to pick bonds, and no single bond is more than about 1%.
HYDR: Follows an index of companies involved in hydrogen technology, such as fuel cells and electrolyzers. It is concentrated and global: Doosan Fuel Cell and Bloom Energy are around 16% each, and Plug Power, Ballard and FuelCell Energy add up to a lot more.
HYDW: US dollar junk bonds, meaning corporate bonds from lower-rated companies, chosen to be less sensitive to swings in the broader high yield market. It holds many bonds, with the largest, EchoStar, around 1% of the fund.
HYEM: Holds US dollar bonds from companies in emerging markets that are rated below investment grade, tracking a VanEck index. These pay higher interest than safer bonds but carry greater default risk, and it is spread over hundreds of issuers.
HYFI: An actively managed fund of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the companies borrowing are riskier. It holds hundreds of different bonds, with none above about 1%, and uses some derivatives.
HYG: Bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest to make up for the greater risk of default. It holds hundreds of bonds, each under 1%, so no single company matters much.
HYGH: A fund that holds the iShares high yield corporate bond fund, which owns bonds from riskier companies, and uses interest rate futures to offset the effect of rising rates. It still carries the credit risk of those bonds, but is less sensitive to interest rate moves.
HYGM: A fund that holds the iShares high yield corporate bond ETF and sells weekly call options on it to aim for a 10% target income. Selling those options brings in extra cash but limits how much it gains when the bond fund rises.
HYGV: US dollar bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, which pay higher interest because they are riskier. Instead of weighting by debt size, an index scores bonds on quality, value and ease of trading, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
HYGW: Holds the iShares high-yield corporate bond fund and sells call options on it to earn extra income. The options premium boosts income, but it can limit gains when the bonds rise, and the cash shown is mostly backing for the options.
HYHG: A fund that holds high-yield (junk) corporate bonds but uses short positions in Treasury futures to reduce its sensitivity to interest rate changes. This aims to keep the credit income while softening losses when rates rise, though it can still lose value when junk bonds fall.
HYIN: An index-based fund of income-focused companies, mostly mortgage REITs and firms that lend to businesses, rebalanced every quarter. Holdings are evenly spread, each about 3% or 4%, and it is roughly half real estate and half financials.
HYLB: A broad basket of US dollar corporate bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds. They pay higher interest than safer bonds in exchange for a bigger risk that the companies fail to repay, and thousands of small positions keep any one bond below about 1%.
HYLS: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds, also called junk bonds, which are loans to companies with lower credit ratings that pay higher interest for more risk. The managers can shift their mix of bonds, loans and cash as markets change, and no single bond is above about 2%.
HYMB: Tax-exempt bonds from US states, cities and agencies with weaker credit ratings, following an ICE index. They pay higher interest but carry more risk, and Puerto Rico bonds are among the biggest holdings at a few percent each.
HYP: Actively managed US stocks the managers expect to grow unusually fast, mostly in technology, energy and health care. It spreads money fairly evenly, with top holdings around 3% each, and tends to hold smaller, fast-moving companies like Argan and Comfort Systems.
HYPG: Gives exposure to the HYPE token of the Hyperliquid platform, and the fund stakes it, meaning it locks tokens up to help run the network and earn extra rewards. It is a single-crypto fund, so its value moves with one volatile digital asset.
HYS: US high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, with five years or less left until they mature, tracking an ICE BofA index. The shorter maturities should make it less sensitive to interest rates, though it still takes the credit risk of lower-rated companies.
HYSA: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other BondBloxx ETFs covering high yield corporate bonds, which are riskier company bonds that pay higher interest. About half is in BB rated bonds, 40% in B rated and 10% in the lowest CCC rated.
HYSD: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds, often called junk bonds, which are loans to companies with weaker credit that pay higher interest. It focuses on shorter maturities, so prices swing less, and it spreads thinly across hundreds of bonds with no holding above about 1%.
HYTI: Holds US Treasuries and uses options on a high-yield corporate bond ETF, selling call options to generate extra income. The option sales cap some of the upside from rising junk bond prices, so it aims for high monthly income rather than price growth.
HYTR: A fund following a rules-based index that shifts between high-yield (junk) bond ETFs and cash-like holdings depending on market trends. Its holdings are three high-yield bond ETFs, so it aims to take part in junk bonds when they trend upward and step aside when they do not.
HYUP: Follows an index of US junk bonds, which are corporate bonds from lower-rated companies, picking those that tend to move more than the broader junk bond market. It holds many bonds with none above about 1%, so it swings more than a plain high-yield fund.
HYXF: US dollar high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, from issuers with better ESG ratings, with extra screens that leave out some businesses. It holds hundreds of bonds, with no single one above about 1%, and pays more income than safer bonds because of higher credit risk.
HYZD: High-yield corporate bonds, meaning bonds from less creditworthy companies that pay more interest, combined with a hedge that reduces the effect of rising interest rates. Each bond is a tiny slice, with no holding above about 1%.
IACL: Uses derivatives to earn income tied to the Nasdaq-100 through an autocallable structure, a contract that pays out when the index is above set levels on certain dates. Its returns depend on that structure rather than simply tracking the index, and the fund is non-diversified.
IAGG: Investment grade bonds from governments and companies outside the US, with currency swings hedged back into US dollars. China government bonds are among its larger holdings, and the hedging removes most of the effect of exchange rates.
IAI: US broker-dealers and securities exchanges, companies like investment banks, brokerages and market data firms, tracking an index of that part of the financial sector. It is top-heavy: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are about 38% of the fund.
IAK: US insurance companies, such as auto, property and life insurers, following a Dow Jones index. It is top-heavy, with Progressive and Chubb together about 27% of the fund and Travelers and Allstate adding roughly another 14%.
IALT: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, bonds and alternative strategies, aiming to hold up in both strong and stressful markets. It works more like a multi-strategy blend than a regular stock or bond fund.
IAPR: Uses options on an iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which tracks developed stock markets outside the US and Canada, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in April. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the whole period.
IAT: US regional banks, tracking a Dow Jones index of mid-sized banks that lend to local customers rather than the biggest national names. It is concentrated, with PNC and US Bancorp each about 14 to 15% and Truist around 9%.
IAU: A trust that holds physical gold bars, so its price follows the price of gold bullion. It is not actively managed, owns no companies and pays no income, so what it is worth depends only on gold.
IAUG: A defined outcome fund tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, using options over a set one-year period starting in August. It aims to cushion part of the losses, and in exchange gains are capped.
IAUI: A fund that gets exposure to gold prices through gold funds, and sells options to generate income. The options give up some gains if gold rallies, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing for the strategy, not the main point of the fund.
IAUM: A fund backed by physical gold held in a vault, so its price follows the gold price. It has a small share price, so it is easy to buy a little, and it pays no income and holds no stocks.
IBAT: Companies that help with energy storage, including hydrogen, fuel cells and batteries, tracking a global index. The holdings come from around the world, and Bloom Energy, Air Products, Air Liquide and BASF are each around 7% of the fund.
IBB: US-listed biotech companies, which develop new drugs and therapies, tracking a biotechnology index. Vertex, Amgen and Gilead are about 23% of it, and it is non-diversified, meaning it can hold larger stakes in fewer companies.
IBBQ: Tracks the Nasdaq Biotechnology Index of drug and biotech companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, from large to small. It is weighted toward the biggest names, with Gilead, Vertex and Amgen together making up about 22% of the fund.
IBCA: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2035. The bonds are held until they mature and then the fund winds down, so it behaves more like a single bond with a set end date than an ongoing bond fund.
IBCB: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in December 2036. The fund pays out interest and then winds up around that date, returning the bonds' face value, so it behaves more like a single bond than an ever-rolling fund.
IBD: A fund of US corporate bonds from large companies, screened by Inspire's values-based rules that avoid companies that conflict with biblical principles. Holdings are spread evenly, with each of the largest positions about 2% of the fund.
IBDR: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2026, from many US and foreign companies. The fund has a set end date in December 2026, returning cash as bonds mature, and no single bond is above about 2%.
IBDS: A basket of bonds from financially solid US companies that all mature in 2027, after which the fund shuts down around December 2027 and hands back what is left. It owns hundreds of bonds, and no single company is more than about 1%.
IBDT: A basket of US investment grade company bonds that all mature in 2028. As the bonds mature the fund winds down and closes in December 2028, so it behaves a bit like a single bond, with holdings spread across hundreds of issuers like CVS and Pfizer.
IBDU: A basket of bonds from financially solid US companies that all mature in 2029, after which the fund shuts down around December 2029 and hands back what is left. It owns hundreds of bonds, and no single company is more than about 1%.
IBDV: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2030, from many US and foreign companies. Each bond is a small slice, with none above about 1%, and the fund is set to close out in December 2030, returning the money as bonds mature.
IBDW: A basket of US investment-grade company bonds that all mature in 2031, so the fund is built to wind down in December of that year. It holds hundreds of companies, each about 1% or less, and pays income along the way.
IBDX: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, tracked by an iBonds index. The bonds are paid back around December 2032, when the fund is designed to wind down, and it spreads across many companies with none above about 1%.
IBDY: A portfolio of US investment-grade corporate bonds all maturing in 2033, which ends in December of that year. As bonds mature the fund winds down and returns cash, and it is spread over many issuers, each around 1% of it.
IBDZ: A basket of US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in December 2034. As they come due, the fund winds down and returns the money, so it acts more like a single bond, spread over many companies with none above about 1%.
IBFR: An actively managed fund of large and mid sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, using options to cushion part of the losses over a set period, in exchange for limits on gains. ASML is the largest holding at about 3%, and financials are about a quarter of it.
IBGA: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2044, held until the fund ends in December 2044 and pays back what is left. It behaves like one long bond, so its price moves a lot when interest rates change.
IBGB: A set of US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2045, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. A few big bond issues make up most of it, and because the bonds are long, its price swings a lot when interest rates move.
IBGC: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2046, so it works like one long bond that slowly winds down. Because the maturity is so far away, its price can swing a lot when interest rates change.
IBGK: A fund of US Treasury bonds that mature in December 2054, held until they mature. The fund then winds down, so it behaves like one very long-term bond with a set end date, and its price moves a lot when interest rates change.
IBGL: A fund of US Treasury bonds that mature in December 2055, held until they mature. The fund then winds down, so it behaves like one very long-term bond with a set end date, and its price moves a lot when interest rates change.
IBGM: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2056, tracked by an index. Since it holds only long-dated government bonds, its price moves a lot when interest rates change, and it is meant to wind down when the bonds mature.
IBHF: A portfolio of US company bonds rated below investment grade and in the BBB range that all mature in 2026, held until the fund winds down. As bonds are repaid, it pays out cash, and it carries more credit risk than government bonds.
IBHG: A basket of US dollar corporate bonds, mostly high-yield with some BBB-rated, that all mature during 2027. As the bonds come due the fund winds down and pays out the money, so it acts like one bond with an end date, spread over many issuers.
IBHH: A basket of US company bonds with lower credit ratings that all mature during 2028, so it winds down and returns cash at the end. Because the issuers are riskier, it pays higher income, and no single company is above about 2%.
IBHI: A basket of US dollar corporate bonds, mostly high-yield with some BBB-rated, that all mature during 2029. As the bonds come due the fund winds down and returns the money, so it behaves like one bond with an end date, spread over many issuers.
IBHJ: A basket of high-yield (lower credit quality) US corporate bonds that all mature in 2030, so it winds down and returns the money at the end of that year. No single bond is more than about 1.5% of the fund.
IBHK: A basket of US dollar high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds because the issuers are riskier, that all mature in 2031. The fund is set to wind down around then, returning money as the bonds mature, and its holdings are spread across many small positions.
IBHL: A basket of US dollar high-yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, tracking an index of them. The fund is designed to end in 2032, when the bonds mature and the fund pays out, and the holdings are spread across hundreds of issuers with none above about 3%.
IBHM: A basket of high yield and BBB-rated US dollar corporate bonds that all mature in 2033. It pays interest and winds down as that date arrives, and it is spread across many issuers, with none above about 2%.
IBID: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) that mature by October 2027, which adjust with inflation. The fund holds them until the end date and then closes, so it behaves more like a single bond than an ongoing fund.
IBIE: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) that all mature in 2028, with the fund set to wind down around October 2028. Because the bonds' principal rises with inflation and everything matures together, it works like a single-year inflation-linked bond ladder.
IBIF: Holds US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, whose value rises with inflation, that mature in 2029. The bonds are held until they mature and the fund then closes, so it works like a bond ladder with one end date, in this case October 2029.
IBIG: Treasury inflation protected securities, called TIPS, that mature by October 2030, whose principal rises with inflation. It holds the bonds until they mature, so the fund winds down in 2030, with only four main bonds making up almost all of it.
IBIH: A basket of US Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) that all mature in 2031, with the fund ending in October 2031. TIPS raise their principal with inflation, and the fund pays back its holdings near the end date instead of lasting forever.
IBII: A basket of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that all mature in 2032, whose principal rises with inflation. The fund ends in October 2032, when it pays back what is left, so it behaves like one bond with a set end date.
IBIJ: A basket of US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that mature in 2033, held until the fund ends in October 2033. Its payouts rise with inflation, and because the maturity is fixed it behaves more like one bond than an ever-rolling fund.
IBIK: Holds US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that mature in 2034, and the fund closes out that year. Principal rises and falls with inflation, and holding to the end date gives a more predictable outcome than a regular bond fund.
IBIL: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds (TIPS) that all mature in 2035, so the fund has a set end date and is meant to be held until then. Its payouts rise and fall with inflation, and it holds only government bonds.
IBIM: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), whose principal rises with inflation, that all mature in October 2036. The fund is designed to wind up around that date, when the bonds mature, and is made almost entirely of government-backed securities.
IBIT: A trust that holds actual bitcoin, so its price tracks the price of bitcoin without needing a crypto exchange account. It owns no companies and pays no income, and as a single asset it can swing sharply.
IBLC: Stocks of companies tied to blockchain and digital assets, such as crypto exchanges, bitcoin miners and chip makers, picked to follow an index. It is concentrated: Coinbase, Iris Energy and Hut 8 are about 26% of it, and it leans heavily toward financials and technology.
IBMO: A basket of investment-grade, tax-exempt US municipal bonds that all mature in December 2026. As the bonds come due, the fund winds down and returns the money, so it behaves like one bond with a fixed end date, and no single issuer is more than about 1%.
IBMP: A basket of tax-exempt US municipal bonds that all mature in December 2027, so the fund winds down that year and returns the money. It holds hundreds of investment-grade bonds from many issuers, and income is generally free of federal income tax.
IBMQ: A basket of tax-exempt US municipal bonds that all mature in December 2028, so the fund winds down that year and returns the money. It holds hundreds of investment-grade bonds from many issuers, and income is generally free of federal income tax.
IBMR: A basket of US municipal bonds that all mature in December 2029, with interest generally free from federal income tax. The fund winds down in that year and returns the money, and no single bond is more than about 1%.
IBMS: A basket of investment-grade municipal bonds that all mature in 2030, so the fund winds down in December of that year. Muni interest is generally free from federal income tax, and it is spread across many issuers, none above about 1%.
IBMT: Investment grade municipal bonds, loans to US states, cities and school districts, that mature by December 2031. It holds the bonds until they mature, so it winds down in 2031, and the interest is generally exempt from federal income tax.
IBMU: Holds municipal bonds, loans to US states and local governments, that mature in December 2032 and pay interest generally exempt from federal income tax. The fund winds down in that year and returns its money, and it is spread across many issuers, none above about 1%.
IBMV: A basket of US municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, that all mature in December 2033. The fund winds down then and returns the money, so it behaves more like a single bond than a normal open-ended bond fund.
IBMW: A fund of US municipal bonds that mature in 2034, tracking an S&P index, so it is designed to wind down in December of that year. The income is generally exempt from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 2%.
IBMX: A basket of municipal bonds all maturing in December 2035, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds end around the same time, the fund closes down at that date and pays out the proceeds.
IBND: Investment-grade corporate bonds issued by companies outside the US, following a Bloomberg index of that market. It holds hundreds of bonds from many issuers, so no single borrower is more than a small piece, and the bonds are in foreign currencies, so exchange rates affect it.
IBOT: Tracks an index of global companies in the robotics and automation business, from factory equipment makers to chip and software firms. It spreads across many names, with ASML, Keyence and ABB each at about 5%, and it is split between technology and industrials.
IBRN: A fund tracking an index of companies working on treatments for the brain and nervous system, mostly small biotech and drug developers. Holdings are spread fairly evenly, with the top names, like Dianthus, Xenon and Praxis, each about 5%, and results depend heavily on trial outcomes.
IBTG: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2026, tracking an index of bonds due by December of that year. The fund closes when the bonds mature and pays back the money, so it has a set end date very soon.
IBTH: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2027, tracked by an index, so the fund has a set end date when the bonds pay back. Because the bonds shorten over time, it behaves like a single bond that steadily pays interest and winds down in December 2027.
IBTI: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2028, tracking an index of bonds due by December of that year. The fund closes when the bonds mature and pays back the money, so it has a set end date.
IBTJ: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2029, with a December end date. As the bonds mature, the fund winds down and pays out, so it behaves like one bond with a set end date and very low credit risk.
IBTK: US Treasury bonds that all mature around December 2030, tracking an index of such bonds. The fund is designed to end that year and return the money, so it works like a ladder of government bonds held until maturity.
IBTL: US Treasury bonds that mature in 2031, held until the fund ends in December 2031 and then paid back as cash. Before that, it works like a bond ladder with a set end date, and the price moves with interest rates.
IBTM: A basket of US Treasury notes and bonds maturing in 2032, with a set end date in December of that year, when the fund pays out its cash. Backed by the US government, it pays income along the way and acts more like a single bond than an ongoing fund.
IBTO: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2033, so it behaves like a bond with a set end date. As the bonds approach maturity the fund winds down and pays back the cash, and it holds only government debt.
IBTP: A basket of US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2034, held in an iShares iBonds fund. The fund is built to end in December 2034, returning its money then, so it works like a bond with a set finish line.
IBTQ: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2035, held until they come due, then paid back. Its price moves with interest rates until then, and because it only holds government debt, credit risk is minimal.
IBTR: US Treasury bonds that all mature in December 2036, so the fund pays interest and then winds down around that date. It is a way to hold a fixed-end-date bond portfolio, though its price still moves with interest rates until then.
IBUF: A defined outcome fund that uses options on an international developed stock ETF, the iShares MSCI EAFE, to cover a set amount of losses over a three month period, in exchange for a cap on gains. It resets every quarter.
IBUY: Global companies that make most of their money selling online, such as web retailers and travel or marketplace sites, picked by an index of the online retail business. It is fairly even across its stocks, with the biggest, like Wayfair and Hims & Hers, each only about 3%.
ICAP: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying stocks, with some preferred shares, chosen by a manager who favors sectors that look undervalued. It holds a fairly small group of stocks, with Marvell, Citizens Financial and Toll Brothers each about 5%, and spans technology, housing and financials.
ICF: US real estate investment trusts (REITs), companies that own and rent out properties like cell towers, warehouses and apartments. It holds about 30 of the biggest, with Welltower, Prologis, Equinix and American Tower making up around 30% of it.
ICLN: About 100 clean energy companies from around the world, such as solar, wind, fuel cell and power producers, tracked by an S&P index. It holds both developed and emerging market firms, and First Solar, a Chinese hydropower company, Nextpower and Bloom Energy are about 30%.
ICLO: An actively managed fund of floating rate notes issued by collateralized loan obligations (CLOs, pools of company loans) rated AAA, the highest credit rating. The interest rates float, so income moves with short-term rates, and the fund sticks to the top-rated slices of CLOs.
ICMO: A fund of mostly other ETFs that holds stocks outside the US, shifting toward countries that have recently done well. About a quarter sits in a broad developed markets fund, and the rest is spread across single country funds.
ICOM: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to commodities, such as energy, metals and farm goods, and aims to generate income as well. Commodity prices can swing widely, so it behaves very differently from a stock or bond fund.
ICOP: Companies that mine copper and other metals around the world, following an index of such miners. It is concentrated: BHP, Anglo American, Grupo Mexico and Freeport-McMoRan are each roughly 8% of the fund, and the whole thing is materials stocks.
ICOW: Large non-US companies in developed markets that produce a lot of cash compared with their price, picking the top 100 and weighting them by cash flow. Holdings are spread across industrials, consumer goods, energy and communications, each about 2%.
ICPI: Short-term US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) with under a year left, whose principal rises and falls with inflation. Because they mature so soon, the price should barely move, and the fund is almost entirely US government debt.
ICPY: An actively managed fund of undervalued stocks outside the US, where company insiders are buying shares or the company is buying back its own stock. Tweedy, Browne picks them, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
ICVT: Convertible bonds, which are bonds from companies that can be swapped for the company's stock, tracked by a Bloomberg index. They sit between bonds and stocks, so they tend to move with the stock market, and no single bond is above about 3%.
IDAU: A defined-outcome fund using options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF (developed markets outside North America) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in August. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
IDEC: A fund using options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed stock markets outside the US and Canada. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in December, and in exchange gains are capped.
IDEF: An actively managed fund of defense and related industrial companies, plus technology firms, from the US and abroad, picked by a manager. RTX, Palantir, Lockheed Martin and Rolls-Royce are about 19% of it.
IDEQ: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US, picked by Lazard using a mix of valuation, quality and momentum measures. It is spread across financials, technology and industrials, and its largest holdings, such as Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung, are each only about 3% to 5%.
IDEV: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Japan, the UK, Canada and Europe, following an MSCI index. It is spread out, with the top holding, ASML, about 2%, and financials the largest sector.
IDGT: Holds US companies that own data centers, cell towers and related equipment, mostly real estate trusts. It is concentrated, with Equinix, Digital Realty, American Tower and Crown Castle among the largest, and the top five about 37% of it.
IDHQ: Quality companies from developed markets outside the US, picked from a broad S&P index for traits like strong profitability and steady earnings. It is spread out across industrials, tech, health care and financials, with Roche, ASML and Novartis the largest at about 5% each.
IDJL: A defined-outcome fund using options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF (developed markets outside North America) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in July. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
IDJN: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 15% buffer, over a set period starting in June. Gains are limited.
IDLV: The 200 least volatile stocks from developed markets outside the US and South Korea, chosen by S&P. It leans toward steady sectors like banks and utilities, and no holding is more than about 1% of the fund.
IDMO: Large companies in developed markets outside the US that have recently been rising faster than others, picked and weighted by an S&P momentum index. At the moment it leans heavily toward European and Canadian banks like HSBC, Santander and Toronto Dominion.
IDMY: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on international developed-market stocks to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in May. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held for the full period.
IDNA: Global companies working in genomics and immunology, such as gene editing, cell therapy and biotech drug developers. It holds many smaller biotech names, and the top ones like Bayer, Twist Bioscience and Revolution Medicines are each near 5%.
IDOG: Stocks from developed markets outside the US, picked by taking the highest dividend payers in each sector of an international index. Spread across sectors and countries such as Finland, Japan, Italy and Poland, with no holding above about 3.5%.
IDRV: Companies around the world involved in electric and self-driving vehicles, including automakers, battery makers and chip suppliers. It is spread across many names, with BYD, Li Auto, Rivian and NIO each around 4 to 5%, and has big exposure to China.
IDSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on a developed-markets stock ETF outside the US to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
IDU: US utility companies, the businesses that supply electricity, gas and water, tracking an index of the utilities sector. It is led by NextEra Energy at about 11%, with Southern Company and Duke Energy also among the biggest holdings.
IDUB: An actively managed fund that holds a broad basket of international stocks, mostly through a Vanguard international stock ETF, and adds options-style swaps to generate extra income. The income boost comes at the cost of giving up some of the stock market's upside.
IDV: About 100 high dividend paying companies in developed markets outside North America, picked by a Dow Jones index. It leans toward banks, energy and utilities, with TotalEnergies, British American Tobacco and Enel among the biggest holdings.
IDVO: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying international companies, mostly held as US-listed ADRs. It also sells call options on some holdings to earn extra income, which limits gains when stocks surge, and it pays out regular income.
IDVY: Companies outside the US that have raised their dividends steadily, following a Nasdaq index of international dividend achievers. It is spread across many names, mostly in Japan and Europe, with no holding above about 2% and financials and industrials the largest sectors.
IDVZ: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying companies outside the US, chosen for steady dividends and quality. Its top holdings, Enel, Intesa Sanpaolo, Petrobras and GSK, are each only about 3% to 4%, so no single name dominates.
IDX: Indonesian companies from a VanEck benchmark index, held in a broad mix of the country's largest businesses. It leans toward banks, with Bank Central Asia and Bank Rakyat Indonesia about 17% of it, and also holds materials and energy firms.
IDYN: An actively managed fund of stocks outside the US that shifts between investing styles, such as value, quality and momentum, depending on which the managers like. It is well spread out, with ASML the largest holding at around 4%.
IEF: US Treasury bonds that mature in seven to ten years, following an index of such bonds. Backed by the government, with a price that reacts to interest rates more than short-term Treasuries do but less than 20 year bonds.
IEFA: Tracks an MSCI index of large, mid-sized and small companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, mainly Europe, Japan and Australia. Financials and industrials are the biggest sectors, and ASML, HSBC and Roche are top holdings, each a small slice.
IEI: US Treasury bonds that have between three and seven years left until they mature, so it sits in the middle of the Treasury range. Government-backed with no credit risk to speak of, but its price still moves with interest rates.
IEMG: Stocks from emerging markets such as China, India, Taiwan and South Korea, following an MSCI index of large, mid-sized and small companies. It is top-heavy in Asian chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 25% together.
IEO: US oil and gas exploration and production companies, plus refiners, tracking a Dow Jones index. It is concentrated, with ConocoPhillips, Valero and Marathon Petroleum making up about 38% of the fund, and nearly all of it is energy.
IETC: US technology companies picked for the evolution of the sector, such as chips, software and cloud services, from large down to small. It is concentrated, with NVIDIA and Broadcom alone at about 22%, and tech is over 80% of the fund.
IEUR: A broad mix of large, mid and small European companies from the UK, Switzerland, France, Germany and others, tracked by an MSCI index. It is well spread: ASML is the biggest holding at about 4%, and financials are about a quarter of it.
IEUS: Small European companies from the MSCI Europe Small Cap Index, from countries like the UK, Sweden and Switzerland. It holds many names, with the biggest under 1% each, and leans toward industrials and financials.
IEV: Large companies across Europe, tracking the S&P Europe 350 Index, which covers about 350 leading businesses from countries including the UK, France, Germany and Switzerland. It holds companies from many countries and sectors, with ASML the largest at about 5% and financials the biggest sector.
IEZ: US companies that provide equipment and services to the oil industry, tracked by a Dow Jones index. It is top-heavy: Baker Hughes and SLB alone are about 43% of the fund, so two companies drive much of the result.
IFEB: Uses options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which holds large companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in February. In return, gains over that period are capped.
IFED: An exchange traded note, which is a debt of the bank that issues it rather than a fund that owns stocks, tracking an index of companies expected to benefit from Federal Reserve policy. It carries the issuer's credit risk and does not hold the stocks itself.
IFGL: Real estate companies in developed countries outside the US, following the FTSE EPRA Nareit Developed ex US Index. It includes landlords and developers like Goodman Group, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan, and is spread across many names.
IFLN: A fund holding corporate bonds that were once investment grade but have been downgraded to high-yield, called fallen angels, and tracks an enhanced version of the Bloomberg index. These bonds pay more interest than safer ones, but with higher risk, and the holdings are spread thinly, each under 5%.
IFLO: A fund of non-US stocks picked by an index that favors companies with strong free cash flow, which is the cash left after running and investing in the business. It holds many companies, each around 2%, across industrials, technology, energy and consumer sectors.
IFLR: An actively managed fund of stocks in developed countries outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, that uses options to limit how much it can lose over a set period. That managed floor comes at a cost, since part of the upside is given up.
IFRA: US companies tied to building and running infrastructure, such as utilities, railroads, construction and materials firms. The stakes are fairly even: the largest holdings, Caterpillar, NextEra and Union Pacific, are each only about 4%.
IFV: A fund of funds that holds five First Trust country ETFs outside the US, picked by Dorsey Wright's momentum rankings. Each pick is about 20% of the fund, so it is concentrated in five countries and the mix can change when the index is reshuffled.
IG: An actively managed fund buying investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies seen as lower risk of default. Managers choose the bonds themselves instead of following an index, and big banks like Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are among the largest issuers it holds.
IGB: Investment-grade US dollar corporate bonds from US and foreign companies, following a FTSE index. Investment grade means the issuers have solid credit ratings, so the fund pays more interest than Treasuries with more risk, and it covers bonds of many lengths.
IGBH: A fund that holds long-term US corporate bonds but uses interest rate futures to cancel out most of the effect of rising or falling rates. It mainly owns an iShares long-term corporate bond fund, so it is mostly exposed to company credit rather than rate moves.
IGCB: An actively managed fund of US corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with a range of maturities. The TCW team picks bonds themselves, so it can differ from a plain corporate bond index, and a small share sits in cash.
IGE: US-listed stocks of natural resource companies in North America, mostly oil and gas producers plus miners and other materials makers. Energy is about 70% of the fund, and ExxonMobil and Chevron together are close to 20%.
IGEB: US investment-grade corporate bonds picked by a computer-driven method that looks at factors like value and quality instead of just following a standard index. It holds many bonds from banks, airlines and other companies, with none above about 0.5%.
IGF: Large infrastructure companies around the world, such as airports, toll roads, electric and gas utilities and pipelines. It is split roughly evenly between utilities and industrials, with some energy, and holds Spanish, Australian, US and Canadian names.
IGGY: An actively managed fund of growth-oriented companies based outside the US, spread across at least three other countries. It leans on technology and industrials, and Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and ASML together are about 18% of the fund.
IGHG: US investment-grade corporate bonds, paired with interest rate hedges meant to offset losses when rates rise. That means it mostly earns the extra income from corporate bonds without taking as much interest rate risk as a normal bond fund.
IGIB: US dollar bonds from financially sound companies, with five to ten years left until they mature. They pay more interest than Treasuries, move more with rates than short-term bond funds, and are spread across hundreds of issuers with none above about 0.2%.
IGLB: Investment-grade US company bonds that mature in ten years or more, from companies like Anheuser-Busch, CVS and Boeing. Because the bonds are long-term, its price moves more than a short-term bond fund when interest rates change, and it pays income.
IGLD: A fund that uses options on gold to try to pay out high income, backed mostly by short-term Treasury bills and cash. The option selling limits how much it gains if gold rises sharply, and the Treasury and options positions shown are the mechanics, not the main investment.
IGM: A wider take on tech that holds technology companies plus some related ones, such as internet and media firms. NVIDIA, Apple, Broadcom and Microsoft are each about 8%, so around 31% of the fund sits in those four.
IGOV: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US, paying in local currencies, tracking an investment-grade international Treasury bond index. Since the bonds are in foreign currencies and the fund is not hedged, currency moves affect results as well as interest rates.
IGPT: US-listed companies that make or use artificial intelligence software, tracking an Invesco index. It is concentrated: Alphabet, NVIDIA, Meta and Advanced Micro Devices are each about 9%, so those four make up over a third of it.
IGRO: International companies outside the US that have a record of growing their dividends, picked and weighted by the dividend dollars they pay. It is spread out, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Nestle and Novartis each only about 3% of the fund, and leans toward financials.
IGSB: US dollar bonds from financially sound companies, but only those maturing in one to five years. Shorter maturities mean its price moves less than longer corporate bond funds when interest rates change, and it spreads across a very large number of issuers.
IGV: US software companies, from enterprise software to security, tracked by an S&P software index. It is concentrated: Palo Alto Networks, Microsoft, Palantir and CrowdStrike together are about a third of it, and it is almost all technology.
IHAK: Companies in cybersecurity and related tech, such as firms that protect networks, identities and data, tracking an index of those businesses. It is spread fairly evenly, with Qualys, Varonis, Palo Alto Networks and Okta each about 5%.
IHDG: Quality dividend-growing companies from developed markets outside the US, such as Japan and Europe. It hedges currency, using contracts to cancel out the effect of foreign currencies moving against the dollar, so returns mostly follow the stocks themselves.
