IHE: US drug makers, covering companies that make prescription and over-the-counter medicines and vaccines, tracking a Dow Jones pharmaceuticals index. It is concentrated: Johnson & Johnson and Eli Lilly are each about 22%, so those two make up nearly half of the fund.
IHF: US health care providers such as insurers, hospital operators and managed care companies, tracking an index of that part of the health care sector. It is very concentrated: UnitedHealth and CVS Health alone are about 37% of the fund.
IHI: US companies that make medical devices, such as heart valves, surgical robots and joint implants, following a Dow Jones index. Abbott, Intuitive Surgical and Stryker are about 44% of the fund.
IHY: High yield bonds, sometimes called junk bonds because the borrowers are riskier, issued by companies outside the US. It follows an index, and it holds a long list of bonds, with none above about 1% of the fund.
IIGD: Holds short-term US investment-grade bonds, choosing those with the highest quality scores from the index provider. It is extremely spread out, with each holding below 1%, aiming for a steadier ride than a regular bond fund.
IINC: A fund that holds a mix of large and mid-size US stocks and also sells options on them to generate extra income. The option premiums add income, but they also limit how much the fund can gain when stocks rise sharply, and a large part of it sits in cash.
IJAN: A fund that uses options on an international developed-markets stock fund to cover part of the losses over a one-year period starting each January, after a first stretch of losses is absorbed. In return, gains are capped, so protection only applies if you hold the full period.
IJH: About 400 mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 index, weighted by size. No single holding is much above 1%, and industrials, technology and financials are the biggest sectors.
IJJ: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that look cheaper compared with their earnings and sales. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 1.5%, and leans toward financials, industrials and consumer companies.
IJK: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that show faster growth, tracked by an index. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward industrials, technology and health care rather than the mega-cap tech giants.
IJR: About 600 small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 index, which also screens for profitability. No holding tops about 1%, so it is very spread out across financials, technology and industrials.
IJS: Smaller US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that look cheap relative to their size and fundamentals, a style known as value. It holds hundreds of stocks with no single one above about 1.3%, leaning toward financials, consumer discretionary and technology.
IJT: Smaller US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that show the strongest growth traits, such as rising sales and earnings. It is very spread out: the biggest holdings are only about 1% each, across technology, industrials, health care and financials.
IJUL: A buffer fund using options on an iShares MSCI EAFE fund (developed markets outside the US and Canada) to absorb the first 15% of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only holds if you stay the whole period.
IJUN: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed markets outside the US and Canada, to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in June. In return, the gains over that period are capped.
ILCG: Large and mid-sized US companies that Morningstar rates as having above-average growth, weighted by company size. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Broadcom and Amazon are about 33% of the fund.
ILCV: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheaper relative to their size, as defined by Morningstar, weighted by company size. It is more varied than many value funds, and Microsoft and Apple are still the top holdings at about 7% each.
ILDR: An actively managed fund of US and foreign companies that may benefit from new technology, using a ranking method to pick them. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Amazon, Alphabet and Broadcom together are about 23% of the fund.
ILF: About 40 of the largest companies in Latin America, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, following an S&P index. It is top-heavy in miners and banks: Vale, Nu Holdings and Itau are about a quarter of the fund.
ILIT: A fund holding lithium miners and producers around the world, picking the companies in a global lithium index. It is a narrow bet on one metal used in batteries, with Mineral Resources, Sociedad Quimica y Minera, Liontown and Albemarle each at about 7% to 8%.
ILOW: Stocks of companies outside the US that the managers expect to move up and down less than the overall market, chosen with a research and risk model. It is actively managed and spread across financials, industrials and technology, with each top holding only about 2% to 3%.
ILS: Mostly catastrophe bonds, which are bonds sold by insurers that pay investors interest but can lose value if a hurricane, earthquake or similar disaster hits. Their returns depend on weather and disaster events rather than the economy, and each single bond is a small slice of the fund.
ILTB: US dollar bonds with more than ten years left until maturity, including many Treasuries, tracking a broad index that holds both investment-grade and high yield bonds. Because the bonds are so long-dated, its price moves a lot when interest rates change.
IMAR: Uses options tied to the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, which covers developed stock markets outside the US, to buffer part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in March. In return, the gains for that period are capped, and the buffer only applies if held for the full period.
IMAY: A fund using options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF to give returns from developed stock markets outside the US, up to a limit, over a one year period starting in May. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, if held for the whole period.
IMCB: Mid-sized US companies, tracking the Morningstar US Mid Cap Index, which covers the stocks in the middle of the US market by size. It holds hundreds of companies and none is more than about 1%, so it is very spread out across technology, industrials and financials.
IMCG: Medium sized US companies that Morningstar's index rates as having above-average growth, like Fortinet, Snowflake and Freeport-McMoRan. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is above about 1.5%, so it is spread out, with tilts toward tech and industrials.
IMCV: US mid-sized companies that Morningstar rates as value stocks, meaning they look cheaper compared with their earnings or assets. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1.5%, and it leans toward financials, energy, health care and industrials.
IMF: An actively managed fund that takes both long and short positions in futures tied to over fifty global markets, including stocks, bonds, commodities and currencies. It tries to follow price trends in either direction, so it behaves differently from a plain stock or bond fund.
IMFL: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed markets outside the US, picked and weighted by an index that shifts between factors like value and momentum depending on conditions. It is widely spread, with Samsung the largest at about 6%.
IMOM: A fund of developed-market stocks outside the US that have shown strong recent price momentum, picked by a rules-based screen. It holds roughly 50 to 200 stocks and changes as the winners change, with financials, industrials and technology the largest groups.
IMTB: A broad bond fund covering US government, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds that mature in about five to ten years. It is meant as a core bond holding, with Treasuries as its largest holdings and moderate sensitivity to interest rate changes.
IMTG: An actively managed fund that mainly holds agency mortgage-backed securities, bonds backed by home loans guaranteed by government-linked agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It aims for income, and its price can move when interest rates change or homeowners pay off loans early.
IMTM: Large and mid size companies in developed markets outside the US that have recently been going up faster than their peers, tracked through an MSCI momentum index. The mix changes as winners change, and it currently includes ASML, HSBC, Royal Bank of Canada and Roche.
IMVP: Follows an index of large and mid sized Indian companies chosen for momentum, value, steady prices and profitability. It holds companies like Bajaj Auto, Tata Consultancy, Infosys and Titan at around 4% each, so it is fairly evenly spread.
INCE: An actively managed fund holding mainly dividend paying US and international stocks, plus some preferred shares. Its holdings are spread over staples, banks, health care and utilities, with names like Chevron, Southern Company and Procter & Gamble each about 3%.
INCM: An actively managed mix of bonds, dividend-paying stocks and preferred securities, which the managers can shift between as opportunities change. About half is bonds and the rest is mostly stocks and preferreds, with a focus on producing income from sectors like consumer staples, energy and utilities.
INCO: Indian consumer companies, such as food, retail and lifestyle brands, tracked with an index of that group. It is concentrated by theme: consumer discretionary is about 60% and staples about 33%, and its largest holdings are each about 5%.
IND: Roughly 500 of the largest companies listed on India's National Stock Exchange, following the Nifty 500 index and holding them mostly by company size. Banks are the biggest group, and HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Reliance Industries together make up about 15% of the fund.
INDA: Large and mid-sized Indian companies, tracking the MSCI India Index. Banks are the biggest group at about 30% of the fund, and Reliance Industries and HDFC Bank are each over 6%, so a few big names matter.
INDE: An actively managed fund buying stocks of Indian companies, picked by managers rather than by following an index. It is fairly concentrated: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Eternal are among the biggest holdings, and financials make up about a third of it.
INDH: A fund of Indian companies that also hedges the Indian rupee against the US dollar, so currency swings matter less to returns. Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are about 24% of it, with financials the biggest sector.
INDQ: An actively managed fund of Indian companies picked for quality using a rules-based method. It is spread over many stocks, with Titan, Eicher Motors, Hero MotoCorp and others each about 4% to 6%, and leans toward consumer companies and health care.
INDS: Tracks an index of developed-market real estate companies focused on industrial properties such as warehouses and self-storage. It is concentrated at the top: Public Storage, Extra Space and Prologis are each around 14% to 16%, which is about 45% combined.
INDY: The 50 largest Indian companies by market size, tracking the Nifty 50 index. It is heavy in banks, with HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank together about 20% of the fund, and Reliance Industries adds around 8%.
INDZ: An actively managed fund of companies tied to India, picked by the managers rather than following an index. Financials are about 30% of it, and Reliance Industries, HDFC Bank and Maruti Suzuki are among the biggest holdings at about 3% each.
INEQ: Holds dividend-paying stocks of large companies outside the US, picked by an active manager for income. It is spread across Europe, Asia and Australia, with names like DBS, UniCredit, Shell, BHP and TotalEnergies each around 4% to 5% of the fund, and financials the biggest sector.
INFL: An actively managed fund that holds companies expected to benefit from rising prices, such as land and royalty owners, precious metals miners and energy infrastructure firms, in the US and abroad. It is concentrated, with the top five holdings about 28% and none above about 7%.
INFO: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked by a quantitative model from PanAgora that looks for stocks with favorable traits. It is fairly top heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft making up about 27% of the fund.
INKM: A fund of funds holding other ETFs across bonds, stocks, real estate and other assets, aimed at producing income. It is actively managed, with mostly bond funds and some dividend and options-income stock funds.
INMU: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term US municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. The managers choose the bonds, aiming for income from a broad mix of issuers.
INOV: Options on an iShares fund that holds developed markets outside the US and Canada, designed to absorb part of the first losses over a set one year period starting in November. The Power Buffer name signals this protection, and gains are capped in exchange.
INQQ: Publicly traded Indian internet and online companies, such as e-commerce, payments and online services, tracked through an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Reliance, Bajaj Finance and a few others each making up about 7% to 8% of the fund.
INRO: An actively managed fund of US stocks that shifts its weight between industries over time, using BlackRock's research models. For now it looks much like the big US market, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 21% of it and technology around 42%.
INTF: Stocks from large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted toward traits like value, quality and momentum. It stays broad, with ASML the largest holding at only about 2%.
INTL: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs covering stocks outside the US, from developed markets and emerging markets. Its biggest pieces are iShares funds, about 38% and 19%, so it is a mix of existing international funds in one ticker.
INTM: An actively managed fund that buys intermediate term municipal bonds, which are debt from US states and cities whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It works as a tax advantaged income holding, and it can also use derivatives that act like municipal bonds.
INVG: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning debt from companies seen as lower risk. It picks bonds with a computer-driven approach that weighs value, quality and momentum, and is spread over many issuers at roughly 1% each or less.
INVN: A fund following an index of US companies the manager sees as innovative but not yet fully recognized by the market, mostly mid-sized. It leans toward technology at about 57%, with health care next, and no single holding is above about 3%.
INYY: Aims to pay high income from Intel stock by using options on it, rather than owning the shares directly. That limits how much of a rise in Intel it can capture, and it holds mostly Treasury bills to back the options.
IOCT: Uses options on the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF, a basket of stocks from developed markets outside the US and Canada, to follow its price over a set one-year period. It buffers part of the losses at the cost of capping gains, and the protection resets each October.
ION: A fund of companies that mine lithium, cobalt and nickel, the metals used in batteries, picked from a broad global stock index. It is almost entirely mining and materials stocks, with Australian lithium producers like Liontown and PLS among the largest holdings.
IOO: About 100 of the world's largest companies, mostly American, from an S&P index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 30% of it, and technology is roughly half.
IOPP: An actively managed fund of Indian companies, picked by the manager from across the country's market. It leans toward consumer-focused businesses like Eternal and Indian Hotels, and the top holdings are each around 5% to 6%.
IOYY: An income fund that sells options on a leveraged ETF tied to IonQ stock, aiming to turn the stock's big swings into payouts. That caps its gains on the upside while keeping most of the downside, and the fund mostly holds Treasury bills as backing.
IPAC: Large and mid-sized companies from developed Pacific countries, mainly Japan and Australia, plus Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand, following an MSCI index. It is well spread out, with banks and big industrial names leading and no stock above about 3%.
IPAV: A fund of companies outside the US that help build infrastructure, mostly materials and industrial businesses like steel makers and cable makers. It follows a Global X index, with Prysmian, ArcelorMittal and Shin-Etsu Chemical among the biggest holdings.
IPAY: Companies that run digital and mobile payment systems, tracking a specialized index. Visa, Mastercard, American Express and Capital One are each about 6%, so it is a blend of payment networks and card lenders spread across financials and technology.
IPB: A trust certificate tied to Merrill Lynch debt, paying a fixed 6.0518% rate, rather than a fund of many holdings. Its price depends on the credit of the company behind it and on interest rates, so it behaves like a single bond.
IPKW: Holds foreign companies that have been steadily buying back their own shares, selected by the Nasdaq International BuyBack Achievers Index. It leans toward banks and other large non-US firms, with ING, UniCredit and Standard Chartered each about 5% to 7% of it.
IPO: Recently listed US companies, following the Renaissance IPO Index, which adds newly public firms and drops them after a couple of years. It is top-heavy: Astera Labs, CoreWeave and Arm are about 30% of the fund.
IPOS: Recently listed companies from outside the US, following an index of international IPOs. It is concentrated, with the top five holdings, like Kioxia, Galderma and CATL, making up about half of it, and tilts toward technology.
IQDF: Large companies outside the US that pay dividends and score well on quality measures like financial strength and profitability, following a Northern Trust index. It has a big tech-chip tilt, with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 5%, alongside many banks and industrial firms.
IQDG: Large and mid-size companies outside the US that have paid dividends and show strong profitability and growth, picked using a WisdomTree index. It is spread widely, with the biggest holdings, such as Toyota, Inditex and LVMH, each around 3 to 4% of the fund.
IQDY: Higher-quality companies outside the US that pay dividends, picked by a Northern Trust index that looks at the quality of earnings and dividend sustainability. It is spread out, with no holding above about 4%, and leans toward financials and tech.
IQGR: An actively managed fund of quality growth companies outside the US, chosen by its sub-adviser for strong, lasting growth. Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and SK hynix are among the biggest holdings, though none is more than about 4%.
IQHI: An actively managed fund of high-yield corporate bonds, from companies with lower credit ratings that pay more interest. It is highly diversified, with no single bond above about 1%, and the managers look for bonds with good yields compared with their risk.
IQLT: Large and mid-sized companies from developed markets outside the US, picked for high quality: strong profits, steady earnings and low debt, from the MSCI World ex USA Quality index. ASML is the largest holding at around 5%, and financials and industrials lead.
IQM: An actively managed fund buying companies that build the technology behind intelligent machines, such as AI chips, robotics and automation. It leans on tech and industrials, with NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor and SanDisk the biggest positions at roughly 6% each.
IQMM: A money market fund that holds only very short-term US government debt and similar safe cash-like holdings. It is built to keep a stable price while paying interest that follows short-term rates, and it is designed to fit rules for backing payment stablecoins.
IQQ: Tracks the Nasdaq-100, the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by company size. It is tech-heavy: technology is about 60% of the fund, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are roughly 21%.
IQQQ: Holds Nasdaq-100 stocks and sells call options on the index to collect extra income, which it pays out often. The options limit gains when the market jumps, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 18% of the fund.
IQSI: Large companies in developed countries outside North America, tracking an index that screens for environmental, social and governance standards. It holds a wide range of stocks, with ASML at about 5% and Roche, Novartis and Nestle each around 2%.
IQSM: US mid-sized companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens set by Candriam, weighted by company size like a regular index. It spreads money across many holdings, with none above about 1%, so no single stock drives results.
IQSU: Large US companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens set by Candriam, weighted by company size like a regular index. It is top-heavy in big tech, with Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon about 20% of it.
IQSZ: An actively managed fund of global stocks from companies that are helping the shift to lower carbon emissions, or plan to. It still looks like the broad market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 14% of it.
IROC: An actively managed fund of high yield municipal bonds, issued by state and local bodies for things like hospitals, utilities and schools. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and it is spread over many issuers at about 1% each.
IRTR: A mix of about 40% stocks and 59% bonds, built from other iShares funds, aimed at people who are already retired. It is actively managed and adjusts the mix over time, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ISCF: Small and mid-size companies in developed countries outside the US, chosen by an index that favors factors such as value, quality, momentum and smaller size. It holds hundreds of stocks, with no single name above about 1%.
ISCG: Small US companies classified as growth stocks by Morningstar, meaning they show above average growth traits. It holds many stocks, with none above about 1%, so it is a broad fund covering small company growth.
ISCV: Small US companies that look cheap compared with their size, picked from a Morningstar small-cap value index. It holds hundreds of stocks, with financials and consumer discretionary the largest sectors, and no holding is above about 1%.
ISEP: Uses options on a developed-markets stock fund outside North America (the iShares MSCI EAFE ETF) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only works if held the full period.
ISHG: Government bonds from developed countries outside the US that mature in one to three years, held in their local currencies. It is not currency hedged, so exchange rates move its value, and holdings include Portugal, Ireland and France.
ISHP: Companies around the world that make their money from online shopping, picked and weighted by the S-Network E-Commerce index. It is spread thinly: the biggest holdings, such as Allegro, Wayfair and Reddit, are each only about 2% of the fund.
ISMD: US small and mid sized companies, chosen by an index that screens for a company's values and impact. It spreads across thousands of tiny holdings, so no single one is above a few percent, and it tilts toward small, lesser known names.
ISMF: An actively managed managed-futures fund that trades futures on stock indexes, bonds, currencies and commodities, aiming to follow rising or falling trends. It can profit in falling markets as well as rising ones, so it behaves differently from a plain stock or bond fund.
ISPY: Holds S&P 500 stocks and uses options to generate extra income, which it pays out. The options limit how much it can gain in strong markets, and part of the fund sits in cash-like holdings, while NVIDIA and Apple are each about 6%.
ISRA: A fund of Israeli companies tracking a VanEck index, so it is a bet on a single small country. Palo Alto Networks is about 13% of it, and technology and banks, such as Leumi and Hapoalim, make up most of the rest.
ISRL: The 120 largest companies in Israel, following a Defiance KSM index. It leans toward banks like Hapoalim and Leumi, plus Tower Semiconductor and defense firm Elbit Systems, so it tracks a single country's economy.
ISTB: US government, corporate and mortgage bonds that mature in one to five years, tracking a short-term investment-grade bond index. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, its price should move less than a fund of longer bonds, and no single bond is above about 1%.
ISTM: Tracks an index of futures contracts on metals used in industry and the energy transition, such as copper and aluminum. It holds futures instead of the metals themselves, so the small positions shown mostly reflect collateral and contracts.
ISVL: Small companies from developed countries outside the US and South Korea, tracking an FTSE index that favors cheaply priced stocks. It holds a wide spread of names, with none above about 1%, and leans toward industrials and financials.
ISWN: A mix of US Treasuries and long dated call options on an iShares fund of developed foreign stocks. Roughly 10% of the index goes to the options, which aim to gain in sharp market swings, while the Treasuries make up most of the fund.
ITA: US aerospace and defense companies, tracking a Dow Jones index of the sector, including makers of jet engines, aircraft and weapons. It is concentrated: General Electric, RTX and Boeing together are about 46% of the fund.
ITAN: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked using a method that tries to value hidden assets like brands, patents and software that regular accounting misses. It is fairly spread out, with Amazon the largest at about 5%, and leans toward technology and health care.
ITB: US home construction companies: homebuilders like DR Horton, Lennar and PulteGroup, plus home improvement and building supply firms. It is narrow and tied to housing, with DR Horton, PulteGroup and Lennar making up about a third of the fund.
ITDB: A fund that bundles other iShares funds in stocks and bonds, with the mix designed for people planning to retire around 2030. It is actively managed and gradually shifts toward bonds as 2030 approaches, so it is a ready-made portfolio in one fund.
ITDC: A target date fund aimed at people planning to retire around 2035, holding a mix of other iShares stock and bond ETFs. It is actively managed and leans toward stocks now at roughly two thirds, shifting more toward bonds as the date nears.
ITDD: A fund of funds that mixes stock and bond funds for people planning to retire around 2040. It holds mostly stocks, about three quarters, and gradually shifts toward bonds over time, a so-called glide path, as that date gets closer.
ITDE: A retirement-date fund for people planning to retire around 2045, built from other iShares funds. It is mostly stocks, about 87%, led by US large companies, with some bonds and real estate, and it shifts toward bonds automatically as 2045 gets closer.
ITDF: A target date fund aimed at around 2050, which holds a mix of other iShares funds covering US stocks, foreign stocks, bonds and real estate. It is mostly stocks now, around 93%, and it is designed to shift toward bonds as 2050 approaches.
ITDG: A retirement fund of funds aimed at people planning to retire around 2055. It is actively managed and mostly holds other iShares funds, with the bulk in US stocks, and the mix is meant to gradually shift toward safer investments as that date gets closer.
ITDH: A target-date fund that mixes other iShares funds, mostly US and international stocks with some bonds, aimed at people retiring around 2060. It is actively managed, and the mix is designed to shift toward safer holdings over time.
ITDI: A target-date fund aimed at someone retiring around 2065. It is actively managed and holds other iShares funds, mostly US and international stocks, and over time it is designed to shift gradually toward safer assets like bonds as that date approaches.
ITDJ: A target-date fund for people planning to retire around 2070, holding mostly stock index funds from iShares in US and international markets. It is nearly all stocks now, and the mix is designed to shift gradually toward bonds as the date gets closer.
ITEQ: Israeli technology companies, tracked by the BlueStar Israel Global Technology Index, covering software, chips and defense tech. Palo Alto Networks is the largest holding at about 12%, with Tower Semiconductor and Elbit Systems next.
ITM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds, loans to US states, cities and agencies whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds hundreds of bonds, so no single issuer is more than a fraction of a percent of it.
ITOT: Almost the entire US stock market, from large to small companies, tracking the S&P Total Market Index. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 16% of it, and technology is about 38%.
ITWO: Holds the Russell 2000, an index of small US companies, and sells call options on it to earn extra income, which the fund pays out. The options cap how much it gains when small stocks rally, and it is spread over a large number of small positions.
IUS: Large US companies weighted by business size, using measures like sales, cash flow, dividends and book value, instead of stock market value. That means big names like Alphabet and Apple lead, but Alphabet is only about 7% and there are many other holdings.
IUSB: A wide mix of US dollar bonds in one fund: Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds, company bonds and some higher-yield and foreign-issued debt, following a Bloomberg index. It is a one-fund take on the whole bond market, with thousands of holdings and no big single position.
IUSG: Large and mid-sized US companies with growth traits from the S&P 900, weighted by size. It is tilted toward tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 26% of it, and technology makes up over half the fund.
IUSV: Large and mid-sized US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, tracking the S&P 900 Value index. Value funds lean toward financials, health care and energy, and Apple is the largest holding at about 7%.
IVAL: Cheap-looking companies outside the US, chosen by a rules-based quantitative screen for low prices compared with their business value. It is spread thinly, with no stock above about 2%, and tilts toward materials, energy and consumer companies.
IVE: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, large US companies that score as value stocks on measures like price relative to earnings and book value. Despite the value label, Apple is about 7% of it and technology is the largest sector.
IVEP: Companies that stand to benefit from the power and infrastructure needs of AI, chosen from a research report by Wedbush analyst Dan Ives. It holds about 30 stocks, such as Schneider Electric, Eaton and Bloom Energy, spread across industrials, utilities and energy.
IVES: About 30 companies from tech analyst Dan Ives' AI list at Wedbush, chosen as likely winners from artificial intelligence. It leans on large tech names, with Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, Broadcom and Alphabet about 26% of the fund combined.
IVLU: Large and mid size companies in developed markets outside the US, picked because they look cheap compared to their earnings and book value, based on an MSCI index. It leans toward banks, carmakers and other cyclical firms, with HSBC, BNP Paribas and Toyota among the top holdings.
IVOG: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that show faster growth characteristics. It is spread over hundreds of stocks, mostly industrials, technology and health care, with no single holding above about 3%.
IVOL: An actively managed fund that mostly holds inflation-protected US Treasuries (TIPS), plus options and swaps that gain when the gap between short and long interest rates changes. It aims to help against rising inflation and rate swings, so it behaves differently from a plain bond fund.
IVOO: About 400 mid-sized US companies, tracking the S&P MidCap 400 Index, which sits between big blue chips and small caps. It is widely spread, with the biggest holdings under 2% each, and industrials, technology and financials are the largest groups.
IVOV: US mid-sized companies that look cheaper relative to their size, tracking the S&P Mid-Cap 400 Value Index. It is spread over hundreds of holdings, none above about 1%, with financials and industrials as the biggest sectors.
IVSI: A fund of large companies in developed markets outside North America, in places like Europe, Japan and Australia. ASML is the largest holding at about 7%, followed by Roche, BHP and Novartis.
IVSS: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, picked with the manager's own research rather than tracking an index. It plans to hold at least 150 positions, so it is spread out, with no holding above about 3%.
IVSX: Small and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside North America, picked by a rules-based method from Applied Finance. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and it leans toward industrials, consumer and materials companies.
IVV: iShares' version of the S&P 500: roughly 500 large US companies, weighted by size. It holds essentially the same stocks as other S&P 500 funds, so about 40% is technology and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are around 18%.
IVVB: A fund holding the S&P 500 through an iShares ETF plus options, with a layered set of quarterly periods that buffers a deeper amount of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held through each period.
IVVM: Holds a laddered set of options-based buffer positions on the S&P 500, staggered by start date so protection resets at different times. Each step cushions part of the losses on large US stocks in exchange for capping some of the gains.
IVVW: Holds the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF and sells one-month call options on the S&P 500 to bring in extra income. That income comes at a price: gains in strong months are capped, while most of the losses in falling markets remain.
IVW: The growth half of the S&P 500: large US companies with faster growth traits, weighted by size. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple around 27% together and technology more than half.
IWB: The roughly 1,000 largest US companies, held in proportion to their size, following the Russell 1000 index. It covers most of the US stock market by value, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 17% of it, with technology around 39%.
IWC: Very small US public companies, microcaps with market values from about $1 million to $3 billion, tracked with a sampling approach that holds a representative selection of the index. It is spread over many tiny positions, none above 1%, with health care and financials the biggest sectors.
IWD: Large and mid-sized US value stocks from the Russell 1000 Value index, meaning companies that look cheaply priced. Amazon and Apple are the top holdings at around 6% each, and financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
IWF: Large and mid-sized US growth stocks from the Russell 1000 Growth index, weighted by size. It is heavy in tech at roughly 57%, and NVIDIA alone is nearly 14% of the fund.
IWFG: An actively managed fund of about 30 large US growth companies chosen by Winslow. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 26% together, and technology makes up over half of it.
IWL: The 200 largest US companies, tracking the Russell Top 200 Index and covering the biggest names in the US stock market. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it, and technology is over 40% of the fund.
IWLG: An actively managed fund holding large US companies that the manager thinks will grow quickly. Alphabet and NVIDIA are each about 12% of the fund, and with Broadcom, Microsoft and Apple the top five are about 40%.
IWM: Nearly 2,000 of the smallest companies in the Russell 3000, making it one of the best known small-company US funds. Each holding is a tiny slice, around 0.4% at most, spread over health care, financials, technology and industrials.
IWMI: An actively managed fund that holds a Russell 2000 small-company ETF and sells call options on the index to pay high monthly income. The options give up some gains when small stocks rally, and the income can vary from month to month.
IWMW: Holds the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which covers US small companies, and sells one-month call options on the Russell 2000 to earn extra income. The options give up some of the gains if small companies rally strongly, in exchange for that income.
IWMY: An actively managed fund that seeks income by selling options tied to the Russell 2000 small company index, paying out distributions weekly. The options limit how much it gains when the index rises, and it still falls when the index falls.
IWN: Small US companies that look cheap relative to their size, a value subset of the Russell 2000 index. Financials are the biggest sector at about 28%, and with hundreds of stocks no single one is above about 1%.
IWO: Small US companies with faster expected growth, a subset of the Russell 2000 index. Health care is the biggest sector at about 30%, followed by technology, and no single stock is more than about 1% of the fund.
IWP: US mid-sized companies expected to grow faster than average, tracking the Russell Midcap Growth index. It leans toward software and tech firms, and the biggest holdings such as Datadog, Snowflake and Cloudflare are only about 2% each.
IWR: Mid-sized US companies, the smaller roughly 800 of the Russell 1000 index, weighted by company size. No single stock matters much here: the biggest holdings are each only about 0.6%, spread across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
IWS: Mid-sized US companies that look cheap relative to their size, tracking the Russell Midcap Value index. It holds hundreds of stocks with no position above about 1%, spread across financials, industrials, technology, energy and real estate.
IWV: Nearly the whole US stock market, about 3,000 companies of all sizes, tracking the Russell 3000 index. It is dominated by big companies: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon make up about 19% of the fund.
IWX: Large US companies from the Russell Top 200 that look cheaper than the rest, with lower prices relative to their book value and slower expected growth. Even so, Amazon, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
IWY: The growth-oriented half of the 200 largest US companies, tracking the Russell Top 200 Growth index. Very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Broadcom are about a third of it, and tech makes up well over half.
IXC: Large energy companies from around the world, mainly oil and gas producers, tracking the S&P Global 1200 Energy index. It is top-heavy: ExxonMobil and Chevron are about 27% of the fund.
IXG: Large financial companies from around the world, such as banks, insurers and payment firms, following the S&P Global 1200 Financials Capped Index. Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase are each about 6% of it, and the whole fund sits in one sector.
IXJ: About 100 of the largest health care companies around the world, like drugmakers, device makers and insurers, tracking an S&P index. It is top heavy: Eli Lilly is about 11% of the fund, and most holdings are US companies.
IXN: Large technology companies from around the world, following an S&P index that caps the biggest names so they cannot dominate. It is still top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 32% of the fund, with Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom next.
IXP: Large communication companies from around the world, such as social media, internet search, streaming, and phone and cable businesses, tracking an S&P index. It is top-heavy: Meta and Alphabet are about 40% together, and Disney and Tencent are each around 5%.
IXUS: Thousands of stocks from developed and emerging countries outside the US, weighted by company size, following an MSCI index of non-US markets. It is spread widely: the largest holding, Taiwan Semiconductor, is only about 4% of it, and financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
IYC: US consumer discretionary companies, the ones selling things people want rather than strictly need, like online retail, cars and restaurants, tracking a FTSE Russell index. Amazon is about 16% and Tesla about 6.5%, so a few names drive it.
IYE: US energy companies, mainly oil and gas producers and refiners, tracking a Dow Jones energy index. It is very top-heavy: ExxonMobil and Chevron alone are about 40% of the fund, and nearly all of it is in the energy sector.
IYF: US financial companies: banks, insurers, asset managers and payment firms, following a Dow Jones index of the sector. Two names dominate: Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan are each about 11% of the fund.
IYG: US financial services companies such as banks, payment processors and insurers, following a Dow Jones financial services index. JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway and Visa are about 35% of it, so a few big names drive the results.
IYH: US health care companies, such as drugmakers, insurers and medical device makers, tracked by an index. It is top heavy: Eli Lilly is about 15% of the fund, and Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie together are about a third.
IYJ: US industrial companies, such as aerospace, machinery and transportation firms, plus payment companies like Visa and Mastercard, which the index counts as industrials. Those two are about 13% of it, so it is not purely factory stocks.
IYK: US consumer staples companies, the makers of everyday goods like food, drinks, household products and tobacco, plus some drugstores, tracking a Dow Jones index. It is concentrated: Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble and Philip Morris are each about 12%, around 36% combined.
IYLD: A fund of funds that holds other iShares ETFs covering floating rate bonds, short-term bonds, broad bonds, preferred stocks and income-focused stocks. It aims to produce income from a mix of bonds and stocks, with about four funds each making up around 15% of it.
IYM: US basic materials companies such as chemical, mining and metals producers, tracking a FTSE Russell index of that sector. It is concentrated: Linde, Newmont and Freeport-McMoRan together make up roughly 38% of the fund, and it holds relatively few stocks.
IYR: US real estate companies, mostly real estate investment trusts that own buildings and pass on rental income, tracked by a Dow Jones index. It is top heavy: Welltower and Prologis are about 20% of the fund.
IYRI: An actively managed fund of US real estate companies, mainly REITs, which also uses options strategies to boost income. It is led by Welltower, Prologis and Simon Property, together about a quarter of it, and the options cap some gains.
IYT: US transportation companies such as railroads, airlines, trucking, shipping and delivery firms, following an S&P Dow Jones transportation index. It is fairly top-heavy: Union Pacific and Uber together are about 30% of the fund, and rail stocks have a big influence.
IYW: US technology companies, covering software, hardware, semiconductors and internet firms, in proportion to their size. It is very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft alone make up about 38% of the fund.
IYY: Tracks the Dow Jones US Index, which covers about the top 95% of US stocks by size, so it spans large, mid and some small companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of the fund.
IYZ: US telecommunications and communications equipment companies, tracking a Dow Jones index. It is top-heavy: Cisco is about 23%, and Arista Networks and Verizon are each around 11%, so it is as much about networking gear as phone companies.
IZRL: Israeli companies, tracking an index of firms based or listed in Israel, with a focus on innovation. It spreads fairly evenly across stocks, with no holding above about 2%, and technology is about half of it, followed by health care and communications.
JA: Investment-grade collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated between AA and A, which are pools of corporate bank loans sliced into layers by risk. It is actively managed and holds many CLOs, each only about 3% of the fund.
JAAA: An actively managed fund of AAA rated collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds, with the safest slices held. Their payments float with short-term interest rates, so it can pay more income than plain short-term bonds.
JABS: An actively managed fund of asset-backed securities, which are bonds backed by pools of loans such as auto loans and corporate loans. It holds many small positions, with the largest only about 2% of the fund.
JADB: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock market ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, it limits how much it can gain, and the protection only works if shares are held for the whole period.
JADE: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, the developing economies such as Taiwan, South Korea, China and India. It is tilted toward chip makers: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 20% of the fund, with Tencent also in the top few.
JAJL: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to protect against losses over a set six-month period starting in January or July. In return, it gives up some of the possible gains, and it works best if held for the full period.
JANB: Uses options on a broad US stock index fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, the upside is capped, so a strong market year will not be fully captured.
JANH: An actively managed fund that holds Treasury bills plus options on the stock market to pay regular income, with a barrier that protects only as long as the market does not fall past a set level. Its gains are limited, and big drops can hurt.
JANI: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an international developed-markets stock ETF (EFA) to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period ending in December 2026. Its upside is not capped, but the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
JANJ: An actively managed fund that uses Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income over a one-year period starting in January. It gives up some protection and upside: a drop in the index beyond a set barrier can mean real losses.
JANM: Uses customized options on US large stocks to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in January. It aims to protect against a large part of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and works as intended only if held for the whole period.
JANP: A fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to give stock market gains up to a limit over a one year period starting in January. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and the stated outcomes only apply if held for the whole period.
JANT: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 10% of losses over a set one-year period starting in January, in exchange for a limit on the gains. The cushion and cap only apply if you hold for the full period.
JANU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in December 2026, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JANW: A defined-outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 to absorb the first 20% of losses over a one-year period that starts each January. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
JANZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a set outcome over a one-year period starting in January. Most of the fund sits in Treasuries and option contracts, so its results depend on the options, not on owning stocks.
JAPN: An actively managed fund of Japanese companies run by owner operators, meaning leaders who hold a significant share of the business. It is concentrated, with Furuno Electric at about 9% of the fund, and many holdings are small and midsize companies.
JAVA: A manager-picked fund of US large companies that look attractively priced relative to their long-term growth potential. It differs from a plain value index fund because the manager chooses the stocks, and Amazon, Microsoft and Apple are among the biggest holdings.
JBBB: An actively managed fund that buys the lower-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are pools of loans to companies sold off in layers by risk. These layers pay higher floating interest than safer ones but carry more credit risk, and it is spread across many CLOs.
JBND: An actively managed bond fund from JPMorgan that aims to beat the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It holds a mix of US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, mostly investment grade, with managers picking them instead of copying an index.
JCAL: A fund of California municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, whose interest is generally free from federal and California state income tax. It is actively managed, so the managers choose which bonds to hold rather than following an index, and it is meant for tax-free income from one state.
JCHI: An actively managed fund that buys stocks of companies tied to China, picked by the manager rather than following an index. It is concentrated at the top: Tencent is about 11% and Alibaba nearly 8%, with financials, consumer and communication companies making up most of it.
JCPB: An actively managed fund that mainly holds US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds, plus a smaller slice of riskier debt. Managers choose the holdings rather than following an index, and the average maturity usually runs five to twenty years.
JCPI: Bonds designed to hold up when inflation rises, mostly US Treasury inflation-protected securities, whose value adjusts with consumer prices. It is actively managed, and the largest few Treasury positions make up over a third of the fund.
JDIV: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large companies from around the world that the managers see as leaders in their industries. Technology and financials are the biggest sectors, and Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor together make up about 12% of it.
JDOC: Large health care companies that the managers believe are leaders, including drugmakers, biotech, medical device and health services firms. It is actively managed, and AbbVie, Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth, Merck and Johnson & Johnson together make up about 30% of the fund.
JDVI: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized companies outside the US that look inexpensive compared with their value. It spreads across countries and sectors, led by financials and industrials, and its biggest holdings, such as Samsung and Novartis, are each around 5%.
JDVL: An actively managed fund of large US companies the manager sees as good value, picked from the range of the Russell 1000 Value Index. It holds a fairly small group of stocks, with Amazon the largest at about 7% and technology, financials and health care leading.
JEDI: Stocks of companies tied to drones and modern defense, such as space, unmanned systems and military technology. It is concentrated in small companies: Redwire and Unusual Machines are over 20% of the fund between them, and it is non-diversified.
JELH: An actively managed fund that holds stocks and equity linked instruments, using options, futures and swaps with the goal of producing high income. Its returns depend on that derivatives strategy, so it will not behave like a plain stock fund.
JELM: An actively managed fund that aims to pay regular income, using stock-linked securities and options. Its holdings are mostly cash and short-term instruments, so its returns come from the income strategy more than from owning stocks.
JEMA: An actively managed fund of emerging markets stocks, with JPMorgan managers choosing companies they think will do well. It has a large technology share, and Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix make up about 26% of the fund.
JEMB: Bonds from governments and companies in emerging markets, issued in US dollars rather than local currencies, picked by an active manager. Pemex, Eskom and other state-linked issuers appear, and about 10% is held in cash.
JEPI: An actively managed fund of large US stocks, picked for lower risk, that also sells call options on the S&P 500 to generate extra income, and those options limit how much it gains in strong markets. Holdings are spread out, none above about 2%.
JEPQ: An actively managed fund of Nasdaq-100 style stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income, and the options cap how much it gains in strong rallies. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Micron about 18% of it.
JETS: Airline stocks from around the world, plus some airports and aircraft makers, tracked by a passive index. It is a narrow bet on air travel: American, United, Southwest and Delta are each roughly 10% of the fund, so the airline industry's swings drive the results.
JFLI: An actively managed income fund that blends bond and stock exposure from around the world, mainly by owning other JPMorgan funds. About a third is a high-yield corporate bond fund and roughly 20% is an options-income fund on the Nasdaq.
JFLX: An actively managed bond fund that can invest across many kinds of debt, including mortgage bonds, corporate bonds, loans and foreign government bonds. Its managers shift between them as they see opportunities, and Ginnie Mae mortgage-backed bonds are among its largest holdings.
JGLO: An actively managed portfolio of large companies from developed markets around the world, picked by the manager rather than by an index. It is heavy in US tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 18% of it, and technology is around a third of the fund.
JGRO: An actively managed fund where JPMorgan picks large US growth companies by hand, rather than following an index. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Alphabet are each about 10%, and about half the fund is in technology.
JGRW: An actively managed fund of large US companies with long records of steady profits and growth. It is fairly top-heavy, with Alphabet, Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA together around a third of the fund.
JHAC: An actively managed fund of US companies of any size, picked by the manager based on a company's fundamentals. It is top-heavy in big tech: Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft together are about 21% of the fund.
JHAI: An actively managed fund of companies around the world tied to artificial intelligence, mostly chip makers and other technology firms. It is concentrated: Taiwan Semiconductor and NVIDIA are about 29% of it, and technology is roughly three quarters of the whole fund.
JHCB: Holds US corporate bonds, which are loans to companies, mostly investment grade, with a small amount of bank loans allowed. It is actively managed and spread out, with no single issuer above about 2%, from names like Bank of America, Microsoft and Amazon.
JHCP: An actively managed fund of bonds, mixing corporate, mortgage-backed, Treasury and other types, with room to add riskier bonds beyond a plain core bond fund. US Treasuries are the largest holdings, though each one is small.
JHCR: An actively managed fund of investment-grade US bonds, meaning bonds from borrowers rated reasonably safe, with a large share in US Treasuries. It aims to be a core bond holding that spreads money across many bonds rather than making one big bet.
JHDG: An actively managed fund of about 100 large US stocks chosen by research, paired with a hedge that is meant to soften market drops. Technology is about a third of it, and Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon together make up roughly 19%.
JHDV: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized US companies chosen by a rules-based approach. Despite the income focus, it holds a lot of technology, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together about 16% of the fund.
JHEM: Emerging market stocks, such as Taiwan, Korea, China and India, picked with a multifactor approach that tilts toward traits like value, size and profitability. It is chip heavy, as SK Hynix, Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor are about 18% of it.
JHHY: Holds US dollar corporate bonds from companies with lower credit ratings (called high yield or junk bonds), which pay higher interest because the borrowers are riskier. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1% of the fund.
JHID: Dividend-paying large and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, selected by a rules-based approach. Financial companies are about a third of the fund, and no single stock is more than roughly 2%.
JHLN: An actively managed fund that mostly holds senior loans, which are loans to companies with weaker credit that are first in line for repayment, from the US and around the world. A good part of it sits in CLOs, bundles of such loans, and the interest rates float with short-term rates.
JHMB: Mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home and commercial property loans that pay out interest and principal. It is actively managed, mixing agency-backed bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with private mortgage trusts, and it is spread across a large number of small holdings.
JHMD: Developed market stocks outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, picked with a multifactor approach that tilts toward cheaper, smaller and more profitable companies. It holds many stocks spread widely, with ASML the largest at only about 2%.
JHML: Large US companies selected and weighted using factors like value, quality and momentum rather than only size. It looks close to the broad market, with NVIDIA and Apple about 4% each, so it is not very top-heavy.
JHMM: About 700 US mid-sized companies, picked and weighted using several factors such as value, quality and momentum rather than just company size. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, across technology, industrials, financials and health care.
JHMU: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds, loans to US states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It can hold bonds of any length, and the manager adjusts the mix, so no single bond is more than about 1% of it.
JHPI: Preferred stocks and other preferred securities, which pay fixed income but rank above common shares, plus some bonds, picked by an active manager. Holdings are widely spread, with no single position above about 1%, and utilities and energy-related issuers show up often.
JHSC: Small US companies chosen by a John Hancock index that favors stocks with factors such as lower prices relative to their value, smaller size and stronger profits. It holds hundreds of companies in small amounts, with none above about 1% of the fund.
JIDE: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed markets outside the US, such as Europe and Japan, picked by a mix of research and quantitative models. It is spread widely, with the top holding ASML at about 4%.
JIG: An actively managed fund buying growth-oriented stocks outside the US, in developed and emerging markets, usually across at least three countries. Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest holding at about 6%, followed by ASML, Safran and Samsung at about 3% each.
JIII: An actively managed fund that mixes many types of bonds, including corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and loans, from the US and abroad, aiming for high income. Because the manager can shift between sectors, it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
JINT: An actively managed fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked using the manager's own models of company fundamentals. It is spread out, with the largest holdings like Novartis, Shell and BHP each under 3%, and about a third of it is in financials.
JIRE: Stocks from developed markets outside North America, actively managed by JPMorgan using company research to try to beat the MSCI EAFE index with similar risk. It is widely spread, with ASML the largest at about 3.5%.
JIVE: An actively managed fund of companies in developed and emerging markets outside the US that JPMorgan's team thinks are priced cheaply. Holdings are spread out, with Samsung, HSBC and Taiwan Semiconductor among the largest, each at only a few percent.
JLCO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that holds a mix of stocks the managers think have good potential. It leans toward big tech, with Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon together about 21% of the fund.
JLQD: An actively managed fund of US dollar corporate bonds, mainly investment grade, meaning borrowers rated as lower risk. It is spread thinly, with no single bond above about 2%, and the managers pick bonds rather than following an index.
JLVP: An actively managed fund of large US companies its managers consider undervalued, using both long positions (bets a stock rises) and short positions (bets it falls). Despite the value label, Amazon, Microsoft and Apple are its biggest holdings.
JMBS: An actively managed fund of mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged together, mostly backed by US government-linked agencies like Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae. A lot of it is held through to-be-announced (TBA) trades, a way of buying mortgage bonds for future delivery.
JMEE: A mix of US small and mid-sized companies, held in a blend that leans toward stocks the managers' research model likes, while staying close to its index. It is very spread out, with no single stock above about 1%, and may use futures to stay fully invested.
JMHI: A mix of municipal bonds, mostly lower-rated or higher-yield ones, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, with Puerto Rico sales tax bonds among the larger positions at about 1% each.
JMID: An actively managed fund of mid-size US companies chosen for growth potential using a computer-driven strategy. It is well spread out, with no holding above about 3%, and leans toward technology, industrials and consumer companies.
JMMF: A money market fund that holds only US Treasury obligations, with some cash kept on hand for redemptions. It works as a place to park cash that earns short-term interest, and the price stays very steady.
JMOM: Large US stocks picked because their prices have been rising strongly, a style called momentum, following an index of those stocks. It holds a broad group, with Broadcom, Apple, NVIDIA and others each around 2%, and about 45% is in technology.
JMSI: A national mix of intermediate-term municipal bonds, issued by cities, states and agencies, with a focus on sustainability. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and holdings include water systems and local authorities, each around 1%.
JMTG: A manager-run fund of mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans whose payments pass through to investors. It is mostly investment-grade agency mortgage bonds, and no single holding is more than about 2%.
JMUB: An actively managed fund of US municipal bonds, loans to states and cities whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It focuses on intermediate maturities and spreads across many issuers and states.
JNEU: An options-based fund that tracks the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in June, with a built-in 15% buffer against losses and no cap on gains up to the period's end. The buffer only applies to those holding for the full period.
JNK: US dollar corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings, called high yield or junk bonds, tracked by a Bloomberg index. They pay more interest than safer bonds but borrowers are more likely to default, and no single bond is above about 1%.
JOET: US large companies chosen for being profitable and well run (quality) and having strong recent price gains (momentum). The index spreads money almost evenly, so each holding is about 1% of the fund and no single giant dominates.
JOJO: An actively managed fund that moves between credit-related investments, and it currently holds mostly two high-yield bond funds: about 70% in one iShares fund and 30% in an Xtrackers fund. It is a fund of funds, so it adds a manager's timing on top of junk bonds.
JOUL: An actively managed fund of companies that make or build high-voltage power grid equipment. Eaton and GE Vernova alone are more than a quarter of the fund, and almost all of it is industrials.
JOYT: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income. Its income comes from dividends and option premiums, though the options can limit gains in strong markets, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
JPAN: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in Japanese company stocks, chosen by the managers rather than an index. Tokyo Electron, Mitsubishi UFJ and Advantest are among the biggest holdings, and technology, industrials and financials make up most of it.
JPEF: An actively managed fund of a fairly small number of US stocks, so a few holdings drive results. NVIDIA, Alphabet and Apple are about 20% of it, and technology is over a third of the fund.
JPEM: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets, selected and weighted by an index that favors lower-risk, value-priced and higher-quality names. It is very spread out: Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest at about 2%, and financials are the biggest group.
JPFP: An actively managed fund that combines two strategies: a managed futures approach that takes long or short positions across markets, and a portfolio of US large company stocks. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are among its biggest stock holdings, at about 3% to 4% each.
JPHY: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds, also called junk bonds, which are bonds from companies with lower credit ratings that pay higher interest to make up for the added risk. It spreads money widely, with no single bond above about 1%.
JPIB: An actively managed bond fund holding government and corporate bonds from countries outside the US, including developed and emerging markets, with currency risk hedged back to the dollar. Canada, Germany, Brazil and Australia are among its biggest government holdings.
JPIE: An actively managed JPMorgan bond fund that spreads money across mortgage bonds, corporate bonds and other debt, looking for income with limited ups and downs. Government-backed mortgage bonds from Ginnie Mae and Fannie Mae are among its largest holdings.
JPIN: Stocks of large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside North America, picked and weighted by an index that favors lower-risk, value-priced and higher-quality names. It is very spread out, with no single holding above about 1%.
JPLD: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities (bundles of loans), along with US Treasuries. It keeps its average maturity short, so interest rate changes should affect its price less than a regular bond fund.
JPMB: Follows an index of US dollar bonds issued by emerging market governments and government related groups, such as Brazil, Turkey, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia. It is spread over many countries, and no single bond is more than about 2% of it.
JPME: US mid-sized companies chosen to represent several factors such as value, quality and momentum, then weighted to keep risk down. It is very spread out, with the biggest holdings around 0.5% each, and it is not tilted toward any one sector.
JPO: A fund that tries to earn high income from JPMorgan stock by selling options on it, rather than owning the shares directly. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and the options mean it gives up much of the gains if the stock rises a lot.
JPRE: An actively managed fund of US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties such as health care buildings, warehouses and data centers. Welltower, Prologis, Equinix and American Tower are about 37% of the fund.
JPRF: An actively managed income fund that holds preferred stocks, hybrids that pay fixed dividends, along with other income-paying debt, with at least a quarter in financial companies. Part of it is held through other funds, and it spreads money across many issuers.
JPSE: Small US stocks chosen by a rules-based index that uses value, momentum and quality factors. It is very widely spread, with no holding above about 0.4%, so it looks more like a broad small-company fund than a bet on a few names.
JPSV: An actively managed fund of US small company stocks that look cheap compared with their worth, drawn from the same size range as the Russell 2000 Value Index. It is spread across many holdings, none above about 2%, and leans toward financial companies.
JPUS: US large and mid-size stocks chosen by a rules-based index that spreads its bets across several factors, such as value and quality, rather than weighting by company size. It is very spread out, with no holding above roughly 0.5%, so no single stock matters much.
JPXN: About 400 Japanese companies chosen for profitability and good governance, following the JPX-Nikkei 400 Index. It spans many industries, with the top holdings, like Tokyo Electron and Murata, each about 3% of the fund.
JPY: An actively managed fund of Japanese companies, bought for their quality and growth rather than by tracking an index. Big banks such as Mitsubishi UFJ, Sumitomo Mitsui and Mizuho, plus Tokyo Electron, are among the largest positions at about 4% to 5% each.
JQTY: US large companies picked for high quality, meaning strong profits and financial health, following the Jensen Quality Index of US stocks. It is a passive index fund, with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple each about 5% and technology around 37% of it.
JQUA: Large US companies with high quality traits, like strong profits and steady earnings, chosen by a JPMorgan index. It is well spread, with Apple, Microsoft, Broadcom and others each about 2%, and technology is roughly 40% of it.
JSCP: An actively managed fund of investment-grade bonds with short maturities, mixing Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, with a limited amount of lower-rated debt. Short lengths mean it should be less sensitive to interest rate changes than a regular core bond fund.
JSI: An actively managed fund of securitized debt, which are bonds backed by pools of loans such as home mortgages. Much of it is in government-backed mortgage bonds, with some in other asset-backed securities, and it aims to pay regular income.
JSMD: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that managers expect to grow faster than average, using a mix of research and quantitative models. It is spread across many stocks, with the top holding only about 2% of the fund.
JSML: Small US companies that Janus Henderson's quantitative models rank as likely to grow, held in an actively managed portfolio. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and it includes industrial, financial and real estate names.
JSTC: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies whose business practices fit a social justice screen, such as how they treat workers and communities. It holds companies from at least three countries, with the biggest, Lam Research, at about 4%.
JTEK: An actively managed fund where JPMorgan's team picks US tech and tech-enabled companies it thinks will keep growing for longer than the market expects. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Intel, Lam Research and Alphabet each about 4% to 5%, and it leans toward chip stocks.
JTNY: Investment-grade municipal bonds from New York issuers, with interest generally exempt from federal, New York State and New York City income tax. It is actively managed with an average maturity between three and twelve years, and a small cash holding.
JUCY: An actively managed fund that holds mostly US government bonds and pairs them with options to boost income. The options give up some gains in exchange for a higher payout, so it is not a plain bond fund.
JUDB: A defined-outcome fund that uses options to protect against a set amount of losses in the US stock market over a one-year period starting in July. In return it gives up some of the gains, so it only works as designed if held through the full period.
JUDO: An actively managed fund of large US companies that also uses options to earn extra income. It is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft making up about 21% of the fund, and the options can limit gains in strong markets.
JULB: A buffer fund that uses options on a broad US stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period beginning in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works as intended only if you hold for the whole period.
JULC: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 10% buffer, over a set period starting in July. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on timing.
JULH: An actively managed income fund that combines Treasury bills with options on the S&P 500, aiming for regular payouts over a one-year period starting in July. It carries a barrier: if the market falls past a set level, losses can pass through, and gains are limited.
JULI: A defined outcome fund using options on a developed markets international stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one year period ending in July. It has no cap on gains, but protection and results depend on when you buy during the period.
JULJ: An actively managed fund that uses Treasury bills and options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for income over a one-year period starting in July. It gives up some protection and upside: a drop in the index beyond a set barrier can mean real losses.
JULM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in July. In return, upside is capped, so it only fully works if held for the whole period, and the options make up nearly the entire fund.
JULP: An actively managed fund using customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in July. It aims to absorb the first 12% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and works best held for the full period.
JULT: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each July, with 10 in the name for the buffer size. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
JULU: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set period ending in mid 2027, to absorb the first 15% of losses. Gains are not capped by a set limit, though the protection only works for someone holding for the full period.
JULV: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the US stock market to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, and the outcome only applies if you hold the full period.
JULW: A buffer fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to absorb the first 20% of losses over a set one-year period starting in July. In exchange, it caps how much of the market's gain you can get, and the buffer only applies over the full period.
JULZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set one-year period starting in July. Most of the money sits in short-term Treasury bills, with options doing the work of tracking part of the market's gains while limiting some losses.
JUNC: A defined-outcome fund using options on a fund tracking the S&P 500 to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in June. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
JUNM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a larger set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each June. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold from the start to the end.
JUNP: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over about a year starting each June, with a 12% buffer. In exchange, gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
JUNT: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cover a set amount of losses over a one year period starting each June, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is meant to be held for the whole period to get that result.
JUNW: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 20% of losses over a one-year period that starts each June. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only applies if shares are held for the full period.
JUNZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500, buying calls and selling puts, to follow a one-year outcome starting in June with limits on both losses and gains. Most of the fund sits in Treasuries as backing for those options.
JUSA: Large US stocks picked using the manager's research to try to beat the broad market while staying close to it. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 19% of it, and it leans toward technology.
JUST: Large US companies picked by an index that ranks them on 'just business behavior', such as how they treat workers, customers and communities. Otherwise it looks like a broad large-cap fund: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
JVAL: Large US stocks picked and weighted for value traits, meaning they look cheap compared with measures like earnings and book value. Despite the value label it still holds big tech names, with Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet each around 2%.
JXI: Global utility companies, such as electric, gas and water providers, tracking the S&P Global 1200 Utilities Capped Index. NextEra Energy and Iberdrola are the largest, and the top five holdings are about 28% of the fund.
JXX: An actively managed fund holding only about 20 to 30 large companies that the managers expect to grow quickly. It is very concentrated: Taiwan Semiconductor, Amazon, Broadcom and Oracle together make up roughly 36% of it.
KAIT: A fund of Asian technology companies linked to artificial intelligence, mostly chip makers and electronics suppliers. Taiwan Semiconductor, SK hynix and Samsung are about 18% of it, and nearly all of the fund is in technology.
KAMO: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds other bond ETFs, including short-term Treasury, AAA-rated CLO and ultra-short bond funds. It can also use derivatives to bet on bonds rising or falling, so it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
KAPR: A defined-outcome fund using options on a small-cap Russell 2000 ETF over a set one-year period starting in April. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in return for a limit on gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
KARS: Global companies tied to electric vehicles and future mobility, including carmakers, battery makers and the miners of materials used in them. Panasonic, STMicroelectronics, Tesla and CATL are each about 4 to 6% of it.
KAT: An actively managed fund of large companies that the manager thinks can grow over the long term with limited downside. It is spread across financials, health care, technology and industrials, with Union Pacific, Occidental and Markel each around 5% of it.
