MMHI: Holds municipal bonds, loans to US state and local governments and related groups, with a focus on higher-yielding, lower-rated ones. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the manager actively picks the bonds.
MMID: An actively managed fund of US medium sized companies, similar in size to those in the Russell Midcap index. It is well spread, with no stock above about 2%, and leans toward industrials, technology, financials and health care.
MMIN: Long-term municipal bonds from US states and cities that are insured, so the interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds many small positions, such as airport and county bonds, with none above about 2%.
MMIT: Intermediate-term municipal bonds, mostly issued by US states and cities, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and holds a wide spread of bonds, with none above about 1%, so no single issuer matters much.
MMK: A money market fund holding short-term, high quality debt like bank deposits and commercial paper, from companies and banks rather than the government. It is built to keep a stable price while paying interest that follows short-term rates, and puts more than a quarter of its money in bank obligations.
MMKT: A money market fund holding short-term US government debt, like Treasury bills, and repurchase agreements, which are very short loans backed by government securities. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, and the price barely moves.
MMMA: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds from state and local governments across the country, mixing different types and credit qualities. The income is generally exempt from federal income tax, and no single bond is more than about 4% of it.
MMSC: An actively managed fund of small US companies, where several outside investment managers each pick stocks and the fund combines their choices. It leans toward technology, health care and industrials, and no single holding is much more than 2% of it.
MMSD: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds issued by US states, cities and other local authorities, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. Holdings are spread thinly across many issuers, with no single bond above about 2%, and the short maturities keep price swings small.
MMTM: US large, mid and small companies from the S&P 1500 that have recently been rising, with the index tilting weights toward those stocks. It is tech heavy, with NVIDIA about 10% of the fund, and its holdings change as momentum shifts.
MN: An actively managed fund holding just a handful of AI and tech giants, in roughly equal slices. NVIDIA, SpaceX, Meta and Alphabet are each about 25%, so it is extremely concentrated, and it targets exposure to private firms like OpenAI and Anthropic as well.
MNA: A merger arbitrage strategy that buys shares of companies being bought out, hoping to collect the gap between the current price and the deal price. It tends to move less with the market, but it can lose money if a deal falls through, and it holds some cash.
MNBD: A fund of intermediate-term municipal bonds, issued by state and local governments, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. It holds many small positions covering schools, toll roads, housing and universities, with the largest each around 2% of the fund.
MNVR: An actively managed defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a one year period starting in November. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
MNVT: An actively managed fund holding only about 15 to 35 stocks from around the world, making it very concentrated. Holdings include smaller, higher-risk names like CleanSpark, Lucid and Pagaya, so it can swing a lot.
MNZL: Tracks a Russell index of large US companies that meet halal standards, meaning it screens out businesses like alcohol, gambling and interest based finance. Apple is about 16% of it, and technology is about half of the fund.
MOAT: US companies that Morningstar believes have lasting competitive advantages, called wide moats, picked when their stock prices look attractive against Morningstar's estimate of value. Holdings are spread out, with the largest only about 3% each.
MODL: US large company stocks, with the mix across the 11 market sectors shifted by a rules-based model that tries to favor stronger sectors. The result is a lot like the broad US market, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 15% of the fund.
MOO: Companies that earn at least half their revenue from farming-related businesses such as seeds, fertilizer, crop chemicals, animal health and farm machinery. It is fairly concentrated: Bayer, Corteva and Deere together are about 27% of the fund, and many holdings are outside the US.
MOOD: An actively managed fund that moves between other ETFs covering stocks, bonds and other assets, depending on market sentiment. About 45% is in a total US stock market fund, and the rest includes short-term Treasuries and a US dollar fund.
MORT: US mortgage REITs, companies that earn money by owning home or property loans, often using borrowed money to do so. Annaly and AGNC are about a third of the fund, and these companies are known for paying high income that can swing a lot.
MOTG: Global companies that Morningstar judges to have lasting competitive advantages, often called wide moats, picked from its index and held when their prices look attractive. It is spread thinly, with the largest holdings around 2% each, across industrials, technology, consumer staples and health care.
MOTI: Companies outside the US that Morningstar rates as having durable competitive advantages, or moats, and that look reasonably priced. It spreads across many countries and industries, with no single holding above about 4% of the fund.
MOTO: Global companies that help build safer, cleaner or connected vehicles, from chipmakers to electric power and automotive suppliers. It is actively managed, leans toward technology, and its top holdings include Taiwan Semiconductor, Infineon, Quanta Services and Amphenol, each around 5% to 6%.
MPDB: Uses swap contracts to follow an HSBC index of large US stocks that is designed to limit part of the losses in falling markets. The cash holdings are collateral, and the buffer comes at the cost of some upside.
MPDY: Uses swaps tied to an S&P 500 futures index that pays out income and can end early when certain conditions are met, an arrangement called an autocall. It is a complex fund where the swaps do the work, and the cash held is just collateral.
MPIA: A defined-outcome fund that uses swaps, contracts that pay the return of an index, tied to the Nasdaq-100. It is an autocall strategy, meaning it can end early and pay out if the index meets certain conditions, with cash backing the swaps.
MPIM: An actively managed fund that gets its exposure through swaps, contracts that pay the return of an index of US momentum stocks with an autocall feature, which can end the strategy early when set conditions are met. It is built around income, and the cash shown is mostly backing for those contracts.
MPLY: An actively managed fund holding companies that dominate their markets with little competition, either alone as monopolies or together as a small group of rivals. It is heavily tilted to big tech, with Alphabet and NVIDIA about 10% each.
MPRO: A fund of ETFs that mixes six to nine funds, about half stock funds and half bond funds, tracking the Monarch ProCap index. Its largest piece is an iShares fund at about half the portfolio, with sector funds making up much of the rest.
MRA: A fund that uses derivatives tied to an autocallable note on MARA Holdings, a bitcoin mining company. An autocallable pays out on set conditions and can end early, so this is a complex, single-stock strategy rather than a basket of shares.
MRCP: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in March, aiming to protect against the first 12% of losses in exchange for a limit on gains. The buffer only works for those who hold the whole period.
MRGR: Follows an index of companies being bought out in announced mergers, a strategy called merger arbitrage. It buys the targets at a small discount to the deal price, so it is meant to move more with deals closing than with the overall stock market.
MRNY: An income fund tied to Moderna stock that uses options to collect payments, rather than owning the shares outright. The options cap how much it gains if Moderna rises, while it still takes much of the loss if the stock falls.
MRSK: A fund that mainly holds an S&P 500 ETF and uses options to limit big drops and calm out the ride. About 87% is in that one ETF, and the options mean it will usually trail the market in strong years.
MSBT: A trust from Morgan Stanley that holds bitcoin and aims to track its price, less the trust's expenses. It owns only the coin, so its value moves with bitcoin, which can swing sharply.
MSEP: Uses options on the S&P 500 to absorb part of the losses over a one-year period starting each September, in exchange for a limit on how much it can gain. The protection only works if you hold through the full period.
MSFO: An options income fund tied to Microsoft that sells call options on the stock to collect payments, then pays most of it out as distributions. The options cap how much it gains if Microsoft rises, and it still loses if the stock falls.
MSFW: An actively managed fund that uses swaps, contracts that pay the stock's returns, plus some Microsoft shares to aim for about 1.2 times Microsoft's return over each calendar week. It is leveraged and resets weekly, so it is a bet on one company, with Treasury bills as collateral.
MSFY: An actively managed fund that aims for regular income from options on Microsoft stock while keeping some exposure to the share price. Mostly Treasury bills sit behind the options, and the strategy limits gains if Microsoft rises sharply.
MSLC: Large US companies chosen from a research based model run by Morgan Stanley, aiming to hold a portfolio close to the broad large company market. NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are about 16% of it, which is typical of large US stock funds.
MSML: Small US companies, tracking the MSCI USA Small Cap index, which covers the smaller slice of the American stock market. It holds a very large number of stocks, with none above about half a percent, so it is a broad, evenly spread small-company fund.
MSMR: An actively managed mix that mostly holds other ETFs, including short-term Treasury bills, pharmaceuticals, small-cap stocks and gold. The managers use trend and sector rotation signals to shift between them, aiming to limit losses in falling markets.
MSOL: A trust that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, directly and tries to track its price. It also earns some staking rewards on part of its holdings, and its value rises and falls with SOL, which can swing sharply.
MSOS: An actively managed fund investing in US companies that grow and sell cannabis, which is still illegal under federal law. It is very concentrated: Curaleaf and Trulieve are over 20%, and a large share of the fund sits in cash and similar holdings used for swaps.
MSR: A fund that uses autocallable contracts tied to MicroStrategy stock, a company known for holding a lot of Bitcoin. Autocallables pay income under set conditions and can end early, so returns differ a lot from owning the stock directly.
MSSE: A trust that holds ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, and aims to follow its price, less expenses. It also stakes part of its ether to earn extra rewards, and its value can swing sharply along with the price of ether.
MSSM: An actively managed fund that buys US small and mid-size company stocks, with managers choosing the holdings instead of following an index. It is spread across hundreds of names, with technology and industrials the biggest sectors, and no holding is above about 2%.
MSSS: A fund of funds holding 10 equal-weighted ETFs, each covering a different US sector or subsector, chosen by an index. Each ETF is about 10% of the fund, so it spreads across areas like health care, technology and financials.
MSST: An actively managed fund that gives synthetic exposure to the price of MicroStrategy (MSTR) stock and sells options to generate income, aiming for a distribution target. Selling those options limits gains, and the stock is very volatile and tied to bitcoin.
MSTB: An actively managed fund that holds an S&P 500 fund and shifts how much stock market exposure it has depending on market conditions, using statistical models and volatility signals. It aims to take less risk in rough markets, and about 82% sits in an S&P 500 ETF.
MSTI: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mixing US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate debt. Holdings are very spread out, with none above about 3%, and short maturities mean its price moves less than longer-term bond funds.
MSTQ: An actively managed fund that mostly holds a Nasdaq-100 ETF, about 64% of it, and shifts its stock exposure based on market conditions. It can add Treasuries or hedges, so it may behave differently from a plain Nasdaq-100 fund.
MSTW: A fund built around MicroStrategy (MSTR), a company that holds a large amount of bitcoin, using options and swaps for exposure and paying income weekly. The option strategy limits how much it gains when the stock rises, and the stock is very volatile.
MSTY: An actively managed income fund tied to the share price of MicroStrategy, a company known for holding bitcoin. It uses options to produce income, which caps how much of the stock's gains it can capture, and the Treasury bills listed are mainly backing for those options.
MTAW: Holds companies tied to Meta's AI ecosystem, such as Meta itself, its suppliers and data center builders. Meta is about 24% of the fund, with Corning, Nebius and Quanta Computer each around 4% to 5%, so it is concentrated.
MTBA: An actively managed fund of mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans, mostly backed by government-linked agencies. It uses to-be-announced contracts, which are forward purchases of mortgage pools, so its holdings can total more than 100% of the fund.
MTGG: Stocks of growth companies from around the world, meaning those expected to grow faster than average. It is actively managed and must hold a significant share of its assets in companies outside the US, so it differs from a US-only growth fund.
MTGP: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of home loans, many backed by Fannie Mae and Ginnie Mae. It can also hold other securitized debt, and the managers choose holdings rather than tracking an index.
MTRA: An actively managed fund of growth-oriented companies based outside the US, picked for strong expected growth. It is fairly concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 9% and ASML at about 6%, and tech, industrials and health care make up most of it.
MTUM: US large and mid-sized stocks that have been rising the fastest recently, picked and weighted by the MSCI USA Momentum index. It follows recent winners, so it changes often, and Micron, AMD, Broadcom and Intel are among its largest holdings.
MTYY: An actively managed fund that sells put options on a leveraged MicroStrategy (MSTR) ETF to pay income, with Treasury bills held as backing. Income can be large, but it takes on much of the loss if the underlying fund falls and gives up gains.
MUB: A broad group of US municipal bonds, loans to states, cities and public bodies whose interest is free of federal income tax. It holds thousands of mostly investment grade bonds of medium length, and no single issuer is more than a small slice.
MUIB: A fund that holds a leveraged position tied to Micron stock using swaps, and sells options to boost income. Micron is the single stock behind it, and the options limit gains if the stock jumps while leaving losses open.
MULT: An actively managed bond fund spread across many types of debt, including US and foreign government bonds, corporate bonds and loans. The manager shifts between sectors to find income, so it is more flexible than a fund tracking one bond index.
MUNA: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature by 2030, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. As bonds mature, the money is returned and the fund winds down, and it spreads across many local issuers, none above about 2% of the fund.
MUNB: A ladder of US municipal bonds maturing through 2035, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It spreads out maturities, with bonds coming due over time, and pays income out to shareholders instead of reinvesting it.
MUNC: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature by 2045, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. As bonds mature, the money is returned and the fund winds down, and it spreads across many local issuers, none above about 3% of the fund.
MUND: A fund of tax-exempt municipal bonds that pays out income instead of reinvesting it, built as a ladder that runs toward 2055. The interest is generally free of regular federal income tax, and it is spread across many local governments and agencies.
MUNF: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature in stages up to 2036, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It is designed to wind down around 2036, and it pays out its income to shareholders rather than reinvesting it.
MUNG: A fund of tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, built as a ladder of bonds maturing around 2046. It pays out income regularly and winds down as the bonds mature.
MUNH: A fund of tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose interest is free from regular federal income tax, built as a ladder of bonds maturing around 2056. Its bonds are very long-term, so the price is more sensitive to interest rate changes.
MUNI: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term municipal bonds, loans to states and cities whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. The managers choose bonds themselves rather than following an index, and it can hold some Treasuries alongside them.
MUNJ: A ladder of US municipal bonds that mature in stages up to 2031, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It is designed to wind down around 2031, and it pays out its income to shareholders rather than reinvesting it.
MUNX: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term US municipal bonds, aiming to pay income exempt from federal income tax. It spreads across many issuers like cities, counties and housing agencies, and no single bond is above about 3% of the fund.
MUNY: Holds New York municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, whose interest is generally exempt from federal and New York state income tax. It follows an index and is spread across hundreds of issuers such as state agencies, bridges and tunnels and water authorities.
MUSE: An actively managed mix of bonds from several parts of the credit market, such as corporate, mortgage-backed and other debt. By spreading across sectors, the managers try to earn higher income than a plain government bond fund, taking on more credit risk.
MUST: Holds US municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, using a rules-based index. It mixes sectors like airports, toll roads and universities, and is spread across hundreds of bonds, none above about 0.5%.
MUY: A fund that aims to pay regular income from options on Micron Technology stock, without owning much Micron directly. The options give up part of Micron's upside, and the fund is still exposed to large drops in the stock.
MUYY: A fund that aims for high income from options tied to Micron stock, using a leveraged Micron fund as its reference. It does not simply own the shares, and Treasury bills back the options, so it follows one volatile company with limited upside.
MVAL: Tracks a Morningstar index of large US companies with durable competitive advantages, called wide moats, that look reasonably priced. It leans toward consumer staples, health care and consumer discretionary, and no single holding is more than about 5% of the fund.
MVFD: Holds 40 US stocks in equal amounts, picked for positive cash flow and the ability to pay dividends, and then screened by trading volume. Because every stock has the same weight, the top holdings are only around 3% each, with energy a big slice.
MVFG: A fund of funds that holds up to 25 equally weighted stock ETFs from around the world, chosen for positive trading-volume cash flow. When flows turn negative, part or all of it can move into Treasury or other defensive ETFs instead.
MVPA: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies that the managers believe are undervalued and have room to grow. It is fairly concentrated, with Crocs, Bread Financial, Bloomin' Brands and Crescent Energy each around 6% of it.
MWHS: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to electricity prices through futures contracts and swaps. It is a bet on power prices rather than on companies, and the cash it holds mostly serves as backing for those contracts.
MXI: Large materials companies from around the world, such as chemical makers, miners and paint producers, following an S&P Global 1200 index. It is fairly concentrated at the top: Linde and BHP are about 15% together, and Rio Tinto, Newmont and Freeport-McMoRan are also large.
MYCF: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2026, so the fund is designed to wind down and return its money around then. Until that point it pays interest, and its largest holdings, like Bayer and VICI, are each under 5% of it.
MYCG: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2027, so it works like a bond that winds down. Because the maturity is close, it moves less with interest rates, and it is spread across many companies with none above about 3%.
MYCH: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2028. As they come due, the fund winds down and returns the money, so it behaves more like one bond than an ongoing fund, and it is spread across many companies.
MYCI: US investment grade corporate bonds that mature in 2029, tracked by an index. Spread across many companies like Philip Morris, Centene, AbbVie and Boeing at roughly 2% each, the fund winds down when the bonds mature.
MYCJ: US corporate bonds that mostly mature in 2030, so the fund is built to wind down around that year. It holds bonds from many companies, such as Boeing, T-Mobile and Anheuser-Busch, each only about 2% of the fund.
MYCK: Holds US corporate bonds that mature in 2031, and the fund is designed to wind down around then. It is very spread out, with no single issuer above about 3%, from companies like Bank of Montreal, Boeing and IBM.
MYCL: A fund of US corporate bonds that mature in 2032, so it is designed to wind down around that year. It holds many companies, such as IBM, Philip Morris, Church & Dwight and AT&T, each only about 3% of the fund.
MYCM: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, so the fund is designed to wind down around then and return the money. Holdings are spread thin, with no single issuer above about 4%, across companies like CVS, Marvell and Verisk.
MYCN: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2034, so the fund is designed to wind down around then and return the money. Holdings are spread thin, with no single issuer above about 3%, from companies like General Motors Financial, BP and AT&T.
MYCO: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature in 2035, so the fund is designed to wind down around that year. It holds hundreds of bonds from many companies, each only about 2% of the fund, and pays out interest along the way.
MYCP: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2036. The fund is set to close around that year, so it behaves more like a single bond that returns your money at the end.
MYHA: A basket of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature around 2027, so the fund is designed to wind down then. Its top holdings, such as DISH Network, Nissan and Live Nation, are each only about 3% to 4%.
MYHB: A basket of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature around 2028, so the fund is designed to wind down then. It is spread widely: no single bond is more than about 3% of the fund.
MYHC: A basket of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature around 2029, so the fund is designed to wind down then. It is spread widely: the largest holdings, like TransDigm and Cloud Software Group, are only about 2% each.
MYHD: A basket of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature in 2030, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It pays higher interest than safer bonds because the companies are riskier, and holds many bonds, each about 1%.
MYHE: A basket of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature in 2031, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It pays higher interest than safer bonds because the issuers are riskier, and holds many bonds, each only about 2%.
MYHF: A basket of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that all mature around 2032, so the fund is designed to wind down then. Because the bonds share a maturity year, it behaves more like holding a bond to the end than a typical open-ended bond fund.
MYLD: An actively managed fund of very small US companies chosen for shareholder yield, meaning how much cash they return through dividends and share buybacks. It is spread across many companies, with the largest, like ManpowerGroup, each only around 1% of the fund.
MYMF: Municipal bonds with income generally exempt from federal income tax, all maturing in 2026, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. Because that date is so near, most of the fund now sits in cash while the last bonds mature.
MYMG: Municipal bonds with income generally exempt from federal income tax, all maturing in 2027, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It is spread over many issuers like school districts and transit authorities, with none above roughly 4%.
MYMH: A basket of US municipal bonds that all mature in 2028, paying interest that is generally free of federal income tax. The fund is set to close around that year, spreading its money across many state and local issuers.
MYMI: A basket of municipal bonds that all mature in 2029, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. Because the bonds are due in one year, the fund is designed to wind down then, returning cash much like a single bond would.
MYMJ: A fund of US municipal bonds that mature in 2030, so it is designed to wind down around that year. The income is generally free from federal income tax, and the bonds come from many issuers, with no single one above about 4%.
MYMK: A basket of municipal bonds that mature in 2031, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. It holds many bonds from issuers like toll roads, hospitals and water utilities, and the fund winds down as the bonds mature.
MYML: A basket of US municipal bonds that all mature around 2032, paying interest that is generally exempt from regular federal income tax. Because the bonds share a maturity year, the fund is designed to wind down around then and return the money.
MYY: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of the daily move of the S&P MidCap 400, a mid-sized US company index, using derivatives. It resets every day, so over longer periods results can drift far from simply the opposite of the index.
NACP: Large US companies picked by an index that scores them on diversity and inclusion, tied to the NAACP's goals. It looks a lot like the broader market, with technology the largest sector at around 40%.
NANC: An actively managed fund that buys stocks which sitting Democratic members of Congress have reported owning in their public disclosures. It is tilted toward big tech and chips: NVIDIA, Applied Materials, Alphabet and Microsoft are together over 25% of it.
NANR: North American companies in natural resources: energy, metals and mining, and agriculture, tracked by an S&P index. It is concentrated in a few giants, with ExxonMobil at about 9% and Chevron at about 6%, so oil prices matter a lot.
NAPR: A defined-outcome fund using options on a Nasdaq-100 ETF over a set one-year period starting in April. It aims to cushion part of the losses in return for a limit on gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
NASA: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the space economy, such as rocket launchers, satellite makers and space data firms. It is concentrated, with Rocket Lab at around 11% and the top five holdings about 36%, and it includes a private SpaceX exposure.
NATO: Tracks an index of aerospace and defense companies based in NATO member countries. It is concentrated, with General Electric, RTX, Boeing and Rolls-Royce about 32% together, so it moves with defense spending and the aerospace industry.
NAUG: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ fund, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period beginning each August. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
NBCE: An actively managed fund investing in Chinese companies, mainly mainland China A-shares plus Hong Kong listings and US-traded depositary receipts. Technology is about 40% of it, and holdings like Montage, CATL and Innolight are each around 4%.
NBCM: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to commodities such as oil, metals and crops through derivatives, which are contracts tied to their prices. The bonds shown as holdings are mainly a cash-like cushion behind those contracts, so the fund is really a bet on commodity prices.
NBCR: Large US companies chosen by Neuberger Berman's managers, who aim for a core stock portfolio that stays close to the broad market. It is actively managed, and NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet together make up about a quarter of the fund.
NBDS: An actively managed, concentrated fund of companies the managers see as disruptors in areas like semiconductors and space. It leans heavily on chip firms: AMD, ARM and NVIDIA are about 25% of it.
NBET: An actively managed fund of energy infrastructure and energy-transition companies, mainly pipeline and midstream businesses that move and process oil and gas. It is heavily energy, about 90%, with Targa Resources, Energy Transfer and Enterprise Products Partners the largest holdings.
NBFC: An actively managed fund that invests across many types of debt, including corporate bonds, loans and CLOs (bundles of corporate loans packaged into bonds). Because it can shift between credit types, it is spread thin: no single holding is more than about 2% of the fund.
NBFR: An actively managed fund holding large US stocks, using options to cushion part of the losses over a set period, in exchange for limits on gains. It is tech heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 24% of the fund.
NBGX: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, similar to those in the Russell 1000 Growth index. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft are about 34% of the fund.
NBIE: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies in developed markets outside the United States, such as Europe, Japan and Australia. The managers pick the stocks themselves, and the top holdings, such as ASML, Novartis and Shell, are only about 2% to 4% each.
NBJP: An actively managed fund of Japanese companies, with the manager picking stocks in industries like manufacturing, insurance and banking. Its biggest holdings, such as Sumitomo Electric, Tokio Marine and Mizuho, are each about 4% of it.
NBOS: An actively managed options fund that earns income by selling put options on the S&P 500, backed by Treasury securities. It collects payments for taking on stock market risk, so it keeps the income but absorbs losses if the market falls sharply.
NBSD: An actively managed fund of mostly investment-grade bonds with short lifespans, from governments, companies and packaged loans like mortgage-backed securities. Short maturities mean the price should swing less than a typical bond fund, with the goal of steady income.
NBSM: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that managers expect to grow. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 3%, and industrials, financials, health care and tech are the largest sectors.
NBTR: An actively managed core bond fund holding a mix of government bonds, corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and asset-backed securities. It aims for a total return of income plus price gains, and US Treasuries make up a large share.
NCIQ: A fund that holds a basket of major cryptocurrencies, mostly bitcoin and ether, and tracks the Nasdaq CME Crypto Index. It holds the digital coins rather than company shares, so its value rises and falls with crypto prices, which can swing a lot.
NCLD: Holds stocks of neocloud companies, which rent out computing power for AI, such as Nebius, CoreWeave, IREN and Hut 8. It is a concentrated bet on a small group of fast moving companies, and it can also get exposure through swaps (contracts that pay the stocks' returns).
NCLO: An actively managed fund of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated AA to BBB. A CLO is a bond backed by a pool of corporate loans, and this fund holds the middle layers, which pay more than top-rated ones but carry more risk.
NCPB: An actively managed bond fund holding a broad mix of income-producing bonds, mainly US Treasuries and mortgage-backed bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Core plus means a base of high quality bonds with room for some higher-yielding ones.
NDAA: An actively managed fund that mostly holds other ETFs, shifting its mix of stocks, bonds and cash using models from Ned Davis Research. Today it is mainly stocks, with large US index and growth funds making up nearly half of it.
NDEC: Uses options tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in December. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
NDIA: An actively managed fund of Indian companies, picked by the manager rather than by an index. Banks lead it: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Reliance Industries are each over 7%, and financials are about a third of the fund.
NDIV: Energy and natural resource companies from an index, with a covered call strategy that sells options on the stocks to earn extra income. That income comes at the cost of limited gains in strong rallies, and the fund is heavy in oil and gas firms.
NDOW: An actively managed mix of stocks, bonds and other funds spread across many asset types, such as international stocks, emerging market debt and managed futures. It aims for a more conservative balance than an all-stock fund.
NEAR: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment-grade US dollar bonds, with US Treasuries a large share of it. Because the average maturity is kept short, its price should move less than a regular bond fund when interest rates change.
NECK: An actively managed fund of companies the manager sees as bottlenecks in the AI boom, like memory chips, optical parts and chipmaking equipment. SK hynix, Lumentum and Samsung are each roughly 8 to 10% of it, so a few names drive it.
NEHI: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to Ether, the cryptocurrency, through an Ethereum ETF and uses options to try to produce high income. The options limit how much it gains if Ether rises, and Treasuries listed in its holdings are mostly backing for them.
NELS: An actively managed fund that mixes individual stocks and other ETFs to cover a broad range of US companies. Its biggest positions are NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, which together make up around 20% of the fund.
NEMD: An actively managed bond fund holding debt from governments and companies in emerging market countries, all paid back in hard currencies like the US dollar. Because the bonds are in dollars rather than local money, currency swings in those countries matter less, though the credit risk of the borrowers still does.
NERD: An actively managed fund buying companies in the video game business, from game makers to platforms. It is fairly concentrated: NetEase, Electronic Arts, Nintendo and Take-Two are each about 8% to 12%, and communication stocks make up most of the fund.
NETL: Real estate companies that own net lease properties, where tenants pay most of the building costs, tracked by an index of such companies. It is concentrated in a handful of names, with WP Carey, NNN REIT and VICI Properties each around 8%.
NEWZ: An actively managed fund of US stocks of all sizes, picked using AI that reads news coverage to score the sentiment around each company. Holdings are spread, with no stock above about 4%, and it leans toward financials, technology and utilities.
NFEB: Options based fund tracking the Invesco QQQ, the Nasdaq 100, that cushions a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in February, but caps the gains. The protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
NFLP: An actively managed fund that aims to pay regular income from Netflix stock by selling options on it, while still giving some exposure to the share price. Selling those options limits the gains if Netflix rises, and it still falls if the stock does.
NFLT: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across many parts of the bond market, such as government, corporate, mortgage and higher-risk bonds. The managers shift between sectors as conditions change, and no single bond is more than about 2% of the fund.
NFLW: A fund meant to return about 1.2 times the weekly move of Netflix stock, using swaps (contracts that pay a stock's returns) and some shares. It pays distributions weekly, and because it is leveraged and tied to a single stock, it can swing sharply.
NFLY: Aims to earn income and track part of the price moves of Netflix stock using options rather than owning the shares. Most of the fund is held in Treasury bills, and the options strategy limits gains when Netflix rises sharply.
NFRA: Infrastructure companies in developed and emerging markets, such as railroads, utilities, airports and telecoms, tracking a STOXX index. It is spread out, with the largest holdings, like Canadian Pacific Kansas City and Canadian National Railway, only about 3% or 4% each.
NFRX: An actively managed fund of companies that run infrastructure such as power utilities, railroads and energy pipelines. It holds a modest number of stocks, with Union Pacific, National Grid and Williams each about 5% of it, and utilities make up almost half.
NFTY: Tracks the Nifty 50 index of India's 50 largest and most liquid stocks, but holds each one in roughly equal amounts. Because of the equal weights, each is about 2%, so the biggest Indian companies matter less than in a standard index.
NGHT: Mixes exposure to bitcoin with US Treasuries and other cash-like holdings, and is actively managed. Treasuries make up most of the fund, and the bitcoin part can swing a lot, so it is a smaller bet on crypto than owning bitcoin directly.
NGIF: An actively managed fund buying stocks of infrastructure companies around the world, such as utilities, pipelines and transport. Utilities lead the holdings, with Entergy, American Electric Power and NextEra each about 5%, and at least 40% must be non-US.
NHYB: US dollar corporate bonds rated just below investment grade, often called junk bonds, but only the higher end of that group (BB to B). It pays higher income than safer bonds in return for more risk of default, and holds many bonds with no issuer above about 1%.
NHYM: A fund of high-yield municipal bonds, which are issued by state and local governments or projects with weaker credit and pay more tax-exempt interest. The bonds are exempt from regular federal income tax, and it is spread across many issuers, with none above about 2%.
NICO: An actively managed fund of global tobacco and nicotine companies, meaning firms that earn at least half their revenue from those products. It is concentrated: Philip Morris, British American Tobacco and Imperial Brands are about 44% of it, and it is all consumer staples.
NIHI: International developed-market stocks, with an options strategy that sells call options to generate extra income. Selling those options limits gains when stocks rise, and the fund holds mostly a single iShares fund as its underlying exposure.
NIKL: Stocks of nickel mining and supply companies around the world, many in Indonesia and Australia. Nickel is used in batteries and stainless steel, and a few names dominate: PT Antam, Nickel Industries and PT Merdeka Battery Materials are about 39% of it.
NISM: Holds small and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, such as Japan, Australia, Italy and Canada. The fund is spread thin, with no single company above about 2% to 3% of it, so no one stock drives the results.
NITE: An actively managed fund that holds a small group of US stocks, typically 15 to 25 companies. Tesla, Amazon and NVIDIA are each about 9% to 10%, so it is concentrated and its results depend on just a few companies.
NIXT: US small and mid-sized stocks that look like cheap value stocks, picked by a Research Affiliates index built around companies removed from other indexes. It holds many positions, none above about 1%, so it is very spread out.
NJAN: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Nasdaq-100 to absorb the first 15% of losses over a one-year period that starts each January. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
NJNK: An actively managed fund of US high yield bonds, also called junk bonds because the companies borrowing have lower credit ratings. Those bonds pay more interest, and the fund holds many of them, with no single bond above about 1%.
NJUL: A fund that uses options on the Nasdaq-100 to cushion the first 15% of losses over a one-year period that starts each July, in exchange for a cap on its gains. The buffer only works if you hold through the whole period, and the cap limits upside.
NJUN: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (a Nasdaq 100 fund) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each June. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection works best if you hold through the full period.
NLR: Companies tied to uranium and nuclear power, including uranium miners, power producers with nuclear plants and reactor suppliers. Cameco, Constellation, PSEG and BWX Technologies are about 30% of the fund.
NLSI: An actively managed fund that buys some US stocks and bets against others, called a long/short approach, and also uses options to produce high monthly income. It is concentrated in a few names: Micron Technology alone is about 18% of the fund.
NMAR: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to follow big tech up to a limit while cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in March. Gains are capped, and timing of purchase matters.
NMAY: Uses options tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each May. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
NMB: An actively managed fund of investment-grade US municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. The manager picks bonds balancing income against risk, and the interest rates can be fixed, floating or variable.
NMBL: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, bonds and commodities worldwide, mostly by holding other ETFs. Roughly 60% is in stocks and about a quarter in bonds, so it works as a ready-made mix in one fund.
NNOV: A defined outcome fund tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, using options over a one-year period starting in November. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and in return gains are capped.
NOBL: S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least 25 years, held in roughly equal amounts. No stock is above about 2%, so it avoids the big tech concentration of the S&P 500.
NOCT: A fund that uses options on the Invesco QQQ fund, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each October. In return, gains are capped, so the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
NODE: Companies building the digital asset economy, such as bitcoin miners and crypto-related businesses, plus some bitcoin-linked funds. It is a concentrated, volatile theme, with the largest holding being a VanEck bitcoin fund at about 7%.
NOEQ: A US stock fund from Northern Trust that appears to hold other index funds and some individual stocks, covering the broad US market. There is little detail on its holdings, so treat the exact makeup as uncertain, and a few ETFs and companies make up much of the top.
NORW: Tracks an index of Norwegian companies, so it is a bet on one small, resource-heavy economy. Equinor and DNB Bank are about 24% together, and energy and financials make up more than half of the fund.
NOVM: A defined-outcome fund using options on the S&P 500 to cushion a large part of the losses over a one-year period starting in November. In return, it caps how much of the market's gains it can keep.
NOVP: An actively managed fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses, up to the 12% buffer in its name, over a one year period starting in November. In return, gains from the index are capped.
NOVZ: An actively managed fund using options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set one-year period starting in November. The options track part of the market's gains while limiting some losses, with most of the money held in Treasuries.
NPFE: An actively managed fund buying US stocks of various sizes, aiming for income and long-term growth. It is fairly concentrated: Microsoft is about 10% of the fund, and technology is more than a third of it.
NPFI: An actively managed fund of preferred stocks and similar income securities, which pay fixed-style dividends and rank between bonds and common stock. Many holdings are issued by banks, such as Banco Santander and NatWest, and no single one is more than about 2%.
NQLT: An actively managed fund of mid and large US companies that the manager sees as high quality, with a few foreign stocks allowed. The big names lead it: Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and NVIDIA together are about 28% of the fund.
NRAM: Follows an index of companies making computer memory and storage, such as Micron, SanDisk, SK hynix, Seagate and Samsung, in part through swaps. It is a narrow technology bet: the top three holdings are about 45% of the fund.
NRES: An actively managed global fund of natural resources companies, mainly in materials such as fertilizer, mining and metals, and energy such as oil majors. It holds a mix of about 50 companies, so it follows commodity driven industries rather than the broad market.
NRR: Holds NEAR, the digital token that runs the NEAR blockchain, so its value follows the token's price. It also stakes part of its NEAR to earn extra tokens as rewards, and the price can swing a lot, like most crypto.
NRSH: Tracks an index of North American companies expected to benefit from production moving closer to home, including logistics, transport and property firms. In practice it also holds software names, and no holding is above about 4%.
NSCI: An actively managed bond fund focused on securitized debt, meaning pools of loans like home mortgages that are bundled and sold as bonds. It holds government-backed and private mortgage securities from names like Fannie Mae, spread over many holdings, each under 4%.
NSEP: Options based fund tracking the Invesco QQQ, the Nasdaq 100, that cushions a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September, but caps the gains. The protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
NSI: Emerging-market stocks chosen by an index that leaves out companies seen as helping adversaries of the US, mainly China-linked firms. That makes it heavy in Taiwan and Korea: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about a quarter of the fund.
NSIG: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet and Apple make up about 34% of it, and technology is well over half the fund.
NSIV: An actively managed fund of US companies the manager considers undervalued, using a disciplined, research-driven approach. It is diversified across financials, technology, health care and industrials, with no single stock above about 7%.
NTRL: An actively managed fund that buys shares of companies involved in announced deals like mergers and sells short others, trying to profit from how those events play out rather than from the market's direction. Its holdings shown here are mostly cash-like collateral held with banks.
NTSD: An actively managed fund that holds large US stocks and adds index futures to get exposure to international stocks too, so the same money works in two places. The top US holdings are NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet, together about 19% of it.
NTSE: Emerging markets stocks weighted by company size, like a standard emerging markets index, with US Treasury futures added on top for some bond market exposure. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 27% of it, so it leans on Asian chipmakers.
NTSI: Developed market stocks outside the US and Canada, weighted by company size, with a currency hedge that reduces the effect of foreign exchange moves on US dollar returns. It is mostly a plain foreign stock fund with that hedge added.
NTSX: An actively managed mix that holds about 90% large US stocks and adds Treasury futures on top, so each dollar gets more than 100% total exposure. The idea is stock-like growth with a bond-like layer added, and the stock part is led by NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet.
NUAG: A broad bond fund that tracks US dollar investment-grade bonds with at least a year left to run, but tilts toward bonds that pay somewhat more income than the standard index. Government bonds are the biggest part, mixed with corporate and mortgage bonds.
NUBD: A broad fund of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed and corporate bonds, selected by an index that screens for environmental, social and governance practices. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings about 1% to 2% each.
NUDG: An actively managed mix of US dividend-paying stocks, picked for companies expected to keep growing their payouts over time. It looks much like the broad market at the top, with Microsoft, Apple and Broadcom around 19% of the fund, and about a third is technology.
NUDM: Large and mid-sized stocks across developed countries outside the US, such as Europe, Japan and Australia, screened for environmental, social and governance factors. It tracks an index in about the same proportions, with ASML the largest holding at about 4%.
NUDV: US companies that pay high dividends and meet environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards, chosen by an index. It is spread across financials, health care, industrials and technology, with no single holding above about 3%.
NUEM: Emerging market stocks chosen by an index that screens for environmental, social and governance practices, from places like China, Taiwan and India. It is top-heavy in chips, as Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 16% of the fund.
NUGO: An actively managed fund of US growth companies with market values of at least $1 billion, chosen by its managers. It is concentrated in a few names: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple, Broadcom and Microsoft together are about 47%, and technology is over 60%.
NUGY: A fund that earns income from options tied to a leveraged gold miners ETF, with most of its money held in Treasury bills. The options bring in high income but cap gains, and the leveraged ETF underneath can lose a lot in a fall.
NUHY: US high-yield corporate bonds, from companies with lower credit ratings that pay more interest, screened for environmental, social and governance standards. It starts from a broad, easily traded high-yield bond index, and no single bond is more than about 2% of it.
NUIB: An actively managed bond fund that mostly holds investment-grade bonds, including government, corporate, municipal and mortgage-backed debt. It focuses on impact bonds, which fund projects with environmental or social goals.
NUIF: US companies that own or run infrastructure, like power utilities, pipelines and waste services. Utilities are about half of it, with energy next at around 30%, so it leans on steady, regulated businesses with American Electric Power at about 9%.
NUKX: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the nuclear industry, including utilities, uranium miners and equipment makers, with a goal of paying income. About 12% sits in a uranium ETF, and it may also use options to add income.
NUKZ: Companies tied to the nuclear industry, from uranium miners and fuel suppliers to reactor builders and nuclear power generators, tracked by the Range Nuclear Renaissance Index. Uranium miner Cameco is about 9% of the fund, and industrials and utilities make up most of the rest.
NULC: Large US companies selected from an index that screens for environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors. It looks much like the broad market, with technology around 40% of the fund and NVIDIA the largest holding.
NULG: Large US growth companies screened for environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. It is concentrated in a few names: NVIDIA, Broadcom, Eli Lilly, AMD and Visa are about 32% of the fund.
NULV: Large US companies that look relatively cheap, screened for good environmental, social and governance (ESG) records, following an index. Microsoft is the biggest holding at about 9%, and technology, financials and health care are the biggest sectors.
NUMG: US mid-sized growth companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, tracked through a Nuveen index. It is spread out, with Datadog the largest at about 5% and no other holding above 4%.
NUMI: Municipal bonds with intermediate maturities from many US states and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread widely, with no single bond over about 2%.
NUMV: US mid-size companies that look inexpensive relative to their size, screened to meet environmental, social and governance standards. It holds a wide mix across financials, technology, industrials and staples, with no holding above about 3%.
NURE: Tracks an index of US real estate investment trusts (REITs), companies that own property and pay out rent, focused on those with shorter lease terms such as apartments and hotels. Each top holding is about 5% of the fund.
NUSA: US investment grade bonds maturing in one to five years, picked from a Bloomberg index and screened on environmental, social and governance measures. Mostly US Treasuries and other high quality debt, with short maturities that keep it less sensitive to interest rate changes.
NUSC: US small companies from an index that screens for environmental, social and governance factors, holding a wide mix of stocks. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1.3%, and has the most in technology, health care and industrials.
NVBT: A fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period from November 1 to October 31. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies when held for the full period.
NVBU: Options on an S&P 500 fund that cushion the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in November, as the name says. It has no cap on gains, though a fee-like cost to the strategy reduces returns versus the index.
NVBW: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cover the first 20% of losses over a one year period from November 1 to October 31. In exchange, gains are limited by a cap, and the protection only applies if held the full year.
NVDW: A fund tied to a single stock, NVIDIA, that aims to pay income weekly. It gets its exposure through derivatives backed mostly by Treasury bills, so it follows NVIDIA's moves but is not simply a holding of the shares.
NVDY: An income fund tied to a single stock, NVIDIA, using options instead of owning the shares directly. It aims to pay high monthly income, but that caps its gains if NVIDIA surges and it can still lose a lot if NVIDIA falls.
NVIB: Gives exposure to NVIDIA stock while aiming to pay out extra income, using swaps and options on the stock. It follows a single company, and the income strategy can limit gains if NVIDIA rises sharply.
NVII: Holds NVIDIA stock exposure and earns extra income from options on it, aiming to pay out regular income. The options can limit how much it gains if NVIDIA jumps, and the large Treasury bill holding is mostly backing for that strategy.
NVIR: An actively managed fund of companies expected to benefit from carbon-based energy production in a cleaner-focused world, such as pipelines, energy services and land owners. It is mostly energy stocks, with a mix of smaller companies like Texas Pacific Land and CES Energy.
NVIT: An actively managed fund built around NVIDIA stock that uses options to aim for a target yearly payout of about 25%, while also seeking some growth. Much of the fund sits in Treasury bills, and the options strategy means it will not fully share in NVIDIA's big gains.
NVOH: Almost entirely Novo Nordisk, the Danish drugmaker, held through its US-traded shares and hedged against changes in the dollar versus the Danish krone. Since it holds a single stock, its results depend on that one company.
NVPS: Companies that supply the chips, memory, cooling and servers that power NVIDIA's AI business, rather than NVIDIA itself, tracked by an index. Mostly technology, with Taiwan Semiconductor, SK hynix and Micron together around 20% of the fund.
NVYY: Aims to pay high income tied to NVIDIA by using options on a related fund rather than owning NVIDIA stock directly. The options cap some of the gains if NVIDIA rises, and the fund's own holdings are mostly cash and short-term bonds.
NXTE: An actively managed global stock fund that invests in companies it considers sustainable, with a big tilt toward the chip and equipment makers behind new technology. SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor alone are about 24% of it, so it is quite concentrated.
NXTG: Companies around the world working on 5G and next-generation wireless technology, tracking an Indxx index. It is mostly chip, tech and telecom names such as Intel, Micron and Taiwan Semiconductor, with no holding above about 2%.
NXTI: Follows an index of US companies picked for the value of their intangible assets, such as brands, patents and know-how, rather than factories or equipment. It holds big, established names like Cisco, Walmart and Johnson & Johnson, each around 4% to 5%.
NXUS: Investment grade bonds issued outside the US, from governments, companies and mortgage-style securities in both developed and emerging countries, with currency swings hedged back to US dollars. This keeps results tied mostly to foreign interest rates rather than currency moves.
NYF: Tax-exempt bonds issued by New York State and its cities and agencies, tracking a broad index of them. Its income is generally free of federal tax, and for New York residents state and local tax too, and no single bond makes up even 1% of it.
NYM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds issued in New York, whose interest is generally free of federal and New York state income tax, mostly rated A or better. It is actively managed, and the largest holdings, such as the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, are each only a few percent of the fund.
NYNY: An actively managed fund of companies based in or closely tied to New York City. About two thirds is in financial companies like Citigroup and JPMorgan, with Pfizer and Verizon among its other largest holdings.
NYSX: Tracks the NYSE 100 Index, which holds 100 of the largest companies listed in the US, including some foreign firms through depositary receipts. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 25% of the fund.
NYYY: A fund that aims to pay frequent income by combining Treasury securities with options-style exposure to NVIDIA stock. Most of its assets sit in cash-like holdings, so it follows NVIDIA only partly, and the income strategy limits how much of the upside it keeps.
NZAC: Holds large and mid-sized stocks from around the world in a way meant to match the Paris climate agreement, cutting down on companies with high carbon emissions. It still looks like the global market, with NVIDIA and Apple about 10% of the fund.
OACP: An actively managed bond fund that mostly buys investment-grade bonds, including US government debt, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, with room for lower-quality bonds. It is spread across many holdings, with Treasuries and agency mortgages among the largest.
OAEM: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and Mexico. Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung are about 13% and 11% of it, so it leans heavily on tech and on a few large companies.
OAIM: An actively managed fund of medium and large companies outside the US, including some in emerging markets. It holds a moderate number of stocks, with the top five, including SK Hynix, Mitsubishi Electric and HSBC, making up about 24%.
OAIW: An actively managed fund of companies tied to the OpenAI ecosystem, such as investors, cloud providers and chip suppliers. It is concentrated and leans toward technology, with SoftBank, Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon among the biggest holdings, and SoftBank alone is about 14%.
OAKG: Large companies from around the world that Oakmark managers think trade for less than they are worth. It is actively managed with about 40 to 60 holdings, spread across Europe, the US and elsewhere, and no single name is above roughly 4% of the fund.
OAKI: An actively managed fund of large companies based outside the US, picked by Oakmark's value focused managers who look for stocks priced below what they think the businesses are worth. It is well spread, with no holding above about 4%.
OAKL: An actively managed fund holding a small number of large US companies that Oakmark's managers think are priced below their worth. Because it holds so few stocks, each one matters more than in a broad index fund.
OAKM: An actively managed fund of about 40 or so large US companies that its managers think are priced below their true worth. It leans toward financials at around 31%, with Citigroup, Keurig Dr Pepper and Delta Air Lines each near 4%.
OALC: An actively managed fund of large US companies, focused on firms that its managers think are of good quality. NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet make up about 20% of it, so it looks a lot like the big names in the S&P 500.
OARK: Aims to pay income and track the ARK Innovation ETF by using a synthetic covered call strategy, a mix of options. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, and the options limit its upside compared to owning the ARK fund.
OASC: An actively managed fund of small and mid sized US companies, with a lean toward financials, technology and health care. It is spread out, with no holding above about 3%, and holds names like Sandisk, Clearway Energy and Flex.
OBIL: A single US Treasury bill with about a year until it matures, held for a month and then swapped for a new one under an index. It holds only US government debt, so its price moves very little and income follows short term interest rates.
OBND: An actively managed bond fund that can hold many kinds of debt, including corporate bonds, bank loans and bonds with equity features. It does this partly through other ETFs, so it blends varied credit types, and the manager chooses where to focus.
OBOR: Companies from around the world that earn much of their revenue from China's Belt and Road infrastructure initiative, tracked by an MSCI index. Despite the China link, it holds firms from many countries, led by Kuwait Finance House and Singapore's OCBC bank, and leans on financials, materials and industrials.
OBTC: A trust that holds bitcoin directly, so its value follows the price of bitcoin, less costs. Bitcoin is a volatile digital currency, and the trust holds the coins instead of stocks, so it moves very differently from a stock fund.
OCDB: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock market ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. In exchange, it limits how much it can gain, and the protection only works if shares are held for the whole period.
OCIO: An actively managed fund of other ETFs, mixing stock and bond funds in a moderate allocation. It typically keeps roughly 30% to 80% in stocks, including Nasdaq 100, value and total market funds, with the rest in more defensive holdings.
OCT: A fund that uses options on US stocks to soften part of the losses over a one year period that starts in October. It also caps how much it can gain over that period, and the protection only applies if you hold the full year.
OCTB: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on a US stock fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. The price of that cushion is a cap on gains, and it only works if held for the whole period.
OCTH: An actively managed fund holding Treasury bills plus options on a broad US stock index, designed to pay regular income from selling those options. A barrier means gains are given up, and some losses can be taken, over a set one-year period starting in October.
OCTI: An actively managed fund using options on international stocks to absorb part of the losses over a set one-year period starting each October. Its buffer is 15%, and it has no cap on gains, though you only get that protection if you hold the full period.
OCTJ: An actively managed fund holding Treasury bills plus options on a broad US stock index, designed to pay regular income from selling those options. A barrier means gains are given up, and some losses can be taken, over a set one-year period starting in October.
OCTM: A fund that uses options tied to a US large-company stock index to absorb a large portion of losses over a one-year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies when shares are held for the full period.
OCTP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped, so it is built to behave differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
OCTT: Uses options tied to an S&P 500 ETF to cushion losses over a set one-year period that starts in October, with a 10% buffer as the name says. In return, gains over that period are capped, so it trades some upside for some protection.
OCTU: Uses options on SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each October, with 15 in the name. It has no set cap on gains, but it uses a cost that trims returns, and protection only applies if you hold the full period.
OCTW: A buffer fund using options on the S&P 500 that absorbs the first 20% of losses over a one year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies to someone holding from the start to the end.
OCTZ: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to aim for a set outcome over a one-year period starting in October, giving up some upside in exchange for some protection. Most of the money sits in Treasury bills to support the options, and the outcome only applies if held the whole period.
ODDS: Companies worldwide that make money from digital entertainment such as online betting, gaming and esports, tracked by a rules-based index. Tencent, Evolution and Flutter are each around 8%, and the fund is split between communication and consumer stocks.
ODDZ: An actively managed fund of companies in sports betting, online gambling and casinos. Casino operators like Las Vegas Sands and Caesars sit alongside Flutter and DraftKings, and about 90% of the fund is consumer discretionary.
ODHY: An actively managed fund of high-yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, with a more cautious approach than most funds of its kind. It is very spread out: the largest holdings, like TransDigm and Terex, are each only about 1%.
ODTE: Holds three funds in roughly equal parts, one each tracking the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 and the Russell 2000, and layers an options strategy on top to produce income. The options bring in regular payouts but can limit the gains if markets rise sharply.
OEF: The 100 biggest US companies, tracking the S&P 100, which is a smaller version of the S&P 500. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together make up about 31% of the fund.
OEFA: Holds dividend paying European companies that screen well on quality, tracked by an index of large and mid sized firms. ASML, HSBC, ABB and Novartis are the biggest names, and industrials, health care and financials make up much of the fund.
OEI: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that aims to produce income, using an optimized mix of stocks and possibly options. It is top heavy in big technology, with NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon and Apple together about 23% of the fund.
OGIG: Tracks an index of global internet companies picked for quality and growth, spanning e-commerce, search, social media, software and cloud. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Oracle and Meta are about 30% of it, and technology is over half of the fund.
OGSP: An actively managed fund of high grade structured products, which are bonds backed by pools of loans and similar assets such as consumer debt and business loans. It spreads money over many small positions, each around 2% to 3%, rather than relying on a few issuers.
OIH: The oil services industry: companies that provide drilling, equipment and field services to oil and gas producers, tracked by the MVIS US Listed Oil Services 25 Index. It holds only about 25 stocks, and SLB alone is about 19% of the fund.
OILK: A fund that tracks crude oil prices by holding oil futures contracts spread across several delivery dates, rather than owning oil directly. It avoids the K-1 tax form that many commodity funds send, and it is mostly backed by cash-like holdings.
OILT: A fund holding oil and gas companies based in Texas, tracking an index of those firms. It is a narrow energy bet, with ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips, Occidental and Diamondback each around 7% of the fund and energy at over 90% of it.
OMAH: Stocks picked to mirror Berkshire Hathaway's well-known holdings, paired with an options strategy that sells call options to generate extra income. Selling those options caps some upside, and Berkshire itself is about 10% of the fund, with Apple near 7%.
OMFL: Large US companies chosen and weighted by an index that shifts its mix of size, value and low volatility depending on whether the market is recovering or not. Apple is the biggest holding at roughly 9%, followed by NVIDIA and Alphabet.
OMFS: Small US companies from the Russell 2000 picked by an index that blends factors such as value, momentum, quality and low volatility, and changes its mix as conditions shift. It holds many stocks, with the top names around 2% each.
ONEH: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500, buying puts and calls, to try to cushion stock market drops while still taking part in gains. Most of the holdings are cash-like and bond-like assets that back the options, so it behaves differently from a plain stock fund.
ONEO: Holds about 1,000 large US companies that have been rising recently, taken from the Russell 1000 index and weighted to favor momentum. No single stock is more than about 1% of it, so it is very spread out across technology, industrials and health care.
ONEQ: Stocks listed on the Nasdaq exchange, tracking the Nasdaq Composite Index and weighted by company size. It is heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon are about 35% of the fund.
ONEV: US large and mid-sized companies from the Russell 1000 selected for lower volatility, then weighted with a focus on stability. It holds many stocks, with Allstate and Progressive at about 1% each, and leans toward steadier sectors like insurance and health care.
ONEY: Large US companies that pay higher dividends, picked from the Russell 1000 with a focus on yield and weighted by it. It is spread out, with insurers Progressive and Allstate, Comcast and UPS among the biggest holdings, each at around 2 to 4%.
ONEZ: An actively managed fund of buffered ETFs that spaces out start dates and follows seasonal patterns in the stock market. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion some losses, but gains are capped, and no single holding is over about 8%.
ONLN: Follows an index of US-listed companies that make most of their sales online, such as e-commerce and online marketplaces. Amazon is about 26% and Alibaba about 12%, so a few names drive it.
ONOF: Large US stocks that shift between fully invested and hedged against market drops, based on a rules-based signal. When hedged it can behave quite differently from a plain index fund, and NVIDIA and Apple are its biggest holdings at about 7% each.
OOSP: An actively managed fund that buys securitized debt, meaning pools of loans such as commercial mortgages and consumer loans bundled into bonds. It is spread across many small positions, with no single holding above about 1%, and the manager picks them instead of tracking an index.
OPPE: A fund of European stocks selected by an index that favors companies with stronger earnings outlooks and valuations, while also keeping some sector balance. Financials and industrials are about half of it, and no single company is above roughly 2.5%, so it is spread widely.
OPPG: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies around the world, with the country decided by where each company does most of its business. Top holdings include Meta, Tokyo Electron and Alphabet at roughly 3% to 5% each, spread across industrials, technology and consumer companies.
OPPJ: Japanese companies picked and weighted by a WisdomTree index that is built around value and cash returned to shareholders. It leans toward Japan's big trading houses: Sumitomo, Marubeni, Mitsubishi and Mitsui are about 27% of it.
OPTO: Companies in photonics, the technology of using light for things like fiber optics, sensors and chips, held as stocks and through swaps. It also uses an options strategy to generate income, which can limit gains when the stocks rise sharply.
OPTZ: A fund that follows a rules-based index aiming to beat the broader US stock market over a full economic cycle by shifting between sectors. Its holdings are mid-sized US companies with a tilt to chips and tech, such as Micron and AMD, so it can differ a lot from the market.
ORBX: Companies in space technology, such as launch, satellites, imaging and communications, tracked by an index. It is concentrated, with Rocket Lab alone around 22% and the top few holdings making up close to half the fund.
ORO: An actively managed fund that shifts between Bitcoin futures, gold futures and cash, guided by an AI-driven index. The goal is to join in Bitcoin's gains while softening the drops, but the mix changes with the model's signals.
ORR: An actively managed fund that buys stocks it likes and bets against others, so it can profit when some fall. It is concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Hikari Tsushin and Grupo Mexico about 28% of it, and the mix is global.
OSCV: An actively managed fund of small US companies that the manager believes are priced below their worth. It is spread across many names, with the biggest around 3% each, and leans toward financials, industrials and energy.
OSEA: An actively managed fund of non-US companies, including some in emerging markets, that the manager expects to keep growing steadily, called compounders. It holds a modest number of stocks, led by Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML at about 6% each.
OTAX: An actively managed fund of US stocks across company sizes, built to hold broad-market exposure while cutting taxes by selling losing stocks. It mostly holds other funds and stocks like NVIDIA and Apple, tilted toward technology.
OTGL: A fund of Latin American stocks, covering companies from across the region. It leans on banks and mining firms, with financials about 27% and materials about 23%, and Vale, Itau Chile and Southern Copper among its biggest holdings.
OUNZ: Physical gold bars held in a vault, with each share backed by gold and redeemable for actual metal. It tracks the price of gold, so it behaves like gold itself and has no interest or dividends.
OUSA: Large and mid-sized US dividend payers screened for high quality and low volatility, from an O'Shares index. It aims for steadier income than a plain dividend fund, with Alphabet, Apple, Johnson & Johnson and Visa each around 5%.
OUSM: Small US companies that pay dividends and score well on quality, like strong profits and low debt, picked by an index from O'Shares. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3.5%, and focuses on steady dividend payers instead of fast growers.
OVB: An actively managed bond fund that holds a broad US investment-grade bond ETF, then sells short-term put options on top to bring in extra income. The options add income but can lose money if prices fall, so it behaves differently from a plain bond index fund.
OVF: An actively managed fund that holds other iShares ETFs covering stocks outside the US, from developed and emerging markets. It also uses an options overlay meant to manage risk, so it differs from simply buying a plain international index fund.
OVL: An actively managed fund that holds an ETF tracking the S&P 500 and adds an options layer meant to change how it responds to market moves. Almost all of it is one underlying fund, a Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, so it mostly moves with large US stocks.
OVLH: Holds a broad S&P 500 fund and adds an options overlay meant to reduce losses when the market falls. It is actively managed, so it tracks large US stocks closely, but the hedge can reduce gains compared with a plain index fund.
OVM: An actively managed fund that holds a municipal bond ETF and also sells short-term put options to earn extra income. Nearly all of it is in that one underlying iShares fund, so it behaves like muni bonds with an options overlay that adds income but also risk.
OVQ: An income fund built around the Nasdaq 100, the index of large non-financial companies on the Nasdaq. It uses an options strategy to generate extra income, which limits how much of the market's gains it captures.
OVS: An actively managed fund that holds mostly an ETF tracking US small companies, about 99%, and then sells call options on top to earn extra income. Selling options can limit gains when small stocks rise sharply.
