OVT: Almost all of this fund sits in one short-term corporate bond ETF, and it sells put options on top to bring in extra income. That options income comes with added risk, because the fund takes on losses if bonds fall sharply.
OWN: One hundred large US companies from the S&P 500 chosen and weighted by how much of each is owned by its own executives and insiders. It leans toward a few big names: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 12% each, with Amazon next at roughly 9%.
OWNB: Companies that hold bitcoin on their balance sheets, such as Strategy, MARA and Metaplanet, following an index of them. It is concentrated, with Strategy about 16% of the fund, and these stocks tend to move strongly with bitcoin's price.
OWNS: An actively managed fund of mortgage-backed securities, bonds backed by pools of home loans, focused on loans made to low- and moderate-income families and underserved areas. The bonds are mostly government-backed, so it is a plain income-oriented bond fund with a housing mission.
OZEM: Holds companies tied to GLP-1 drugs and weight loss, the medicines behind Ozempic and Wegovy, including makers, developers and related businesses. Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly are about 26% of it, so it leans on a few drug companies.
PAAA: Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) rated AAA, the safest slice of bundles of corporate loans packaged into bonds. It is actively managed and floating-rate, so its income moves with short-term interest rates, spread across dozens of issuers.
PAB: An actively managed fund of US investment grade bonds, holding a broad mix of Treasuries, mortgage backed securities and corporate debt, all in US dollars. It works as a core bond holding, and up to 25% can be foreign issuers, including emerging markets.
PABD: Large and mid sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, weighted to cut carbon exposure in line with the Paris Climate Agreement. It holds a broad spread, with ASML the largest at about 3%, and leans toward financials and industrials.
PABU: Large and mid-size US stocks chosen and weighted so the overall portfolio follows a path of falling carbon emissions in line with the Paris climate agreement. It is top-heavy in technology: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 24% of the fund.
PALC: Holds about 100 large US companies and rotates every year between several different stock-picking styles (such as value, momentum and quality) based on a rules-based index. No single stock tops about 3%, though Mastercard, Visa and Apple are among the largest.
PALL: A fund that holds physical palladium, a precious metal used mainly in car exhaust systems, stored in vaults. It has no companies or income: the price simply follows the price of palladium, which can swing a lot.
PAMC: US mid sized company stocks chosen by a rules based method that combines several factors, such as value, quality and momentum, and shifts between them over time. It is spread widely, with no holding much above 2% of the fund.
PAPI: An actively managed fund of US stocks that also sells call options on them to earn extra income paid out as distributions. That income strategy limits gains in strong markets, and the stock holdings are small, each about 1% or less.
PAPR: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to buffer the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in April. In return, gains are capped at a set level, so the buffer only works fully if held for the whole period.
PATN: Large and mid-sized companies from outside the US that own highly valuable patent portfolios, picked by a Nasdaq index. It is heavy in tech and chips, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK Hynix about 22% of it.
PAUG: A defined outcome fund using options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion some losses over a set one-year period starting in August. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
PAVE: US companies that benefit from building and upgrading roads, rail, power and other infrastructure, including engineering, construction, equipment and materials firms. About three quarters is industrials, with Quanta Services, CSX and Eaton among the top names at roughly 3% to 4% each.
PAWZ: About 50 companies that stand to benefit from pet ownership, such as pet health, pet food and pet retail, tracked through an index. Four companies, IDEXX, Chewy, Freshpet and Zoetis, are about 40% of the fund, so it is fairly concentrated.
PAYH: A fund that gets its returns from an index of autocallable notes, structured products tied to a volatility measure that pay high income and can end early. The fund mostly holds cash-like assets as backing, and is built for income but with complex risks.
PAYM: An actively managed income fund that mostly holds Treasuries and cash, and uses swaps tied to autocallable notes on US stocks to generate extra payouts. The swaps carry the risk, so it works differently from a plain bond fund despite the safe-looking holdings.
PAYR: An actively managed fund of high dividend-paying US and international stocks, with an options strategy added to bring in extra income. The options can limit gains in strong markets, so it focuses on income over growth.
PBAP: An actively managed fund using customized options on large US stocks to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in April. It aims to absorb the first 20% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and is meant to be held for the full period.
PBAU: An S&P 500 fund that uses options to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in August. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies to investors who hold for the full period.
PBCS: Holds consumer staples companies from around the world, the makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks and household products. These businesses tend to have steadier demand than most, and the fund spans many countries.
PBD: Companies around the world in clean energy, such as renewable power, efficiency and electric vehicle businesses, tracked by an index. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and many are small and mid-sized companies, with industrials the biggest sector.
PBDC: A fund that holds business development companies, or BDCs, which lend money to smaller private US companies and pay most of their earnings out as dividends. It is concentrated in a few lenders: Ares Capital, Blue Owl Capital and Blue Owl Technology Finance each make up about 10%.
PBDE: An actively managed fund using customized options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in December. It aims to absorb the first 20% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and is meant to be held for the full period.
PBE: US biotechnology and genomics companies, picked by an Invesco-tracked index, covering firms that research and make new drug and genetic treatments. It holds about 30 stocks in nearly equal amounts, with Regeneron, Amgen and Vertex among the largest at about 5% each.
PBEU: Banks in Europe, selected by a fixed rules-based index. It is concentrated in one industry: HSBC, Santander, BBVA and UniCredit are over a third of the fund, and everything in it is a bank.
PBFB: An S&P 500 fund that uses options to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in February. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies to investors who hold for the full period.
PBFR: A fund of twelve PGIM S&P 500 Buffer 20 funds, each starting in a different month, so the dates of the protection are staggered through the year. Each underlying fund uses options to cushion a set amount of losses, but gains are capped.
PBJ: US food and beverage companies, tracked by an index, including makers of drinks, packaged food and restaurants. Monster Beverage, Coca-Cola, Starbucks and Archer Daniels Midland are each around 5% of the fund, and it is mostly consumer staples.
PBJA: Uses options that follow the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period that starts in January, while capping how much of the gains it can capture. The buffer is 20% as named, and it only works if shares are held for the full period.
PBJL: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cover the first 20% of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are capped, so it only works as designed if held for the full period.
PBJN: Uses options on the S&P 500 to buffer part of the losses over a one-year period starting each June, with 20 in the name pointing to the buffer size. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
PBL: An actively managed fund that aims to capture part of the stock market's gains while limiting swings and losses. It mostly avoids buying stocks directly, instead using other funds, options and Treasuries to get stock exposure with a cushion.
PBMR: An actively managed fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses, up to the 20% buffer in its name, over a one year period that starts in March. In return, gains from the index are capped.
PBMY: An actively managed fund using customized options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in May. It aims to absorb the first 20% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and works as intended only if held through the full period.
PBNV: An actively managed fund using customized options on the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a set period starting in November. It aims to absorb the first 20% of losses in exchange for a cap on gains, and is meant to be held for the full period.
PBOC: An actively managed fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period beginning in October. In exchange, its gains are capped, so it gives up some upside for the protection.
PBOG: Large integrated oil and gas companies and oil producers from around the world, selected by a fixed rules-based index. It is concentrated: ExxonMobil and Chevron make up about 30% of the fund, and everything in it is an energy company.
PBOT: An actively managed fund of technology companies tied to artificial intelligence and automation, such as chip and equipment makers. It is concentrated, with Alphabet, KLA, Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom each making up about 6% to 7%.
PBP: Holds the S&P 500 stocks and sells call options on the index to collect extra income. The options limit gains in strong markets, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of the fund.
PBPH: Large pharmaceutical and biotech companies from around the world, tracking a rules-based index. It is top-heavy, with Eli Lilly about 15% and Johnson & Johnson about 10%, so a few drugmakers drive most of its results.
PBQQ: Holds a ladder of four buffered Nasdaq-100 funds, each resetting at a different time of year. Each one follows the Nasdaq-100 up to a limit while cushioning a set amount of losses, and staggering them smooths out when the protection starts.
PBSC: An actively managed fund holding mostly secured credit, such as loans backed by collateral and pools of loans called CLOs, picked by Barings. It spreads money across many small positions of about 1% each, and the loans pay floating rates that move with interest rates.
PBSE: An actively managed fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in September. The trade-off is a cap on gains, so it passes on only part of a strong market.
PBTP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) maturing in zero to five years, whose principal rises with inflation. Holdings are roughly 5% each, and the short maturities mean its price reacts less to interest rate changes than longer TIPS.
PBUB: A basket of US bank stocks, held according to an index of the sector. It is top-heavy: JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo together are about a third of the fund.
PBUS: Large and mid sized US companies, tracking an MSCI USA index weighted by company size, so bigger firms count for more. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of it.
PBW: US-listed stocks of companies tied to cleaner energy and conservation, picked by the WilderHill Clean Energy Index. Holdings are mostly small, varied companies, and no single stock is more than about 2% to 3% of the fund.
PBWN: Industrial companies from developed countries outside the US, such as aircraft makers, electrical equipment firms and machinery makers. Siemens, Schneider Electric and Rolls-Royce lead it, and the top eight are about 32% of the fund.
PCEB: Bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, issued in euros rather than dollars. Because the bonds are in euros, changes in the euro's value against the dollar can affect what a US holder earns, on top of the bonds' own ups and downs.
PCEF: A fund of funds that owns shares of closed-end funds, which are income-focused funds that trade on exchanges, often at a discount or premium to their holdings. It targets high income from a mix of bonds and stocks, and many of these funds use borrowing, which adds risk.
PCFI: An actively managed fund of bank loans, also called floating-rate loans, whose interest payments rise and fall with short-term rates. It aims to beat the broader bank loan market over a full credit cycle, and the loans are made to lower-rated companies.
PCHI: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, which come from companies with weaker credit and pay more interest to make up for the extra risk. It aims to beat the broader high yield market over a full credit cycle, the several year stretch when borrowing gets easier and then harder.
PCI: Investment-grade corporate bonds with medium maturities of about five to ten years, largely from big banks and other large companies. It is spread thin, with the biggest holdings around 2% of the fund each.
PCL: Bonds issued by US companies that mature in ten years or more, from big names like JPMorgan, UnitedHealth and Wells Fargo. Long maturities mean the fund's price swings more when interest rates change, in exchange for higher interest payments.
PCLC: An actively managed fund of large US growth companies, picked by Polen Capital using a five-part framework for spotting high quality businesses. It is fairly concentrated and tech heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet, AMD, Tesla and SpaceX together are about a third of it.
PCLG: An actively managed fund of a limited number of large US growth stocks that Polen believes have lasting competitive strengths. It is concentrated: Microsoft, NVIDIA, ServiceNow and Alphabet are about 30% of the fund.
PCLN: An actively managed global stock fund investing in companies helping solve environmental problems, such as cleaner energy, water and efficient technology. It leans heavily on technology and industrials, with Applied Materials, ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor among the biggest holdings.
PCLO: Private credit CLOs rated AAA, which are pools of loans made by private lenders to mid sized companies, packaged and sliced into bonds, with AAA the highest rating. Holdings are evenly split, with the largest positions each about 5% of the fund.
PCMM: A fund that mainly buys collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) backed by private credit, which are bundles of loans to companies sliced into bonds. It is a niche way to earn floating-rate income, with returns tied to how well those underlying loans are repaid.
PCOV: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying stocks that also uses options to generate extra income. Apple, Microsoft and JPMorgan are the biggest holdings at roughly 4% to 5% each, and the options income limits some upside.
PCPC: US property and casualty insurers, the companies that cover homes, cars and businesses, tracked by an index from Porter & Company. It is fairly concentrated: Slide Insurance, HCI Group, RenaissanceRe and Kinsale together are about a quarter of the fund.
PCPI: An actively managed fund from PIMCO that mainly holds inflation-linked bonds, whose value adjusts with inflation, from the US and other governments and companies. It may use derivatives like futures and swaps as well, so the bonds listed are only part of how it works.
PCPP: Follows the Porter Portfolio Index, a mix that spreads money across stocks, short-term bonds and gold-related companies, tilted toward insurers and financial firms. It owns several other ETFs too, and it is non-diversified, so a few holdings matter a lot.
PCR: An actively managed bond fund that aims for income and some price growth by investing in a mix of private credit related debt and other bonds. It is a manager's judgment call rather than an index, and a large slice sits in a short-term Treasury fund.
PCS: US corporate bonds that mature in about five years or less, mostly from large banks and other companies. Short maturities mean the price is less sensitive to interest rate changes, and JPMorgan, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley are each around 2% of the fund.
PCSG: An actively managed fund buying US small and mid-sized growth companies, chosen by the manager using a mix of business quality and growth potential. It is spread thin, with DigitalOcean, Twist Bioscience and Twilio each only about 3% to 4%, and leans toward technology.
PCY: US dollar bonds issued by governments of emerging market countries such as Poland, Pakistan and Angola. Each country is only a small slice, around 1% to 1.5% for the largest, and the bonds carry more credit risk than developed market government debt.
PDBA: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to farm commodities like grains, sugar and livestock, mainly through futures contracts. It avoids the K-1 tax form, and the large money market and Treasury holdings are collateral, not the point of the fund.
PDBC: An actively managed fund that gets exposure to widely traded commodities like oil, metals and farm products through futures contracts rather than holding the goods themselves. It is run without a K-1 tax form, and most of the fund sits in cash and short-term securities backing those contracts.
PDEC: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to buffer the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in December. In return, gains are capped at a set level, so the buffer only works fully if held for the whole period.
PDN: About 1,500 smaller and mid-sized companies from developed countries outside the US, picked and weighted by fundamentals like sales and cash flow instead of size. It is extremely spread out, with no holding above about 0.3%.
PDP: About 100 US stocks from a Nasdaq index that picks companies whose prices have recently been rising fastest, according to Dorsey Wright's momentum ranking. The list is reshuffled regularly, so it follows whatever is hot and is spread fairly evenly, with no holding above about 3.5%.
PEJ: US leisure and entertainment companies, such as travel booking, cruises, restaurants and hotels, picked and weighted by a rules-based index. It is a narrow slice of the economy, with Expedia, Viking and Airbnb each about 5% to 6% of it.
PEMX: Stocks of companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, South Korea and India, deliberately leaving out China, chosen by an active manager. It is top-heavy in chip makers: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung together are about a third of the fund.
PEPS: An actively managed fund of large US stocks, mainly tilted to the biggest companies, that also uses options to try to manage risk. It is fairly top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 17% of it, and technology is around 40%.
PEPT: A fund tracking the VettaFi Peptide Index, which holds companies working on peptide-based products, small chains of amino acids used in medicines, supplements and cosmetics. It is a narrow health care theme and concentrated in one area of the sector.
PEVC: Tries to copy the returns of private equity and venture capital by holding public companies that such firms have backed. Its biggest holdings are Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Broadcom and Amazon, each around 4% to 5%, so it looks a lot like a tech-heavy stock fund.
PEX: Companies that invest in private businesses, like Ares Capital, 3i Group and Onex, which are listed on stock exchanges so they can be bought like any stock. It is a way to get private equity style exposure, and the top five holdings are about 40% of it.
PEXL: Holds about 100 large and mid-sized US companies that earn a high share of sales from exports, weighted equally. Equal weights spread it out, with no stock above about 6%, and it leans toward tech.
PEY: US companies with at least ten straight years of rising dividends, picked for their higher yields from an index of dividend achievers. It is a mid-cap value fund spread across financials, consumer staples and utilities, with no holding above about 4%.
PEZ: At least 30 US consumer discretionary stocks, such as retailers, airlines and carmakers, chosen for strong momentum, meaning they have recently beaten their peers, using the Dorsey Wright index. It is spread fairly evenly, with Victoria's Secret, Amazon and eBay each around 4% to 6% of the fund.
PFDE: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen with a disciplined, rules-based process. It looks a lot like the big US market, with NVIDIA, Apple, Amazon and Microsoft together about 27% of it and technology over 40%.
PFEB: A fund using options on the S&P 500 to cushion losses over a one-year period that starts each February. It buffers the first 15% of drops while capping how much gain is possible, so the outcome depends on when you buy within that period.
PFF: Preferred stocks, a hybrid of stocks and bonds that pay fixed dividends and get paid before common shareholders if a company struggles. It tracks an ICE index, and these shares are often issued by banks and other financial companies, so income is the main feature.
PFFA: An actively managed fund of US preferred stocks, a hybrid between stocks and bonds that pays fixed dividends, from companies such as banks, REITs and energy firms. It also uses borrowed money to boost income, which adds risk and is why its holdings add up to more than 100%.
PFFD: Preferred stocks from US companies, a hybrid security that pays a fixed dividend like a bond but trades on the stock market. Most holdings are bank and financial preferreds, and it is built for regular income rather than growth.
PFFR: Preferred shares issued by real estate investment trusts, called REITs, tracking an index of those securities on US exchanges. Preferred shares pay fixed income and sit between bonds and stocks, and the fund is spread over many REITs with none above about 3%.
PFFV: Preferred stocks, which are hybrid securities that pay set dividends, whose payments float with interest rates instead of staying fixed. Most holdings are financial companies like Morgan Stanley, KeyCorp and Bank of America, each only a few percent of it.
PFI: Holds at least 30 US financial companies picked for strong momentum, meaning their stocks have recently done better than others in the sector. It is spread across banks, brokers and other financial firms, and the biggest holdings are each only about 4% of the fund.
PFIG: Holds US dollar investment grade corporate bonds, picking and weighting them by the issuing company's size and financial fundamentals rather than by how much debt each has. It is widely spread across many issuers, with banks and big industrial names each around 1% or less.
PFIX: A fund built to gain when long-term interest rates rise, using interest rate options and swaps alongside a pile of Treasuries and income-producing debt. It is a hedge, not a regular bond fund, and it can lose value when rates fall.
PFLD: Preferred securities, a mix of stock and bond that pays fixed income, from US-listed issuers, with a focus on lower sensitivity to interest rate changes. Many holdings are big banks and other large companies, and no single one is more than about 1% of the fund.
PFM: US companies with at least ten years of steadily raising their dividends, following the Nasdaq U.S. Dividend Achievers Select Index. It is spread over many sectors, with Microsoft, Eli Lilly, Apple and Broadcom each around 3% to 4%.
PFOE: An actively managed fund holding only 15 to 30 stocks picked by its managers, so each position matters. Alphabet, Universal Music, UnitedHealth and ASML are each about 6% of it, and it mixes tech, health care and financial companies.
PFRL: A fund of floating-rate loans and similar debt, where the interest payments rise and fall with short-term rates. It holds many loans and CLO slices from many borrowers, with none above about 2%, and these loans are often made to lower-rated companies.
PFRX: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked from Putnam's own company research. It holds a focused list of companies rather than the whole market, so it can look quite different from a plain index fund.
PFXF: Preferred stocks, hybrids that behave partly like bonds by paying steady fixed dividends, from US-listed companies that are not banks or other financials. The mix leans toward utilities, and Boeing and Strategy are about 16% of it, so a few issuers matter a lot.
PGF: Preferred shares issued by financial companies, mostly big banks, which are a mix between stocks and bonds that pay fixed income and rank ahead of regular stock. It follows an ICE index, and JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo preferreds are the largest holdings.
PGHY: US dollar bonds from lower-rated companies outside the US, in the high-yield (junk) category, tracking an Invesco index. They pay more interest than safer bonds, but carry more risk, and the fund is spread out with no single issuer above about 1%.
PGJ: Chinese companies listed on US exchanges, tracked by the Nasdaq Golden Dragon China Index. It leans toward consumer and internet names, with JD.com, Yum China and Alibaba among the biggest holdings at about 8% to 9% each.
PGRI: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized companies outside the US, chosen for growth potential. Technology and industrials lead, and Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML are the biggest holdings at about 9% and 7% of the fund.
PGRO: An actively managed fund of about 40 large US growth companies, a more focused bet than an index fund. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple and Microsoft together are roughly 35% of it, and technology is more than half the fund.
PGX: Preferred stocks, a hybrid that pays fixed dividends like a bond but trades like a stock, following an ICE index. Big banks such as JPMorgan and Wells Fargo issue many of them, so it leans heavily toward financials.
PHDG: The S&P 500 paired with a hedge that uses volatility futures, plus some cash, so it tries to lose less when markets drop sharply. It holds the big index names like NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft, but the hedge can hold back gains in rallies.
PHEQ: A fund of large US stocks combined with an options strategy meant to dampen swings in the market. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of it, and the hedge means it may fall less in drops but gain less in rallies.
PHO: US-listed companies that make products and services for conserving and purifying water, tracked by the Nasdaq OMX US Water Index. It holds a wide mix of industrial, health care and technology firms, and the top three, Roper, Ecolab and Ferguson, are about 24% of it.
PHOX: Invests in companies that make optical and photonic technology, the light-based components that move data inside AI data centers and networks. It is almost all technology, and Lumentum, Coherent and a few others make up a big chunk, roughly 40% in the top five.
PHYL: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, issued by companies with weaker credit ratings. They pay more interest than safer bonds but carry more risk of default, and no single bond is above about 1%.
PHYS: A trust that holds physical gold bullion in storage, so its price follows the price of gold. It owns the metal itself rather than mining companies or futures, and it pays no income.
PICB: Investment-grade corporate bonds from companies outside the US, issued in major currencies other than the dollar. It leaves currency swings unhedged, and is spread across many issuers, mostly banks, each about 0.5% of the fund.
PICK: Global metals and mining companies, including miners of iron ore, copper and gold and producers of steel and aluminum, from both developed and emerging markets. It is concentrated at the top: BHP and Rio Tinto (both share classes) are about 20% of it.
PID: Companies outside the US that have a long record of raising their dividends, held through shares and depositary receipts that trade in the US and London. It is spread across many countries and sectors, with banks, utilities and telecoms the biggest groups, and no holding above about 4%.
PIE: Emerging market stocks picked for strong recent price momentum, meaning the ones that have been rising fastest, following an index from Dorsey Wright. It leans heavily toward technology (about 45%) and the list of holdings is rebalanced often, so it shifts over time.
PIEL: Large companies outside the US that earn a big share of their sales from exports, selected by a rules-based index. Holdings are spread out, with ASML, SK Hynix, Novartis, Samsung and Roche each making up roughly 4% to 5%.
PIEQ: An actively managed fund of stocks outside the US, including emerging markets such as China, across companies of all sizes. The top holdings are large names like Samsung, Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML, which together are around 22% of the fund.
PIFI: An actively managed fund of US dollar investment grade bonds, mostly Treasuries with some agency debt, aiming for an average maturity of zero to ten years. It works as a core bond holding, and it is spread across many bonds.
PINC: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds securitized credit, which are pools of loans such as mortgages, car loans and other debts bundled into bonds. It can also use derivatives to get the same exposure, and it aims to earn income from those pools.
PINK: An actively managed US health care fund that picks from drugmakers, insurers, devices and other medical firms, using a rules-based approach from Simplify. It is concentrated, with PureCycle, United Therapeutics, Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and UnitedHealth about 6% to 7% each.
PIO: Companies around the world tied to water, such as makers of pumps, filters and testing gear plus water utilities, tracked by an index. It is concentrated, with Roper, Ecolab and Pentair together making up around a quarter of the fund.
PIPE: Master limited partnerships (MLPs) and other companies that run oil and gas pipelines and related energy infrastructure, mostly in North America. It is all energy, and Targa, Plains, Williams, TC Energy and Cheniere are about 30% of it.
PIT: An actively managed fund giving exposure to commodities such as energy, metals and farm goods, mainly by using futures contracts instead of owning the goods. Most of the fund's assets are held in cash-like investments backing those contracts.
PIZ: Developed-market stocks outside the US that show the strongest recent price momentum, picked by the Dorsey Wright index, so the list changes as trends shift. Financials and industrials dominate, and top holdings like Constellation Software and Bombardier are around 3% each.
PJAN: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion losses of up to about 15% over a one-year period starting in January. In exchange, gains are capped at a set level, so it only fully works if held for the whole period.
PJFG: An actively managed fund of a small number of large US growth companies chosen by Jennison. It is highly concentrated: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Amazon and Apple make up around 36% of the fund.
PJFM: An actively managed fund of about 30 to 40 mid-sized US companies that the managers believe can grow strongly. It is spread across technology, financials and industrials, with no single holding above roughly 5%, though it holds far fewer stocks than a typical mid-cap index fund.
PJFV: An actively managed fund of a small number of large US companies that the manager thinks are priced below what they are worth. It is concentrated: Advanced Micro Devices and Alphabet are around 12% of it, with technology, financials and industrials the biggest areas.
PJIN: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies from around the world, picked by the managers rather than following an index. It spreads money across many countries and industries, so its mix can differ from a standard global stock index fund.
PJIO: An actively managed fund of growth companies outside the US, including some in emerging markets. It is concentrated and tech heavy: SK Hynix, Samsung and Taiwan Semiconductor are about 20% of it.
PJP: An index of 30 US pharmaceutical companies, including drug makers such as AbbVie, Amgen, Johnson & Johnson, Merck and Eli Lilly. Holdings are fairly evenly split, with the top eight each around 4.5% to 5.7%, so it spreads across one narrow industry.
PJSM: An actively managed fund that buys US small and mid-sized companies, mixing the two size groups in one portfolio. The managers pick stocks themselves rather than following an index, so what it holds can differ quite a bit from a standard small or mid-cap index fund.
PJUL: A buffer fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each July, in exchange for a cap on gains. The protection only applies if you hold for that full period, and the cap limits upside.
PJUN: A fund using options on the S&P 500 to cushion losses over a one-year period that starts each June. It buffers the first 15% of drops while capping how much gain is possible, so the outcome depends on when you buy within that period.
PJUS: An actively managed fund of US companies, mostly large ones, chosen by the manager at Jennison for their growth and quality. Technology is the biggest slice, and NVIDIA, Alphabet and Apple together are about 20% of the fund.
PKB: US building and construction companies, from home improvement retailers to makers of cement and aggregates, picked by an index. It is fairly concentrated, with Home Depot, Johnson Controls and Vulcan Materials each about 5% of the fund, and it leans toward industrials and materials.
PKW: US companies that have bought back at least 5% of their own shares over the past year, picked by a Nasdaq index. It leans heavily toward financials at about 40%, and Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Adobe are each roughly 5% of the fund.
PLA: A fund built on derivatives tied to an autocallable note on Palantir stock, a contract that pays out if the stock holds above a set level on check dates and can end early. Most of the fund sits in cash backing those contracts, so it is a narrow, complex bet on one company.
PLGI: An actively managed mix of growth stocks and income-producing holdings such as options strategies and high-yield bond funds, with the manager free to trade often. Tech giants lead it: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about 16% of the fund.
PLIB: Gives exposure to Palantir stock while aiming to pay out extra income, using swaps and options on the stock. It holds a single company's performance, and the income strategy can limit gains if Palantir rises sharply.
PLTM: Physical platinum bars held in a vault, so the fund's value follows the platinum price. It holds the metal itself rather than mining companies, and it pays no income, so platinum price changes are the whole story.
PLTW: A fund aiming for about 1.2 times the weekly return of Palantir stock, using swaps (contracts that pay the stock's return) and some shares, backed by Treasury bills. It resets weekly, pays weekly distributions, and is a leveraged bet on a single stock.
PLTY: Earns income by selling options tied to Palantir stock, using a mix of options and Treasuries instead of owning the shares directly. The strategy caps how much it gains if Palantir jumps but still leaves it exposed to most of a decline.
PLYY: An income fund built around Palantir that uses options on a leveraged Palantir fund to generate payouts, with Treasury bills held as backing. Selling options caps its upside, and the leveraged underlying makes it very volatile.
PMAP: An actively managed fund that holds options on the S&P 500 to cushion a large part of losses over a set one-year period, starting each April. In return, gains are capped, so it will lag the index in strong years.
PMAR: A fund using options on the S&P 500 to cushion losses over a one-year period that starts each March. It absorbs the first 15% of losses but caps the gains at a set level, so you only get the buffer if you hold through the full period.
PMAU: A defined outcome fund that follows the S&P 500's price up to a limit over a set one year period, using options to absorb a large share of the losses. Buying mid-period changes what protection and upside remain, and it does not pay S&P 500 dividends.
PMAY: An options-based fund that tracks the S&P 500 over a one-year period starting in May, with a buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses. In return, gains are capped, so you get a cushion but give up some upside.
PMBS: An actively managed bond fund that mainly holds mortgage-backed securities, bonds backed by pools of home loans, and may use derivatives such as futures and swaps. The managers choose among mortgage bonds of different maturities, so it differs from a fund that simply tracks a mortgage bond index.
PMDE: Uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a large part of the index's losses over a one-year period that starts in December, while capping how much of its gains you can keep. It is actively managed, and the protection only works if held through the full period.
PMFB: A defined outcome fund that follows the S&P 500's price up to a limit over a set one year period, using options to absorb a large share of the losses. Buying mid-period changes what protection and upside remain, and it does not pay S&P 500 dividends.
PMIO: An actively managed fund of intermediate-term municipal bonds from state and local governments, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds toll roads, housing and energy authority bonds, with the top holdings each only about 2% to 3%.
PMJA: A fund that follows the S&P 500 using options designed to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works best if you hold from the start of that period to its end.
PMJL: Uses options on the S&P 500 to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in July, with a maximum buffer meant to absorb a large share of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
PMJN: An actively managed fund tied to the S&P 500 that uses options to cushion a large part of the losses over a set period starting in June, in exchange for a limit on gains. The protection only applies if shares are held for the full period.
PMMF: A money market fund that holds very short-term US dollar debt, such as government, bank and corporate IOUs and repurchase agreements. It aims to keep a steady price while paying interest that follows short-term rates, and it works like a place to park cash.
PMMR: A fund that follows the S&P 500 using options designed to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works best if you hold from the start of that period to its end.
PMMY: A fund that follows the S&P 500 using options designed to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection works best if you hold from the start of that period to its end.
PMNV: An actively managed fund that holds options on the S&P 500 to cushion a large part of losses over a set one-year period, starting each November. In return, gains are capped, so it will lag the index in strong years.
PMOC: An actively managed fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to buffer a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if shares are held for the whole period.
PMSE: Uses options on the S&P 500 to give a set outcome over a one-year period starting in September, with a maximum buffer meant to absorb a large share of losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
PMTL: Tracks an Indxx index of gold and silver mining companies picked for their quality. Newmont, Agnico Eagle, Barrick and Wheaton Precious Metals are the largest, so it rises and falls with metal prices and mining costs.
PNOV: An options-based fund that tracks the S&P 500 over a one-year period starting in November, with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses. In exchange, gains are capped, so it gives up some upside for that cushion.
PNQI: Follows an index of the largest US-listed internet companies, including search, shopping, social media and streaming. It is top-heavy, with Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, Alphabet and Meta together making up about 40% of the fund.
POCT: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to buffer the first 15% of losses over a one year period starting in October. In return, gains are capped at a set level, so the buffer only works fully if held for the whole period.
POMG: An actively managed fund of mid-sized and smaller US growth companies, picked by the PRIMECAP team for long-term growth. It holds a limited number of stocks, which makes it more concentrated than a typical index fund.
POW: An actively managed fund of global companies that benefit from the growing need for electricity, such as makers of electrical equipment, power components and utilities. It holds companies like LS Electric, Delta Electronics and Powell, and industrials are about 60% of it.
POWA: Large US companies with steady profit margins, which suggests they can keep prices up even when costs change. It follows a Bloomberg index and holds a wide mix, with no stock above about 3%, across technology, health care and industrials.
POWR: US companies tied to the power grid, including electricity utilities, equipment makers and builders of power infrastructure, following an S&P index. It is top-heavy: GE Vernova, Eaton and Quanta Services are about 20% of the fund, and utilities are roughly half of it.
PPA: US aerospace and defense companies, such as makers of jets, missiles, ships and defense electronics. It is fairly concentrated, with RTX, GE Aerospace, Boeing and Lockheed Martin each making up roughly 7%, and about 90% of it is in industrials.
PPH: Large drug companies listed in the US, including foreign ones trading as depositary receipts, tracked by an index of the pharmaceutical industry. It is top heavy: Eli Lilly is about 20% of it, and Lilly, Novartis and Merck together are about 40%.
PPI: An actively managed fund that invests in real assets: things like infrastructure, energy, materials, real estate and gold. Industrials, energy and materials make up around 80% of it, and a gold fund is its largest single holding at about 6%.
PPLT: A fund that holds physical platinum bars kept in a vault, so its price follows the platinum market. It owns the metal itself rather than mining companies, and platinum is used mainly in car exhaust systems and jewelry.
PPTY: US real estate companies, including data center, warehouse and apartment landlords, chosen by a rules-based index. It is fairly spread out, with Equinix, Prologis, Four Corners and Digital Realty each around 4% to 5% of the fund.
PQAP: A fund that uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in April. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies when held for the full period.
PQDI: An actively managed fund of preferred securities and similar income-paying securities, many issued by large banks, including contingent convertible bonds that can turn into stock in a crisis. Holdings are spread out, with the top names each around 3%.
PQJA: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ fund, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, to cushion part of the losses over a set one year period starting in January. In return, gains are capped, and the fund is very tech heavy, with technology about 60% of it.
PQJL: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Nasdaq-100 (through the QQQ fund) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in July. In return, it caps how much of the gains it can keep.
PQNT: An actively managed fund of large companies outside the US, where artificial intelligence tools help pick and weight the stocks. It is spread widely, with the biggest holding, ASML, only about 4% of the fund.
PQOC: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Nasdaq-100 (through the QQQ fund) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in October. In return, it caps how much of the gains it can keep.
PQUS: An actively managed fund of large US companies where Pictet uses artificial intelligence to help pick and weight stocks. It looks a lot like the big US market, with NVIDIA and Apple each about 7% and technology over 40%.
PQV: Holds options tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion a set amount of losses over each three month period, in exchange for limiting gains. The protection only applies if you hold through a full period, and the upside is capped.
PQX: An actively managed fund that holds options on the S&P 500 to cushion the first 10% of losses over a quarter, resetting each quarter. In return, gains are capped, so it will lag the index in strong periods.
PQXV: Tracks the S&P 500 using options that aim to absorb a set amount of losses over each three-month period, in exchange for limiting the gains. The 15 in the name refers to its buffer level, and the protection only applies if you hold through a full period.
PQXX: A fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to take a set amount of losses off the table for a three-month period, in exchange for limiting the gains. The protection resets every quarter, and the fund's name says the buffer covers the first 20%.
PRAB: Holds investment-grade asset-backed securities, bonds backed by pools of loans such as credit cards, car loans, student loans and mortgages. It mixes public and private deals, which aim to earn a bit more income, and is spread across many different issuers.
PRAE: An actively managed fund of funds mixing other ETFs holding US and international stocks with extras like futures, commodities and currencies. The point is broad stock exposure plus alternatives for diversification, so it holds many other funds rather than individual companies directly.
PRAM: A fund focused on companies tied to computer memory chips and photonics, the use of light to move data. Much of its exposure may come through derivatives rather than owning the stocks directly, and it is a narrow, concentrated theme.
PRAY: An actively managed fund of US and international stocks screened to fit Christian values, excluding companies that conflict with them. It is a mix of big and small names, with technology the largest sector at around 30%.
PRCS: An actively managed portfolio of a small number of large US companies, picked by Parnassus with a focus on quality and responsible business practices. It is concentrated: Applied Materials, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 28% of it.
PREF: An actively managed fund of preferred securities, which are hybrids that pay fixed income like bonds but rank above common stock. Mostly issued by banks and insurers such as Bank of America and MetLife, it spreads across many issuers and none is more than about 3%.
PRF: About 1,000 of the largest US companies, but weighted by business size such as sales, cash flow, dividends and book value, instead of by stock market value. That makes it less tilted to the biggest names: Apple is about 4% and Alphabet about 4%.
PRFD: An actively managed fund holding preferred securities, which are hybrids that pay fixed income like bonds but rank above regular stock, mostly issued by big banks and financial firms. The managers pick and weight them, so it spreads across many issuers such as JPMorgan, Royal Bank of Canada and Bank of America.
PRFZ: About 1,500 small and mid-sized US companies, chosen and weighted by business size measures like sales, cash flow, dividends and book value rather than by share price. This approach tilts away from the most expensive stocks, and no holding is above about 1%.
PRIV: An actively managed bond fund that mixes traditional investment-grade bonds with private credit, meaning loans made outside public markets, aiming for extra income. Its biggest listed holdings are US Treasuries and Fannie Mae, so it blends government and agency bonds with higher-yielding lending.
PRIZ: A fund of preferred stocks, which are shares that pay a fixed dividend and rank ahead of regular shares if a company runs into trouble. It also holds some bonds, and it is built mainly for steady income rather than growth.
PRMR: An actively managed fund of US large company stocks that trades often rather than following an index. It is spread widely, with Palantir, CrowdStrike, Microsoft and Dell each only about 3%, though around 40% is in technology.
PRN: US industrial companies picked for strong recent price momentum by the Dorsey Wright index, with the list refreshed regularly. It is fairly concentrated: Comfort Systems, Howmet and Quanta Services are about 14% of it, with a tilt to construction and aerospace.
PRNT: Companies involved in 3D printing, from the software and design tools to printers, materials and medical uses. It tracks an index of companies spread across the US and Europe, with no holding above about 6%.
PRSD: An actively managed fund of investment-grade bonds with short maturities, mixing public bonds such as Treasuries and mortgage securities with private credit loans sourced through Apollo. The private credit portion is the main difference from a plain short-term bond fund.
PRTO: An actively managed fund that shifts between asset classes, using trend and momentum signals to decide the mix. Today it holds mostly other ETFs, including small-cap stock funds, a gold fund and a Nasdaq-100 fund.
PRVS: An actively managed fund holding a concentrated group of large companies its managers think are priced below their worth. Its biggest positions, including Amazon, Alphabet and Taiwan Semiconductor, are each about 5% to 6%, and it leans toward technology.
PRXG: Tracks the CRSP US Large Cap Growth Index, with a screen for companies Praxis considers good for society. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 32% of the fund, and nearly 60% is technology.
PRXI: Stocks of large companies outside the US in developed markets, aiming to reflect that broad market while screening for positive social and environmental impact. It is spread widely, with ASML, HSBC, Roche and Novartis among the larger names, none above about 4%.
PRXV: Tracks the CRSP US Large Cap Value Index, with a screen for companies Praxis considers good for society. It is fairly spread out, with Micron, JPMorgan Chase and Johnson & Johnson the biggest at around 3% to 5%.
PSAI: Tracks an index of 100 S&P 500 companies picked by an artificial intelligence model that scores them on factors like momentum and value. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 4%, and the sector mix can shift as the model updates.
PSC: An actively managed fund of US small companies, where the managers pick stocks they like rather than copying an index. It is spread over many holdings, with the biggest each around 1%, and leans toward health care, financials and technology.
PSCC: Tracks an index of small US consumer staples companies, which sell everyday items like food and household goods. It is fairly top heavy, with Lamb Weston, PriceSmart, Vita Coco and Cal-Maine making up more than a third of it.
PSCD: Small US companies that sell consumer goods and services people buy when they feel comfortable spending, like retail, restaurants and homebuilding, tracked by an S&P index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 3%.
PSCE: Tracks the S&P SmallCap 600 energy companies, which are smaller US oil, gas and energy services firms. It is concentrated in a handful of names, with SM Energy, Archrock and Noble each around 6% to 7%, so it rises and falls with energy prices.
PSCF: Holds small US financial and real estate companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, such as banks, insurers and property owners. It is widely spread, with no single company above about 2%, and is mostly financials with a large real estate share.
PSCH: Small US health care companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, covering things like biotech, drugmakers and health services. It is spread across many names, with the largest, Molina Healthcare, at about 5%.
PSCI: Small US industrial companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, such as builders, machinery makers and electrical equipment firms. It is moderately concentrated, with Argan, Powell Industries, Everus and ESCO each around 3%, and is more volatile than large-company funds.
PSCJ: An actively managed options fund tied to the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in July, designed to be conservative by guarding against a set amount of losses while capping gains. The outcome only applies to those who hold for the full period.
PSCM: Small US materials companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, covering chemicals, packaging, metals and mining, and paper. It is fairly concentrated for a sector fund: Element Solutions and Eastman Chemical are together about 23% of it.
PSCQ: A defined-outcome fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to protect against part of the losses over a one-year period starting in October. The conservative tilt means more downside protection but a lower cap on gains.
PSCT: Tracks the information technology part of the S&P SmallCap 600, so it holds small US tech companies such as chip makers, electronics and software firms. Its largest holdings are Sanmina and Semtech at about 5% each, and smaller companies tend to swing more than big ones.
PSCU: Follows an index of small US companies in the utilities and communication services sectors, such as phone, media and entertainment firms. It is a narrow slice, with Lumen, Match Group and Madison Square Garden among the largest holdings at 6% to 10% each.
PSCW: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to protect part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in April, with a limit on the gains. This is the conservative version, which uses a bigger cushion and a lower cap on gains.
PSCX: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options tied to the S&P 500 to protect against part of the losses over a set one-year period. The trade-off is a cap on gains, and the protection works best if shares are held for the whole period.
PSDM: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds from several parts of the bond market, including government, corporate and mortgage bonds. Because the maturities are short, its price moves less with interest rates than a typical bond fund, and it pays regular income.
PSEP: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion the first 15% of losses over a one-year period starting each September. Gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only works for the full period.
PSFD: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to protect part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in January, with a limit on the gains. This is the flex version, which balances the cushion and cap more evenly.
PSFF: A fund of other Pacer Swan SOS ETFs, each of which uses options to limit losses on the S&P 500 for a one-year period, in exchange for capping the gains. The funds start at staggered times through the year, so the protection is spread out rather than all resetting at once.
PSFJ: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow large US stocks while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period starting each July. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
PSFM: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow US large company stocks over a set one-year period that starts in April. It is actively managed and aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for a limit on gains, so results depend on when you hold it.
PSFO: Uses customized options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to give a defined outcome over a set period starting in October. It aims to follow part of the S&P 500's gains while shielding against a set amount of losses, and the fund is non-diversified.
PSH: A bond fund holding US companies' high yield bonds, which are rated below investment grade, with a shorter average maturity than most funds of this type. Shorter maturities usually mean smaller price swings, though these borrowers carry more risk of missing payments than safer issuers.
PSI: About 30 US semiconductor companies, the businesses that design and make computer chips, picked and weighted by an index. It is a narrow, single-industry fund where the top names like Applied Materials, AMD, NVIDIA and Micron are each around 5% to 6% of it.
PSIL: An actively managed fund investing in companies working on psychedelic based medicines, such as treatments for depression and anxiety. It is a narrow, all health care bet where just three companies, Definium, Compass Pathways and AtaiBeckley, make up about 35% of the fund.
PSK: Preferred securities, a mix between stocks and bonds that pay fixed income and rank ahead of regular stock, tracking an ICE index of US-listed preferreds. Most come from banks and other financial companies, and the fund pays regular income, with no single holding above about 4%.
PSL: US consumer staples companies, such as food, grocery and household product makers, chosen by recent price momentum under a Dorsey Wright method. It holds about the same weight in each top name, with Casey's, US Foods and Costco each around 5%.
PSLV: A trust that holds physical silver bars in storage, so its price follows the price of silver. It owns the metal itself rather than mining companies or futures, and it pays no income.
PSMD: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a set period starting in January, in return for a cap on gains. It is actively managed, and the protection only applies if held for the full period.
PSMJ: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting each July to cushion part of the losses. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold for the full period.
PSMO: Uses options tied to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period that starts each October, with a moderate buffer against part of the losses. In return, the gains for that period are capped, and it is actively managed.
PSMR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to follow the US market up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period starting in April. Gains are capped, and results depend on when you buy.
PSOX: A thematic stock fund focused on companies that make power chips and multilayer ceramic capacitors, the tiny parts that manage electricity inside electronics. It is narrow, concentrated in a small corner of the semiconductor and electronics industry.
PSP: Listed companies that invest in private equity, such as 3i, Blackstone, EQT and KKR, drawn from around the world. It gives stock market access to a private equity business, and the largest names are each about 5% to 6% of the fund.
PSQA: A fund that holds the highest-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), bundles of corporate loans, rated AAA or AA when issued, tracking a Palmer Square index. These senior slices are the first to be paid, so they are designed to be safer than other CLO tiers.
PSQO: An actively managed fund that mostly owns debt, including bonds and loans of any maturity and credit quality, with room for lower-rated and unrated ones. It aims to find extra income in corporate credit, so it carries more risk than a safe bond fund.
PSR: An actively managed fund of US real estate companies, mostly REITs, which own properties like cell towers, warehouses and data centers and pay out rental income. American Tower, Prologis and Welltower are about 27% of it.
PSTP: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period, with the buffer stepping up in a defined way. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
PSTR: An actively managed fund that rotates between US sector funds, such as financials, technology and health care, holding mostly other ETFs. It also uses options to bring in extra income, which can limit some of the upside when markets rise.
PSWD: A fund that follows the Solactive Cyber Security Focus Index, holding companies that make cybersecurity software and services. It is concentrated, with CrowdStrike, Okta, Fortinet, Rubrik and Palo Alto Networks each about 6% of the fund, and nearly all in technology.
PTBD: A rules based trend following bond fund that moves between high yield corporate bonds and 7 to 10 year Treasuries depending on a risk signal. It can hold all high yield, half and half, or all Treasuries, so its bond mix changes over time.
PTEU: Large companies from the eurozone, following a trend rule that decides how much to hold. It can be fully in European stocks, half in stocks and half in Treasury bills, or fully in Treasury bills, depending on market trends, so it can step aside in downturns.
PTF: Technology companies chosen by Dorsey Wright for strong recent price momentum, meaning stocks that have been rising, reshuffled regularly. It holds at least 30 companies, around 94% in tech, and leans toward storage and chip makers like Western Digital, Micron and Seagate.
PTH: Health care stocks picked for strong recent price momentum, meaning they have been rising faster than others. It is heavy on smaller biotech and health services firms, no holding is above about 5%, and the group is re-picked regularly.
PTIN: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed markets outside the US, held under a trend-following rule from Pacer's own index. When the index's trend signal turns weak, part or all of the fund can shift into Treasury bills to cut stock exposure.
PTL: The 500 large US companies in the Inspire 500 Index, picked using an impact score that screens for values-based factors. It is not an ordinary index fund: Broadcom is about 13% of it, a lot more than a plain S&P 500 fund would hold.
PTLC: Follows the S&P 500 but shifts its mix based on a trend rule using the index's 200 day average. It can hold all stocks, half stocks and half Treasury bills, or all Treasury bills, so it sometimes steps out of the market after declines.
PTMC: US mid-sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400, with a trend-following rule that moves part or all of the money into Treasury bills when prices weaken. This aims to reduce losses in a downturn, though it can also miss some of a rebound.
PTNQ: Follows the Nasdaq-100 using a trend-following rule: it holds the stocks when the index is above its 200-day average, half stocks and half Treasury bills when mixed, and all bills when weak. Its stock exposure changes over time, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
PTNT: An actively managed fund focused on companies that earn money from patents, licensing and royalties on their intellectual property. Holdings were not listed, so the mix is not clear, though it sits in the global large-company category.
PTRB: An actively managed US bond fund that spreads money across government, corporate and other bonds to earn income and some price gains. It is a broad core holding rather than a narrow bet, and about a third of it sits in US Treasuries at the top.
PUI: Utility companies picked by momentum, meaning those whose share prices have been rising faster than peers, tracked by a Dorsey Wright index of at least 30 stocks. It is about 84% utilities, with ONEOK, Sempra and Evergy among the largest holdings at around 4% each.
PVAL: An actively managed fund holding a concentrated set of large US companies that managers judge to be priced below their worth. Unlike many value funds it owns big tech: Microsoft and Apple together are about 17% of it.
PVEX: An actively managed fund that holds part of its money in US large-cap stocks and uses options to soften the hit from big market drops. The rest sits in Treasury bills and other funds, so it moves with the market only partly.
PVI: Tracks an index of tax exempt US municipal bonds with floating interest rates, which reset often and have very short maturities. Because the rates adjust, its price tends to be steady, and income follows short term rates.
PWB: Fifty large US growth stocks, picked by an index for strong price growth and other growth traits. It is concentrated in few names: Mastercard, Visa, Applied Materials, Amazon and Apple are each about 3% to 4%, and over half is technology.
PWER: A fund of companies tied to the shift away from fossil fuels, including utilities, metals and mining firms, and energy producers. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Steel Dynamics, Hudbay, ERO Copper and Valero each around 5% to 6%.
PWRD: An actively managed global stock fund betting on companies that help power and move the modern world, like electrical equipment, aerospace and chips and networking gear. It is concentrated, with GE Aerospace, Arista Networks, Safran and KLA about 24% of it.
PWRX: An actively managed fund of companies tied to power generation and infrastructure, such as GE Vernova, Vistra and Quanta Services. It is fairly spread out, with each of its top holdings around 4%, across industrials, energy and utilities.
PWRZ: An actively managed fund of global companies that own or run renewable energy assets, mostly utilities. It aims to pay income, and the biggest holdings include American Electric Power, RWE and Enel, with the top three about 27% of the fund.
PWS: Follows an index that shifts between US stocks, Treasuries or a mix, based on a rule for managing risk. It currently holds a lot of Treasuries, around 16%, plus stocks spread across sectors, and the mix can change as the rules dictate.
PWV: Large US companies chosen by Invesco's index for strong value traits like low prices compared with their fundamentals. It leans toward financials, energy and health care, with the largest holdings including Bank of America, AbbVie and JPMorgan at about 3% to 4% each.
PWZ: Tax-exempt bonds issued by California and its local governments, following an index of such long-term municipal debt. Interest is generally free of federal and California income tax, and the holdings are spread thinly, with no single issuer much above 1% of the fund.
PXE: US energy companies that find and produce oil and natural gas, plus refiners, held in a rules-based index. It is a narrow bet on one industry: Valero, Marathon Petroleum, EOG and Diamondback are each about 5% to 6%, and results follow oil and gas prices.
PXF: About 1,000 of the largest companies in developed markets outside the US, weighted by fundamentals like sales, cash flow and dividends instead of market size. That gives more weight to cheaper, established firms, and Samsung is the largest holding at about 4%.
PXH: Large emerging market companies, picked and weighted by size measures like sales, cash flow and dividends instead of stock market value. This gives bigger weights to value-type firms in oil, banks and manufacturing than a plain emerging markets index would.
PXI: US energy companies that have shown strong recent price momentum, selected by a Dorsey Wright index of at least 30 stocks. It tilts toward refiners and pipeline companies like Marathon Petroleum, Cheniere and Targa, and the list gets reshuffled regularly.
PXJ: Holds US companies that provide services and equipment to oil and gas producers, such as drilling and offshore support firms, chosen by an index. Frontline, TechnipFMC, NOV and Baker Hughes are each about 5% of it, so it is a narrow bet on energy services.
PY: An actively managed fund of US large companies the manager considers cheap compared with their value, mixing in financials, health care and tech. Apple is the biggest holding at about 8%, and Amazon, Walmart and Bank of America follow at 2% to 3% each.
PYLD: An actively managed PIMCO bond fund that spreads money across many parts of the bond market, such as corporate, mortgage and foreign debt, with managers choosing the mix. It aims to pay steady monthly income and uses derivatives, so its exposure can exceed the fund's size.
PYPY: An actively managed fund that tries to earn high monthly income from PayPal's stock price moves by using options, rather than owning much PayPal stock directly. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills, and the options approach limits how much it gains if PayPal rallies.
PYZ: US basic materials companies, such as steel makers, specialty metals and chemicals, that have shown strong recent price momentum, picked by a Dorsey Wright index. ATI and Carpenter Technology are each about 7% of the fund, and the list is reshuffled regularly.
PZA: Long term municipal bonds from across the US, tracking an index of bonds whose interest is exempt from federal income tax and not subject to the alternative minimum tax. It holds a very large number of bonds, and none is more than a fraction of a percent.
PZIV: An actively managed fund of stocks of large companies outside the US, picked by Pzena as cheap compared with their long-run earning power. That value approach has led it to hold many Japanese and European electronics and industrial firms like Murata and TDK.
PZLV: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the managers think are cheap compared to what they are worth. It leans toward health care and financials, with Humana, Baxter and Skyworks among its biggest holdings.
PZT: Holds investment grade bonds issued by New York State and its cities and agencies, whose interest is generally free of federal and New York income tax. It spreads across hundreds of issues, with no single bond above about 2%, and it focuses on longer maturities.
QABA: Small, mid sized and large US banks and thrifts that are listed on Nasdaq, tracked by the Nasdaq ABA Community Bank Index. It is all banks and spread across many names, with the largest, Wintrust, only about 4% of the fund.
QAI: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mostly bond funds plus some stock funds, to mimic the average results of hedge fund strategies like long/short and global macro. It is a mix of bonds and stocks, led by short-term Treasury and floating rate bond ETFs.
QALT: An actively managed fund that takes both bets for and against global stocks, bonds and currencies, mostly through futures, to try to deliver steady returns in different markets. Because it uses derivatives backed by cash and short-term holdings, it is not a plain stock or bond fund.
QARP: Large US companies that look high in quality yet are reasonably priced, picked by a Russell index. It is top-heavy, with Apple, NVIDIA, Amazon and Alphabet about 22% of the fund, and it leans toward technology.
QAT: Tracks the MSCI Qatar index, holding large companies from the small Gulf country of Qatar. It is concentrated in banks: Qatar National Bank and Qatar Islamic Bank are about 37% of it, and financials are over half.
QAU: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in August. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QB: A fund tracking the Nasdaq-100 that also uses options to cushion some losses, in exchange for giving up part of the gains. It follows a set strategy rather than just owning the index, with NVIDIA and Apple making up about 15% of it.
QBF: A defined-outcome fund giving exposure to bitcoin through options, with no cap on gains, while limiting part of the losses over a quarterly period. The protection comes at a cost, and the stated outcome only applies if held for the full period.
QBIF: Tracks international developed-markets stocks through options on an EFA ETF, with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped at a set level, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
QBIG: An actively managed fund giving exposure to the largest companies in the Nasdaq-100, using the index's Mega version as its guide. NVIDIA is about 7% of it, and a large share of the fund sits in a government money market fund, so it is a concentrated bet on big tech.
QBIV: Tracks the performance of an international developed-markets stock ETF (EFA) using options, with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 5% of losses over a set one-year period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies to investors who hold for the full period.
QBKF: Tracks small US companies through options on a Russell 2000 ETF (IWM), with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
QBKV: Tracks small US companies through options on a Russell 2000 ETF (IWM), with a built-in buffer meant to absorb the first 5% of losses over a set one-year period. Gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held through the whole period.
QBQF: Uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year outcome period. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only works if you hold the fund for the whole period.
QBQV: Uses options tied to a Nasdaq 100 ETF to cushion a small set amount of losses over a one-year period ending in September, with a 5% buffer as the name says. In return, gains are capped, and the underlying index is about 60% technology.
QBSF: Options contracts tied to the S&P 500 that aim to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period, in exchange for a limit on the gains. The cushion and cap only apply if you hold from the start to the end of that period.
QBSV: A defined-outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period ending in September. In exchange, it limits how much of the market's gains it can capture.
QBUF: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to cushion the first 10% of losses over a three-month period. In exchange, the upside over that period is capped, and the protection resets every quarter.
QBY: An income fund built around D-Wave Quantum stock that sells put options on a 2 times leveraged fund tied to it, aiming to pay weekly. It is a highly volatile strategy, with Treasury bills held as backing.
QCAP: Uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in April. It is built to cushion part of the losses in exchange for a cap on gains, so timing within the period matters.
QCJA: Options contracts tied to the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, that aim to cushion part of the losses over a set one-year period starting in January. Gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
QCJL: Uses options tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to buffer part of the losses over a one-year period that starts in July. In return, the gains over that period are capped, and the buffer only works if held for the full period.
QCLN: Clean energy companies listed in the US, of all sizes, tracking a Nasdaq Clean Edge index. It covers fuel cells, solar, electric vehicles and chip makers, and is fairly concentrated: Bloom Energy and Tesla are about 18% of the fund.
QCOC: Uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100 to cushion part of the losses over a one year period that starts in October, with a conservative level of protection. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it works best when held for the full period.
QDEC: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the Nasdaq-100 (through the QQQ fund) to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each December. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold the full period.
QDEF: Follows a Northern Trust index of high-quality US stocks that pay income, with a lean toward steadier companies. It aims to swing less than the broad market, though Apple and NVIDIA are still about 15% of it, so tech has a large weight.
QDF: Large and mid-size US companies chosen for high quality and steady dividends by a Northern Trust index, aiming for long-term growth with income. It still has a tech tilt: Apple, NVIDIA, Broadcom and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund.
QDIV: Holds companies from the S&P 500 that score well on quality and pay high dividends, following a Global X index. It is spread across consumer staples, financials, industrials and health care, with no single stock above about 3%.
QDPL: The S&P 500 plus extra exposure to its dividends through futures, using a design that multiplies the dividend part of the index. Its stock holdings are about the same as the S&P 500, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 18% of it, but the dividend futures add extra risk.
QDTE: A fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 while selling call options that expire within a day (0DTE) to produce income paid out weekly. The options limit gains when the market rises, and the fund's holdings are mostly options and Treasury bills.
QDTY: Gives exposure to the Nasdaq 100 index while selling call options on it, aiming to pay out income every week. Those options cap how much of a big rally the fund keeps, and it holds a fairly concentrated mix, mostly technology.
QDVO: Growth-oriented US stocks, led by NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft, plus an options strategy that sells call options to earn extra income. That income comes with a trade-off, since selling calls limits how much the fund gains when stocks surge.
QEFA: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside North America, such as Europe, Japan and Australia, picked with a tilt toward factors like value, quality and low volatility. ASML, Novartis and AstraZeneca lead, but each is only about 2%.
QEMM: Large and mid-sized stocks across 26 emerging markets, picked and weighted for value, low volatility and quality instead of just company size. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 7% of it, and tech and financials are the biggest sectors.
QETH: A trust that holds ether, the digital currency of the Ethereum network, directly rather than owning company stocks. Its price follows the market price of ether, which can swing sharply, and it earns no interest or dividends.
QEW: The 100 companies in the Nasdaq-100 index, but each held in roughly equal amounts instead of weighted by size. That means the giant tech names matter far less than in the regular index, and no single holding is much above 1% of the fund.
QFF: An actively managed, concentrated fund of large US growth companies that the managers see as lasting compounders: durable advantages, owner-minded management and high returns on reinvested money. NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 24% of it, and technology and financials make up over half.
