QFHD: US large companies from the S&P 500 that pay dividends and have strong free cash flow, which is cash left after running the business. Holdings are weighted by dividend yield rather than size, so it is spread widely with no single stock above about 3%.
QFLR: An actively managed fund giving exposure to the Nasdaq-100 stocks while using options to set a floor that limits how much it can lose. In exchange, upside is typically limited too, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 24% of it.
QFRD: Holds S&P 500 companies picked for strong free cash flow and heavy spending on research and development. It leans toward technology, about 65%, and health care, about 25%, with Datadog the largest holding.
QGRD: Uses options on the Nasdaq-100 Index to manage risk and generate income, aiming to limit part of the losses in exchange for giving up some of the gains. Its returns follow the Nasdaq-100 only partly, so it can lag in strong rallies.
QGRO: US large and mid-size companies that have strong growth in earnings and sales and are financially sturdy, chosen by American Century's quality growth index. It is fairly spread out: Apple, TJX and NVIDIA are each only about 3% to 4% of it.
QGRW: US companies with strong profits and growth, picked and weighted by WisdomTree's quality and growth rules, then rebalanced twice a year. It is concentrated in big tech: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta are about 39% of the fund.
QHY: US corporate bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, called high yield or junk bonds, which pay more interest because they carry more risk of default. It follows a WisdomTree index and holds hundreds of bonds, each only about 0.5% of the fund.
QIDX: Mid-sized US companies that an index-based adviser thinks have steady, high-quality earnings. It holds a broad mix of about 100 or more stocks, led by technology, industrials and health care, with no single holding above roughly 4% of the fund.
QIG: Investment-grade US corporate bonds, meaning loans to companies with solid credit, picked to follow a WisdomTree index. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings, such as Bank of America and Wells Fargo, around 1% each.
QINT: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked by American Century's index, which favors companies with strong quality and value measures. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 1.5%, across companies like Rio Tinto, Equinor and BNP Paribas.
QIS: An actively managed fund that uses swaps, contracts that pay the return of rule-based trading models, to spread bets across stocks, interest rates, commodities and currencies. The Treasury bills and fund holdings that show up are largely backing for those swaps, and it aims to behave differently from stocks and bonds.
QJL: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in July. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QJN: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100 to cushion the first 10% of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
QJUN: A fund using options on the Nasdaq-100 to cushion losses over a one-year period starting each June. It buffers the first stretch of drops, about 10%, but caps the gains, so the protection only applies if you hold through the full period.
QLC: Large US companies chosen by Northern Trust for a mix of quality, value and momentum traits, rather than just by size. It still ends up top-heavy in tech, with Apple and NVIDIA each around 7% and technology about 38% of the fund.
QLDY: An actively managed income fund that aims to give exposure to the Nasdaq 100's price while earning income from options, with payouts meant to be made twice a week. It is about 60% technology, and the options can limit gains compared with owning the index.
QLTA: US corporate bonds rated from AAA to A, the higher quality end of investment grade, from a broad index of large companies. It is widely spread across issuers, with no single bond above about a third of a percent.
QLTI: An actively managed fund of high-quality companies outside the US, chosen by the manager GMO for strong profits and stable finances. It is moderately concentrated, with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 6% and Inditex, SAP and Novartis each around 4 to 5%.
QLTY: An actively managed fund of US large companies that its manager GMO judges to be high quality, meaning strong, stable profits and sturdy finances. Technology and health care are around 62% of it, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Lam Research are the largest holdings.
QLV: Large US companies chosen for strong quality and lower expected ups and downs than the broader US market, tracking a Northern Trust index. It still holds the big tech names: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple are each about 6% of the fund.
QLVD: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, picked for being high quality companies with steadier prices. It is well spread across industries and countries, led by names like Novartis, Royal Bank of Canada and Unilever, each only a few percent of the fund.
QLVE: Emerging market stocks chosen for high quality and lower price swings than the broader emerging market universe. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 15% of it and Samsung is another large holding, so it leans toward technology.
QMAG: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to follow big tech stocks up to a limit while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period starting in August. Gains are capped, and results depend on when you buy.
QMAR: A fund that uses options on the Invesco QQQ ETF, which follows the Nasdaq-100, to buffer against the first 10% of losses over a one-year period that starts each March. In return, it caps the gains, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
QMFE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq-100) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting in February. In return, gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full period.
QMID: Holds mid-sized US companies with high quality and growth traits, chosen by a WisdomTree index. It is spread widely, with no stock above about 1.5%, across technology, health care, industrials and consumer companies.
QMMY: A defined outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, over a set one-year period starting in May. It aims to gain with the market up to a cap, with a buffer against part of the losses.
QMNV: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq-100) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting in November. In return, gains are capped, and the protection works best if held for the full period.
QMOM: A fund of US mid-sized companies chosen because their stock prices have been rising strongly, using a rules-based momentum screen. It is spread across about 50 stocks, with no single holding above roughly 2%, and it shifts toward whatever sectors are trending.
QMY: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to a growth and technology ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 10% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and it is tilted toward tech.
QNDX: A low-cost fund tracking the Nasdaq 100, the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange. It is heavy in technology, at about 60%, and top-heavy too: NVIDIA, Apple and Micron are around 20% of the fund.
QNXT: Holds the roughly 70 Nasdaq-100 companies ranked 31st through 100th by size, leaving out the 30 biggest like Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA. That makes it a way to own the Nasdaq-100's smaller names, with technology the largest slice at about 44%.
QOWZ: A fund following a Nasdaq index of US-listed companies with steady, growing free cash flow, meaning the cash left over after running the business. It is heavy in technology at about two-thirds, and NVIDIA and Broadcom together are close to 18%.
QPX: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other ETFs across stocks, bonds and gold, shifting among them over time. At present it leans toward technology funds, with gold and small company stocks making up a large share.
QQA: A fund that holds Nasdaq-100 stocks (large US technology-leaning companies) and also sells options on the index to collect extra income. The options income comes with a trade-off, as it limits some gains when the market surges, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 16% of it.
QQAU: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in August. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QQBF: Uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (the Nasdaq-100) to cushion the first 15% of losses over each quarter. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, and the buffer resets every three months.
QQDH: An actively managed fund that holds the Nasdaq-100 through the QQQ fund and/or options, then adds two options strategies: one to earn income and one to hedge against falls. The options bring extra income and some protection but limit how much of the upside it keeps.
QQEW: The 50 Nasdaq-100 companies with the best combined growth, value and momentum style scores, held in roughly equal amounts rather than by company size. That equal weighting means no giant dominates: the largest holdings are only about 3% each, and technology is about 70% of the fund.
QQH: A fund built around large US growth stocks like Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft, following the Nasdaq-100 idea but actively managed with a defensive, rule-based approach. A big part of it is held through another ProShares fund, so it is top-heavy in tech.
QQHG: A fund that holds the stocks of the Nasdaq-100 and adds an options hedge meant to soften sharp drops. NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet are about 28% of it, and technology is around 60%, so it is very tech-heavy.
QQI: About 100 of the largest non-US companies listed on Nasdaq's international market, following the Nasdaq International Innovators 100 index. It tilts to technology and health care, and Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 11% of the fund.
QQJL: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in July. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QQJN: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in June. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QQLV: Picks the 100 or so Nasdaq-100 stocks that have been calmer, meaning their prices have swung less, and holds them as an index fund. As a result it leans toward utilities, consumer staples and industrials, and away from the usual tech giants.
QQMG: The Nasdaq-100 with companies screened and weighted on environmental, social and governance (ESG) measures. It looks much like the regular Nasdaq-100, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together about 25% of the fund.
QQMY: Uses options on the Invesco QQQ fund, which tracks the Nasdaq 100, to protect against a set amount of losses over a set period starting in May. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
QQQ: Tracks the Nasdaq-100: about 100 of the biggest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by size. It is tech-heavy, with technology around 60% of the fund and NVIDIA and Apple together about 14%.
QQQA: Holds the 21 stocks in the Nasdaq-100 with the strongest momentum, meaning recent price strength, based on a Dorsey Wright ranking. It is concentrated and tech-heavy: ARM, AMD and Intel are about 23% of it, and technology is around two thirds.
QQQB: Aims to follow the Nasdaq-100 while using options to protect against part of the losses. Because of that protection, it gives up some of the gains when the index rises, and its holdings are mostly cash and option contracts rather than stocks.
QQQE: The same companies as the Nasdaq-100 but held in equal amounts instead of by size, so each holding is only about 1%. This makes it less top-heavy than the usual Nasdaq-100 fund, which leans on a handful of giants.
QQQG: Fifty Nasdaq-100 companies picked for strong cash generation and growth, instead of the whole index. It is heavily tilted to technology at about 80%, with data storage and chip equipment makers like Western Digital, Seagate and Applied Materials near the top.
QQQH: An actively managed fund holding Nasdaq-100 stocks, with options on top: a put spread to hedge against drops and call options sold for income. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron together are about 20% of the fund, and the options trade some upside for protection.
QQQI: The Nasdaq-100 stocks, mostly big tech, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to generate monthly income. The options pay the fund extra cash but cap how much it gains when the market rises sharply.
QQQJ: The next 100 largest Nasdaq companies just below the Nasdaq-100, mostly mid-sized growth firms in tech and health care. It is evenly spread, with no holding above about 3%, and changes often as companies move in and out.
QQQM: Another fund tracking the Nasdaq-100: about 100 of the biggest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange. Technology is about 60%, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 21%, making it a close twin of QQQ.
QQQS: Small US companies from the Nasdaq market that are not big enough to be in the Nasdaq-100, with an index picking those with growth potential. It is spread across many tiny positions, with over half in health care and about 30% in technology.
QQQT: An actively managed fund that holds the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100, and uses options to try to produce regular income. Almost all of the fund sits in that one ETF, so it behaves like a technology heavy fund with income as the goal.
QQQY: An actively managed fund that uses options on the Nasdaq-100 index to generate income, paid out weekly. That strategy limits how much it gains when the index rises, while most of the losses from a drop can still come through, and it holds mostly Treasury bills and options.
QQSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the Invesco QQQ Trust, which tracks the Nasdaq-100 to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
QQWZ: A rotation strategy that, based on an index rule, holds either the Nasdaq 100 or a basket of high free cash flow US companies, so it can shift between growth and value styles. Its current holdings are led by NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon, together about 26% of it.
QQXT: The companies in the Nasdaq-100 that are not technology businesses, such as health care, consumer, industrial and communications firms. Each stock is held in roughly equal amounts rather than by size, so no single name dominates, and the biggest holdings are only about 2% each.
QRMI: Holds Nasdaq-100 stocks and sells call options while buying put options, a collar strategy, to earn monthly income and soften some losses. That means it gives up part of big rallies, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of it.
QSE: A defined-outcome fund using options on the Invesco QQQ Trust (Nasdaq 100) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in September. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
QSIG: US corporate bonds from companies with strong credit ratings that mature within a few years, tracking a WisdomTree index. Holdings are spread across many issuers, with big banks like Goldman Sachs and Bank of America each only around 1% of the fund.
QSIX: Holds the stocks of the Nasdaq-100 and adds futures contracts on the index's dividends, which is meant to boost the dividend income it captures. It is tech heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 20% of the fund, and it holds a fairly small number of names.
QSML: A fund of small US companies picked by an index that favors strong profitability and growth. It holds hundreds of stocks, with none above about 1%, so it is very spread out, and technology and consumer discretionary are the largest sectors.
QSOL: A fund that holds Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, directly rather than through stocks or futures. It also aims to stake most of its coins, which means locking them up to help run the network in exchange for extra rewards, and its value swings with Solana's price.
QSPT: A fund using options on the Nasdaq-100 to cushion losses over a one-year period starting each September. It buffers the first stretch of drops, about 10%, but caps the gains, so the protection only works if you hold through the full period.
QTAC: An actively managed fund that mixes stock index futures, leveraged ETFs and Treasuries, and can shift its mix based on market conditions. About half sits in a Nasdaq-100 ETF, and its leveraged holdings make it riskier than a plain index fund.
QTAP: Uses FLEX options, customizable exchange traded options, tied to the Invesco QQQ Trust, a Nasdaq-100 fund, to magnify gains, up to a limit, over a set period that starts each April. It can still lose money if the index falls.
QTEC: The tech stocks of the Nasdaq-100, with each company given roughly the same weight rather than by size. That makes it very different from a normal tech fund: small and mid sized chip and software firms matter as much as giants, and no holding is above about 3.5%.
QTJA: A defined outcome fund using options tied to the Invesco QQQ, a Nasdaq-100 tracker, over a one-year period starting in January. It aims to magnify gains up to a cap while taking on losses if the index falls, so results depend on when you buy and sell.
QTJL: A defined outcome fund using options tied to the Invesco QQQ, a Nasdaq-100 tracker, over a one-year period starting in July. It aims to magnify gains up to a cap while taking on losses if the index falls, so results depend on when you buy and sell.
QTOC: An actively managed fund using options on the Invesco QQQ (Nasdaq-100) fund over a set one-year period starting in October. It aims to give some amplified gains if the index rises, with a cap, but you can lose money if the index falls.
QTOP: The 30 biggest non-financial companies from the Nasdaq-100, a narrower and more concentrated version of that index. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron alone are about a quarter of the fund, and roughly two thirds is technology.
QTPI: An actively managed fund of preferred stocks and bonds whose dividends are meant to qualify for lower US tax rates. Preferreds pay steady income, and the biggest holdings are large US banks like Bank of America, Goldman Sachs and Citigroup at about 3% each.
QTR: The Nasdaq-100 stocks combined with protective put options that pay off if the index drops sharply. The options act as insurance against big falls, which costs some return, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of it.
QTUM: Companies tied to quantum computing and machine learning, such as chip makers and equipment firms, held in roughly equal amounts by a Defiance-sponsored index. The biggest holdings are only about 2% each, so it is a spread-out bet on an early, speculative area.
QTUP: An actively managed fund of companies focused on quantum computing, meaning at least half their revenue or activity comes from it. It is very concentrated in small, young firms, with Quantinuum and IonQ together about 34% of the fund.
QUAL: Large US companies chosen for quality traits: high profitability, steady earnings and low debt, following an MSCI index. It looks a lot like the broad market at the top, with Microsoft, Apple and NVIDIA about 20% of it, and technology around 41%.
QUIZ: Actively managed fund of large international stocks outside the US, chosen with a quality focus on strong, profitable companies. It is spread widely, with ASML, HSBC and Siemens each only a few percent, and tilts toward financials and industrials.
QUS: Large and mid-sized US companies picked and weighted by an MSCI index that blends quality, value, smaller size and lower volatility traits. The result looks like the US market but is more evenly spread, with Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA each only about 3% of the fund.
QUSA: US high-quality companies, with a combination of stocks and options that aims to pay a steady income. The largest holdings are Microsoft, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, NVIDIA and Broadcom at about 5% each, and it leans heavily toward technology.
QVAL: About 50 to 200 undervalued US stocks, picked by a rules-based screen for cheap, high-quality companies, held in roughly equal amounts. It is very evenly spread, with each top holding near 2%, and leans toward energy, consumer discretionary and health care.
QVML: About 400 to 450 of the S&P 500's companies, chosen for being cheaper, higher quality and having stronger momentum, and weighted by those traits rather than just size. It still leans on big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about 22% of the fund.
QVMM: About 400 US mid-sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400, picked and weighted for quality, value and momentum together rather than by size. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
QVMS: About 600 US small companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, with the weights tilted toward cheaper, higher-quality stocks with strong recent price gains. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings only about 1% each.
QVMT: Holds 100 stocks from the S&P 500 that score best on quality, value and momentum, a mix of company strength, cheap prices and recent price strength. It is far more concentrated than the full index, with Apple, Johnson & Johnson and Visa each around 4% to 5%.
QVOL: Holds Nasdaq-100 stocks and sells options on them to generate income. Selling options can limit gains in a strong market, and it is tech-heavy, with NVIDIA, Amazon and AMD together about 22% of it.
QVOY: An actively managed fund of funds that moves between other ETFs across four categories, shifting its mix as market conditions change. Its top holdings are other ETFs, each about 14%, so it is a tactical mix and not a fixed allocation.
QWLD: Large and mid-sized stocks from 23 developed countries, picked and weighted by factors like value, quality and low volatility rather than size. The top holdings, Microsoft, Apple and NVIDIA, are each only about 2%.
QXQ: Holds Nasdaq 100 companies, often through options or other funds, and adds options strategies meant to produce income. This tilts it toward big tech names, and the options can limit gains in a strong market.
QYLD: The Nasdaq 100 stocks, but with an options strategy called a covered call that sells away much of the future upside in exchange for regular income payments. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 22% of it, and gains are capped in strong markets.
QYLG: Holds the Nasdaq 100 stocks and sells call options on about half of them, collecting option income in exchange for giving up part of the gains in big rallies. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 21% of the fund.
RAA: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, bonds and alternatives like commodities, gold and managed futures, mostly by holding other ETFs. It uses a real-assets strategy meant to hold up better when inflation rises, and about 60% of it is in stocks.
RAAA: An actively managed fund holding the safest, top-rated AAA slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are pools of loans made to companies. No single manager's deals dominate, with each of the largest holdings around 6%, and it aims for income above ordinary bonds.
RAAR: Holds an underlying fund of the safest AAA-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds. Unlike its annual-payout sibling, this one reinvests the income, so it grows rather than paying distributions.
RAAX: An actively managed fund of funds aimed at assets that tend to hold value as prices rise: commodities, gold, infrastructure, energy and natural resources companies. About 40% sits in just two funds, a commodity strategy fund and a gold fund, and it also tries to limit losses in long market declines.
RAAY: Holds one other fund that invests in the safest, AAA-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds. It aims for more yield than ordinary bonds of similar rating and pays out income annually.
RACK: Companies that supply what data centers need, such as memory chips, cables and connectors, power equipment and electricity-related firms, following a VanEck index. It is spread across many names, with Micron, Amphenol and Sandisk each around 5% of it, and it leans heavily toward technology.
RAFE: Large US companies selected and weighted by PIMCO's RAFI method, which uses company size measures such as sales and cash flow, then screens for ESG (environmental, social and governance) factors. Apple and Microsoft are about 9% of it.
RANK: A fund that follows an index of large US stocks chosen using Wall Street analyst ratings and forecasts. Technology makes up over 40%, and Micron, Applied Materials, Walmart and General Electric are each roughly 5% to 7% of it.
RAUS: US listed companies weighted by fundamentals such as sales, cash flow and book value, instead of by market size like most index funds. It still holds the big names, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet about 20% of the fund.
RB: Holds the Russell 2000 small-company index and adds a layer of very short-term options that aim to soften part of the losses on a rolling basis. The buffer is reset every day, so protection is partial and gains are limited when the market rises sharply.
RBLD: US companies and REITs (real estate investment trusts) building the infrastructure of the future, such as data, power and network systems, picked by the Alerian index. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 2%, and mixes tech, energy and real estate names.
RBLY: A fund that uses options to earn income from Roblox stock without owning much of the shares directly, with most of the money held in Treasury bills. The options can bring in high income, but they limit gains if Roblox rises and losses can still be large.
RBTX: An actively managed fund that buys stocks of companies building robotics and related technology, plus derivatives that give similar exposure. The managers choose the holdings themselves instead of following an index, so it is a themed bet on robotics rather than a broad tech fund.
RBUF: Uses options tied to the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which follows small US companies, to buffer part of the losses over a repeating three-month period. In return, the gains for each period are capped, and the buffer only works if held for the full period.
RCGE: An actively managed fund of global stocks from companies that show a commitment to gender balance in management and on their boards. It spreads money across many companies, with no holding above about 1% of the fund, and leans toward financials.
RCLO: An actively managed fund holding the lower-rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, which are bundles of loans to companies. These slices pay higher interest than safer bonds but carry more risk, and the fund spreads money across many CLOs from different managers.
RCLR: An actively managed fund that puts nearly everything into one underlying fund of CLOs, pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds, focusing on the lower investment grade and below slices. These pay more income than most bonds but carry more credit risk.
RCLY: Holds one other fund that invests in BBB to B rated slices of collateralized loan obligations, pools of corporate loans packaged into bonds. These slices pay higher income than safer ones but carry more risk, and this version pays out annually.
RCTR: Follows a Bloomberg index of companies tied to nuclear power, including utilities that run reactors, builders of equipment, and uranium and metals suppliers. It is split mainly between utilities at about 42% and industrials at about 40%, with GE Vernova and Rolls-Royce at the top.
RDFI: An actively managed fund that buys closed end bond funds, which often trade at a discount or premium to their holdings, and pays regular distributions. Some of those funds hold foreign and emerging market debt, making it a fund of funds with extra layers.
RDOG: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) chosen for their high dividend yields, with the highest payers from each property type held in roughly equal amounts. That equal weighting leaves it spread out, with no holding above about 3%.
RDTE: Gets its exposure to the Russell 2000 small-cap index through options, selling very short-term call options that expire the same day to generate income. This brings in cash payouts but limits how much it can gain when small stocks rally.
RDTY: An income fund that aims to follow small US companies in the Russell 2000 while selling very short-term options, mostly with one-day lifespans, to pay out weekly. Those options cap how much of a rise it can capture, and it uses derivatives rather than owning the stocks directly.
RDVI: US companies with long records of raising dividends, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to bring in extra income. That extra income comes at a cost: it limits how much the fund gains when stocks rise a lot.
RDVY: Large and mid-sized US companies that have raised their dividends and have the cash flow to keep doing so, picked using the Nasdaq US Rising Dividend Achievers index. Despite the income theme, chip equipment makers Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA are its largest holdings at about 13% together.
RDYY: A fund that tries to pay high monthly income from Reddit's stock by using options, without actually owning the shares. Selling those options limits how much it can gain if Reddit rises, and it holds Treasury bills to back the strategy.
REAI: An actively managed fund of real estate companies around the world, chosen with the help of AI-driven analysis. It leans toward data centers and storage, with Equinix and Digital Realty each about 9% of the fund.
RECI: A US stock fund chosen with in-house research that also uses options to bring in extra income. Technology is about 40% of it, with NVIDIA and Apple each around 10%, and the options income comes in exchange for limiting some gains.
RECS: US large and mid-sized companies from the Russell 1000, but chosen and weighted using the manager's research to try to beat the plain index. In practice it is top-heavy: Apple and NVIDIA are each around 11%, and technology is about 39% of the fund.
REET: Real estate investment trusts (companies that own buildings like apartments, warehouses and data centers and pass on rental income) from around the world, tracking a FTSE EPRA Nareit index. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are about 20% of the fund, and most holdings are in the US.
REFA: An actively managed fund of large companies outside the US, picked with in-house research and aiming to beat a standard international stock benchmark. Its largest holdings include ASML, Roche, Novartis and BHP, and each is only about 3 to 4% of the fund.
REGL: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that have raised their dividends every year for at least 15 years, equally weighted so each is a small slice. Because it is built around long dividend growth, it leans toward financials, industrials and utilities.
REGS: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen for above-average growth potential. It leans heavily on technology, and NVIDIA, Apple, Broadcom and Alphabet together make up about 30% of it.
REIT: An actively managed fund of US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties like data centers, warehouses and apartments and pay out rental income. Equinix, Prologis and Welltower are about 28% of it.
REIX: Holds real estate and infrastructure companies around the world, such as apartment and health care landlords, utilities, pipelines and railways. It is spread widely, with Welltower the biggest at about 7%, and real estate makes up about half.
REK: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of the daily move in a US real estate stock index, so it tends to rise when real estate falls. It resets every day, which makes it a short-term tool that can drift from the index over longer periods.
REM: Mortgage real estate investment trusts, companies that own mortgages instead of buildings and earn money from the interest. It is concentrated: Annaly and AGNC are about 38% of the fund, and these companies are known for high payouts.
REMC: An actively managed fund of US mid-sized company stocks, chosen with in-house research and aiming to beat the Russell Midcap benchmark. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings such as Phillips 66, Snowflake and Datadog each only about 2%.
REMG: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, with Taiwan Semiconductor, SK Hynix and Samsung making up about 28% of it together. Technology is its biggest sector at over 40%, followed by financials.
REMX: Companies that mine, refine and recycle rare earths and strategic metals such as lithium, tungsten and cobalt, tracked by a MarketVector index. Many of these businesses are in China and Australia, and the top holdings are each only about 7% of the fund.
RESM: An actively managed fund of US small company stocks, chosen using in-house research and aiming to beat the Russell 2000 style small-cap benchmark. It holds many companies, with no single holding above about 1%, so it is very spread out.
REVS: Large US value stocks from the Russell 1000 Value Index, reweighted by a rules-based method that favors higher-quality, cheaper companies. It is a bit top-heavy in big tech, with Apple and Microsoft about 15% of it, plus banks and energy.
REXC: Mining and processing companies for rare earths, the metals used in magnets, electronics and electric motors, outside of China. It is very concentrated: MP Materials and Lynas Rare Earths together are about 39% of the fund, so it rides on a few producers.
REZ: US real estate companies tied to housing and other property types, mostly health care facilities, self-storage and apartments, following an iShares-chosen index. It is top-heavy in health care property: Welltower is about 23% of the fund, and Public Storage and Ventas follow at 8% to 9%.
RFCI: An actively managed bond fund that mixes US Treasuries, corporate bonds and some preferred stocks, from the US and abroad. Managers shift between these types as conditions change, so it differs from an index fund that tracks one fixed slice of the bond market.
RFDA: US dividend-paying stocks and real estate investment trusts, picked using a dynamic approach by ALPS. It is a fairly spread-out large-company fund, with NVIDIA, Alphabet and Microsoft each around 4%, and financials, technology and health care the biggest areas.
RFFC: An actively managed fund of US stocks across many sectors, run by a manager who picks stocks and uses some other tools. Large tech companies lead: Alphabet, Microsoft, Apple and NVIDIA are about 20% of it, with technology around a third overall.
RFG: US mid sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that score highest on growth measures, such as how fast their sales and earnings are rising. It is evenly spread, with no holding above about 2.5%, and leans toward industrials, health care and technology.
RFLR: Holds US small company stocks along with options designed to set a floor, limiting part of the losses over a set period. In return, gains are limited too, so it behaves differently from a plain small-cap index fund.
RFV: US mid sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that score as the cheapest on value measures. It is spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and leans toward consumer companies, financials, energy and tech.
RGEF: An actively managed portfolio of stocks from around the world, chosen by Rockefeller's managers rather than by tracking an index. Alphabet, Microsoft, AMD and Samsung are the largest positions, each between about 4% and 6%, so it is spread out but leans toward technology.
RGLO: An actively managed fund of stocks from around the world, mostly large companies, adjusting its mix with Russell's research. It is top-heavy in US tech: NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft are about 17% of it.
RGYY: A fund aiming for weekly income by selling put options on a leveraged fund that moves twice as much as Rigetti Computing each day. It is very risky, since a big drop in that stock can cause large losses, and the Treasury bills it holds are collateral.
RHRX: An actively managed fund that rotates among other ETFs to pursue growth instead of following an index. A single SPDR fund is about 47% of it, with others including a semiconductor ETF, so the mix can shift as the manager changes it.
RHTX: An actively managed mix of other ETFs, shifting between US stocks, gold, silver and cash depending on the manager's view of the market. About two-thirds of it sits in two S&P 500 ETFs, so its results depend on the manager's timing calls.
RIET: Tracks an index of 100 US-listed real estate companies chosen for their high dividend yields. It holds many REITs in small slices, with storage and net lease landlords like National Storage Affiliates, Lineage and WP Carey, and no holding above about 2%.
RIFR: Companies around the world that own or run infrastructure, such as utilities, toll roads, airports, pipelines and railroads. Utilities are about 44% of it, and the biggest holdings, like Aena and NextEra Energy, are each about 5%.
RIGS: An actively managed global bond fund that mixes government and corporate debt of various maturities, credit ratings and currencies, aiming for income. It uses derivatives too, and US Treasuries are a big share, but no single holding is more than about 7%.
RILA: An actively managed fund of US growth stocks of any size, picked by its adviser for growth potential. It leans toward tech, with Broadcom, NVIDIA and Palo Alto Networks among the biggest holdings, though no single stock is above about 5%.
RINF: A fund that aims to gain when inflation expectations rise, based on the gap in yield between regular US Treasury bonds and inflation-protected ones. It uses derivatives rather than owning bonds directly, so it is a narrow bet on one measure rather than a bond fund.
RING: Gold mining companies from developed and emerging markets, following an MSCI index. The fund tends to move with gold prices, and it is concentrated: Newmont and Agnico Eagle are about 29% of it, with Barrick and Wheaton close behind.
RINK: An actively managed bond fund that spreads across several kinds of bonds, such as government, corporate and mortgage debt. The manager shifts between those areas, so it is more flexible than a fund tracking one bond index.
RINT: A fund of stocks from developed countries outside the US, managed by Russell Investments using a mix of strategies. It is widely spread, with financials, industrials and technology the largest groups and ASML the top holding at about 3%.
RISE: An actively managed fund of stocks in emerging markets, which are developing economies, aiming at companies tied to growing consumer demand. It holds three India funds at about 5% each, and the rest is spread over many names, led by financials and materials.
RISN: An actively managed fund that uses chart-based signals to move between US large company stocks when the market trends up and safer assets like short-term Treasuries when it does not. It currently holds a sizable chunk in a short-term Treasury fund.
RISR: An actively managed bond fund focused on mortgage-related securities, seeking income while also hedging against rising interest rates. It aims to hold up better than a typical bond fund when rates rise, and the mortgage bonds it holds are mostly government-backed.
RITA: A fund of real estate investment trusts (REITs) in developed markets, screened to meet socially responsible and green criteria. It is fairly concentrated, with Welltower, Simon Property and Prologis each around 13%, and it pays income from rents.
RIZE: Mostly short-to-medium term US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, whose value adjusts with inflation. It is actively managed, and the top holdings are Treasuries of about 6% each, so it is very low in credit risk.
RJCA: An actively managed fund of US companies with strong growth in earnings, picked by a quantitative research approach. It is top-heavy in technology: NVIDIA is about 15%, and with Microsoft and Apple the top three are roughly 30%.
RJDI: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying US stocks, aiming for a higher yield than the S&P 500 and dividend growth that beats inflation. Broadcom is the largest holding at about 7%, and tech is the biggest sector.
RJMI: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds issued by states, cities and local agencies, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It holds intermediate maturities across many issuers, with no single bond more than about 2% of the fund.
RJVI: An actively managed income fund that mixes corporate bonds, preferred stocks and some regular stocks, picking among the types of a company's debt and equity wherever yield looks best. About two thirds is bonds, from well-known names like Union Pacific and Honeywell.
RKNG: An actively managed fund of stocks the manager picks to match a theme the fund calls Retail Kings, and its current holdings are mostly technology and industrial firms like Micron, Sandisk and Bloom Energy. Its top holdings are each only about 4%, so it is fairly spread out.
RKSG: A mostly US stock fund that follows a custom growth-focused index built by Ruk Indexes. It is tilted toward technology, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet making up around 22% of the fund, plus sizable health care and financial holdings.
RLY: An actively managed fund of funds spread across assets that tend to hold up when inflation rises: natural resources and infrastructure companies, commodities, and inflation-protected Treasury bonds. About half of it sits in just two ETFs, natural resources and infrastructure, so it leans toward energy and materials.
RMCA: An actively managed fund of California municipal bonds, aiming to pay income that is free from federal and California state income tax. Its holdings are spread widely, with no single bond above about 3%, and they come from local agencies, schools and housing authorities.
RMHY: A fund that holds a single other fund, an Xtrackers high yield corporate bond ETF, and adjusts its exposure based on market risk. High yield bonds come from companies with weaker credit, so they pay more income but carry more risk of loss.
RMME: A government money market fund holding cash, short-term US government securities and repurchase agreements backed by them. It is built to keep a stable value while paying interest that follows short-term rates, working like a place to park cash.
RMNY: An actively managed fund of New York municipal bonds, issued by state and local bodies like transit and power authorities. It aims to pay income exempt from federal and New York state income tax, which mainly suits New York residents.
RMOP: An actively managed fund of municipal bonds that aims for income exempt from federal tax plus some growth, and it can buy lower-rated bonds. It holds many bonds from different issuers, with the largest each around 2%.
RMRC: An actively managed fund that spreads money across ETFs for the S&P 500's sectors, such as consumer staples, utilities and health care. It can shift between them to manage risk, and it owns funds rather than individual stocks.
RND: A fund following a Bloomberg index of US companies that pour money into their own growth through research and development. Alphabet, NVIDIA, Amazon and Apple are each around 8% of it, and technology is about 46%.
RNEM: Emerging market stocks drawn from an index, with a tilt that favors more attractive companies than a plain market-size weighting would. Financials are over a third of it, and holdings include Tencent, Reliance and Anta Sports.
RNIN: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that the managers believe are priced below their worth. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward technology, consumer discretionary and energy companies.
RNMN: A market neutral fund, meant to ignore the market's direction by balancing long and short bets. Many of its top holdings are SPACs, shell companies formed to buy other businesses, each around 2% of the fund, and it is actively managed.
RNRG: Companies that generate power from renewable sources such as wind, solar and hydro, tracked through a global index. Almost all of it is utilities, spread across about a dozen or so names from Brazil, Austria, Denmark, Portugal and Israel, each around 6%.
RNTY: A portfolio of US real estate companies, such as Welltower, Prologis and Digital Realty, paired with an options strategy designed to generate extra monthly income. The options can limit gains when real estate stocks rally, and the fund is mostly property companies.
ROAM: Stocks from emerging markets chosen with a multifactor approach, meaning it favors companies with qualities like value and quality, tracked by a Hartford index. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2.5%, and leans toward tech and financials.
ROBO: Robotics and automation companies from around the world, such as factory equipment, sensors and chip makers, tracking the ROBO Global index. It holds a lot of names in roughly equal amounts, with none above about 2%.
ROBT: Companies involved in artificial intelligence and robotics around the world, chosen by a Nasdaq index and held in fairly equal amounts. Because it spreads evenly instead of by size, no holding is above about 2%, and it includes software, health tech and industrial firms.
ROBX: Companies in the robotics business, such as makers of motion-control parts and factory automation, picked by a rules-based Amplify index. It has a lot of Japanese industrial names, with Harmonic Drive and Panasonic each about 10% of the fund.
ROCQ: Large Nasdaq-listed stocks, mainly technology companies, combined with an options strategy that sells call options to generate extra income. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron are about 22% of it, and the options income comes at the cost of limiting some gains when stocks surge.
ROCY: A basket of large US stocks that also sells call options on the market to earn extra income, which is paid out regularly. Selling those options limits how much it gains in a strong rally, and NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are about 20% of it.
RODM: Large and mid-sized companies in developed countries outside the US, picked with a multifactor approach that favors cheaper, higher quality and lower volatility stocks. It is spread across many companies, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward financials, especially Canadian banks.
ROE: An actively managed fund that holds about equal amounts of high-quality US companies, picked for strong profitability and good financial health. Equal weighting means giant companies do not dominate it, though it still leans toward technology, with no single stock above roughly 2%.
ROKT: Companies tied to space and deep-sea exploration, such as satellite, aerospace and defense suppliers, tracked by the S&P Kensho Final Frontiers Index. It is evenly spread, with the top holdings each around 3% to 4%.
ROMO: Follows an index that moves among US, international and emerging market stocks depending on which are showing positive momentum compared with Treasuries. It holds iShares ETFs, and over half of it is the iShares Core S&P 500 fund.
RONB: An actively managed fund holding growth companies of any size, mostly US ones. It is very concentrated: SpaceX is about a third of the fund and Tesla is another 12% or so, so just two names drive a lot of the result.
ROPE: An actively managed stock fund, mainly US large companies, that can shift up to all of its money into cash when the managers want downside protection. The largest holdings, like Target, Exxon and ConocoPhillips, are each around 5% to 6%.
ROSC: Small US companies chosen by a multifactor index, which scores stocks on measures such as value, quality and momentum. It is spread across many small holdings, with the largest about 1%, and leans toward financials and health care.
ROUS: Large US companies picked from a broad index using several traits together, such as being cheap, profitable, and recently strong. It spreads across hundreds of stocks with none above about 2%, and leans toward technology.
RPAR: An actively managed fund that spreads money across stocks, Treasury bonds, inflation-protected bonds and commodities such as gold, aiming for each to contribute a similar amount of risk. It mostly holds other ETFs, and may use leverage, which means borrowing to increase exposure.
RPG: S&P 500 companies with the strongest growth in sales, earnings and share price, weighted by how strong that growth is rather than size. The result is a tilt toward tech and industrials, and it can move more than the broad S&P 500.
RPV: The cheapest stocks in the S&P 500, picked and weighted by how strong their value traits are, such as low prices compared with sales and earnings. It looks very different from the usual index: Centene, Archer Daniels Midland and Humana top it, and no holding is above about 3%.
RSBA: A fund that stacks two strategies in one: a bond portfolio and a merger arbitrage strategy that buys stocks of companies being acquired. Because both run on the same money, it is built to add a second source of return on top of the bonds.
RSBT: An actively managed fund that stacks two strategies: a bond portfolio plus a managed futures strategy that bets on price trends across markets like commodities and currencies. It uses leverage, so total exposure is more than the money invested.
RSBY: Stacks two strategies in one fund: a core of US bonds, and an overlay of futures aimed at earning extra yield across markets. The futures use borrowed exposure, so the fund aims for more return than its bonds alone, with added risk.
RSDE: A fund that uses options on an equal-weight S&P 500 fund to absorb part of losses over a one-year period starting in December. Equal-weight means every company counts the same, so big tech matters less, and gains are capped in return for the protection.
RSEE: An actively managed fund that holds other ETFs covering US large and small companies, developed markets outside the US, and emerging markets, shifting the mix using its own rules. It also uses a hedging approach meant to reduce losses in rough markets, so it differs from a plain stock index fund.
RSIT: A stacked fund that holds international stocks and a managed futures strategy at the same time, so each dollar gets both exposures. The futures use leverage, meaning borrowed-style exposure, so it is more complex than a plain international stock fund.
RSJN: Uses options on an equal weighted S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in June, but caps the gains. The protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
RSMC: An actively managed fund of US small and mid-sized companies, picked by a manager who looks for quality businesses. It is spread across industrials, financials and technology, and its biggest holdings are each only around 3% to 4%.
RSMR: Uses options on an equal-weighted S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts each March. In return, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if you hold the full period.
RSMV: An actively managed fund of US growth stocks that tries to limit big swings in value, partly by holding other funds alongside individual stocks. Roughly a third of it sits in other ETFs, so what you own is a mix of broad funds and a few tech names.
RSP: Holds the same roughly 500 companies as the S&P 500, but gives each about the same weight instead of weighting by size. That means the biggest companies matter far less, and no holding is much above 0.3%.
RSPA: US stocks matching the S&P 500 Equal Weight index, where each company gets a similar share, combined with an options strategy meant to generate extra income. The options give up some gains in strong markets, and a good chunk is held in cash-like funds.
RSPC: All the communication services companies in the S&P 500, held in roughly equal amounts rather than weighted by size. So smaller names like Roku and Take-Two matter as much as the giants, and each top holding is only about 5% of the fund.
RSPD: The consumer discretionary stocks of the S&P 500 (things like restaurants, travel, retailers and carmakers), with each stock given the same weight instead of weighting by size. Because of that, smaller companies matter more than in a normal index, and no holding is above about 3%.
RSPE: About 500 US companies from the S&P 500 that pass environmental, social and governance screens, each held in roughly equal amounts. Because every company counts about the same, it leans less on the biggest tech names than a regular index fund.
RSPF: The financial companies in the S&P 500, each weighted about equally instead of by size. That makes it more evenly spread across banks, insurers, payment firms and others, with no holding above about 2%, unlike a typical market-weighted financial fund.
RSPG: The energy companies in the S&P 500, held in equal amounts rather than weighted by size. That means smaller names like Valero, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 count as much as the giants, and the fund is all energy, so it moves with oil and gas.
RSPH: The health care companies in the S&P 500, with each stock given about the same weight instead of weighting by company size. That means smaller health care firms count more than in a standard health care fund, and no holding is above about 2%.
RSPM: The materials companies in the S&P 500, such as chemicals, packaging and mining, each given about the same weight. Because no stock dominates, the top holdings like International Paper and Ball are only around 4% to 5% each.
RSPN: The industrial companies of the S&P 500, with each stock given the same weight instead of being weighted by size. That means it is not top-heavy: the largest holdings are only about 1.5% each, spread across airlines, defense, machinery and more.
RSPR: The real estate companies in the S&P 500, each held in roughly equal amounts instead of by size. That makes it less dominated by the largest names, with Welltower, Ventas, CBRE and Simon Property each at about 3% to 4%.
RSPS: The consumer staples companies in the S&P 500, such as discount stores, food makers and household goods firms, each held in roughly equal amounts. Equal weighting means smaller companies count as much as the giants, so no holding is much more than 3% to 4%.
RSPT: The tech companies of the S&P 500, but each is held in roughly equal amounts instead of by size. That makes it far less top-heavy than most tech funds: the biggest holdings are only about 2% each, and smaller software and hardware firms count as much as giants.
RSPU: The utility companies in the S&P 500, such as electric, gas and water providers, each held in about the same amount rather than by size. Because it is equal-weighted, smaller names like NRG, Constellation and Vistra count as much as the giants.
RSSB: An actively managed fund that stacks stock and bond exposure on the same dollar, holding global stocks and also using futures to add US Treasury bond exposure. That means it can be exposed to more than 100% of its value, which adds risk.
RSSE: Uses options on an equal weight S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September. In return, upside is capped, and the options are nearly the whole fund.
RSSL: The Russell 2000, a broad index of about 2,000 small US companies, held in proportion to their size. It is very spread out, with no single holding above about half a percent, so it moves with the small-company part of the market.
RSST: An actively managed fund that stacks two strategies on the same money: US large-company stocks, mostly through an S&P 500 fund, plus managed futures, contracts that trade trends across markets. Using futures means total exposure goes above 100% of the fund's value.
RSSX: A fund that stacks two bets in one: about 100% in US large-company stocks, mainly through an S&P 500 ETF, and another 100% in a gold and bitcoin strategy. The stacking uses borrowed money and derivatives, so total exposure comes to about twice the fund's size.
RSSY: An actively managed fund that stacks two things on the same money: a large slice in a US stock fund tracking the S&P 500, plus a bond and futures yield strategy on top. Because of that layering, total exposure adds up to more than 100% of what is invested.
RTAI: Mostly shares of closed-end funds that hold municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, bought when they trade at a discount to their underlying value. It is a fund of funds, with about 70% in a handful of BlackRock, Neuberger and Eaton Vance muni funds.
RTH: The 25 largest US retail companies, including online sellers, grocery chains and drugstores, held in a fund tracking a MarketVector index. It is top-heavy, with Amazon at about 20% and Walmart and Costco together at about 19%.
RTHY: A fund of long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, US government bonds whose value adjusts with inflation, with maturities of 20 years or more. Because the bonds are so long, its price can swing a lot when interest rates change.
RTOO: Companies around the world in robotics and automation, such as Yaskawa, Nabtesco, Keyence and Rockwell Automation. It is a narrow industry theme, but fairly evenly spread, with no holding above roughly 4% of the fund.
RTRE: An actively managed bond fund that mixes corporate, mortgage, government and other bonds. Some of its money is held in other Rareview funds and long Treasury funds, so it is more flexible than a plain bond index fund.
RTYY: An actively managed income fund that uses options contracts tied to a leveraged fund on Riot Platforms stock, rather than owning the shares directly. It aims to pay out option income, but that strategy limits gains if the stock rises and still carries large losses if it falls.
RULE: An actively managed fund that mixes individual stocks with stock and bond ETFs, shifting the blend as its managers see fit. Right now it is heavily weighted toward technology, with Seagate, Micron and Corning among its largest holdings at roughly 5% to 6% each.
RUNN: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US companies that the manager sees as efficient at turning profits into growth. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 2.5%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
RUSC: US small companies, aiming to track the performance of smaller US stocks, with thousands of holdings spread thinly. No single stock is above about 1%, so it is very diversified, with health care, industrials and financials the biggest areas.
RVER: An actively managed fund of growth stocks that the manager believes can beat the S&P 500. It is concentrated and unusual: Hewlett Packard Enterprise, NVIDIA, EQT and ImmunityBio are about 37% of it.
RVNU: An actively managed fund of US municipal bonds that pay for public infrastructure like airports, toll roads, bridges and utilities, with interest generally exempt from federal income tax. It is spread across many issuers, with none above about 2%.
RW: An actively managed global stock fund that looks for high-quality companies of any size, mostly mid and large ones in developed markets. It is fairly concentrated, with Loar, HEICO and Diploma each near 6% to 7%.
RWEM: Emerging market stocks chosen with a systematic, data-driven approach that favors cheaper, higher-quality companies. It is top-heavy in chip makers, with TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung together about a quarter of the fund.
RWIN: Stocks of large companies in developed countries outside the US, picked using several measures at once rather than company size alone. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 3%, and financials are the biggest sector at about 27%.
RWJ: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, weighted by their sales instead of their stock market value. This puts more of the fund in big-revenue, low-margin businesses like health plans, fuel distributors and car dealers.
RWK: US mid-sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400, but weighted by how much revenue each makes rather than by stock market value. This pushes it toward big-revenue businesses like food distributors and airlines, and no single stock is more than about 4%.
RWL: The companies of the S&P 500, but weighted by their yearly revenue instead of their stock market value. Big sellers like Amazon, Walmart and UnitedHealth get the largest slices, and no company is above about 5%.
RWLC: An actively managed fund of US large companies, weighted using a method that mixes company size with other measures instead of just market value. Technology is the biggest part, with Apple and NVIDIA together about 15% of it.
RWO: Real estate companies around the world, such as apartment, warehouse, data center and retail landlords, tracking a Dow Jones global real estate index. Welltower and Prologis are about 17% of the fund together, and it pays income from rents.
RWR: US real estate investment trusts, or REITs, which are companies that own and run properties like apartments, warehouses, cell towers and shopping centers. It follows the Dow Jones Select REIT index, and Welltower and Prologis are about 20% of the fund.
RWX: Real estate companies outside the US, such as property owners and developers across Japan, Europe, Australia and more, following the Dow Jones Global ex-US Select Real Estate Securities index. It is diversified, with the largest name, Mitsui Fudosan, at about 6%.
RXI: Global consumer discretionary companies, the ones that sell things people want rather than need, such as online retail, cars and home improvement. It is top-heavy: Amazon is about 15% and Tesla about 8%, and Home Depot is next at about 5%.
RYLD: Holds the stocks of the Russell 2000 small-company index and sells one-month covered call options on it to earn extra monthly income. That income comes with a cost: gains are capped when the market rallies, while losses on the stocks are only partly cushioned.
RYLG: Holds a Russell 2000 small-company stock ETF and sells call options on part of it to generate income, while keeping some of the upside. The options bring in extra payouts but cap some gains, and small-company stocks can swing a lot.
RZG: Small US companies with the strongest growth traits, taken from the S&P SmallCap 600 Index and held in a pure growth subset of it. It is spread thin, with no holding above about 2%, and leans toward health care, industrials, financials and technology.
RZV: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that look cheapest on measures like price compared with earnings and sales, weighted toward the strongest value scores. It spreads across hundreds of holdings, with no single stock above about 2%, and leans toward consumer and industrial businesses.
SAGP: An actively managed fund of US and international stocks of companies that are active in influencing public policy, such as through lobbying. It is spread widely, with health care and industrials the biggest sectors.
SALI: A fund that gets its returns from swaps, contracts that track an index of autocallable notes, structured products that pay income and can end early. It aims for a steady income stream, but it carries stock market risk and complexity.
SAMM: An actively managed fund that picks US stocks and other assets based on a macro and momentum approach, shifting toward areas the managers see gaining strength. It can hold a mix of company shares, REITs and other funds, so it is not a plain index fund.
SAMT: An actively managed US stock fund where Strategas picks companies it thinks fit big themes in the economy and markets, such as industrial, energy and tech trends. It holds a modest number of names with the largest, like FuelCell Energy and Timken, around 3% each.
SAPH: A way to own SAP, the German software company, through its US traded shares while hedging out changes in the euro versus the dollar. It holds one company, so it rises and falls with SAP alone, minus the currency swings.
SASS: An actively managed fund holding a small group of US companies the manager thinks are undervalued. It is concentrated, with top names like Henry Schein, Primo Brands, AMETEK and Williams each about 6 or 7%.
SATO: Companies in the crypto economy, such as bitcoin miners and firms holding crypto, tracked by an Alerian Galaxy index, plus some direct bitcoin exposure through a bitcoin ETF. About 10% is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust, and it can swing sharply with crypto prices.
SAUG: Uses options tied to small US companies, through the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in August. It is built to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains.
SAWG: An actively managed fund buying large US companies the manager sees as high quality with solid growth. It is top-heavy in big tech: NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet together are about 20% of the fund.
SAWS: An actively managed fund of small US growth companies that the manager considers high quality. It spreads across health care, industrials and technology, with no holding above about 4% of the fund.
SBAR: An income fund that mostly sits in a government money market fund for interest, then adds option spreads that pay extra income as long as the market stays above a set level. The options can lose money in a sharp drop, so the income is not guaranteed.
SBB: A bet against small US companies, aiming to move opposite to the S&P SmallCap 600 Index each day. It uses derivatives and resets daily, so over longer periods the results can drift away from simply the opposite of the index.
SBIL: A government money market fund holding very short term US Treasury bills and similar government securities, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. The price stays steady and the income follows short term interest rates.
SBIO: Small and mid-sized biotech companies with drugs in later stages of testing, tracked with a Poseidon index of such firms. It holds many stocks, none above about 5%, and results depend heavily on trial outcomes and approvals.
SBND: A bond fund holding short-term US investment-grade bonds, with a large share in mortgage-backed securities, which are pools of home loans. Shorter maturities usually mean smaller price swings than longer-term bond funds, and the fund is spread across many positions.
SCA: Uses derivatives called autocallables tied to Super Micro Computer stock, which pay out and end early if the stock reaches a set level. It is built around one company's shares and is a complex income strategy.
SCAP: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen for value and income, with some preferred stock mixed in. No single stock is above about 4%, and it spreads across industrials, technology, consumer and financial companies.
SCAU: A defined-outcome fund using options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (small US companies) to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in August. The name points to a 15% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
SCCR: An actively managed core bond fund of mostly investment-grade US bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It is meant to be a broad, steady bond holding, and it is spread over a large number of bonds with no single one above about 3%.
SCDS: About 95% in small US companies, picked by JPMorgan using data science models that score each company on measures of value, quality and momentum. It is spread thin: no holding is much more than 1% of the fund, across health care, financials and technology.
SCDV: Small US companies that pay and grow dividends, picked by the manager for steady earnings. It tilts toward industrials and health care, and the largest holding, Ensign Group, is only around 7%.
SCEC: An actively managed fund of mostly investment-grade bonds, mixing US Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities and corporate bonds, with room for some lower-rated junk bonds. It is broadly spread, with the largest holdings each only a few percent of the fund.
SCEP: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US stocks that sells options to collect extra income and also buys protection against market drops. Apple, NVIDIA and Alphabet are each about 6%, and the options limit some upside in return.
SCHA: Small US companies, tracking the small-cap part of the Dow Jones U.S. Total Stock Market index. It holds well over a thousand stocks, so no single holding is large, though Sandisk is the biggest at about 5%.
SCHB: Almost the whole US stock market, around 2,500 of the largest publicly traded companies, weighted by size. Because big companies get the most weight, NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is close to 40%.
SCHC: Small companies in developed countries outside the US, tracking an international small-cap index. It holds many names in tiny slices, with none above about 0.5%, and industrials, materials and financials are the biggest groups.
SCHD: About 100 US companies with long records of paying dividends and solid finances, picked by the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index. Built around steady income, so it leans toward consumer staples, health care, energy and technology rather than the big tech giants.
SCHE: Large and mid sized companies in emerging markets such as Taiwan, China and India, tracking the FTSE Emerging Index. It leans on one company: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 17% of the fund.
SCHF: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, covering roughly the top 90% of each market. Financials, technology and industrials lead, and Samsung, SK Hynix and ASML are the biggest holdings at about 2% to 3% each.
SCHG: Large US growth stocks from the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Growth Total Stock Market Index, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 28% of it, and technology is more than half.
SCHH: US real estate investment trusts, companies that own properties such as apartments, warehouses, data centers and malls, tracking a Dow Jones index that excludes mortgage REITs. Welltower and Prologis are about 19% of it.
SCHI: Investment grade US company bonds maturing in 5 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. They pay more than Treasuries of similar length because companies are riskier borrowers, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 0.3%.
SCHJ: Investment-grade US corporate bonds that mature in one to five years, tracking a Bloomberg index. Because the maturities are short, it should be steadier than longer bond funds, and it holds a very large number of bonds, each a tiny share.
SCHK: The 1,000 largest US companies, held in proportion to their size, covering most of the US stock market by value. It is top-heavy at the top: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of the fund, and technology is around 39% of it.
SCHM: About 500 mid-sized US companies, those ranked 501 to 1,000 by size in the US market, tracking a Dow Jones index. It is spread out: no holding above about 5%, with industrials, technology and financials the largest sectors.
SCHO: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, held all in one portfolio and tracking a Bloomberg index. Backed by the government, and with such short maturities the price moves little when interest rates change.
SCHP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, across a range of maturities from one year up. It tracks a Bloomberg TIPS index, so it holds all those Treasuries and its price still moves with interest rates.
SCHQ: US Treasury bonds with 10 or more years left until they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index of them. Because the bonds are so long, its price moves a lot when interest rates change, and it holds many bonds with none above about 2%.
SCHR: US Treasury bonds with roughly 3 to 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index of them. They are backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, but prices still move up and down as interest rates change.
SCHV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their size, tracking the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Value index. It is a mix of financials, technology and health care, with Micron, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan among the biggest holdings at about 3% each.
SCHX: Large US companies from the Dow Jones U.S. Large-Cap Total Stock Market Index, weighted by size. It is much like an S&P 500 fund, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 19% together and technology near 40%.
SCHY: Stocks of higher-dividend companies from developed and emerging countries outside the US, picked by a Dow Jones index. It holds about 100 stocks, with no single one above about 5%, and is built for dividend income rather than growth.
SCHZ: The broad US investment grade bond market, including Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, tracking the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is very spread out, with no single bond above about 0.4%.
SCIN: A broad fund of investment-grade bonds issued outside the US, tracking an international bond index from Schwab. It spreads money across many governments and companies in other countries, which adds currency effects on top of interest rate moves.
SCIO: An actively managed bond fund that puts at least 80% of its money in structured credit, meaning loans and mortgages bundled into interest-paying securities. It is spread across hundreds of small positions, with no single holding above about 1.5%, and aims to pay income.
SCJ: Small Japanese companies, following the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index, which covers roughly the smallest 14% of the Japanese stock market. It spreads across industrials, consumer companies, financials and technology, and no single holding is above about 2%.
SCJL: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in July. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCJN: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in June. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCLZ: An actively managed fund of dividend-paying large and mid sized US stocks that also uses options to try to boost income. Micron, Apple and NVIDIA make up about 20% of it, and the options can limit gains when stocks rally.
SCMB: A broad basket of investment-grade municipal bonds, which are loans to US states, cities and other local governments with interest generally free of federal income tax. It holds many bonds in tiny slices, with none above about 0.2%, so no single issuer matters much.
SCMC: An actively managed fund that invests in a mix of bonds across sectors, such as corporate, government and securitized debt, aiming for income. The manager decides where to invest, so it is more flexible than a fund that follows a bond index.
SCMY: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to a US small-cap stock ETF to cushion a set amount of losses, with a stated 15% buffer, over a set period starting in May. In return, gains over that period are limited, and results depend on timing.
SCNM: An actively managed fund buying US municipal bonds of medium length, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. The manager chooses bonds from many states and issuers, so it is a flexible approach rather than a fixed index.
SCOP: A trust that holds physical copper, so its price follows the price of copper itself rather than copper mining companies. It owns the metal directly and pays no income, so what happens to it depends on swings in the copper market.
SCOW: Holds small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that have produced positive free cash flow, meaning real cash left over after expenses, for at least seven years in a row. It also favors high cash margins and returns, and is spread across technology, financials and more.
SCSB: An actively managed fund of investment-grade bonds with short maturities, which can include municipal bonds, convertible bonds and preferred stocks. Because the bonds mature soon, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than a typical bond fund, and it is meant to supply income.
SCSE: A defined-outcome fund that uses exchange-traded options on the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, which tracks small US companies to cushion the first 15% of losses over a set one-year period starting in September. In exchange, gains are limited to a cap, so it suits holding through the whole period rather than trading in and out.
SCYB: Corporate bonds from US companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because they carry more risk of default. It holds hundreds of them, so no single issuer is above about half a percent of the fund.
SCZ: Small companies in developed markets outside the US and Canada, mainly in Europe, Japan and Australia, tracking the MSCI EAFE Small Cap index. It is very spread out: even the largest holdings are only about 0.4% of the fund each.
SDCI: A broad basket of commodity futures, such as energy, metals and farm goods, picked each month by a rule-based index, with Treasury bills held as collateral for the futures. It issues a normal 1099 tax form, not a K-1.
SDCP: An actively managed fund of mostly investment-grade US bonds, with an average maturity of about one to three years, so prices move little when rates change. It holds Treasuries, mortgage and auto-loan bonds, and aims for income with low volatility.
SDEM: Tracks 50 emerging market stocks that pay some of the highest dividends, each held in equal amounts. It leans toward financials and spreads across many countries, so no one company is above about 3%, and its high yield is the main focus.
SDFI: An actively managed fund of income-producing bonds with short maturities, so its price should move less when interest rates change than longer bond funds. It holds a mix of corporate, government and securitized debt chosen by the managers.
