SDG: Global companies whose products and services help meet UN Sustainable Development Goals, like clean energy, health and nutrition, tracking an MSCI index. It is spread over many countries and sectors, with Marvell Technology at about 10% the biggest holding.
SDIV: One hundred of the highest-yielding stocks worldwide, picked for dividend yield and weighted roughly equally, with many in real estate, finance and energy. It aims at income, and the high yields can signal risky companies.
SDMF: A fund that follows an index mimicking managed futures, or trend-following strategies that bet on rising or falling prices in commodities, currencies, bonds and stock indexes. It gets this through futures contracts, with Treasury bills held as backing, so it tends to move differently from stocks.
SDOG: Fifty US large-company stocks, the highest dividend yielders in each of the market's sectors, with an equal share given to each sector and reshuffled once a year. Because it picks by yield across all sectors, it holds more of the older, steadier names than the big tech giants.
SDSI: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mixing safer investment-grade and riskier high-yield debt, plus government, mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, it is less sensitive to rate changes, and US Treasuries are about a fifth of it.
SDTY: An actively managed fund that uses a synthetic covered call strategy on the S&P 500, with options expiring the same day, to pay income weekly. Its gains are capped, and it holds mostly option contracts and Treasury bills rather than the stocks themselves.
SDUR: An actively managed fund of short-term, investment grade bonds, such as corporate debt, mortgage-related and asset-backed securities and US government bonds. Short maturities are meant to keep the price steadier than a bond fund of longer-term bonds.
SDVD: Small and mid-sized US companies with a history of raising dividends, combined with an options strategy that aims to add income. The options can limit gains when stocks surge, and the fund is spread over many stocks, each about 1%.
SDVY: Small and mid sized US companies with a record of raising their dividends, chosen by a rules-based index. Holdings are spread out, with none above about 1.3%, and it leans away from the largest companies.
SDY: About 100 US companies with the longest records of raising their dividends year after year, tracking the S&P High Yield Dividend Aristocrats index. It tilts toward utilities, consumer staples and financials, and it pays regular income.
SEA: Global shipping and freight companies: ocean tankers and container lines, air cargo and ports, following an index of them. Holdings are fairly even at around 5% each, and it moves with world trade and shipping rates.
SECA: An actively managed fund that rotates between market sectors, mostly by holding other sector ETFs plus some individual stocks. The manager shifts the mix over time, and it currently leans heavily on technology, with about 44% in tech companies.
SECR: An actively managed fund that invests mainly in securitized debt, which means pools of loans like mortgages bundled into bonds. Holdings are spread widely, with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac issues among the larger ones, each only about 2% of the fund.
SECT: An actively managed fund of funds that holds other sector ETFs, shifting money between sectors like technology, financials and industrials as its managers see fit. Because it picks sectors rather than tracking an index, it can look quite different from the overall market, with about half in tech.
SECU: An actively managed bond fund focused on securitized debt, meaning bundles of loans like mortgages, car loans and credit card debt that are packaged and sold as bonds. The manager chooses which types to hold, and it may use derivatives to adjust exposure.
SEEM: An actively managed fund buying stocks in emerging market countries, with managers choosing holdings instead of tracking an index. Taiwan Semiconductor is about 11% and Samsung about 7%, so a few large technology names carry a good share of it.
SEF: A fund that aims to deliver the opposite of the daily return of US financial stocks in the S&P 500, so it tends to rise when they fall. It resets daily, so over longer periods the results can drift well away from the simple reverse.
SEIE: An actively managed fund of stocks from outside the US, across companies of all sizes in at least three other countries, with at least 40% of assets held abroad. It is widely spread, with HSBC, Murata Manufacturing and ASML among the larger holdings at only about 2% each.
SEIM: Large US companies with strong recent price momentum, meaning stocks that have been rising, picked by SEI using a rules-based approach. It is tilted toward technology at about 44%, and Alphabet and NVIDIA are the biggest holdings at around 6% to 7% each.
SEIQ: Large US companies that score well on quality traits like strong profits and steady finances, chosen by an actively run, rules-guided process. Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 20% of it, so it leans toward big technology.
SEIS: Stocks of small US companies, similar in size to those in the Russell 2000 Index, with at least 80% of the fund held in them. It is widely spread, with the biggest holdings, such as Bloom Energy and Enova, each only around 1% to 1.5% of the fund.
SEIV: Large US companies that look cheap and are picked by SEI using a rules-based approach that favors value traits like low prices compared with earnings. It still has sizable tech holdings, led by NVIDIA, Micron and Apple, which are each about 3%, so it is spread out.
SEIX: Senior loans, which are loans to companies with below-investment-grade credit that are paid back before other debts and carry floating interest rates that move with market rates. It holds many loans, with each one around 1%.
SELV: US large company stocks screened to be less jumpy than the market, using a model that favors steadier shares. Holdings are spread out, with Cardinal Health and Johnson & Johnson each around 3%, and it leans toward tech, health care and consumer staples.
SEMG: An actively managed fund of high quality US growth companies. It is top-heavy: Alphabet, NVIDIA and Microsoft together make up about 30% of the fund, and technology is the largest sector at around 45%.
SEMI: An actively managed fund that puts at least 80% of its money in chip makers, chip equipment makers and related technology companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Broadcom and Apple are about 30% of the fund.
SEMY: An income fund that sells options on a leveraged semiconductor ETF to produce high payouts, with Treasury bills backing the contracts. Because it sits on a leveraged fund and options cap the gains, results can swing a lot and depend on semiconductors.
SEPC: A defined-outcome fund using options on a fund tracking the S&P 500 to aim for a set amount of protection against losses, with a cap on gains, over a one-year period starting in September. The name points to a 10% buffer, which applies only if held the full period.
SEPI: An actively managed fund of large US stocks that also sells call options to earn extra income, which tends to cap how much it gains when stocks surge. Technology is about 38% of it, and the top holdings are AMD, Caterpillar and Micron at roughly 7% each.
SEPM: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September. In return, upside is capped, so it works best when held for the full period, and the options are nearly the whole fund.
SEPP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in September. In return, gains are capped, so it behaves differently from a plain S&P 500 fund, and the outcome only applies when held for the full period.
SEPQ: An actively managed fund holding large Nasdaq stocks while using options to lower risk and earn some income. NVIDIA, Apple and Micron are about 20% of the fund, and nearly 60% is technology.
SEPT: A defined-outcome fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a set period starting in September. It aims to cushion the first 10% of losses, in exchange for a cap on gains, and works as intended only if held for the whole period.
SEPU: Uses options on the S&P 500 to follow it over a one-year period starting each September, with a set amount of losses absorbed first. Its name says buffer 15 and uncapped, so gains are not limited by a cap, though a fee reduces the upside.
SEPW: A fund that uses customized options on an S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each September. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only fully applies if you hold through the whole period.
SEPZ: An actively managed fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in September. It is meant to give part of the market's gains while cushioning some losses, so results depend on when you buy within that period.
SEQ: An actively managed fund holding a small number of companies the manager thinks are undervalued and can grow, from around the world. It is concentrated: Rolls-Royce, Alphabet, Formula One owner Liberty Media and Universal Music are about 35% of it.
SETH: An inverse fund that aims to move opposite to the price of ether, the second largest cryptocurrency, on a daily basis. It rises when ether falls and falls when ether rises, and because it resets each day, it is a short-term trading tool rather than a long-term hold.
SETM: Holds companies mining or processing materials needed for the energy transition, such as copper, uranium, lithium and rare earths. It is spread across miners like Freeport-McMoRan, Kazatomprom, Lynas and Cameco at about 5% each, so it follows commodity-linked stocks.
SEUS: An actively managed fund of US stocks of all sizes, chosen using factors such as value, quality and momentum rather than just company size. Even so, it looks a lot like the market: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 15% of it and technology is over a third.
SFEB: Uses options tied to small US companies, through the iShares Russell 2000 ETF, to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in February. It is built to absorb a set amount of losses in exchange for a cap on gains.
SFGV: A global stock fund that mostly buys other ETFs, covering developed markets, emerging markets, small companies and real estate, with a tilt toward cheaper-looking value stocks. It is a fund of funds, so about 10% each sits in a Vanguard developed markets ETF and an iShares fund.
SFLO: Small US companies that produce a lot of free cash flow, meaning cash left over after running and investing in the business, chosen and weighted by a Victory index. It spreads money across many names with none above about 2%, so it is not top-heavy.
SFLR: An actively managed fund holding large US stocks alongside options meant to limit how much it can lose over a set period. That protection comes with a cost, since the options also cap some gains; the stocks come from the Solactive US 500 index, led by NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft.
SFTX: An actively managed fund of large stocks outside the US that adds a risk-control layer, which can hedge with futures to cut losses in falling markets. Taiwan Semiconductor, ASML and Samsung are among the top holdings, and the hedge may reduce gains in rallies.
SFTY: An actively managed fund that mostly owns large US stocks, including the Magnificent Seven, and adds a risk-control layer that can hedge with futures to cut losses when markets fall. NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are each around 6%, and the hedge may reduce gains in rallies.
SFY: 500 large US-listed companies weighted by a mix of size and company fundamentals, instead of size alone. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA is about 15% of it, and technology is about half of the fund.
SFYF: Fifty US stocks that are the most widely held in self-directed brokerage accounts at SoFi, a snapshot of what individual investors own. It is concentrated: Tesla and NVIDIA are about 17% of the fund, and technology is roughly 40% of it.
SFYI: Holds stocks popular with retail investors, chosen from social media and trading activity, and sells options on them to produce income. Tesla, Amazon and NVIDIA are about 25% of it, and the options limit how much it gains in strong rallies.
SGDJ: Smaller, "junior" gold mining companies, mostly in the US, Canada and Australia, tracked through an index of their shares. It is a narrow, volatile corner of the market, with no single miner above roughly 6% and every holding in the materials sector.
SGDM: Gold mining companies in the US and Canada, tracked by a Sprott index that favors stronger growth and cash flow. Agnico Eagle, Barrick, Newmont and Wheaton Precious Metals are about 30% of the fund, and prices can swing with gold.
SGLC: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen by a quantitative model, so it can differ from the S&P 500. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 20% of the fund, and technology is about 40%.
SGOL: A fund that holds actual gold bars stored in vaults, so its price follows the price of gold. It owns no stocks or bonds and pays no income, so its value rises and falls with gold alone.
SGOV: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
SGRT: An actively managed fund of large US companies picked for strong earnings growth. It is concentrated and tilted to tech hardware: Vertiv, Western Digital and Micron are roughly 31% of it, with Energy and health care names making up the rest.
SGRW: An actively managed fund of US small companies that its manager thinks can grow faster than average, mostly in technology, health care and industrials. It is spread widely: no single holding is more than about 4% of it.
SGVT: A money market fund holding short-term US government debt, like Treasury bills and agency securities, to keep the price steady while paying interest. The income moves with short-term interest rates, and it is meant as a place to hold cash.
SHAG: Short-term US bonds, including Treasuries, mortgage-backed bonds and corporate debt, following an index of those bonds with a tilt to boost yield. Because the bonds mature soon, the fund's price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds.
SHDG: A fund that mostly holds a big S&P 500 index fund and adds an options overlay meant to soften market drops. That hedge means it may fall less in a downturn, but it can also lag when stocks rise.
SHE: US large company stocks that the index picks for having more women in leadership and on their boards. It is tech heavy, with Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Intel and NVIDIA making up about 18% of the fund.
SHEH: A fund tied to a single stock, Shell, the big energy company, with currency moves hedged so the US dollar value follows the share price more closely. Almost all of it, about 96%, is that one company, so it moves with one oil and gas giant.
SHLD: Companies involved in defense technology, such as aircraft, missiles, cybersecurity and military software, from the US and abroad. It is fairly concentrated, with Lockheed Martin, RTX, General Dynamics and Palantir each about 7 to 8%, and Rheinmetall at about 6%.
SHM: Short-term bonds from US states and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, following an ICE index. Short maturities keep price swings small, and no single bond is above about 1%.
SHOC: US semiconductor companies, such as chip designers, memory makers and equipment suppliers, following a Strive index of the sector. It is concentrated: NVIDIA, Micron and Broadcom make up about 40% of the fund.
SHPP: Tracks an index of global industrial and logistics companies, including railroads, engineering firms and software. SAP, ABB and Union Pacific are about 28% of the fund, and it holds both US and foreign stocks.
SHRD: A bond fund tracking an index of US investment-grade bonds screened to follow Catholic values, so some issuers are excluded. Treasuries make up a big share of the top holdings, so it behaves much like a core bond fund focused on steady income.
SHRT: An actively managed fund that both buys stocks it likes and bets against stocks it expects to fall, a strategy called long/short. It is built to hold up better than the market when stocks drop, and no single position is more than a small slice.
SHRY: Follows a Bloomberg index of large and mid-sized US companies that return cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. It is spread out, with no holding above about 5%, and leans toward value-style companies like MetLife and Fox.
SHUS: Holds large US stocks weighted by a method that tries to avoid piling too much into any one business area, then uses index options to hedge against market losses. The options can limit gains in strong markets.
SHV: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in under a year, so it works like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves, and the income follows short-term interest rates.
SHY: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they mature, tracking an index of those government bonds. Because the maturities are short, its price moves much less than longer bond funds when interest rates change.
SHYD: A fund of high-yield municipal bonds with shorter maturities, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. These bonds carry more credit risk than ordinary municipal bonds, and holdings include Puerto Rico and California issuers.
SHYG: Short-term US corporate bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (called high yield or junk bonds), limited to those maturing within about five years. They pay higher interest than safer bonds, but the borrowers are more likely to struggle, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
SHYL: Short-term, lower-rated corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, that mature within a few years. Shorter maturities mean less sensitivity to interest rates than a regular high-yield fund, though the bonds still carry real credit risk, and no issuer is above about 1%.
SHYM: An actively managed fund of high yield municipal bonds with short maturities. These are bonds from state and local governments that pay higher interest because they are riskier, and the short length helps limit swings from interest rates.
SIFI: An actively managed fund of bonds from many sectors, mainly corporate debt, including higher-risk issuers, selected with a rules-based computer approach. It uses derivatives such as credit default swaps and Treasury futures to manage risk, and is spread across lots of small positions.
SIHY: An actively managed fund of high yield corporate bonds, sometimes called junk bonds, which pay more interest because the companies carry more risk. A systematic, rules-based approach picks them, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
SIL: Companies that mine silver, tracked by a Global X index, so it moves with silver prices and mining costs rather than holding silver itself. It is concentrated: Wheaton Precious Metals, Pan American Silver and Coeur Mining make up almost half of the fund.
SILJ: Smaller silver mining companies, following an index of firms mainly focused on silver. It is concentrated: Hecla, Coeur and First Majestic are about 31% of the fund, so it swings with silver prices.
SIMS: About 100 US-listed companies worldwide that build and run smart infrastructure, such as clean power, smart grids, water systems and automation, following the S&P Kensho Intelligent Structures Index. It is spread thinly, with no holding above roughly 3% of the fund, and leans toward industrial and tech names.
SIO: An actively managed bond fund that mixes many types of income-producing debt, including US Treasuries, corporate bonds and other higher-yielding bonds, to aim for steady income. It spreads across several kinds of bonds instead of following one index, so its risk depends on the manager's choices.
SIOO: An actively managed fund holding large US stocks from the S&P 100 and selling options on them to earn extra income, with a target of paying out about 15% a year. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 25% of it, and the options can limit gains when stocks surge.
SIVR: Physically owned bars of silver held in a vault, so the share price follows the price of silver. It holds no stocks or bonds, pays no income, and moves up and down with the silver market.
SIXA: Holds the largest US companies, the top 10% of the Russell 3000 by size, chosen with a focus on firms with strong financial health. It leans toward steady payers, with Altria, Philip Morris, Verizon and AT&T each about 4% to 5% of it.
SIXD: Uses stock-index options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion the first 10% of losses over a six-month period that resets each June and December. In exchange, gains over that period are capped, and the protection only works if shares are held for the full period.
SIXF: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to follow large US companies over a six month period starting in February and August. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for limiting gains, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
SIXH: A fund of US stocks, mostly in steady, dividend-paying areas like tobacco, telecom and health care, combined with options meant to cushion losses when the market falls. The hedge costs some upside, and Altria, Philip Morris and Verizon are each about 4 to 5% of it.
SIXJ: A defined outcome fund using S&P 500 options over a set six-month period starting in January or July. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses, and in return gains are capped.
SIXL: Mid-sized US stocks picked for being less jumpy than the overall market, meaning a low beta, so it favors steadier areas like financials, consumer staples, utilities and health care. It is spread thinly, with no holding above about 1% of the fund.
SIXO: A defined outcome fund that uses options tied to the S&P 500 to give a set amount of protection against losses over a six month period, in exchange for a cap on gains. It resets twice a year, April and October, and the protection applies only over the full period.
SIXP: A fund that uses options on the S&P 500 to follow large US companies over a six month period starting in March and September. It aims to cushion a set amount of losses in exchange for limiting gains, and the protection only fully applies if held for the whole period.
SIXS: An actively managed fund of small US companies, similar in size to those in the S&P SmallCap 600. It tilts toward lower-priced value stocks, spread across real estate, health care, energy and financials, with no holding above about 2%.
SIXZ: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to cushion a set amount of losses over six months, from November to May and May to November. In return, the gains it can capture are capped, so it is designed to be held for the full period.
SIZE: US stocks from the MSCI USA index weighted to tilt toward smaller companies, so it holds a broad mix of large and mid-sized firms with more weight on the smaller ones. No single stock is more than a sliver of the fund, so it is very spread out.
SJB: Aims to go up when US high yield corporate bonds fall, delivering roughly the opposite of their daily return. It resets every day, so over longer periods results can drift away from the opposite of the bond market.
SJCP: An actively managed bond fund holding mostly investment-grade US corporate and government bonds, plus some preferred stocks, which pay fixed dividends. US Treasuries are about a third of the fund, so it is aimed at steady income.
SJLD: An actively managed fund of short-term, high-quality debt, aiming to keep its average sensitivity to interest rates low. It mixes Treasury bills with corporate debt and preferred shares, so it is a bit riskier than a plain Treasury fund.
SJNK: Bonds from companies with weaker credit ratings (so they pay higher interest), limited to ones that mature in about one to five years. The short timeline reduces sensitivity to interest rate swings, and holdings are very spread out, with none above about 1% of the fund.
SKOR: US dollar corporate bonds of medium length from investment grade companies, chosen by an index that scores credit strength and value. It holds many bonds from big names like Salesforce and Broadcom, and none is more than about 1% of the fund.
SKYY: US and global companies in cloud computing, such as providers of data storage, networking and software delivered over the internet. It is spread fairly evenly, with no single holding above about 4%, so it is less dominated by the biggest tech names.
SLDR: A ladder of US Treasury bonds with short maturities, tracking an index that spreads money evenly across different end dates. As each bond matures, the money is reinvested, so the fund stays short-term and is less sensitive to interest rate changes.
SLJY: Holds shares of junior silver mining companies, mostly through another Amplify silver miners ETF, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. The options cap gains when silver miners surge, while the miners can still fall sharply.
SLNZ: An actively managed fund buying senior secured loans, which are floating-rate loans to companies that get paid back first if a borrower runs into trouble. The interest rates reset as short-term rates move, so income changes with interest rates.
SLQD: Investment-grade US corporate bonds with 0 to 5 years left until they mature, tracking an index of bonds from financially solid companies. Spread across many companies, none above about 0.2%, and the short maturities mean its price moves less than longer-term bond funds.
SLV: Physical silver held in a vault, so the fund's price follows the price of silver. It holds no companies and pays no income, and silver tends to swing in price more than gold because it is also used in industry.
SLVI: A fund tied to the price of silver that also aims to pay high monthly income, using options on silver investments to earn extra cash. Selling those options gives up some of silver's gains in strong rallies, so it trades some upside for income.
SLVO: An exchange-traded note that follows a covered call strategy on the iShares Silver Trust, meaning it tracks silver while collecting option income. That income is paid out regularly, but it caps gains if silver rises sharply, and as a note it also carries the issuer's credit risk.
SLVP: Companies that mine silver and other metals around the world, tracked by an MSCI index of silver and metals miners. It is concentrated in a few miners, with Hecla, Penoles, Fresnillo and First Majestic about 44% of it, and these stocks swing with metal prices.
SLVR: A mix of silver mining company stocks and a holding of physical silver through a Sprott trust. About 80% is in miners such as First Majestic and Wheaton Precious Metals, so it moves with silver prices and with mining company results.
SLVX: Silver mining companies, a silver trust, and options on silver stocks, aimed at producing income. About 15% of the fund is a physical silver fund and the rest is miners like First Majestic, SSR Mining and Silvercorp, and selling options caps some of the upside.
SLVY: Aims to follow the price of silver while also paying income, using options on silver-related investments. Selling options for income caps how much of silver's rise it can capture, and it holds no physical silver bars itself.
SLWS: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds from many sectors and countries, including corporate debt and securities backed by loans. Because the bonds are short, prices move less than in a typical bond fund, and it is spread across many small holdings.
SLX: Companies in the steel industry worldwide, from iron ore miners to steel producers, tracking a VanEck index. It is concentrated in a few names, with BHP, Vale and Rio Tinto about 23% together, so it follows a cyclical corner of materials.
SLYG: Smaller US companies picked from the S&P 600 index because they show faster growth traits, like rising sales and earnings. It holds hundreds of stocks and no single one is much above 1% of the fund, so it is very spread out.
SLYV: Smaller US companies from the S&P 600 index that look cheap compared to their earnings and assets, the 'value' end of small caps. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is much above 1%, so it is spread out across many industries.
SMAX: Holds an iShares S&P 500 fund and options to cushion a larger amount of losses over a one-year period starting in September. The tradeoff is a cap on gains, so a strong market will not be fully captured.
SMAY: Uses options on a small-company stock fund (the iShares Russell 2000 ETF) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each May. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
SMB: Short term, tax exempt municipal bonds issued by US states, cities and agencies, tracked through a VanEck index. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the shorter maturities mean the price moves less than longer muni funds.
SMBS: A broad basket of US mortgage-backed bonds, which are pools of home loans guaranteed by government-linked agencies such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. It tracks an index of investment-grade ones, and it is spread across thousands of pieces, so no single holding matters much.
SMCO: An actively managed fund of 50 to 75 small and mid-sized US companies that the manager sees as solid and fairly priced. It spreads across industrials, tech, health care and financials, with no holding above about 3%.
SMCP: An actively managed fund of mid-sized companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. It is a concentrated mix of miners, energy and drug companies, with the largest few holdings each around 6% to 8% of the fund.
SMCY: Aims to pay high income from Super Micro Computer stock by selling call options on it, rather than holding the shares. That caps the gains if the stock climbs but leaves much of the downside, and the Treasury bills are collateral.
SMDV: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that have raised their dividends every year for at least 15 years, following a ProShares index. It holds around 100 stocks in similar amounts, so no single holding is above about 2%.
SMDX: Holds small and mid sized US companies drawn from the S&P Small-Mid Cap index, with the weights adjusted by a math-based method meant to beat the index a little. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings only around 1% each.
SMH: A concentrated group of the largest semiconductor companies listed on US exchanges, including foreign chipmakers held through depositary receipts. NVIDIA and Taiwan Semiconductor alone are about 27% of the fund, so it rides on a single industry.
SMHC: Tracks an index of the largest and most traded Chinese semiconductor companies, around 25 stocks. It is concentrated and all technology: Cambricon, Hygon and Eoptolink are each roughly 7% to 9% of the fund.
SMHX: Fabless semiconductor companies, meaning chip designers that have others manufacture their chips, tracked by the VanEck Fabless Semiconductor index. It is concentrated: NVIDIA and Broadcom make up about a third of it.
SMIG: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies that pay and grow dividends. It aims for steady income plus growth, and the top holdings, like Silicon Motion, Targa Resources and Snap-on, are each about 5% to 7% of it.
SMIN: Small-sized Indian companies, tracking an MSCI index of them. It is spread across many stocks with none above about 2%, covering industrials, consumer companies, financials and health care in a single emerging market.
SMIZ: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies picked with Zacks research that ranks stocks by earnings outlook. It holds many companies in small slices, with none above about 2%, and tilts toward technology, industrials and financials.
SMLF: Small US companies picked and weighted by an index that favors four traits: recent price momentum, high quality, cheap prices and low volatility. It holds hundreds of stocks and none is much above 1%, so it is very spread out.
SMLL: An actively managed fund of smaller US companies chosen by the managers rather than an index. Holdings are fairly spread out, with Pool Corp, Morningstar, WillScot and Wintrust each around 4% to 5%, and industrials and financials are the largest sectors.
SMLV: Small US companies with lower price swings, picked from the Russell 2000 for being less volatile than the group as a whole. It holds many small positions of about 0.6% each and leans toward financials, industrials, technology and real estate.
SMMD: US small and medium sized companies, covering roughly the 2,500 smallest stocks in the Russell 3000 index, weighted by company size. Holdings are spread very thinly across many industries, with individual stocks well under 1% each.
SMMU: Actively managed short-term municipal bonds whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, with maturities of a few years or less. Because the bonds are short, it carries less interest-rate risk than longer municipal funds, and it is spread over many issuers.
SMMV: Small US companies chosen and weighted to have lower price swings than the overall small-company market. It leans toward steadier areas like real estate, utilities, health care and insurance, with no holding above about 2%.
SMNG: A fund holding stocks of companies in the Samsung group, the large South Korean conglomerate, which spans electronics, finance, shipbuilding and more. It is concentrated in one corporate family and one country, so it depends on a small group of related businesses.
SMOG: Holds companies tied to low carbon energy, such as clean power producers, electric vehicle makers and fuel cell firms, from around the world. Tesla, Iberdrola and Bloom Energy are each about 8% of it, so a few names have a big influence.
SMOM: An actively managed fund of funds that holds sector ETFs from the S&P 500, shifting toward the sectors with the strongest recent momentum. This means it can be heavily tilted, with technology and energy funds being about half now.
SMOT: Small and mid-sized US companies that Morningstar judges to have lasting competitive advantages, sometimes called moats, and that look reasonably priced. Holdings are spread out, with the largest, like Acuity and Bio-Techne, only about 2% each.
SMOX: An actively managed fund of small and mid-size US companies, which also can include real estate trusts. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings, like Twilio, TD Synnex and Okta, each only about 1 to 2%.
SMRF: Holds companies tied to nuclear energy, including uranium miners and nuclear power producers around the world, plus small modular reactor developers. It is a narrow theme, with uranium names like NexGen and Uranium Energy among the top holdings.
SMRI: An actively managed fund holding US mid-size companies that the managers think are priced below their worth. Technology and health care are the largest sectors, and the top holdings like Tenet Healthcare, Workday and Accenture are each around 2 to 3%.
SMRZ: A fund holding companies involved in small modular reactors, compact nuclear power plants built in factories, including those that build them, supply fuel or provide parts. It is narrow and non-diversified, so a few companies can drive its results.
SMTH: An actively managed core bond fund that puts at least 80% in bonds, including government, company and convertible bonds. US Treasuries are among its largest holdings, and the manager can move between bond types.
SMTJ: An actively managed fund of Japanese stocks, chosen to benefit from long-term shifts in society and industry. It is fairly concentrated: big banks like Mitsubishi UFJ, plus Hitachi and Sony, lead the list, and industrials and financials are about half the fund.
SMYY: An income fund tied to Super Micro Computer stock that uses options and swaps instead of owning the shares directly, aiming to pay large distributions. Most of the money sits in Treasury bills as backing, and the strategy limits how much it can gain if the stock rises.
SNAV: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs, mainly an equal weight S&P 500 fund and sector funds such as technology and health care. The manager shifts between them, so it is a US stock mix that can change over time.
SNOV: Uses options on a small-company stock fund (the iShares Russell 2000 ETF) to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period that starts each November. In return, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
SNOY: A fund that gives income and partial exposure to Snowflake's stock price using options, rather than owning the shares. Its option strategy caps how much it gains if Snowflake rises, while losses can still be large, and most assets are held in Treasury bills.
SNPD: US companies from the S&P High Yield Dividend Aristocrats, which have raised their dividends for decades, screened for certain environmental and other concerns. It leans toward consumer staples, industrials and utilities, with each holding only about 2 to 3%.
SNPE: US large companies that follow the S&P 500's industry mix but screen out or hold less of firms that score poorly on environmental, social and governance (ESG) measures. It is still top-heavy: NVIDIA and Microsoft alone are about 21% of the fund.
SNPG: US large companies from the S&P 500 that show strong growth, screened and scored on environmental, social and governance measures and weighted by company size. It is top-heavy: Micron, Microsoft and NVIDIA are each about 8% of it, and technology is nearly half the fund.
SNSR: Companies tied to the Internet of Things, meaning everyday devices connected to the web, including chip makers and sensor and medical device firms. Technology is about 80% of it, with STMicroelectronics the largest holding at roughly 9%.
SNTH: An actively managed fund that uses options and Treasury bonds to mimic stock market returns without holding stocks directly. Most of the fund sits in US Treasuries, with options supplying the stock exposure, so it behaves like a stock fund built from different parts.
SNTQ: An actively managed fund that mixes options with Treasuries to get Nasdaq-100 type returns in a different way than owning the stocks. It is a defined outcome style fund, so its results can differ noticeably from the index in both directions.
SOCL: Social media and online networking companies from around the world, tracked by a Global X index. It is concentrated in a few big names: Tencent, Naver and Meta are each about 9% to 10% of the fund, and nearly all of it is communication companies.
SOEZ: A fund that aims to follow the price of Solana, a cryptocurrency, by holding it directly rather than owning company shares. Its value can swing sharply, and it behaves like a single crypto asset rather than a diversified basket.
SOFR: An actively managed fund that aims to match the SOFR rate, the short-term interest rate set by the New York Fed that banks use for overnight loans. It keeps its money in very short-term cash-like holdings, so its income follows short-term rates.
SOLC: Holds actual Solana (SOL), a cryptocurrency, in a trust, so its price follows the price of the coin. A portion of the coins may be staked through Marinade to earn extra rewards, and the value can swing sharply, as with other crypto.
SOLM: Aims to follow Solana's price while selling monthly options on Solana funds to bring in extra income. It holds a Solana staking fund and cash like holdings, and the options limit gains if Solana jumps.
SOLZ: A fund giving exposure to Solana (SOL), a digital currency that runs on its own computer network. It invests in SOL-linked instruments rather than only holding the coin, so its price follows Solana, which can swing sharply, and part of the fund sits in cash.
SOVF: An actively managed fund of US companies, mostly small and mid sized, picked by its adviser. It leans toward tech and financials, and no single stock is much above 4%, with names like Molina, Paycom and Repay at the top.
SOXQ: Tracks the PHLX Semiconductor index of the 30 largest US-listed chip companies, from designers to equipment makers. It is concentrated: Micron, NVIDIA, Broadcom, AMD and Intel are about 42% of the fund.
SOXX: Roughly 30 of the biggest US-listed semiconductor companies, the chip designers and makers, following the PHLX Semiconductor index. It is a narrow, single industry bet: Micron, AMD, NVIDIA, Intel and Broadcom are each roughly 6% to 9%, together about 36% of it.
SOXY: Holds semiconductor stocks such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and ASML, and sells options on them to generate income. Those options cap how much it can gain when chip stocks rise, so it trades some upside for monthly payouts.
SOYB: Gets exposure to soybean prices by holding futures contracts on soybeans, rather than the beans themselves. Its value follows soybean futures, which can move sharply with weather and crop news, and the fund also holds cash to back its contracts.
SPAB: A broad basket of US investment grade bonds, mainly US Treasuries, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds, following the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. It is the kind of core bond fund meant to give steady income, and no single bond is more than about 1% of it.
SPAM: Companies in the cybersecurity industry, such as Palo Alto Networks, Okta and CrowdStrike, following a Themes index. It is concentrated in tech, and each of the top holdings is around 6% of the fund.
SPAQ: An actively managed fund of SPACs, shell companies that raise money in a stock market listing so they can buy a business later. It aims to beat what bank CDs pay, and holds many SPACs, each around 4% to 5% of the fund.
SPBC: Mostly a fund tracking the S&P 500, about 90% of it, plus a smaller slice, around 8%, in a Bitcoin ETF. It is actively managed, so it gives large US stocks with a modest dose of Bitcoin exposure added on top.
SPBO: A broad basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds, meaning bonds from financially solid companies, tracking an index of that market. It is highly spread out, with no single bond above about 0.3%, and banks are among the larger issuers.
SPBU: A fund of twelve other buffer funds that stagger their one-year periods across the calendar, each aimed at cushioning part of the losses on the S&P 500. It has no cap on gains, so each period's upside is not limited, though the protection costs a fee.
SPBW: A mix of one-year buffered funds that follow the S&P 500, each cushioning a set amount of losses while capping gains. The funds start at different times of year, so protection is staggered rather than all resetting at once.
SPBX: A mix of six-month buffered funds that follow the S&P 500 and cushion a set amount of losses at the end of each period. In exchange, each caps how much of the market's gain you can capture, and the funds are staggered across the year.
SPCI: A fund giving exposure to space industry companies using stocks, call options and synthetic positions, and earning extra income with a put spread, a paired options trade. The options strategy trades away some upside in exchange for that income.
SPCK: Special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs), empty shell companies that raise money to buy a business later, plus companies that recently went public. Because SPACs are mostly cash waiting for a deal, its holdings are small, with none above about 5%.
SPCT: Large US companies with a strong record of raising their dividends, picked by the managers rather than an index. It is spread widely, with the top names such as Apple, Amazon, Caterpillar and Eli Lilly each around 3% of the fund.
SPD: Holds the S&P 500 through an iShares ETF, about 95% of the fund, and adds put options that pay off if the market drops sharply. The options cost money to carry, which can drag on gains in calmer markets.
SPDF: An actively managed fund that holds US large company stocks, mostly through a single S&P 500 index fund. A rules based risk overlay can move the fund toward cash when markets look weak, so it differs from simply owning the index.
SPDG: US dividend-paying large companies, weighted so that no sector gets far bigger than the others, tracking an S&P index. Even so, tech is the largest sector at about 40%, with Cisco, Verizon, IBM and Texas Instruments among the biggest holdings.
SPDV: Tracks an index of S&P 500 companies with high dividend yields and dividends that look sustainable, weighted equally instead of by size. It spreads across many sectors, with the largest holdings at only about 2% to 3% each.
SPDW: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as Japan, the UK, Canada and Europe, weighted by company size. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings, Samsung, SK Hynix and ASML, about 8% together, and financials the largest sector.
SPEM: Large and mid-sized companies from emerging markets such as China, Taiwan, India and Brazil, weighted by company size. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 15% of the fund, and technology and financials together make up around half of it.
SPEU: A broad mix of large and mid-sized companies across developed European countries, tracking an index with a sampling approach. ASML is the largest holding at about 5%, and it leans toward financials, industrials and health care.
SPFF: Preferred shares, which are stock-like securities that pay a fixed dividend, selected to follow a Global X preferred stock index. It is built for income, and the holdings are a mix of companies from many industries instead of just banks.
SPGM: A low-cost index fund of stocks from around the world, covering both developed and emerging countries, tracking an MSCI index. It is mostly US-weighted and tech-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 10% of the fund.
SPGP: S&P 500 companies picked for a mix of growth and fair pricing (growth at a reasonable price), using earnings growth, valuation and quality. It is evenly spread: no holding is above about 2%, and financials and tech lead the mix.
SPHB: The 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have been the most sensitive to market swings, so it tends to rise and fall by more than the market. It leans on tech, chips and trading firms like Micron and Robinhood, with none above about 2%.
SPHD: Holds the 50 stocks in the S&P 500 with the highest dividend yields and the lowest recent price swings. It leans toward real estate, utilities, consumer staples and similar areas, with Verizon, Altria and Healthpeak among the largest holdings.
SPHQ: The 100 stocks in the S&P 500 with the highest quality scores, based on measures like profitability, earnings stability and low debt. It is concentrated, with Mastercard, Visa and Apple together making up about 17% of the fund.
SPHY: High yield bonds from companies with lower credit ratings, often called junk bonds, tracking a Bloomberg index. They pay more interest because the chance of default is higher, and the fund is very spread out, with no holding above about 0.4%.
SPIB: Investment grade bonds from US companies maturing in roughly 1 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. It pays more than Treasuries because companies are riskier borrowers, and it is spread across many issuers with none above about 0.5%.
SPIN: Holds large US companies, then adds a strategy to earn extra income from selling options on them. NVIDIA, Alphabet, Microsoft and Apple are about 27% of it, and the option income can limit how much it gains in strong markets.
SPIP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), government bonds whose principal rises with inflation, across a range of maturities. It tracks a broad TIPS index, so it holds many separate bonds, and all of them are backed by the US government.
SPIT: An actively managed fund buying US companies in special situations, such as ones going through restructurings or other major changes. It leans toward mid and small sized companies, spread across technology, health care and industrials, with no one holding above about 5%.
SPLB: Long-term US investment-grade corporate bonds, those maturing in more than ten years, from a broad index of large companies. Long maturities make the price quite sensitive to interest rates, and no single bond is more than about half a percent.
SPLS: A fund that holds S&P 500 stock exposure and adds an actively managed bond portfolio on top, using funds, futures and swaps to do both at once. It gives stock market returns plus a bond manager's attempt to earn extra, so it differs from a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPLV: The 100 stocks from the S&P 500 that have swung the least in price over the past year, so it is built to be steadier than the market. It leans toward utilities, financials and real estate, and no stock is more than about 1.3%.
SPMB: Mortgage-backed bonds from agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which pool home loans and pass the payments to investors. These are backed by government-linked agencies, and the fund holds thousands of these bonds, none more than about 1%.
SPMD: Mid-sized US companies, tracking the S&P MidCap 400 index and holding its stocks in the same proportions. It sits between large and small companies, and no single holding is more than about 1% of the fund.
SPMO: About 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have been rising the fastest over the past year, so it follows recent winners. It is concentrated and changes often: Micron, NVIDIA and Broadcom make up about 27% of the fund.
SPPP: A trust that holds physical platinum and palladium bars in storage, so its price follows those two metals. They are used heavily in car exhaust systems, and the fund owns the metal itself and pays no income.
SPRE: Holds real estate investment trusts (REITs) from around the world that pass a Sharia (Islamic law) screen, tracking an S&P index. It is concentrated, with Goodman Group, Prologis, Equinix and Welltower each around 12% of the fund.
SPRX: An actively managed fund of technology companies that the manager thinks benefit from big shifts like AI, cloud and chips, with nearly 90% in tech. It is concentrated: Astera Labs, KLA, Coherent and Arm are about 35% of the fund.
SPSB: Investment grade bonds from US companies maturing in 1 to 3 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. The short maturities mean smaller price swings, and holdings are spread widely, with none above about 0.6%.
SPSK: Sukuk, which are Islamic finance certificates that work like bonds but are structured to follow Islamic law, tracked by the Dow Jones Global Sukuk index. Many are issued by Saudi Arabia and similar governments and companies, all in US dollars.
SPSM: About 600 small US companies that are profitable, from the S&P SmallCap 600 index, which requires positive earnings to be included. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and financials, technology and industrials are the biggest sectors.
SPTB: US Treasury bonds with intermediate maturities, from a broad Treasury index, held by sampling the index instead of buying every bond. It spreads across hundreds of government bonds, with no single bond near 1%.
SPTE: Large global technology companies that pass Shariah screens, which exclude businesses and finances that conflict with Islamic investing rules. It is very concentrated: NVIDIA, Apple and Taiwan Semiconductor are each about 11%, and Microsoft adds about 9%.
SPTI: US Treasuries with roughly 3 to 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index. They are backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, though prices still move with interest rates.
SPTL: US Treasury bonds with more than 10 years left before they mature, tracking a Bloomberg index. The long maturities make its price swing more with interest rates than shorter Treasury funds, while credit risk is minimal.
SPTM: The whole US stock market in one fund: large, mid and small companies from the S&P 1500 index, weighted by size. Because big companies weigh most, NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 17% of it.
SPTS: US Treasury notes and bonds that mature in one to three years, so it is a government bond fund with low sensitivity to interest rates. It holds many separate Treasury issues, each only about 1 or 2% of the fund, and income follows short-term rates.
SPUC: Holds an S&P 500 index fund and adds an options strategy that aims to give more of the market's gains on strong rises while also paying income. Nearly all of it is the underlying S&P 500 fund, so tech giants drive most of its movement.
SPUS: Holds S&P 500 companies that pass Sharia (Islamic) screens, which exclude sectors like defense, financial exchanges and data processing, plus companies that fail financial tests. It ends up very tech-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 34% of the fund.
SPUT: An actively managed income fund that sells put options on a broad US stock index to collect payments, alongside holding stocks. It aims for steady income while still keeping some growth, though selling puts means it can lose money in sharp market drops.
SPVM: 100 stocks from the S&P 500 that rank high on both value (looking cheap) and momentum (recently rising). It leans toward financials, energy and utilities, with Allstate, General Motors and United Airlines each about 2%.
SPWO: Companies outside the US, in developed and emerging markets, that pass screens for following Islamic (Shariah) rules, following the S&P Shariah World ex-US index. It is top-heavy with Taiwan Semiconductor at about 20%, and technology makes up over half of it.
SPXD: The S&P 500 reweighted so sectors are more balanced and no single giant dominates. Compared with a plain S&P 500 fund, it holds less of the biggest tech names and more of areas like health care and consumer staples.
SPXE: The S&P 500 with every energy company removed, so it holds the other US large companies in similar proportions to the index. It is top heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 20% of the fund.
SPXN: The S&P 500 without its financial companies such as banks and insurers, held in index proportions. Technology dominates: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund, so it works as a US large-company fund that skips the financial sector.
SPXP: A fund that follows an index which pairs exposure to the S&P 500 with extra investments in other assets, hence the "plus" in its name. It can use derivatives, and it is non-diversified, so it can behave differently from a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPXT: The S&P 500 without its information technology companies, so it holds the other large US companies in the index in the same proportions. With tech removed, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla become the biggest holdings, and financials, communication and health care carry more weight.
SPXV: The S&P 500 with the health care companies taken out, so it holds the other large US companies in similar proportions to the index. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together make up about 22% of the fund.
SPY: The first ETF, launched in 1993, and the classic way to own the S&P 500: about 500 of the biggest US companies, weighted by size. It's the most traded fund in the world, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 18% of it.
SPYA: A fund in the equity hedged category, meaning it generally holds stocks alongside a hedge meant to soften market drops. It is a careful middle ground between owning the stock market outright and staying out of it.
SPYC: Mostly an S&P 500 index fund, with a small side of options bought to try to gain more when stocks fall sharply. The options are meant to add a cushion in bad markets, but they cost money, so in calm or rising markets it can trail a plain S&P 500 fund.
SPYD: The 80 highest dividend-yielding stocks in the S&P 500, weighted by how much they pay out, so it is built for income. It leans toward real estate, consumer staples, financials and utilities, and each stock is only about 1 or 2% of the fund.
SPYG: The faster-growing companies within the S&P 500, picked by their growth traits and weighted by size. It is heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Microsoft and Apple together are about 27% of it, and technology is over half the fund.
SPYH: S&P 500 stocks combined with an options collar: sold call options bring in income, while bought put options protect against drops. This limits both big losses and big gains, and the top holdings NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it.
SPYI: Holds the stocks of the S&P 500 and sells call options on them to produce extra income. The options cap how much it can gain when the market surges, and as an actively managed fund it is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 18% of it.
SPYM: Another way to own the S&P 500: about 500 large US companies, weighted by size. It holds the same stocks as other S&P 500 funds, so about 40% is technology, with NVIDIA and Apple the biggest names.
SPYT: Holds an S&P 500 index fund and sells daily call spreads on the index, an options strategy that earns extra income. That income is paid out as distributions, but the options limit how much the fund gains when the market jumps.
SPYV: The cheaper-looking half of the S&P 500, large US companies that score as value stocks on measures like price relative to earnings and book value. Despite the value label, Apple is about 7% of it and technology is the largest sector.
SPYX: The S&P 500 with companies that own fossil fuel reserves such as coal, oil and gas removed, so it otherwise tracks the big US companies in the usual way. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 19% of the fund.
SQBA: A fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a three-month period, in exchange for a cap on gains. The protection resets every quarter, and the 15 in the name refers to the buffer level.
SQBR: A fund using options on US stocks to protect against losses over a set quarterly period, as long as the market does not fall past a barrier level. In return, gains are capped, and the protection can end if the barrier is breached.
SQLT: A fund tracking US small company stocks screened for quality, meaning high profitability, steady earnings and low debt. It is spread across technology, industrials, health care and financials, with no stock above about 1%, so no single company dominates.
SQLV: Small US companies that an actively run quantitative model rates as both high quality and reasonably priced. It spreads money across many tiny positions, each around 1% or less, and trades often, so the mix changes frequently.
SQMX: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow large US stocks while protecting against a larger part of losses over a set period that resets each quarter. In return, gains are capped, and protection only fully applies if you hold the whole period.
SQS: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked for high quality, meaning strong finances and steady profits. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple and Amazon are about 30% of it, so it behaves a lot like a big-tech-heavy market fund.
SRET: Real estate investment trusts, or REITs, that pay high dividends, picked from around the world by a Global X index. Holdings are equally spread across many names, none above about 5%, and it focuses on yield.
SRHQ: A fund of US companies with steady, moderate revenue growth that are not priced too richly, following an index built on that growth-at-a-reasonable-price idea. It spreads across many mid-sized stocks, with no holding above about 2% and the most weight in technology, health care and industrials.
SRHR: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) listed in the US, with the fund selling covered call options on them to earn extra income. That income comes at the cost of capping some of the upside, and Lamar Advertising is the largest holding at about 10%.
SRLN: Senior loans, which are loans banks make to companies with lower credit ratings, first in line for repayment and with interest rates that float with short-term rates. It is actively managed and aims to beat a leveraged loan index.
SROI: An actively managed global stock fund that picks companies using sustainability criteria rather than following an index. It still ends up top-heavy in big tech: Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 18% of it.
SRVR: Real estate companies tied to data and infrastructure, such as data centers, cell towers and storage. Digital Realty, Equinix and American Tower alone are about 48% of the fund, so a few companies drive most of the result.
SSCP: An actively managed fund of small companies listed on US exchanges, including some based abroad. Its top holdings are a mix of aerospace, aluminum, food and firearms makers, each about 5% to 7%, so a few names matter a lot.
SSFI: A fund of funds that holds other bond ETFs, moving among bond types like emerging market, high yield and Treasury bonds depending on the manager's view. Its top four holdings are each about 19% of it, so it is made of only a few funds.
SSK: A fund giving exposure to the Solana cryptocurrency, held partly directly and partly through other crypto products, with staking, where coins are locked up to earn rewards. Solana is about half of it, so it moves with the price of one crypto asset.
SSMG: An actively managed fund buying small and mid-sized US growth companies, mostly in technology, industrials and health care. It is well spread out, with the biggest holdings, such as Sterling Infrastructure and TechnipFMC, each only around 3%.
SSPY: Tracks an index of large US companies that are weighted by a mix of company fundamentals rather than by size alone, created by Syntax. It is spread very evenly, with no holding above about 1%, so it looks quite different from a standard S&P 500 fund.
SSS: About three quarters of this fund is in the S&P 500, the 500 largest US companies, and about a quarter is in Solana, a cryptocurrency, held directly and through another fund. It mixes a broad stock index with a risky crypto bet.
SSUS: An actively managed fund that holds the Select Sector SPDR ETFs, one for each part of the US market, and shifts the mix based on a strategy meant to favor stronger sectors. It is currently tilted to technology, with that sector fund about 36% of it.
SSXU: An actively managed fund of funds that holds international stock ETFs, aiming to beat the MSCI ACWI ex USA Index by owning more or less of certain countries. Japan, the UK, China and South Korea ETFs are the biggest holdings.
STAX: Short-term US municipal bonds, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed and spread across many issuers, such as cities, states and hospitals, with no single bond above about 2.5%.
STBF: An actively managed fund of short term bonds that can include both investment grade and lower rated ones. Because the bonds mature soon, it is less sensitive to interest rate changes, and it is spread widely with no holding above about 3%.
STBQ: Holds companies involved in the technology behind stablecoins, which are digital coins pegged to the dollar, tracked by a rules-based index. It also holds some crypto funds such as Chainlink, Solana and Ethereum, so it is a niche and volatile mix.
STCE: Stocks of companies tied to crypto, such as bitcoin miners and digital asset firms, tracking a Schwab index that uses language analysis of company filings to find them. It holds no cryptocurrency itself, and the top holdings like Bitdeer, Hive and Core Scientific are about 6% to 8% each.
STEN: A defined-outcome fund that holds options tied to the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF over a set period starting in September. It aims to cushion the first 10% of S&P 500 losses, in exchange for a cap on gains, and works best when held for the full period.
STHH: A single stock fund holding American depositary receipts of STMicroelectronics, the European chip maker, with a currency swap meant to hedge the euro against the dollar. It is a bet on one company's shares.
STIP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) maturing in five years or less. TIPS have a principal that rises with inflation, and the short maturities mean the price moves less when interest rates change than longer inflation-protected bonds.
STLR: Gives exposure to XLM, the digital coin of the Stellar network, through futures contracts traded on a regulated US exchange rather than holding the coin directly. It is actively managed and tied to a single, volatile crypto asset.
STNC: An actively managed fund of US stocks selected for strong finances and sustainable business practices. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 4%, and has a mix of technology, health care and consumer companies.
STOT: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mixing US Treasuries with mortgage-backed and other bonds, run by DoubleLine. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, the price swings less than for longer-term bond funds, and it pays regular income.
STOX: An actively managed fund that mostly holds big US stocks, plus some other ETFs, and blends in some exposure to the biggest tech names. NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet are each about 6%, and a Roundhill Magnificent Seven fund is another big slice.
STPZ: Holds US Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) with 1 to 5 years left, following an ICE BofA index. TIPS raise their principal when inflation rises, and with the shorter maturities the fund's price is less sensitive to interest rates.
STRN: An actively managed fund of large US companies chosen using a trend-following approach, which favors stocks that have been rising. It holds only a small number of stocks, with Eli Lilly, Vertiv, Welltower and Howmet each near 7%, so it is fairly concentrated.
STXD: Large and mid-sized US growth companies that also have a record of paying and growing dividends, tracking a Strive index. It holds a mix of tech, financials, industrials and health care, with Eli Lilly, Broadcom, JPMorgan and Microsoft each around 4% to 6%.
STXE: Large and mid-size companies from 24 emerging markets, leaving out China. It is concentrated in technology and in Asia: Taiwan Semiconductor, Samsung and SK hynix together are about 40% of the fund.
STXF: Large US companies, tracking the Bloomberg 500 index, so it looks much like the broad US market. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 18% of the fund and technology around 40%.
STXG: A fund of large US growth stocks from the Strive 1000 index, which covers the biggest 1,000 US companies. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 23% of it, and technology is nearly half.
STXK: US small-company stocks, following a Strive index of small caps. It is very widely spread, with every top holding around 0.5%, and technology, financials and industrials are the biggest areas.
STXT: An actively managed bond fund holding bonds of varying maturities, including mortgage bonds from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, Treasuries and some Strategy Inc preferred shares. It is aimed at a mix of income and price gains, and the top holdings are each only a few percent.
STXV: About 1,000 large US companies that look cheap compared with their size, such as banks, health care and energy firms, following a Strive value index. It is spread widely, with no single stock above about 3% of the fund.
STYL: An actively managed fund of consumer lifestyle brands, covering apparel, footwear, accessories, outdoor gear and specialty retail. Ferrari and Nike are each about 8% of it, and nearly all of the fund is in consumer discretionary companies.
SUB: Short-term municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, tracking an ICE index. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the short maturities mean its price moves less than longer muni funds, with no single issuer above about 0.4%.
SUIS: A trust that holds SUI, the digital token of the Sui blockchain, and tracks its price. It also stakes the coins, meaning they are used to help run the network, which may earn extra rewards, and it carries the large price swings of crypto.
SUPP: An actively managed fund of companies that help move and make goods around the world, such as chip makers and industrial firms, in the US and abroad. Taiwan Semiconductor, NVIDIA, Carpenter Technology and Eaton are each about 6% to 8%.
SURE: An actively managed fund that picks from the 3,000 largest US companies, with a focus on company insider activity, as the name suggests. It leans toward technology at about a quarter of the fund, and positions are small, with the biggest around 2% each.
SURI: An actively managed fund that puts its money into a small number of biotech, pharmaceutical and healthcare companies, plus some energy holdings. It is concentrated in a few names, and it also uses Treasury bills and other instruments alongside the stocks.
SUSA: Large US companies from the MSCI USA index, reweighted to favor those with better environmental, social and governance scores while staying close to the overall market. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 19% of it, similar to a regular large company index.
SUSB: US dollar investment-grade corporate bonds maturing in one to five years, tracking a Bloomberg index that screens companies using ESG (environmental, social and governance) ratings from MSCI. Short maturities mean its price is less sensitive to rate changes, and it spreads across hundreds of issuers, none above 1%.
SUSC: Investment-grade US corporate bonds from companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, tracking an ESG-aware corporate bond index. It is spread across hundreds of issuers, with no single bond more than about 0.3% of the fund.
SUSL: Large US companies with strong environmental, social and governance ratings, based on an MSCI index that keeps sector weights close to the broad US market. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA and Microsoft alone are roughly 25% of the fund, and tech is about 40%.
SVAL: A fund tracking the Russell 2000 Focused Value Select Index, which picks cheaper small US companies and weights them equally. Because of equal weighting, no holding is above about 1%, so it is spread evenly across many small firms.
SVOL: Earns income by selling insurance-like options on VIX futures, which track expected stock market swings, while holding Treasuries as collateral. It does well when markets are calm but can lose a lot in sudden sell-offs, so it is a risky income strategy.
SVTN: US Treasury bonds with between seven and ten years left until they mature, following a FTSE index. It sits in the middle of the bond maturity range, so its price moves moderately when interest rates change.
SWAN: A fund that mostly holds US Treasury securities, with a smaller part in long-dated call options on the S&P 500 for stock market gains. The Treasuries aim to protect the money while the options give some upside.
SWP: An actively managed fund of US income-paying stocks that also show strong growth traits, picked by the adviser. It tilts toward technology, with Microsoft, Broadcom, Apple and Oracle each about 4 to 6%.
SXQG: An actively managed fund of large US companies that the manager sees as high quality and growing. It leans toward tech and health care: Alphabet, Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft are about 23% of the fund.
SYFI: An actively managed fund of corporate bonds from lower-rated (junk) companies that mature in a relatively short time. The shorter timeline is meant to make its price swing less than a regular high yield bond fund, and it holds hundreds of bonds, none more than about 1%.
SYLD: An actively managed fund of US stocks with high shareholder yield, meaning companies that return cash through dividends, share buybacks and paying down debt. It is spread evenly across many mid-sized stocks, with none above about 1.5%.
SYSB: A bond fund that follows a BlackRock index mixing US Treasuries, mortgage-backed securities, and investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds, with weights set by a rules-based model. Treasuries make up many of the top holdings, and the model shifts the mix between bond types over time.
SYZ: An actively managed fund of small US companies chosen by Lazard using a systematic, rules-based process. It is very spread out, with no holding above 1%, which is much less top-heavy than most funds.
TABD: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade and some lower-rated bonds, including mortgage-backed securities, aiming for income plus some price growth. A manager picks the bonds rather than following an index, and no single holding is more than about 3% of it.
TACK: An actively managed fund that holds sector ETFs, such as energy, health care, materials and consumer staples, and shifts between them based on a model of which sectors are doing best. It can also move into bonds when markets look weak, so its mix changes over time.
TACN: An actively managed fund of large companies from developed countries outside the US, such as ASML, HSBC, AstraZeneca and Roche. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 3%, and the manager picks stocks rather than copying an index.
TACU: An actively managed fund of US stocks that mixes research with computer models, aiming to beat the broad US market. It resembles the market, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft about 17% of it and technology near 40%.
TAFI: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds from US states, cities and agencies, mainly paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. It holds many small positions, none above about 1.5%, and keeps maturities short to limit how much prices move when interest rates change.
TAFL: A national mix of long-term municipal bonds from US states, cities and public agencies, with interest that is mostly exempt from federal income tax. It is actively managed with an eye on taxes, and holds many bonds, none above about 3%.
TAFM: Mostly intermediate-term municipal bonds, issued by US states, cities and agencies, whose interest is generally free from federal income tax. Managers aim to keep tax costs low, and the fund is spread across many issuers, with none above about 1%.
TAGG: An actively managed fund of US investment-grade bonds, mostly Treasuries, that aims to beat the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index, the standard measure of the US bond market. It uses a quantitative approach to pick bonds and pays income from interest.
TAGS: Holds four Teucrium funds, each tracking futures contracts on one crop: soybeans, sugar, wheat and corn, in roughly equal amounts. It follows farm commodity prices rather than company stocks, and futures can behave differently from the day to day price of the crops themselves.
TAIL: A hedging fund that holds mostly US Treasuries and buys put options on the S&P 500, which pay off when the stock market falls sharply. Over time it tends to lose a little in calm markets, since the puts cost money to hold.
TALV: An actively managed fund of large US companies the managers think are undervalued. It is broadly spread across financials, tech and health care, with Amazon, JPMorgan and Apple the largest holdings at about 4% to 5% each.
TAN: Companies in the solar energy business, from panel makers to inverter and project companies, tracked by the MAC Global Solar Energy Index. It is a narrow theme, and First Solar, Nextpower and Enphase make up about 30% of it.
TAOZ: An actively managed fund of US-linked companies that the managers believe are good businesses selling below their worth. It holds a modest number of stocks, with Alphabet, Apple, Eli Lilly and Coherent each around 4% to 5%.
TAPR: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to protect against a set amount of losses over a two-year period ending in April 2027. In exchange, it gives up some gains, and the protection only applies if you hold through the whole period.
TAX: An actively managed fund of US mid and large companies that picks value stocks with lower dividends, to keep taxable income down. It is spread across many holdings, none above about 2%, and leans toward health care, technology and industrials.
TAXE: An actively managed fund of investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by US states, cities and agencies, with income that is generally free from federal income tax. It holds many bonds with intermediate maturities, and each is roughly 2% or less of the fund.
TAXF: A diversified mix of US municipal bonds of intermediate length, issued by state and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. It holds many hundreds of bonds, so no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
TAXI: Investment-grade municipal bonds from across the US with maturities under 15 years, following an ICE index. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the fund is very spread out, with each bond only about 0.2% of the total.
TAXM: A fund of investment-grade bonds chosen to give Massachusetts residents income that is generally free of federal and state income tax. It is actively managed, so it picks bonds rather than following an index, and almost all of it is in bonds.
TAXS: Short-term bonds issued by US states and local governments, whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. It follows an ICE index of investment-grade municipal bonds maturing in under five years, spread across hundreds of issuers.
TAXT: Investment-grade municipal bonds, issued by US states and local governments, following an ICE index. The interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the fund is very spread out, with no single bond above about 1%.
TAXX: An actively managed fund of short-term municipal and taxable bonds, aiming to produce income that is mostly tax-aware while keeping interest rate sensitivity low. It holds many bonds from different issuers, each around 1% or 2%, such as transit, gas and housing authorities.
TBFC: An actively managed fund of other ETFs, mixing stocks and bonds across the world. It shifts the blend using two in-house strategies and leans toward bonds, with top holdings being Vanguard, Xtrackers and iShares bond funds, which fits its conservative label.
TBFG: An actively managed fund of funds that spreads money across other ETFs holding US and global stocks and some bonds. It adjusts the mix over time, and the largest holdings are broad S&P 500 and growth funds, each under about 12% of the total.
TBG: An actively managed fund of US companies that its manager thinks can raise their dividends over time, across small, mid and large sizes. It is fairly spread out, with Blackstone, Merck, Verizon and Chevron each around 4%, and leans toward value stocks.
TBIL: A single three-month US Treasury bill, swapped for a fresh one each month, so it acts like a place to park cash that earns interest. Because the bill is so short and backed by the US government, the price barely moves while income follows short-term rates.
TBJL: Uses options on a long-term US Treasury bond ETF to cushion part of its losses over a one-year period starting in July, while capping gains. The protection works only if the fund is held for the full period, and long-term bonds can swing a lot.
TBLL: Very short-term US Treasury bills, tracking an index of government debt that matures in a year or less. The price barely moves because the bills are so short, and the income follows short-term interest rates, so it works like a place to park cash.
