UXAP: An actively managed fund using options on the SPDR S&P 500 fund over a one-year period starting in April. It aims to give extra gains if the market rises with no cap, but you are exposed to losses if it falls, since its protection is limited.
UXJA: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to try to deliver a multiple of the index's gains over a set one-year period that starts each January. It has no cap on those gains, but it also gives up some protection, so you can lose money if the market falls.
UXJL: A fund that uses options on an S&P 500 ETF to follow the US stock market over a one-year period, with some boosted exposure to gains and no cap on them. It also uses options to cushion a set amount of losses, and the outcomes only apply over the full period.
UXOC: Uses FLEX options, customizable exchange traded options, on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to seek boosted gains with no upper limit over a set period that starts each October. Results are designed for those who hold the full period, and losses are still possible.
VABS: A bond fund that mostly holds asset-backed securities and mortgage-backed securities, which are bundles of loans like car loans, mortgages and business debt that pay out as borrowers repay. It is actively managed and spread across many small positions, none above about 3%.
VAIC: Uses contracts that follow an NYSE index of 500 US stocks to pay regular income, with a payoff that can end early if the index reaches a set level (an autocallable). It does not hold the stocks directly, and losses are possible if the index falls.
VAIE: An actively managed income fund that gets its exposure through autocallable contracts tied to a US 500 stock index, which pay income and can end early if the index reaches set levels. It does not simply own the stocks, so it behaves differently from a plain index fund.
VALQ: US large and mid sized companies picked for looking cheaply priced while also showing quality and steady income. It is well spread across tech, health care and consumer firms, with no single holding above about 4%.
VAMO: An actively managed fund of US stocks picked for being cheap and having strong price momentum, with the option to hedge part of its holdings. A lot of the portfolio sits in cash, and energy refiners like PBF Energy and Valero show up among the larger holdings.
VAVX: A fund that directly holds AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain, and tracks its price. It holds no stocks or bonds, and because crypto prices swing sharply, its value can change a lot in short periods.
VAW: US materials companies of all sizes, such as chemicals, mining, metals and building materials firms, following a Vanguard-run index. It is top heavy: Linde is about 15% of the fund and Newmont and Freeport-McMoRan add roughly 14% more.
VB: Small US companies, tracked by the CRSP US Small Cap Index and weighted by size. It holds a very large number of names, the biggest only about 0.5%, so it is widely spread across technology, industrials and health care.
VBCA: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2027, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCB: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2028, so the fund is designed to wind down around that date. It holds hundreds of bonds, with large banks and companies like CVS each under 1% of the fund.
VBCC: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2029, tracking a Bloomberg index. As bonds mature, the fund winds down, so it behaves more like one bond with a set end date, and it is spread across hundreds of issuers.
VBCD: Investment grade US corporate bonds that mature in 2030, held until the fund ends. It holds many bonds, with T-Mobile the biggest at about 1%, so it behaves more like one bond than a fund that keeps rolling.
VBCE: A basket of investment grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2031, so the fund is designed to wind down around then. It is spread across many companies, such as Amazon, Goldman Sachs and Oracle, each around 1% of the fund.
VBCF: US investment grade corporate bonds that mature in 2032, tracked by an index. It is very spread out, with big banks like Bank of America and JPMorgan each only about 1% of the fund, and it winds down once the bonds mature.
VBCG: A basket of investment-grade US corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, tracking a target-maturity index. As the bonds near maturity, it winds down, so it pays interest and returns the bond principal around that year; large banks like Wells Fargo and Bank of America are among the issuers.
VBCH: A basket of US corporate bonds that all mature around 2034, tracking a Vanguard target maturity index. Because the bonds end near the same date, it behaves a bit like a single bond, with large banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America among the borrowers.
VBCI: A basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds that mature in 2035, from companies like Meta, Morgan Stanley and Broadcom. Each bond is a tiny slice of the fund, and it is designed to wind down around its target year rather than run forever.
VBCJ: Holds US investment-grade corporate bonds that mature around 2036, tracking a Bloomberg index of such bonds. The fund shuts down at that time and pays back its holders, and it is spread across many companies, none above about 2%.
VBIL: Very short-term US Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, tracking a Bloomberg index. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, with a price that barely moves and income that follows short-term rates.
VBK: Small US companies with growth traits, following a Morningstar index and weighted by size. It holds hundreds of stocks with none above about 1.3%, leaning toward technology, health care and industrials, and small companies tend to swing more than large ones.
VBNB: A fund that holds BNB, the digital coin tied to the Binance crypto ecosystem, directly, rather than owning stocks or futures. Its price follows the market price of BNB, which can swing sharply, and it pays no income.
VBND: An actively managed bond fund aiming for income and some price growth, holding mostly US Treasuries and other bonds picked by the managers. Treasuries make up the largest positions, with the top four around 20% of the fund combined.
VBR: Small US companies that look cheaply priced, known as value stocks, tracking the CRSP US Small Cap Value Index. It is very spread out, with no holding above 1%, and leans toward financials, industrials and consumer companies.
VCEB: US investment-grade corporate bonds from companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, with maturities over one year. It is very spread out across many issuers, with no single bond above about half a percent of the fund.
VCHY: Tracks an index of US dollar corporate bonds rated below investment grade, often called junk bonds, from many different companies. No single issuer is more than a fraction of a percent of the fund, so default risk is spread very thin.
VCIT: Investment-grade corporate bonds from US and foreign companies, maturing in 5 to 10 years, tracking a Bloomberg index. It pays more interest than Treasuries because companies carry more risk, and holdings are spread out, none above about 0.3%.
VCLN: A fund of clean energy companies, such as solar, fuel cell and wind businesses, picked by the managers. It is concentrated, with First Solar, Bloom Energy and China Yangtze Power each making up about 7 to 8% of the fund.
VCLT: US investment grade corporate bonds that mature in more than 10 years, from a Bloomberg index. Long bonds pay more income but their prices move a lot when interest rates change, and the fund is spread across hundreds of companies.
VCOB: An actively managed US bond fund holding government, corporate and mortgage-backed bonds, aiming for income plus some price growth. It is broadly spread across hundreds of bonds, with Treasuries the largest piece at under 10%.
VCR: US consumer discretionary companies of all sizes, meaning businesses that sell things people want but don't strictly need, like online shopping, cars, restaurants and home improvement. Amazon and Tesla alone are about 42% of the fund, so two stocks drive much of it.
VCRB: A broad mix of US investment-grade bonds, including Treasuries, corporate bonds and mortgage-backed bonds, chosen by a Vanguard team rather than a fixed index. It is very spread out, with the biggest holding only about 1%, and works as a core bond holding.
VCRM: An actively managed fund of US municipal bonds, loans to states, cities and agencies whose interest is exempt from federal income tax and the alternative minimum tax. It spreads across many issuers, none above about 1%, and uses a core mix of higher-quality bonds.
VCSH: Investment grade US company bonds that mature in one to five years, following a Bloomberg index. Because the bonds are short, the price moves less than with longer bonds, and it holds thousands of issues so no single borrower is more than a tiny share.
VDC: US consumer staples companies, the makers and sellers of everyday items like food, drinks and household goods, tracked by a Vanguard index. It is top-heavy: Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola are about 45% of it.
VDE: US energy companies of all sizes, mostly oil and gas producers and pipeline firms, tracking an index of the energy sector. It is very top-heavy: ExxonMobil and Chevron together are over a third of the fund.
VDG: Large and mid-sized growth companies in developed markets outside the US, tracked by a Vanguard-chosen index. It spans Europe, Japan, Canada and others, and SK Hynix, ASML and Samsung are the largest holdings at about 13% combined.
VDI: Dividend-paying stocks from outside the US, picked by a rules-based process aimed at income. Financials are over 40% of it, and holdings such as ASML, HSBC and Roche are each only around 2% to 3%.
VDIG: An actively managed fund of US companies that pay dividends and are expected to raise them over time, run by the Wellington team. It holds large companies in tech, finance and health care, with Broadcom, Eli Lilly and Microsoft together around 17% of the fund.
VDV: Tracks developed stock markets outside the US, but only the companies that look cheap compared to their size and earnings. It holds names like Samsung, Nestle, Shell and BHP, and leans toward financials, industrials and energy rather than growth stocks.
VEA: Stocks from developed countries outside the US, such as those in Europe, Japan and Australia, across large, mid-sized and small companies. It follows the FTSE Developed All Cap ex US Index, and financials, industrials and technology are the biggest sectors.
VEEM: A fund of emerging-market stocks picked from the MSCI Emerging Markets Index for positive analyst sentiment, meaning analysts are leaning favorable on them. It is concentrated in chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 17%, and technology is nearly half the fund.
VEFA: A fund of developed-market stocks outside the US and Canada, picked from the MSCI EAFE Index for positive analyst sentiment, meaning analysts are leaning favorable on them. It is fairly broad, with ASML the largest holding at about 5% and financials the biggest sector.
VEGA: An actively managed fund of other ETFs covering global stocks and bonds, which sells call options to earn extra income. Selling those options limits the upside in strong markets, and about 40% sits in one big US stock fund.
VEGI: Companies across the agriculture chain, such as tractor makers, seed and fertilizer firms and crop processors. It is top-heavy: Deere is about 26% of the fund, and Corteva and Archer Daniels Midland add around 17%.
VEGN: Follows an index built from about 500 of the largest US companies, screened to leave out businesses tied to animal products and fossil fuels. It leans heavily into technology, which is around two thirds of the fund, led by Micron, Apple, AMD and Broadcom.
VEGX: International companies outside the US selected by an index screening for vegan-friendly and climate-conscious practices. It ends up heavy in technology and industrials, with ASML, Shopify and Advantest among the largest holdings, each about 3% to 5%.
VEM: Dividend-paying companies from emerging markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, picked by an active manager. It is top-heavy in tech, with Taiwan Semiconductor alone about 16% and Samsung and SK Hynix adding roughly another 16%.
VEMY: An actively managed fund of high yield bonds, often called junk bonds, issued by governments and companies in emerging market countries. They pay higher interest because the issuers are riskier, and the fund is spread thinly, with each top holding only about 1% to 2%.
VETZ: Mostly holds mortgage-backed bonds guaranteed by US government agencies such as Ginnie Mae, which pool home loans and pass the payments on to bondholders. It is actively managed with a veteran-focused mission, and no single bond is more than about 6% of it.
VEU: Stocks from large and mid-sized companies outside the US, across both developed and emerging markets, tracking the FTSE All-World ex US Index. Financials and technology are the biggest sectors, and Taiwan Semiconductor is the top holding at about 4%.
VEXC: Large and mid-sized companies in emerging markets with China left out, tracking an index of about 1,000 stocks. It is top-heavy in one name: Taiwan Semiconductor is around 22% of the fund, with Taiwan, India and other markets making up most of the rest.
VFH: US financial companies of all sizes, such as banks, insurers, payment firms and asset managers. It is top-heavy: JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway, Mastercard and Bank of America are about 26% of the fund.
VFLO: About 50 US companies picked for strong free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and investing in it, using a rules-based index. Holdings are spread out, with the largest around 3% each and a mix of energy, software and travel names.
VFMF: US stocks, mainly mid-sized and value-leaning, chosen by a computer model that looks for strong recent performance, solid fundamentals and low prices. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 1.2%, and tilts toward financials, tech and health care.
VFMO: A broad mix of US stocks of all sizes that have recently had strong price gains, chosen by a rules-based momentum screen. Because the winners change over time, it holds many companies and leans toward technology, industrials and health care, with no single holding above about 1.5%.
VFMV: US stocks selected to move less than the overall market, using a model that looks at how volatile each stock is. It spreads across many companies, with Qualcomm, Cisco, Microsoft and Apple each around 2%, and has a tilt toward technology and health care.
VFQY: US stocks from companies with strong profits and financial health, picked by Vanguard's quant team using quality measures. It spans companies of many sizes, and no holding is over about 2%, with tech names like Fortinet, Apple and Adobe near the top.
VFVA: US stocks that look cheap compared to measures like earnings and company assets, picked by a rules-based Vanguard approach. It holds several hundred companies in nearly equal slices, none above about 1%, and leans toward financials, health care and consumer companies.
VGHY: An actively managed fund of high yield corporate bonds, often called junk bonds, which pay higher interest because the companies borrowing are riskier. It holds many bonds, with none above about 1%, plus a small amount of Treasuries.
VGIT: US Treasury bonds that mature in about three to ten years, following a Bloomberg index. It is backed by the US government, so credit risk is minimal, but its price still moves when interest rates change, more than short-term Treasuries.
VGK: Stocks of companies across developed European countries, large, mid-sized and small, weighted by size, following a FTSE index. It holds names like ASML, HSBC, Roche and Nestle, and financials and industrials are the biggest sectors.
VGLT: US Treasury bonds with maturities longer than ten years, tracking a Bloomberg index of long-term Treasuries. Backed by the government, but because the bonds run so long, its price swings much more than short-term bond funds when interest rates move.
VGMS: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several bond sectors of varied credit quality, aiming for steady income. It holds a wide mix, including Treasuries, corporate and foreign bonds, and no single position is above about 2%.
VGRO: An actively managed fund of US companies with higher-than-average growth potential, all with at least $1 billion in market value. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA and Alphabet are about 30% of it, and technology and communication make up about 70%.
VGSH: US Treasury bonds maturing in one to three years, following a Bloomberg index. Backed by the government and short in length, so its price moves very little when interest rates change, and its income tracks short-term rates fairly closely.
VGSR: An actively managed fund of real estate companies around the world, mostly REITs, picked with a focus on sustainability. Equinix, Simon Property, Welltower and Prologis are each roughly 5% of it, so it is fairly spread out.
VGT: US technology companies of all sizes, such as software, hardware and chip makers, weighted by size. It is extremely top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together are about 41% of the fund.
VGTX: A fund holding technology company stocks and tech-focused ETFs, then selling options on them to earn extra income. Selling options brings in cash but caps some of the gains when tech rallies, so it trades part of the upside for income.
VGVT: An actively managed fund of bonds issued or backed by the US government and its agencies, including Treasuries and mortgage securities from Fannie Mae and similar groups. It can hold any maturity and aims for steady income with low credit risk.
VHT: US health care companies of all sizes, such as drug makers, insurers, device makers and biotech firms, held roughly in proportion to their size. Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie and UnitedHealth make up about 34% of the fund.
VIDI: Stocks of companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging markets, chosen by a rules-based index rather than by company size. It holds many smaller positions, with the biggest around 2%, and leans toward industrials, financials and technology companies in places like South Korea and Taiwan.
VIG: Large US companies that have raised their dividends steadily for years, rather than the ones paying the highest yields. Broadcom, Apple, Microsoft and JPMorgan are the biggest holdings, and it leans toward technology, financials and health care.
VIGI: Large companies outside the US that have raised their dividends for years, picked by a Vanguard index. It is not heavy in tech, with banks, food and drug makers like Royal Bank of Canada, Nestle and Novartis among the biggest holdings.
VIOG: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that are classified as growth stocks, meaning faster expected growth. It holds hundreds of stocks with none above about 2%, so it is a broad small company growth fund.
VIOO: About 600 small US companies that meet profitability rules, following the S&P SmallCap 600 Index. It holds a lot of names in small amounts, with the biggest each under 1% of the fund, spread across financials, technology and industrials.
VIOV: Small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600 that look inexpensive compared with their size, book value and earnings. It holds hundreds of stocks across financials, consumer, technology and industrials, and no single holding is above about 1%.
VIS: US industrial companies, like aerospace, defense, machinery, airlines and rail, tracked by a Vanguard index. Caterpillar, General Electric and GE Vernova are about 14% of the fund, and it holds large, mid and small firms.
VLU: A fund tracking the S&P 1500, covering large, mid and small US companies, but weighting cheaper stocks more heavily than a plain market-size index would. It still holds household names like Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway and Microsoft, each only about 2% to 3%.
VLUE: Large and mid-sized US stocks that look cheap compared with their earnings, sales and book value, picked and weighted by an MSCI index. It is unusually concentrated for a value fund: Micron is about 19% of it, and technology is over 40%.
VMAX: US large companies that look cheap compared to their size, picked by a rules-based value index, with a tilt toward banks and financials. It is widely spread, with the top holdings such as BNY Mellon, State Street and US Bancorp each only about 2%.
VMBS: US government-backed mortgage bonds, which are pools of home loans packaged together and sold to investors, tracking a Bloomberg index of agency mortgage securities. Homeowners' payments flow through as income, and each of the many holdings is a tiny slice, under 1%.
VMHY: Higher-yield municipal bonds, meaning loans to US state and local governments or related projects that pay more but carry more risk. Income is generally exempt from federal income tax, and it spreads across a large number of issuers.
VMSB: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several bond types, such as corporate, government-backed mortgage and other income-producing bonds, to earn high current income. Each holding is small, with the biggest positions around 1% to 2% of the fund.
VMSD: Short-term municipal bonds, which are loans to US states, cities and local governments, with income that is generally exempt from federal income tax. Short maturities mean its price moves less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates change.
VNAM: Vietnamese stocks from a broad MSCI Vietnam index. It is very top-heavy: Vingroup alone is about 24% of the fund, and real estate and financial companies make up around 60% of it.
VNIE: An actively managed fund of companies outside the US, picked by Vontobel for quality and growth in at least three countries. Its biggest positions include Taiwan Semiconductor, Tokyo Electron and ASML, each around 6% to 7%, and it is mixed across technology, industrials and financials.
VNLA: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mostly from banks and companies, with a goal of steady income and small price moves. It is spread over many holdings, none above about 1%.
VNM: Stocks of companies based in or doing most of their business in Vietnam, following the MVIS Vietnam Index. It is concentrated in a few firms, as property developers Vingroup and Vinhomes together are about 17% of the fund.
VNQ: US real estate companies, mostly REITs, which own things like apartments, warehouses, data centers and health care buildings. REITs pay out much of their rental income, and Welltower, Prologis and Equinix are among the biggest holdings.
VNQI: Real estate companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging markets, weighted by company size, following an S&P index. It is spread out, with the largest holding, Australia's Goodman Group, only about 4%.
VNSE: An actively managed fund holding a focused set of mostly large US and global companies picked by the manager rather than following an index. About 40% sits in technology, and NVIDIA, Taiwan Semiconductor, Eli Lilly and Alphabet are each roughly 7% to 8%.
VO: Hundreds of mid-sized US companies, bigger than small caps but smaller than the giants, tracked by the CRSP US Mid Cap Index. It is spread out, with no holding above about 1%, and leans toward industrials and technology.
VOE: Mid-sized US companies that look cheap on measures like price relative to earnings or book value, following a CRSP index. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings only about 1% to 2% each, and has more energy, financials and utilities than the broad market.
VOLT: An actively managed fund of global companies tied to electrification, such as power equipment makers, grid builders, utilities and clean energy firms. It is concentrated, with the top five holdings around 30% of it, and mostly industrials and utilities.
VONE: About 1,000 of the largest US companies, tracking the Russell 1000 index and weighted by company size, so bigger firms count for more. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft together make up about 18% of it.
VONG: Large US companies from the Russell 1000 index that show growth traits, such as fast-rising sales and earnings, weighted by company size. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up about 34% of it, and technology is well over half.
VONV: Large US companies that look cheap compared with their earnings and assets, tracking the Russell 1000 Value index. It holds hundreds of stocks, with Micron, Berkshire Hathaway, Alphabet and JPMorgan among the largest at roughly 2% to 3% each.
VOO: The 500 biggest US companies in the S&P 500 index, each weighted by its size. Technology is about 40% of it, and NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft alone make up close to 18%.
VOOB: Aims to follow the S&P 500 while using options to protect against part of the losses. Because of that protection, it gives up some of the gains when stocks rise, and its holdings are mostly cash and option contracts rather than stocks.
VOOG: The growth half of the S&P 500: large US companies whose earnings and sales are growing faster than average. It is top-heavy, with NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet together making up about 36% of the fund.
VOOV: The cheaper half of the S&P 500, meaning large US companies that look inexpensive relative to their size and fundamentals. It still holds big names, with Apple at about 8% and Amazon at about 4%, and spreads across technology, financials, health care and industrials.
VOOY: Holds the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF and adds an options strategy designed to produce extra monthly income. The options can limit gains when the stock market rises strongly, and it still falls when large US companies fall.
VOT: Mid-sized US companies with growth traits, following a CRSP index and weighted by size. Holdings are spread out, with the largest, such as Vertiv and Quanta, around 2% to 3% each, and it leans toward technology and industrials.
VOTE: US large companies from an S&P 500-style index, held in roughly market-cap proportions, so it behaves much like the broad US stock market. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 20% of the fund, and technology is around 40%.
VOX: US communication services companies of all sizes, such as social media, streaming, phone and media firms, following a Vanguard sector index. It is very concentrated: Meta and Alphabet (Google's parent, held in two share classes) together make up around 48% of the fund.
VOXP: A fund of mostly large US stocks, led by NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet, which together are about 20% of it. The managers pick holdings by their own approach, so it can differ from a plain index fund even though it looks much like one at the top.
VPC: Follows an index of US-listed closed-end funds and business development companies that make private loans to companies, so it is a private credit fund of funds. Oxford Lane, Eagle Point and Horizon Technology Finance are among its top holdings, and it aims for income.
VPFF: Preferred shares and similar hybrid securities, which pay fixed dividends and rank ahead of common stock but below bonds. It is actively managed, with no holding above roughly 2%, with a focus on income.
VPL: Stocks from developed Pacific countries such as Japan, Australia, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore, weighted by company size. Technology and financials lead, and Samsung and SK Hynix are the two biggest holdings at about 12% combined.
VPLS: An actively managed bond fund holding US government, mortgage, corporate and asset-backed bonds, with some emerging market debt. Its goal is to earn more income than the standard US bond market while staying mostly in investment-grade bonds.
VPU: US electric, gas and water utility companies, held by market size through a Vanguard index. Utilities are known for steady dividends, and NextEra Energy is about 12% of the fund, with Southern Company and Duke Energy next.
VPX: An actively managed US stock fund that shifts its mix of sectors depending on where it thinks we are in the economic cycle. About 20% sits in a broad US market fund, and the rest is in stocks such as Broadcom, NVIDIA and ExxonMobil.
VRAI: Stocks of companies tied to real assets such as energy, real estate, utilities, materials and agriculture, picked from an index built by Indxx. The idea is income from businesses that own physical things, and it is spread out, with no holding above about 2%.
VRIG: Investment-grade debt with floating interest rates that reset regularly, so the income follows short-term rates and the price stays steadier than regular bonds. It mixes floating rate Treasuries with corporate and other issuers, and is actively managed.
VRP: Preferred stocks and similar securities whose dividend rates float or reset, mostly from banks and other financial companies, tracking an Invesco index. They sit between stocks and bonds, and the changing rates make the income follow interest rates more than fixed-rate preferreds do.
VSDA: US companies with a record of raising dividends year after year, picked by the Nasdaq Victory Dividend Accelerator Index. It leans toward consumer staples and financials and holds firms like Franklin Resources, Kimberly-Clark and Altria, each near 4%.
VSDB: A mix of short-term bonds such as corporate bonds and US Treasuries, with maturities of only a few years. Because the bonds are short, its price moves less than longer bond funds, and the income follows interest rates fairly closely.
VSDM: Short-term bonds from US states, cities and agencies whose interest is generally exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds mature fairly soon, its price moves less than longer municipal bond funds, and no single issuer is more than about 0.5% of it.
VSGX: Large, mid and small companies from developed and emerging markets outside the US, with companies screened out for environmental, social and governance reasons. Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest holding at about 5%, and financials and technology are each about 28%.
VSHY: An actively managed fund of high-yield bonds with shorter maturities, meaning bonds from weaker-credit companies that pay more interest. Shorter bonds usually swing less when rates change, and the fund is spread across many issuers, with none above about 1.5%.
VSLU: Large US companies picked using a valuation approach, with at least 80% in stocks worth $5 billion or more. It is top-heavy in tech: NVIDIA, Apple, Alphabet and Microsoft are about 33% of the fund.
VSMV: A US stock fund tracking an index that picks stocks using several factors, then aims for lower price swings than the market. It is more concentrated than most, with Apple at about 10% and chip makers Lam Research and KLA near the top.
VSOL: A fund that holds the Solana cryptocurrency, SOL, directly instead of stocks or bonds. Its value follows the price of Solana as measured by a MarketVector benchmark, and like other crypto it can swing a lot.
VSS: Small companies from developed and emerging countries outside the US, tracking a FTSE index of small caps. It holds thousands of stocks, none above about 0.3%, with industrials, technology and materials the largest sectors.
VT: Stocks from all over the world in one fund, covering the US plus developed and emerging markets, of all sizes, following the FTSE Global All Cap Index. US companies are the biggest share, led by NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft at about 3% to 4% each.
VTC: A broad collection of US investment-grade corporate bonds, meaning loans to financially sound companies, tracking the Bloomberg US Corporate Bond Index. It invests through other Vanguard bond funds and holds thousands of bonds, so no single company is more than a tiny share.
VTEB: A broad basket of US municipal bonds, which are loans to states, cities and public agencies whose interest is exempt from federal income tax. It holds thousands of bonds of medium length, and no single issuer is more than a sliver of the fund.
VTEC: Investment-grade bonds from California state and local issuers with medium-term maturities. Their interest is generally free of federal and California income tax, and it is spread over many bonds, none above about 1%.
VTEI: Intermediate-term US municipal bonds, which are loans to state and local governments that pay interest generally exempt from federal income tax, with maturities up to 20 years. It holds thousands of investment-grade bonds, so no single issuer is a large share, and it leans toward California.
VTEL: Long-term US municipal bonds, mostly from states, cities and public agencies, tracking an index of investment-grade muni bonds maturing in over ten years. The interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and longer maturities mean prices move more when interest rates change.
VTES: Short-term bonds from US states and local governments, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax. Short maturities keep price swings small, and it is spread over many bonds, none above about 0.3%.
VTG: A fund holding US Treasury bonds of all kinds, tracking a Bloomberg index of government debt, with middle-length maturities. Its holdings are spread across hundreds of Treasury issues, so no single bond is more than about 1%.
VTHR: The 3,000 biggest US companies, covering about 98% of the US stock market, weighted by size. It is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is around 38% of the whole fund.
VTI: Nearly the whole US stock market in one fund: thousands of companies of every size, from giants to small firms, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are together about 16% of it, so the biggest names still steer the results.
VTIP: US Treasury bonds that adjust with inflation, known as TIPS, limited to ones maturing in under 5 years. Their value rises with inflation, and the short maturities mean it is less sensitive to interest rate changes than longer bond funds.
VTP: US Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) of all maturities, whose principal rises with inflation, tracking a broad Bloomberg TIPS index. It holds hundreds of government bonds, so credit risk is very low, but prices still move with interest rates.
VTV: Large US companies that look cheaply priced relative to their size or earnings, known as value stocks, weighted by size. It leans toward financials and health care, with JPMorgan, Berkshire Hathaway and Johnson & Johnson among the larger holdings.
VTWG: Small US companies with growth traits, tracking the Russell 2000 Growth Index, which holds the faster-growing stocks of the smallest 2,000 companies in the Russell 3000. It holds well over a thousand stocks, none above about 4%, and about 30% is health care, much of it smaller biotech.
VTWO: About 2,000 smaller US companies, tracking the Russell 2000 index, which is the standard yardstick for US small caps. It is very spread out, with no holding above about 2%, and health care, financials and technology are the biggest sectors.
VTWV: Small US companies that look cheaper relative to their size, tracking the Russell 2000 Value Index by holding each stock in about the same proportion as the index. It is spread across hundreds of companies, with banks and other financials the largest group and no single stock above about 1%.
VUG: Large US companies picked for growth traits, like faster expected sales and earnings growth, weighted by size. It is concentrated, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 32% and technology around 60%.
VUS: US stocks that pay dividends, chosen by a rules-based process that looks for dividend income. Despite the income focus it is heavy in big tech, with Apple, NVIDIA and Microsoft making up about 15% of the fund.
VUSE: US large company stocks picked by a rules-based Vident index that screens for strong fundamentals, quality and reasonable price. Technology is about 40% of the fund, and the top holdings such as Broadcom, Oracle and Alphabet are each around 3%.
VUSG: An actively managed fund of large and mid-sized US companies that Wellington expects to grow earnings faster than average. It is very top-heavy and tech-driven: NVIDIA, Alphabet, Micron and Broadcom together are about 39% of the fund.
VUSV: An actively managed fund of US value stocks, meaning companies that look cheap relative to their earnings or assets, run by the Wellington team. It is spread widely, with Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft about 3% each, across financials, tech and health care.
VV: Large US companies making up roughly the top 85% of the US market by value, weighted by size. NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft are about 18% of it, and technology is around 40%.
VWO: Stocks from emerging markets like China, India and Taiwan, tracked by an FTSE index that includes China A shares. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 16% of it, and technology is roughly a third.
VWOB: Bonds issued by governments and government-owned companies in emerging markets, priced in US dollars. They tend to pay more than US government bonds but carry more risk, and the holdings are spread out, with Argentina and Pemex among the largest.
VXF: Everything in the US stock market except the S&P 500: mid-sized and small companies, tracking the S&P Completion Index. It is spread thin, with top holdings around 1% each, and leans toward technology and industrials.
VXUS: Stocks from companies outside the US, in both developed and emerging countries and of all sizes, following the FTSE Global All Cap ex US Index. Financials and technology are the biggest sectors, and Taiwan Semiconductor is the largest single holding at about 4%.
VYM: Large US companies that pay higher than average dividends, leaving out real estate companies, weighted by size. It leans toward financials, technology and health care, and Broadcom is the biggest holding at about 7%.
VYMI: Stocks of large companies outside the US that pay above-average dividends, in developed and emerging markets, tracking the FTSE All-World ex US High Dividend Yield index. It is spread across many countries and holds banks, drug makers and energy companies, with no holding above about 2%.
WABF: An actively managed bond fund holding a broad mix of US government, corporate and other debt of different maturities. It can also hold some lower-rated and credit-linked bonds, so the managers have room to depart from a standard bond index.
WAGN: An actively managed, concentrated fund of small and mid-sized stocks from around the world, chosen using value investor Mohnish Pabrai's style of buying cheap companies. Warrior Met Coal and Transocean are about 10% each, and holdings range from energy to airports and retail.
WAMA: US large-company stocks that switch between full stock exposure and a defensive position depending on a moving-average trend signal, following a WisdomTree index. When the signal is positive it looks like a big-company index, with NVIDIA, Apple and Alphabet about 21% of the fund.
WAR: An actively managed fund of companies tied to technology and national defense, such as drones, cybersecurity, semiconductors and aerospace, including many outside the US. It is fairly concentrated: Astera Labs, Axon and Micron are about 27% of it.
WARP: Companies tied to the space industry, such as rocket launchers, satellite operators and space communications firms, tracked by an index. It is concentrated and non-diversified: SpaceX and Rocket Lab together are about 35% of the fund.
WATS: An actively managed fund of companies that make or support battery energy storage, such as batteries and the systems that store power. Tesla is about 17% and Bloom Energy about 12%, so a couple of names drive much of the result.
WBEM: An actively managed fund of stocks from emerging markets, developing economies such as China, India and Brazil, picked by William Blair's managers. It does not follow an index, and being non-diversified it can place larger bets on fewer companies.
WBIE: An actively managed fund of stocks from companies outside the US, mostly large ones with strong growth prospects, picked by William Blair's managers. It invests mainly in common stocks and does not follow an index, so results depend on the manager's choices.
WBIF: An actively managed fund of value-priced stocks of all sizes, in the US and abroad, that can shift a large part of its money into cash when its model turns cautious. About a quarter is currently held back in cash, and individual stocks are each under 4%.
WBIG: A tactical fund that shifts between stocks, bonds and cash depending on market signals, focusing on dividend-paying US and foreign stocks. Holdings are spread widely, and a good part of it can sit in cash when the managers turn defensive.
WBIL: An actively managed fund that holds US and foreign stocks of all sizes, picked for quality, and can shift toward safer assets such as cash or Treasuries when the manager sees trouble. Technology is about 38% of it, with chip firms like Astera Labs and Marvell near the top.
WBIY: Holds about 50 higher-dividend US mid- and smaller-sized stocks picked by the Solactive index using a rules-based screen of yield and quality. No company dominates: Best Buy, HP, Altria and Campbell's are each about 5% of it.
WCAP: An actively managed stock fund that can invest in companies of any size, in any sector and anywhere, and does not follow an index. It holds mostly large US names plus a few ETFs, with Microsoft and Alphabet about 6% each.
WCBR: Global companies that make cybersecurity and security software, tracking a WisdomTree index of firms getting a meaningful share of revenue from it. It is a narrow technology theme, with CrowdStrike, Datadog and Palo Alto Networks about 21% of the fund.
WCEO: An actively managed fund of US companies that are led by women CEOs, leaning toward smaller and mid-sized firms. Holdings are spread thinly across many industries, with no single stock above about 2.5%, so it is not dominated by a few names.
WCLD: A fund of companies that sell software over the internet, known as cloud computing, tracked by an index that weights them about equally. Because no company dominates, with the top holdings each around 3%, it behaves more like a basket of many small tech bets.
WCME: Stocks of companies in developing countries, picked by an active manager looking for quality businesses. It leans on Asia: Taiwan Semiconductor is about 13% and Korean names like SK Hynix and Samsung add another 15% or so.
WCMG: An actively managed fund buying stocks of companies around the world, chosen by WCM using a focus on firms with strengthening competitive advantages. It is spread across health care, technology, communication and financials, and Nebius is the largest holding at about 7%.
WCMI: An actively managed fund of companies outside the US, picked for strong competitive advantages and improving business quality. It holds a mix of tech, banks and industrials, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Rolls-Royce and Kioxia the largest at about 20% combined.
WCPB: An actively managed fund of bonds that mostly invests in investment-grade debt but can reach into lower-rated bonds for extra income, hence the 'core plus' name. Weitz picks holdings by hand rather than following an index, across government, corporate and mortgage bonds.
WDAF: Defense and aerospace companies in Asia, tracked through a WisdomTree index, with a big focus on India, South Korea and Japan. It is concentrated, with Hindustan Aeronautics, Bharat Electronics and Korea Aerospace each about 8%.
WDAI: Roughly 300 large companies from around the world picked by a rules-based S&P index that ranks firms using AI-driven scoring. Holdings are spread thinly, with no single company above about 1% of the fund.
WDE: Securitized debt, meaning loans like commercial mortgages, auto loans and equipment leases packaged into bonds. It uses futures and swaps to hedge and manage sensitivity to interest rates, and its holdings are spread out, with none above about 5%.
WDEF: European defense and aerospace companies, such as BAE Systems, Thales, Rheinmetall and Safran, picked to follow a WisdomTree index. It is a narrow theme: the top four holdings are about 34% of the fund, and nearly all of it is industrials.
WDGF: A fund of defense and aerospace companies from around the world, such as RTX, General Dynamics, BAE Systems, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman. Each of those is about 5% of the fund, and nearly all of it is in industrials.
WDIG: A fund investing in companies that mine or process rare earths and strategic metals, such as Lynas, MP Materials and Materion, partly through futures contracts. It is a narrow bet on a small, volatile corner of the metals market.
WDIV: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, chosen from the S&P Global BMI for high yields and a record of managed dividend policies. It holds many positions, none above about 2%, and tilts toward financials, industrials, utilities and real estate.
WDNA: Global companies in biotech and genetic science, such as gene editing, DNA sequencing and new drug discovery. It holds a sample of the stocks in the WisdomTree BioRevolution index, with Twist Bioscience, Moderna and Eli Lilly among the largest at about 4% to 6%.
WDRN: Companies building physical AI such as humanoid robots, drones and the batteries and parts behind them, following a theme index. Tesla and NVIDIA lead at about 5% each, so it is a narrow, tech-heavy basket of fast-changing businesses.
WDTE: An actively managed fund that holds S&P 500 exposure through options and pays out income every week. Selling options caps how much it gains when the market rises, so it trades upside for income and still holds downside risk.
WEAT: A fund that tracks wheat prices by holding wheat futures contracts, which are agreements to buy wheat at a set price later, rather than real grain. Its returns follow wheat prices, which can swing a lot with weather and supply, and the cash-like holdings are just collateral.
WEED: An actively managed fund giving exposure to cannabis companies, including Curaleaf, using stocks and swaps, which are contracts that pay a stock's returns. The Treasury bills are collateral for the swaps, and the fund is concentrated in a small, volatile industry.
WEEI: An actively managed fund of energy companies that also sells options on some of its stocks to earn extra income. Oil giants dominate: ExxonMobil and Chevron together are about 39% of it, so the options income comes with limited upside on those stocks.
WEEK: Treasury bills maturing in three months or less, aiming to pay out income weekly. It works like a place to park cash that earns interest, and because the bills are so short, the price barely moves while the income follows short-term rates.
WEEL: An actively managed income fund that holds sector ETFs and some stocks, then sells options on them in a repeating strategy called the wheel. The option income can add yield, but it limits gains in rising markets and does not protect against falls.
WELD: An actively managed fund of mid-sized US companies that benefit from more manufacturing returning to America, such as makers of industrial parts and automation tools. It is concentrated in roughly 30 stocks, with the top four, including Cognex and Timken, each around 7%.
WEPN: An actively managed fund mixing defense and rare earth companies with other funds and options, aiming to produce income. Cybersecurity firms Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are each about 10%, and part of it holds metals and steel funds.
WGMI: An actively managed fund of companies that mine bitcoin or supply the power and data center capacity around it. It is very concentrated, with its top four holdings around half the fund, and its fortunes tend to swing with bitcoin's price.
WIMA: Large and mid-sized stocks from developed countries outside the US, with a rules-based twist: it adjusts how much it holds in stocks versus cash-like assets depending on recent market trends. Top holdings such as ASML, HSBC and Novartis are each only a few percent.
WINC: An actively managed fund of bonds from emerging market countries, such as developing economies in Latin America, Asia and Africa, chosen by William Blair's managers. These bonds usually pay more interest than US ones but carry higher risk, and the fund may use derivatives to get exposure.
WINN: An actively managed fund of mostly large US companies the manager expects to grow faster than average over the long run. It holds a small group of stocks, and NVIDIA, Alphabet, Apple and Broadcom together make up roughly a third of it.
WIP: Government bonds from countries outside the US whose payments rise with inflation, such as those from Germany, the UK, Spain and Turkey. It is spread across many countries and none of the bonds is above about 2% of the fund.
WISE: Holds companies tied to artificial intelligence, following a theme index and mostly picking technology firms. It is fairly concentrated, with Advanced Micro Devices at over 10% and a mix of big names like NVIDIA and smaller, lesser-known companies below that.
WLDR: A global stock fund tracking an index of roughly 150 to 250 companies in the US and at least three other countries. Right now it leans toward technology, with Dell, Micron and Seagate each making up about 5% to 7% of it.
WLTG: A fund of funds that holds other ETFs, mainly US stock funds, and shifts between asset classes and sectors based on market trends. It is actively managed and aims for long-term growth rather than tracking one index.
WMSB: An actively managed bond fund that spreads money across several types of bonds, such as corporate, government and securitized debt. The manager chooses the mix rather than following an index, so the holdings can shift over time.
WMTI: A fund built around Walmart stock that aims to pay income while keeping some exposure to Walmart's share price, using options and derivatives. It holds mostly Treasury bills as backing, so it follows a single company and does not match owning the stock.
WNDR: An actively managed fund of companies tied to travel and leisure, such as airlines, hotels, cruise lines, ride sharing and entertainment. Disney, American Express, Uber and Booking are among its biggest holdings, each around 4% to 7%.
WNTR: Pays income while giving inverse exposure to MicroStrategy stock, meaning it aims to gain when the stock falls, using options and swaps. Most of the fund sits in Treasury bills as backing, and it loses when the stock rises sharply.
WOMN: Holds large US companies picked for their record on women's leadership and gender equality, following an index built around that idea. Holdings look like a broad market mix, with Alphabet, Microsoft and NVIDIA each around 4 to 5%.
WOOD: Global companies tied to forests and timberland, such as landowners, paper and packaging makers and wood product producers, following the S&P Global Timber & Forestry Index. It is fairly spread out, but Weyerhaeuser, Smurfit Westrock and West Fraser are each about 7% to 9% of it.
WQTM: A fund tracking an index of companies working on quantum computing, a new kind of computer, including hardware makers, software firms and big tech. It is a narrow theme with some small, volatile names: Quantinuum, D-Wave and Rigetti together are about 18% of it.
WR: An actively managed basket of US companies that could benefit from geopolitical conflict, higher defense spending and US energy security. It leans heavily on energy, at roughly 60% of the fund, with defense and industrial firms and Palantir making up most of the rest.
WRND: Large companies around the world that spend heavily on research and development, picked by an index that treats that spending as a sign of innovation. It is top-heavy with big tech, as Alphabet, NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 30% of it.
WRTH: An actively managed income fund that sells options to collect premiums, run by a sub-adviser named Worth Charting Group. It keeps most of the money in Treasuries and cash as collateral for the options, which can limit gains when markets rise.
WSDB: An actively managed fund of short-term bonds, mostly US Treasuries and other government-backed debt. Because the bonds mature soon, its price tends to move less than longer-term bond funds when interest rates change.
WSGE: An actively managed fund that gets worldwide stock exposure mostly by holding other ETFs, covering companies of all sizes in the US, developed markets and emerging markets. The top holding, a global equity factor ETF, is about 17% of it.
WSLS: A mix of two US small-company stock approaches: one that buys some stocks and bets against others (long/short), and one that only buys. Because part of it bets against stocks, it can behave quite differently from a plain small-cap index fund.
WSMD: An actively managed fund of small and mid-sized US companies, selected by Wasatch's research team with an eye on growth. It invests at least 80% in these stocks, so it tends to be more volatile than funds of big companies.
WSML: Small companies from developed countries around the world, held in index-like proportions based on the MSCI World Small Cap Index. It is very spread out, with the largest holdings only about 2% or less, and the US makes up the biggest share.
WSPC: An actively managed fund of global companies in the space economy, such as launch firms, satellite makers and space services. SpaceX is about 16% of the fund, with Rocket Lab next at around 5%, so it leans heavily on a few names.
WTAI: Companies around the world involved in artificial intelligence, such as chip and memory makers, software firms and data infrastructure businesses, tracked by a WisdomTree index. Technology is about 80% of the fund, and memory makers Micron, Samsung, Sandisk and Kioxia are each around 4 to 5%.
WTAL: An actively managed long-short fund that uses swaps and other derivatives to bet on some assets rising and others falling, aiming to profit whichever way markets move. Treasuries and cash are held as collateral for those contracts, not as the main investment.
WTBN: An actively managed bond fund that holds a mix of 5 to 20 other bond ETFs, following an index built by Bianco Research that weights them to hit target factors. It covers Treasuries, corporates and TIPS, so it works as a one stop mix of US bonds.
WTIB: An actively managed fund combining crude oil exposure and bitcoin exposure, mostly through futures contracts and another bitcoin fund, with a lot of cash held as backing. It mixes two very volatile markets, and its returns do not simply follow either one.
WTIP: An actively managed fund mostly holding US Treasury bonds, especially inflation-protected ones (TIPS) whose value adjusts with inflation. It also adds a small amount of other assets, including a bitcoin fund of about 5%, so it is not just plain Treasuries.
WTLS: An actively managed, model driven fund that combines a long/short US stock strategy, betting on some stocks rising and others falling, with a long only strategy. It gets much of its exposure through derivatives, backed by Treasury bills.
WTMF: An actively managed fund that uses futures and currency contracts to follow price trends across assets like stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, and holds a small bitcoin fund. Most of what it holds is Treasury bills as collateral, not the point of the fund.
WTMU: A broad mix of US municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, spread out over different years in a ladder, where bonds come due steadily. The interest is generally free from federal income tax, and no single issuer is more than about 4% of the fund.
WTMY: A ladder of higher-yielding municipal bonds whose interest is generally exempt from US federal income tax. Many are riskier, lower-rated issuers, such as Puerto Rico and Chicago's school board, so it pays more income but with more credit risk than plain muni funds.
WTPI: An options income fund that sells put options on the S&P 500 and keeps cash collateral in Treasury bills, collecting premiums as income. It takes on stock market losses in exchange for that income, so a sharp market drop would hurt.
WTRE: Follows an index of real estate companies tied to the digital economy, such as data centers, cell towers and warehouses, from around the world. Equinix, Prologis and Digital Realty are among the top holdings at around 5% each.
WTV: US mid-sized companies that look inexpensive based on measures like earnings and cash flow, chosen and weighted by WisdomTree's rules. It is spread out, with the biggest holdings, NVIDIA, Dell and Berkshire Hathaway, each only about 3%.
WUGI: An actively managed fund of companies tied to 5G and the digital economy, mostly chipmakers and equipment makers. It is heavy in technology, with Taiwan Semiconductor, Micron and Applied Materials about 21% of the fund.
WWJD: Large foreign and emerging market stocks chosen by an index that screens companies with a faith-based Inspire Impact Score, keeping those scoring zero or higher. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 1%, across industrials, financials and materials.
WZRD: An actively managed fund that trades a mix of stocks, other ETFs and derivatives, with the manager shifting positions opportunistically. Its holdings lean toward technology and consumer companies, and its results depend on the manager's choices rather than an index.
XA: An actively managed fund of cybersecurity companies, firms that make software to defend computers and networks. It is concentrated, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike making up about 24% of it, and the whole fund is in technology.
XAGG: An actively managed multi-sector bond fund that shifts between corporate bonds, mortgage-backed securities and other debt in search of higher income. Government-backed mortgage securities lead the holdings, and most of it is bonds, so it takes more credit risk than a simple government fund.
XAIW: Invests in companies tied to the SpaceX and AI ecosystem, from SpaceX itself to chips and servers from NVIDIA, Dell, Super Micro and TSMC. It is concentrated, with SpaceX alone about 21% of the fund, and mostly technology and industrials.
XAIX: Global companies in artificial intelligence and big data, including chipmakers and software firms, tracking an index of developed and emerging markets. It is tech heavy, with memory makers Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix about 25% of the fund.
XAPR: A fund using options tied to the S&P 500 to give stock market gains up to a limit over a one year period starting in April. It aims to cushion a moderate amount of early losses, and the stated outcomes only apply if held for the whole period.
XAR: US aerospace and defense companies, tracking an S&P index that holds them in roughly equal amounts rather than by size. That keeps it from being dominated by giants like Boeing: the largest holdings are only about 3% each, and it includes smaller, newer firms.
XAUG: Uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to give extra upside, up to a limit, while cushioning part of the losses over a one-year period that resets each August. Gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the whole period.
XB: A basket of US dollar corporate bonds rated B, a middle tier of high yield (also called junk) debt that pays more interest but carries more risk of default. It is spread across hundreds of issuers, and no single bond is more than about 1% of the fund.
XBAP: Uses options tied to the S&P 500 to aim for a defined outcome over a one-year period starting in April. It is built to boost gains up to a cap while absorbing a set amount of losses, so what you get depends on when you buy within the period.
XBB: Holds US dollar corporate bonds rated BB, the higher tier of high-yield or junk bonds, which pay more interest than safer bonds but carry more risk of default. It is spread over many issuers, with none above about 1%.
XBCI: An income-focused fund tied to Bitcoin, using Bitcoin funds, a Cayman subsidiary and options-style strategies, with a large pile of Treasury bills alongside. Bitcoin prices drive its results, and the options income it aims for can limit gains when Bitcoin rallies.
XBFR: A fund using options on large US stocks to soften a set amount of losses over a one year period, in exchange for limiting how much it can gain. Its stock exposure is top heavy, with NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft making up about 20% of it.
XBI: US biotech companies from the S&P Biotechnology Select Industry Index, which spreads money across many holdings in nearly equal slices. No single company is more than about 1.5% of the fund, so it is much less top-heavy than most sector funds, but many holdings are small, unprofitable drug developers.
XBIL: US Treasury bills that mature in about six months, held to track an index of those short-term government bonds. Because the bills are so short, the price barely moves and the income follows short-term interest rates.
XBJA: Uses options on US large-company stocks to chase more than the market's gains up to a limit, while cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in January. Results depend on when you buy relative to that period.
XBJL: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF over a one-year period starting in July, aiming to absorb a set amount of losses and to speed up gains up to a cap. Protection only applies if held for the full period.
XBOC: Uses options tied to a US large company index to absorb losses, with a 9% buffer, over a one year period that starts in October. In return, it is able to capture a boosted share of gains up to a cap, so it works best when held for the full period.
XBTY: An options income fund built around Bitcoin, using derivatives on a Bitcoin ETF rather than owning coins directly. It aims to pay high income by selling options, which limits how much it gains if Bitcoin rises, and the Treasury bills it holds are mainly backing.
XC: Emerging market stocks, picked by an index that tries to reflect true emerging economies by leaving out state-owned companies. It is spread widely, with no holding above about 3%, and financials are around a third.
XCCC: US dollar corporate bonds rated CCC, the lowest tier of high-yield (junk) bonds, from companies with weaker finances. They pay higher interest than safer bonds, but there is more risk that borrowers fall behind on payments, and no single bond is above about 2%.
XCEM: Emerging market stocks from countries like Taiwan, South Korea and India, deliberately leaving out China. It is heavily weighted to chipmakers: Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung together are about 25% of it, and technology is roughly half of the fund.
XCHG: An actively managed fund of US companies, chosen by the manager rather than by an index. It has a small number of holdings and is top-heavy: NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon and Alphabet are about 29% of it.
XCNY: A fund following an S&P index of emerging-market stocks outside China, in places like Taiwan and South Korea. Taiwan Semiconductor alone is about 20% of the fund, and technology is around 40%.
XCOR: An actively managed fund that holds a changing mix of other ETFs, mostly US stock funds with growth, momentum and value styles. The managers rotate between them, and the top few holdings are each about 11% to 13% of the fund.
XCSH: A very short-term fund that uses box spreads, paired options trades that work like a short loan, with an average life under 90 days. It is meant to behave like a cash-like holding that earns interest, with little price movement.
XDAT: Companies that create, store, secure or analyze huge amounts of data, such as cloud, software and cybersecurity firms. It is concentrated, with Cloudflare and Alphabet each around 10% of the fund and technology plus communication stocks making up about 95%.
XDEC: A defined-outcome fund using options on an S&P 500 ETF over a set one-year period starting in December. It aims to cushion part of the losses while taking part of the gains, and results depend on buying at the start of the period.
XDEF: European companies that earn much of their revenue from defense, space and cybersecurity, tracked by a STOXX index with a passive, rules-based approach. It is concentrated in aerospace names: Airbus, Rolls-Royce, Safran and BAE Systems together are about a third of the fund.
XDIV: Gives exposure to the S&P 500 by holding an S&P 500 ETF, but is designed to avoid dividends, tilting returns toward price growth instead of income. Nearly all of it sits in the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF, so it looks like the index of large US companies.
XDQQ: Gives about two times the gains of the Nasdaq-100, through the Invesco QQQ fund, up to a set limit over a three-month period. Losses are not cushioned, so it can fall as much as the index when prices drop.
XDSQ: Gives about two times the gains of the S&P 500 up to a set limit over a three-month period, using options on an S&P 500 fund. In exchange, losses are not cushioned, so it can lose as much as the market if prices fall.
XDTE: A fund that gives exposure to the S&P 500 and sells short term call options on it, collecting that income and paying it out. Because those options are sold with very short lives, they cap gains on big up days while still leaving most of the losses.
XEMD: Bonds issued in US dollars by governments and companies in emerging markets, limited to those with average lives of one to ten years. It holds many countries, some riskier ones like Argentina and Ecuador, and each bond is only about 1 or 2% of it.
XEML: Large, high-quality European companies picked by a rules-based index, rather than simply the biggest by size. It holds a mix of well-known names like ABB, Novo Nordisk, Richemont, ASML and L'Oreal, each around 5% of the fund.
XES: US companies that make equipment or provide services for oil and gas drilling, tracking an S&P index that weights them roughly equally. That makes it a fairly even mix of smaller firms, with each top holding about 4% to 5%.
XEY: A fund that uses options tied to Ether, the second largest cryptocurrency, to generate income. Selling options brings in cash but limits gains if Ether rises, and it does not simply hold Ether like a plain crypto fund.
XFEB: Uses customized options on the SPDR S&P 500 ETF to follow the large US companies of the S&P 500 while cushioning a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting each February. In exchange, gains are capped, and the protection only applies if you hold for the full period.
XFIV: US Treasury bonds picked so the average duration, a measure of sensitivity to interest rates, is about five years. It is spread across many Treasuries, each only about 4% of it, so it sits in the middle between short and long.
XFLX: A fund of funds that mostly owns other bond ETFs, mixing corporate, high-yield, floating-rate and investment-grade bonds of different maturities. The manager shifts between them actively, and no single holding is more than about 11% of it.
XHB: US homebuilders and companies that sell to them, such as building materials and home improvement, tracking an S&P index that holds them in roughly equal amounts. No holding is above about 4%, so no single company dominates it.
XHE: US makers of medical equipment such as devices and diagnostics, from the S&P Health Care Equipment Select Industry Index. It is equally weighted, so smaller companies count as much as bigger ones, and no stock is more than about 3% of the fund.
XHLF: US Treasury securities held so their average time to maturity is about six months. Because they are so short-term, the price barely moves and the income follows short-term interest rates.
XHS: Small and mid-sized US health care service companies such as clinics, labs and insurers, tracked with the S&P Health Care Services Select Industry Index. It holds many stocks in roughly equal amounts, so no company is above about 2%.
XIDE: A defined-outcome fund that uses options on a US stock ETF to absorb a set amount of losses over a one-year period starting in December. It also aims to pay extra income by selling options, which limits how much it can gain.
XIDV: Tracks an index of stocks from developed countries outside the US, chosen to deliver a higher dividend yield without being much more volatile than the broader market. It leans toward financials and energy, with European banks and insurers among the biggest holdings.
XIGV: A fund that tracks an index of 100 large US tech companies with the software businesses left out. That leaves chips, hardware, internet and electric vehicle names, and its biggest positions each make up only about 5%.
XIJN: Uses options tied to a US stock ETF to cushion a set amount of losses over a one-year period that starts in June, and also sells options to earn extra income. That mix of buffer and income means gains over the period are limited.
XIMR: Uses options tied to a US large company ETF, plus short-term Treasuries, to aim for protection from a set amount of losses over a one-year period that resets each March. It also seeks income from selling options, which limits how much of the market's gains it can capture.
XISE: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to cushion a set amount of losses over a one year period starting in September, and also aims to pay extra income. In return, upside is capped, and it holds some short term Treasuries alongside the options.
XITK: About 50 to 100 US-listed technology companies picked for being in innovative parts of the sector, held in roughly equal amounts. That makes it less top-heavy than most tech funds, with its top holdings each only around 3% to 5%.
XJAN: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to give a boosted share of gains up to a limit, while softening part of the losses over a one-year period starting in January. It holds options rather than stocks, so the outcome depends on when you buy.
XJH: About 400 US mid-sized companies from the S&P MidCap 400, with firms removed if they fail certain environmental, social or governance screens, such as those tied to controversial weapons or tobacco. It is widely spread, with no holding above about 1%.
XJR: Holds small US companies from the S&P SmallCap 600, leaving out those involved in controversial businesses or facing controversies. It is spread thinly across hundreds of stocks, with no holding above about 1%, and no one sector dominates.
XJUL: An options-based fund tied to the S&P 500 through a one-year outcome period starting in July, with a moderate buffer against losses and an enhanced cap on gains. The outcome only applies to those who hold for the full period.
XJUN: A fund that uses customized options on the S&P 500 to cushion part of the losses over a one-year period starting each June. In return, it limits how much of the market's gains you can capture, and the protection only works if held for the full period.
XLB: The materials slice of the S&P 500, such as chemicals, metals and mining, and building materials. It is top-heavy: Linde alone is about 14%, and Newmont, Freeport and Corteva each add around 5% or more.
XLBI: Holds the Materials Select Sector SPDR fund, which covers chemicals, metals, mining and packaging companies from the S&P 500, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. That options income is meant to boost payouts, but it limits how much the fund gains when materials stocks rally.
XLC: The communication services slice of the S&P 500, covering internet platforms, media, entertainment and telecom companies. It is top-heavy: Meta and the two classes of Alphabet stock together make up roughly 43% of the fund.
XLCI: Holds the communication services stocks of the S&P 500 through a Select Sector SPDR fund, and adds an options strategy that generates extra income. The options bring in premium payments, but they can limit how much the fund gains when those stocks rally.
XLE: The energy companies of the S&P 500, mainly oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline firms, held in roughly the index's proportions. It is very concentrated: ExxonMobil and Chevron are about 39% of it, so those two drive much of the result.
XLEI: The energy sector of the S&P 500, with an options strategy layered on top to produce extra monthly income. Selling call options caps some of the upside, so it can lag when energy stocks rally strongly.
XLEM: The energy companies of the S&P 500, such as oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline firms. It tracks the sector slice of the index, so its results are tied closely to oil and gas prices and a few giant companies.
XLF: The financial companies of the S&P 500, such as banks, insurers, payment firms and asset managers, held in roughly the index's proportions. It is fairly concentrated: Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase and Visa alone are about 31% of the fund.
XLFI: A fund that holds the Financial Select Sector SPDR, the financial companies of the S&P 500, and adds options to produce extra income. Nearly all of it is financials, and the income comes in exchange for limiting some of the upside.
XLG: The 50 largest companies in the S&P 500, held in proportion to their size, so it is a narrower slice of the index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Amazon together are about 39% of the fund.
XLI: The industrial companies of the S&P 500, such as aerospace and defense, machinery, transport and electrical equipment makers, held in roughly the index's proportions. Caterpillar, GE and GE Vernova are about 21% of it.
XLII: Holds the industrial companies of the S&P 500 through the Industrial Select Sector SPDR fund, and sells call options on them to earn extra income. That income can be paid out, but the options give up some gains when industrial stocks rally.
XLK: The technology slice of the S&P 500, holding the index's tech companies in about the same proportions as the index. It is very top-heavy: NVIDIA, Apple and Microsoft make up around 36% of the fund.
XLKI: A fund that holds the Technology Select Sector SPDR (XLK) and sells options on it to generate extra monthly income. Selling those options limits how much it can gain if tech rallies, so it is built for income more than growth.
XLKM: The technology companies of the S&P 500, holding them in roughly the same proportions as the index. It tracks the tech slice of the market, so a handful of giant companies tend to make up a large share of it.
XLP: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: companies that sell everyday essentials like groceries, household goods, drinks and tobacco. Very concentrated: Walmart, Costco, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola are about 35% of the fund.
XLPM: The consumer staples companies of the S&P 500, makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks and household products. It tracks the sector slice of the index, which is typically steadier than the overall market but concentrated in a few large companies.
XLRE: The real estate slice of the S&P 500, holding the index's property companies such as landlords, cell tower owners and data center operators. Welltower, Prologis and Equinix together are about 27% of it, so a few big names carry a lot of weight.
XLRI: Holds the real estate stocks of the S&P 500 through a Select Sector SPDR fund, and adds an options strategy that generates extra income. The options bring in premium payments, but they can limit how much the fund gains when real estate stocks rally.
XLSI: Holds the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR fund, covering makers and sellers of everyday goods like food, drinks and household products, and sells options on it to earn extra income. The options can limit gains when the sector rises, in exchange for that income.
XLSR: An actively run fund of funds that shifts money among the Select Sector SPDR ETFs, each covering one slice of the S&P 500 like tech or energy. It picks which sectors to favor, so its mix can differ a lot from the plain index.
XLU: The utilities slice of the S&P 500: electric, gas and water companies, plus some power producers. It is steady-leaning and top-heavy, with NextEra, Southern Company and Duke Energy making up about 27% of the fund.
XLUI: Holds the Utilities Select Sector SPDR, the utility companies of the S&P 500 such as electric and gas providers, and sells call options on it to earn extra income. The options give up some gains if utilities rally sharply, in exchange for that income.
XLV: The health care companies of the S&P 500, including drugmakers, insurers, device makers and hospital operators, in roughly the index's proportions. It is concentrated: Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson alone are about 27% of the fund.
XLVI: Holds the Health Care Select Sector SPDR fund, which owns the health care companies of the S&P 500, and also sells call options to bring in extra income. The options cap some of the upside in strong markets, so it trades some growth for income.
XLY: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: companies selling things people want but do not strictly need, like online retail, cars, restaurants and home improvement. Amazon and Tesla alone make up about 42% of the fund.
XLYI: Consumer discretionary stocks from the S&P 500, such as Amazon, Tesla and retailers, combined with options that bring in extra income. The income can be higher than regular dividends, but selling options can limit gains when the stocks rally.
XLYM: The consumer discretionary companies of the S&P 500, which sell things people buy when they have spare money, like cars, retail goods, hotels and restaurants. It tracks that slice of the index, so a few large companies carry much of the weight.
XMAG: Tracks an index of the 500 biggest US companies, with the Magnificent 7 tech giants removed. Without them it is more evenly spread, and its biggest holdings, like Broadcom, Micron and Eli Lilly, are each under 5%.
XMAR: A defined outcome fund that uses options on the S&P 500 over a set one-year period starting in March. It aims to gain with the market up to a cap, while cushioning a set amount of losses, and the options are held through a Cboe exchange.
XMAY: Uses options on an S&P 500 fund to aim for about double the market's gains up to a set cap, while cushioning a set amount of losses. This only applies over a one-year period starting each May, so buying midway through the year gives a different result.
XME: Metals and mining companies, including miners of uranium, gold, steel, copper and rare earths, held in roughly equal amounts rather than by size. Because of that, small miners matter as much as big ones, and no holding is above about 5%.
XMHQ: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that score best on quality: high profitability, strong accounting and low debt. It holds a limited set of firms, with the largest each about 3% to 4%, and industrials are about 30% of it.
XMLV: The 80 or so least volatile mid-size US companies in the S&P MidCap 400, so the price tends to swing less than the broader mid-cap market. It leans heavily toward financials, real estate and utilities, and no single holding is more than about 3%.
XMMO: Mid-size US companies from the S&P MidCap 400 that have the strongest recent price momentum, meaning they have been rising fastest. The list is reshuffled periodically, so it chases whatever has been working, and it leans toward technology, industrials, health care and energy.
XMPT: Holds closed-end funds that themselves own municipal bonds, whose interest is generally free of federal income tax, so it is a fund of funds. Many of these funds trade at a discount or premium and use borrowing, which can make it bumpier than ordinary muni funds.
